Module 1·Weeks 1–2Must

Spring fundamentals

19 topics · about 2 h of reading

Spring Boot is how most Java back-ends are built today. Behind it sits the Spring Framework, whose core idea is simple: instead of your classes creating their own collaborators with new, a container creates the objects, wires them together and manages their life. Once you understand that one idea (Inversion of Control and dependency injection), the rest of Spring — configuration, auto-configuration, transactions, security, data access — becomes a set of small, learnable parts.

This module is the foundation for everything else in the page. Module 2 builds REST controllers on top of beans, Module 3 uses injected repositories, Module 4 and Module 5 rely on profiles, proxies and test slices, and Module 6 and Module 7 deploy what you build. The plain Java behind it (interfaces, polymorphism, reflection, annotations) is in Core Java · Module 2. Examples work on Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x; where they differ, a version note says so.

After this module you will be able to:

  • explain Spring vs Spring Boot, and create and run a project from Spring Initializr;
  • explain Inversion of Control and dependency injection, first in plain Java and then with the ApplicationContext;
  • define beans with stereotype annotations and @Configuration / @Bean, and use constructor injection with @Qualifier and @Primary;
  • read and fix the common bean errors from the startup failure report;
  • choose bean scopes and describe the bean lifecycle step by step;
  • configure an app with application.yml, profiles, @Value and @ConfigurationProperties;
  • explain how @SpringBootApplication, auto-configuration, starters and the embedded server work, and why @Transactional fails on self-invocation.

What Spring and Spring Boot are

Spring is a framework whose container creates and wires your objects; Spring Boot sits on top of it and adds starters, auto-configuration, an embedded server and sensible defaults so an app runs with almost no setup.

Java was designed for large business applications, but writing them with plain Java means a lot of repeated work: creating objects, connecting them, opening database connections, handling transactions, reading config files. The Spring Framework (first released in 2003) took over that repeated work. You write business classes; Spring creates them, connects them and adds features such as transactions around them. A class managed this way is called a bean.

Early Spring needed pages of XML and a separate server (Tomcat) to run. Spring Boot (2014) removed that pain. You add one dependency, write one class with a main method, and you get a running web server with JSON support, logging and database connection pooling already configured. Boot does not replace Spring: it is Spring, with the setup done for you.

The Spring ecosystem map

"Spring" is also the name of a family of projects. All of them use the same container and the same annotations, so learning the core once helps everywhere.

ProjectWhat it gives youWhere in these notes
Spring FrameworkThe container (IoC/DI), AOP, Spring MVC, transactions, RestClient, eventsThis module and Module 2
Spring BootAuto-configuration, starters, embedded server, Actuator, executable JARThis module and Module 6
Spring DataRepositories for JPA, MongoDB, Redis and more — you write an interface onlyModule 3
Spring SecurityAuthentication, authorization, JWT/OAuth2, CSRF, CORSModule 4
Spring CloudGateway, config server, service discovery, resilience for microservicesModule 7
Spring BatchLarge scheduled jobs: read, process and write millions of records in chunksLater, on the job

Spring vs Spring Boot

QuestionSpring Framework aloneSpring Boot
SetupYou choose and configure every pieceStarters and auto-configuration do it
Dependency versionsYou pick matching versions of each libraryThe Boot parent / BOM fixes a tested set
ServerBuild a WAR and deploy to an external TomcatEmbedded server; run java -jar
Configuration styleXML or Java config you write fullyDefaults first; override in application.yml
Production supportYou add monitoring yourselfActuator: health, metrics, info

What Boot adds, in six points

Opinionated defaults
Boot makes a sensible choice for you (Tomcat, Jackson for JSON, HikariCP for the connection pool, Logback for logs). You override only what you disagree with.
Starters
One dependency that brings a whole feature with compatible versions: spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson and Tomcat.
Auto-configuration
Boot looks at your classpath and your properties and creates the beans you would otherwise write by hand.
Embedded server
Tomcat runs inside your application, started from main. No separate server install.
Executable JAR
One "fat" JAR holds your code, all libraries and the server. Run it with java -jar app.jar.
Actuator and no XML
Production endpoints (/actuator/health) and Java/YAML-only configuration.

Version note: which Spring Boot should you learn?

Spring Boot 4.x (released November 2025) is built on Spring Framework 7 and Jakarta EE 11 and needs Java 17 or newer. Spring Boot 3.x (Spring Framework 6, Jakarta EE 10, Java 17+) is still on most company servers. Since Boot 3, all enterprise packages are jakarta.*, not javax.* (for example jakarta.persistence.Entity, jakarta.validation.Valid); old tutorials with javax.* are Boot 2 and will not compile. Everything in this module works on both. Learn on the latest stable Boot, use Java 21 or 25, and read the official migration guide when a project upgrades. Boot 4 also reorganised some starters and modules, so always copy dependency names from Initializr instead of from an old blog.

Rule: Boot never replaces Spring knowledge

Auto-configuration is just Spring beans created for you. When something goes wrong (a missing bean, a wrong config value, a transaction that does not roll back), you debug it with Spring Framework concepts: beans, scopes, proxies, properties. The rest of this module teaches exactly those.

Mistake: thinking Spring Boot is a different framework

"Boot is faster than Spring" or "Boot replaces Spring MVC" is wrong. Boot configures Spring MVC for you. If someone asks "Spring vs Spring Boot" in an interview, the answer is "Boot is an opinionated layer on top of Spring that removes configuration".

Interview: "What is Spring Boot and why use it?"

  • Spring is a container-based framework for building enterprise apps; Boot is a layer on top that gives starters, auto-configuration, an embedded server, an executable JAR and Actuator.
  • Benefits: faster start, less configuration, tested dependency versions, production-ready features, easy deployment (one JAR, Docker friendly).
  • Mention that you can still override any default, and that Boot is still plain Spring underneath.

Creating a project: Spring Initializr and project structure

start.spring.io generates a ready-to-run Maven or Gradle project from a few choices; its main class calls SpringApplication.run, and everything else lives in the standard src/main and src/test folders.

Spring Initializr is a web tool at start.spring.io. IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code and Spring Tools for Eclipse have the same tool built in (New Project → Spring Initializr). It writes a pom.xml (or build.gradle), a main class and a test class, so you start from a working build.

The form, field by field

FieldWhat to choose
ProjectMaven (most common in companies) or Gradle. These notes use Maven.
LanguageJava.
Spring BootThe newest stable release (no SNAPSHOT or milestone M1/RC1 labels) — or the version your company uses.
GroupReverse domain of your organisation, such as com.example. It becomes the base package.
Artifact / NameThe project name, such as orderservice. It becomes the JAR name.
PackagingJar (default, runs with the embedded server). War is only for deploying to an external server.
Java17, 21 or 25. Pick a Java version you have installed; 21 is a safe choice.
DependenciesAdd the starters you need: Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, PostgreSQL Driver, Validation, Spring Boot DevTools, Lombok.

Press Generate, unzip the download and open the folder in your IDE. You can add dependencies later by editing pom.xml; nothing is locked in.

The generated structure

  • src/main/java — your code. src/main/resources — non-code files that go onto the classpath.
  • application.properties — starts empty except for spring.application.name. Rename it to application.yml if you prefer YAML (see the configuration article).
  • static/ and templates/ matter only for web pages. A pure REST API leaves them empty.
  • src/test/java — tests, mirroring the package of the code they test.
  • mvnw — the Maven Wrapper downloads the right Maven version on first use, so every developer and the CI server build the same way.

The main class

package com.example.orderservice;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class OrderserviceApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderserviceApplication.class, args);
    }
}

SpringApplication.run does the whole startup: it reads the configuration, creates the ApplicationContext (the container), scans for beans, applies auto-configuration, starts the embedded Tomcat and keeps the JVM alive. What @SpringBootApplication means is explained in its own article.

The generated pom.xml, trimmed

<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.0</version>   <!-- the Boot version you picked -->
</parent>

<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
</properties>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

Your version number will be whatever Initializr wrote; the one above is only an illustration. Notice that the starters have no version: the parent supplies it (see the starters article). The spring-boot-maven-plugin is what builds the executable fat JAR.

Running the application

$ ./mvnw spring-boot:run              # during development (mvnw.cmd on Windows cmd)
$ ./mvnw clean package                # build target/orderservice-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
$ java -jar target/orderservice-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
$ java -jar target/orderservice-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --server.port=9090

In the IDE you can also click the green run arrow next to main. When startup works, the log ends with lines like these (the port and timing vary):

Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'
Started OrderserviceApplication in 1.9 seconds (process running for 2.3)

A web starter keeps running until you stop it with Ctrl+C. Without a web starter, the app starts, runs its beans and exits, because there is nothing to keep the JVM alive.

Package by layer or by feature

Where do your own classes go under com.example.orderservice? There are two common styles.

By layerBy feature
Layoutcontroller/, service/, repository/, model/order/, customer/, payment/, each holding its own controller, service, repository
Good forSmall apps, learning, quick scanning of "all controllers"Bigger apps; a feature's code sits together; easy to extract into a microservice later
WeaknessOne feature is spread over four folders; everything tends to be publicNeeds discipline about what one feature may call in another

Start with layers while learning; move to features when the project grows past a handful of entities. Both work with component scanning as long as the sub-packages sit under the main class's package.

Rule: keep the main class in the root package

The main class must sit in a package above all your other code (com.example.orderservice), because scanning starts there. Never leave it in the default (empty) package: Spring would scan the whole classpath and Boot logs a warning.

Conventions

  • Commit pom.xml, mvnw, .mvn/ and the sources. Add target/ to .gitignore.
  • Use the wrapper (./mvnw) in README and CI so nobody needs a local Maven.
  • Name the application class XxxApplication.

Edge cases

  • Port 8080 already in use: the app fails with Web server failed to start. Port 8080 was already in use. Stop the other program or set server.port.
  • Unsupported class file major version or a compile error about the release version: your installed JDK is older than the java.version in the pom.
  • On Windows PowerShell use .\mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run; in Git Bash ./mvnw works.

Interview: "Walk me through a Spring Boot project and its startup"

  • Main class annotated @SpringBootApplication calls SpringApplication.run; the resources folder holds application.yml; the pom inherits from the Boot parent and uses starters.
  • Startup creates the context, scans for beans, applies auto-configuration, starts Tomcat, then runs any CommandLineRunner beans.
  • Packaging is a fat JAR run with java -jar.

Inversion of Control and dependency injection, in plain Java first

Dependency injection means a class receives the objects it needs instead of creating them; Inversion of Control means something else (the Spring container) decides which objects to create and hand over.

Before any annotation, understand the problem with plain Java. A dependency is any object your class needs to do its work. An OrderService that sends a confirmation needs something that can send messages; that "something" is its dependency.

Step 1: tight coupling with new

public class EmailSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) {
        System.out.println("EMAIL to " + to + ": " + text);
    }
}

public class OrderService {
    private final EmailSender sender = new EmailSender();   // hard-wired

    public void placeOrder(String customerEmail) {
        // ... save the order ...
        sender.send(customerEmail, "Your order is confirmed");
    }
}

This works, but it hurts in four ways. (1) OrderService is welded to EmailSender: to switch to SMS you must edit OrderService. (2) You cannot unit-test it without really sending an email, because you cannot replace the sender. (3) If EmailSender itself needs an SMTP host and a password, OrderService must know how to build it. (4) You cannot share one instance across classes. This is called tight coupling.

Step 2: program to an interface, receive it through the constructor

public interface NotificationSender {
    void send(String to, String text);
}

public class EmailSender implements NotificationSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) {
        System.out.println("EMAIL to " + to + ": " + text);
    }
}

public class SmsSender implements NotificationSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) {
        System.out.println("SMS to " + to + ": " + text);
    }
}

public class OrderService {
    private final NotificationSender sender;           // only the interface

    public OrderService(NotificationSender sender) {   // given from outside
        this.sender = sender;
    }

    public void placeOrder(String customer) {
        sender.send(customer, "Your order is confirmed");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NotificationSender sender = new EmailSender();      // you wire it
        OrderService service = new OrderService(sender);    // by hand
        service.placeOrder("ravi@example.com");
    }
}
EMAIL to ravi@example.com: Your order is confirmed

This is dependency injection (DI): OrderService no longer creates its sender, it is given one. Now switching to SMS needs no change inside OrderService, and a unit test can pass a fake sender. DI is only a technique — a constructor that takes its collaborators. You can do it with no framework at all.

Step 3: the wiring grows, so let a container do it

In a real app you have 50 or 200 classes, each with dependencies, which have their own dependencies. Writing that wiring by hand in main becomes a long, fragile list: you must create objects in the right order and share singletons correctly.

DataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(config);
OrderRepository repo = new OrderRepository(ds);
PaymentClient payment = new PaymentClient(httpClient, apiKey);
NotificationSender sender = new EmailSender(smtpHost, user, pass);
OrderService service = new OrderService(repo, payment, sender);
OrderController controller = new OrderController(service);
// ... 40 more lines, in the right order ...

Inversion of Control (IoC) means you hand this job to a framework. Normally your code is in control: you decide what to create and when. With IoC the framework is in control: it creates the objects, finds each one's dependencies, builds them in the right order and gives them out. You only declare what is a bean and what each class needs. The container that does this is Spring's ApplicationContext.

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final NotificationSender sender;

    public OrderService(NotificationSender sender) {   // Spring passes it in
        this.sender = sender;
    }
    // ...
}

@Component
public class EmailSender implements NotificationSender { /* ... */ }

The classes did not change much. What disappeared is the new calls and the main wiring. Spring sees that OrderService needs a NotificationSender, finds the EmailSender bean, creates it first, then creates OrderService with it.

IoC vs DI

Inversion of ControlDependency Injection
What it isA design principle: the framework calls your code and controls object creation ("Hollywood principle: don't call us, we call you")A technique that implements IoC for object dependencies
ScopeWider: also covers callbacks, event listeners, the servlet container calling your controllerNarrower: how an object gets its collaborators
In SpringThe container manages the life of beansConstructor, setter or field injection

Why this is worth it

  • Easy testing. Pass a fake NotificationSender into the constructor; no Spring needed for a unit test (Module 5).
  • Swappable parts. Change the implementation by changing configuration, not business code (the demo project uses this with profiles).
  • One place for lifecycle. Singletons, creation order, startup and shutdown callbacks are the container's job.
  • Cross-cutting features. Because the container creates your objects, it can wrap them in proxies to add transactions, caching and security (the AOP article).

Rule: depend on interfaces, not on concrete classes

Declare the field and constructor parameter as the interface (NotificationSender), not EmailSender. The container supplies whichever implementation is configured. If you write the concrete class, you lose the swapping and testing benefit.

Convention: do not use new for your own beans

Inside a Spring app, never write new OrderService(...) for a class that is a bean. The object you create is not managed: it gets no injection, no proxy and no transactions. Ask for it as a dependency instead. Plain value objects (DTOs, records, entities) are fine to create with new.

Edge cases

  • Not every class should be a bean. Beans are services and components with behaviour and shared state-free logic; data holders are not beans.
  • You can still use DI without Spring (Guice, Dagger, Jakarta CDI, or by hand). Spring just also bundles lifecycle, AOP and configuration.
  • Too many constructor parameters (more than about five) is a design smell: the class probably does too much. Split it.

Interview: "What is IoC? What is DI? What problem do they solve?"

  • Without DI, classes create their dependencies with new — tight coupling, hard to test, hard to change.
  • DI gives the object its dependencies from outside (best through the constructor). IoC means the framework controls creation and wiring.
  • Spring's IoC container reads bean definitions (annotations or Java config), builds the object graph in dependency order and manages scope and lifecycle.
  • Benefits: loose coupling, testability, one place for configuration, ability to add proxies for transactions and security.

The container: ApplicationContext, BeanFactory and bean definitions

The ApplicationContext is the Spring container: it reads bean definitions, creates the beans in dependency order, injects them into each other and manages their life until shutdown.

When SpringApplication.run returns, it hands you back a ConfigurableApplicationContext. That object is the container. It holds every bean in a registry (a map from bean name to bean), knows how each was built and keeps singleton beans alive until the application stops.

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

BeanFactoryApplicationContext
RoleThe basic container: create beans, look them up, inject dependenciesA BeanFactory plus enterprise features
Singleton creationLazy: when first requestedEager: all singletons are created at startup
ExtrasNoneEvents, Environment and properties, message sources (i18n), resource loading, annotation processing, BeanPostProcessor registration
You use itAlmost never directlyAlways (Boot creates it)

Eager creation is a feature: a wrong configuration makes the application fail at startup, not hours later when a user hits that code path.

Bean definitions: the recipe

Before the container builds any object, it collects bean definitions. A definition is a recipe: the class, the scope, the init and destroy methods, the dependencies. Definitions come from three places:

  • Stereotype annotations found by component scanning (@Component and friends).
  • @Bean methods inside @Configuration classes.
  • Auto-configuration classes from Boot libraries (they are ordinary @Configuration classes, just loaded conditionally).

Every bean has a name (id) and a type. For a scanned class the default name is the simple class name with a lowercase first letter: OrderService becomes orderService. For a @Bean method the name is the method name.

How the container builds the object graph

The creation step in detail, for this tiny app:

Spring reads constructor parameter types, finds a matching bean for each, creates missing ones recursively, and only then calls the constructor. That "dependencies first" rule is why a circular dependency (A needs B, B needs A) cannot be solved by constructors (see the errors article).

Using the context directly

In application code you almost never call the container; you declare dependencies. But it helps to see it once, for example to understand what Boot does or in a quick experiment:

@SpringBootApplication
public class OrderserviceApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConfigurableApplicationContext ctx =
                SpringApplication.run(OrderserviceApplication.class, args);

        OrderService byType = ctx.getBean(OrderService.class);
        OrderService byName = (OrderService) ctx.getBean("orderService");
        boolean same = byType == byName;
        System.out.println("Same singleton? " + same);
        System.out.println("Bean count: " + ctx.getBeanDefinitionCount());
    }
}
Same singleton? true
Bean count: 164

Calling getBean yourself is the service locator style and is an anti-pattern in normal code: it hides dependencies and brings back the testing problems DI solved. Use it only in framework-style glue code.

The ApplicationContext in a plain Spring program (no Boot)

@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example.shop")
class AppConfig { }

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)) {
            ctx.getBean(OrderService.class).placeOrder("ravi@example.com");
        }   // close() destroys singleton beans and runs @PreDestroy
    }
}

Boot does the same thing with SpringApplication.run, plus auto-configuration and an embedded server. You can even list all beans with ctx.getBeanDefinitionNames() to see what auto-configuration created for you.

Rule: beans are found by type first, then by name

Injection matches the type of the parameter. If several beans have that type, Spring falls back to matching the parameter name against bean names, and then you need @Primary or @Qualifier (see the injection article).

Convention: let Boot own the context

Do not create a second ApplicationContext inside a Boot app. Tests use @SpringBootTest or slice annotations, which create one for you (Module 5).

Edge cases

  • Only singleton beans are created eagerly. Prototype and request-scoped beans are created on demand, and @Lazy singletons wait until first use.
  • A web app uses a web-aware context (AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext) that also starts the embedded server. You do not need to remember the class name.
  • Contexts form hierarchies (parent and child), used in older Spring MVC setups and in some Spring Cloud setups. Boot apps normally have one.

Interview: "BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext? What happens at startup?"

  • BeanFactory is the basic lazy container; ApplicationContext adds events, property/environment handling, i18n, resource loading and eager singleton creation. Use the latter.
  • Startup: collect bean definitions, run post-processors, create singletons in dependency order, inject, run init callbacks, then the context is ready.
  • Eager singleton creation makes wiring errors fail fast at startup.

Component scanning and the stereotype annotations

Component scanning finds classes marked @Component (or @Service, @Repository, @Controller) in the main class's package and its sub-packages and registers each as a bean.

You do not list your beans anywhere. Instead you put an annotation on the class, and at startup Spring walks the packages looking for those annotations. This is component scanning. It is switched on by @ComponentScan, which is part of @SpringBootApplication.

The scanning rule

@SpringBootApplication scans the package of the class it is on, and all sub-packages — nothing else.

Mistake: a bean outside the base package

The most common beginner failure: a class is annotated @Service but lives in a sibling package, so nobody finds it. The app fails with "required a bean of type … that could not be found".

Wrong: service outside the scanned tree

// main class: com.example.shop.ShopApplication
package com.example.common;     // sibling of com.example.shop

@Service
public class AuditService { }

Right: move it under the base package, or widen the scan

package com.example.shop.common;     // under the main class

// or, if it must stay where it is:
@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = {"com.example.shop", "com.example.common"})
public class ShopApplication { }

Moving the class is nearly always better than widening the scan. Use scanBasePackages (or @ComponentScan with basePackages) only for shared libraries from other modules.

The stereotype annotations

A stereotype annotation marks a class as a bean and also tells readers its role. @Component is the generic one; the others are specialisations of it (they are meta-annotated with @Component).

AnnotationLayerExtra behaviour
@ComponentAny class that fits no other role (a mapper, a helper, a client)None. Just a bean.
@ServiceBusiness logicNone today; documents intent and is a good pointcut target.
@RepositoryData accessTranslates persistence exceptions (such as SQLException or Hibernate errors) into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy.
@ControllerWeb layer returning HTML viewsHandler methods are found by Spring MVC; return values are view names.
@RestControllerWeb layer returning JSON@Controller + @ResponseBody: return values are written to the response body.
 
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderController {
    private final OrderService service;
    public OrderController(OrderService service) { this.service = service; }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; }
}

@Repository
public class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { /* ... */ }

With Spring Data (Module 3) you will not annotate repository interfaces yourself; Spring Data creates and registers them. You still use @Repository on hand-written data-access classes.

Exception translation in @Repository

Each persistence technology throws its own exceptions. A @Repository bean is wrapped by a post-processor (PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor, which Boot registers for you when data access is present) so those exceptions turn into DataAccessException subclasses, such as DuplicateKeyException or DataIntegrityViolationException. Your service code then does not depend on JPA or JDBC exception types.

Bean names and conflicts

  • Default name: class name, first letter lowercase (OrderService → orderService). An exception: names like URLService keep their case, because the first two letters are capitals.
  • Custom name: @Service("orders").
  • Two scanned classes with the same simple name in different packages produce the same default name and fail with ConflictingBeanDefinitionException. Give one an explicit name.

Customising what is scanned

  • @ComponentScan(basePackages = "...") sets other packages (this replaces the default, so list the original one as well).
  • Include/exclude filters (@ComponentScan.Filter) can drop classes by annotation or pattern.
  • @Profile("dev") on a class keeps it out of the context unless that profile is active (profiles).

Rules

  • A scanned class must be concrete (not an interface or abstract class) and needs a constructor Spring can call.
  • Use the most specific stereotype: @Service for services, @Repository for data access, @RestController for JSON endpoints.
  • Scanning only finds classes you annotate; third-party classes cannot be annotated, so use @Bean for them (next article).

Conventions

  • Do not put @Component on everything. Entities, DTOs and records are data, not beans.
  • Keep the dependency direction one-way: controller → service → repository. A repository must never call a controller.
  • Use @Component (not @Service) for technical helpers such as a JSON mapper or a filter.

Edge cases

  • @Service and @Component behave the same; using the wrong one never breaks the app, but it misleads readers and can break AOP pointcuts written for a stereotype.
  • In tests with @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest, only a slice of beans is loaded; a scanned @Service is missing unless you add it with @Import or @MockitoBean (Module 5).
  • A class with two constructors and no @Autowired on one makes Spring look for a no-argument constructor and fail (see injection).

Interview: "@Component vs @Service vs @Repository? What does @ComponentScan do?"

  • All three register a bean. @Service and @Repository are specialisations of @Component that express the layer; @Repository also enables exception translation.
  • @Controller adds web handling; @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody.
  • Component scanning looks in the main class's package and sub-packages; a bean outside gives NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.
  • For classes you cannot annotate (third-party), declare a @Bean method.

@Configuration and @Bean: defining beans in Java code

A @Configuration class holds @Bean methods; each method's return value becomes a bean, which is how you register third-party classes and objects that need custom set-up.

Stereotypes only work on classes you own. You cannot put @Component on ObjectMapper, RestClient or BCryptPasswordEncoder, because you do not edit their source. For those, and for any object that needs set-up code, you write a method that builds the object and tell Spring to treat the result as a bean.

import java.time.Clock;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public Clock clock() {                         // bean name: "clock"
        return Clock.systemUTC();
    }

    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {     // bean name: "passwordEncoder"
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);
    }
}

Now any class can ask for a Clock or a PasswordEncoder in its constructor. Putting a Clock in the container is also a good testing habit: tests inject a fixed clock instead of calling LocalDateTime.now() directly.

Beans that depend on other beans

A @Bean method can take parameters; Spring resolves them as beans, exactly like a constructor.

@Configuration
public class PaymentConfig {

    @Bean
    public PaymentClient paymentClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
                                       PaymentProperties props) {
        RestClient client = builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl()).build();
        return new PaymentClient(client, props.apiKey());
    }
}

Here RestClient.Builder is provided by Boot's auto-configuration and PaymentProperties by your own configuration properties.

Bean names and customising

  • The name is the method name. Change it with @Bean("fastEncoder") or @Bean(name = {"a", "b"}) for aliases.
  • Several methods can return the same type with different names; choose between them with @Qualifier or @Primary.
  • Other attributes: initMethod and destroyMethod (lifecycle callbacks on a third-party class), and @Scope, @Lazy, @Profile, @ConditionalOnProperty next to @Bean.
@Configuration
public class HttpConfig {

    @Bean
    @Primary                        // chosen when nobody says which
    public RestClient paymentRestClient() {
        return RestClient.create("https://pay.example.com");
    }

    @Bean
    public RestClient shippingRestClient() {
        return RestClient.create("https://ship.example.com");
    }
}

@Service
class ShippingService {
    ShippingService(@Qualifier("shippingRestClient") RestClient client) { /* ... */ }
}

@Configuration, proxyBeanMethods and "full" vs "lite" mode

A @Configuration class is itself a bean, and by default Spring wraps it in a CGLIB subclass (proxyBeanMethods = true). The proxy makes one promise: if one @Bean method calls another, the call goes through the container, so you still get the singleton and not a new object.

@Configuration
public class ServiceConfig {

    @Bean
    public AuditLog auditLog() {
        return new AuditLog();
    }

    @Bean
    public OrderService orderService() {
        return new OrderService(auditLog());   // same AuditLog singleton
    }
}

With @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) (called lite mode) the proxy is skipped: startup is slightly faster, but auditLog() inside orderService() is a plain method call and creates a second object. Boot's own auto-configuration classes use proxyBeanMethods = false and take dependencies as method parameters instead. Your rule: keep the default, or use false and always pass dependencies as parameters.

@Component with @Bean ("lite" beans)

@Bean methods also work inside any @Component class. They follow the lite rules: inter-method calls are plain Java calls. Use @Configuration for classes whose job is to define beans.

When to use which

SituationUse
Your own classA stereotype annotation (@Service, @Component)
A class from a library@Bean method
An object needing builder code, parameters or a condition@Bean method
Several differently configured instances of one classSeveral @Bean methods with distinct names
Swap a Boot default (your own ObjectMapper, security chain)@Bean; Boot's version backs off (auto-configuration)

Rules

  • @Bean methods must not be private or final inside a @Configuration class that is proxied (CGLIB must override them).
  • The @Configuration class itself must not be final when proxyBeanMethods is true.
  • Return the interface or the most useful type; the declared return type is what Spring uses for type matching before the bean is created.

Conventions

  • Split configuration by concern: SecurityConfig, JacksonConfig, HttpClientConfig. Do not make one giant AppConfig.
  • Prefer parameters over calling other @Bean methods.
  • Name beans for what they are, not how they are built (paymentRestClient, not bean1).

Mistake: creating a bean with new in business code

Writing PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder() inside every service gives each one its own object and hard-wires the choice. Define it once as a @Bean and inject it.

Interview: "@Component vs @Bean? What does proxyBeanMethods do?"

  • @Component is class-level and found by scanning; @Bean is method-level and used inside configuration classes, so you control construction and can register third-party classes.
  • With proxyBeanMethods = true (default) calls between @Bean methods return the same singleton; with false they are plain calls, which is faster to start.

Injection types: constructor, setter, field, and choosing between beans

Prefer constructor injection: it makes dependencies required, lets fields be final and lets you test with plain new; use @Qualifier and @Primary when several beans match.

Spring can hand a bean its dependencies in three ways. They differ in what they guarantee, not in what they can reach.

Constructor injection (preferred)

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final NotificationSender sender;

    // Only one constructor: @Autowired is not needed (Spring 4.3+)
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository, NotificationSender sender) {
        this.repository = repository;
        this.sender = sender;
    }
}

If a class has one constructor, Spring uses it automatically. With several constructors, mark the one to use with @Autowired. With Lombok you can drop the boilerplate:

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor      // generates a constructor for all final fields
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final NotificationSender sender;
}

Records and Java 21 make this even lighter for small cases, but Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor is what you will see in most projects.

Setter injection

@Service
public class ReportService {
    private AuditLog auditLog;   // optional: the app works without it

    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setAuditLog(AuditLog auditLog) {
        this.auditLog = auditLog;
    }
}

Use it for dependencies that are truly optional or that must be changeable after creation. The object can exist without them, which is both the benefit and the risk.

Field injection (avoid)

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository repository;     // set by reflection
    @Autowired
    private NotificationSender sender;
}

Why constructor injection wins

ConcernConstructorSetterField
Fields can be final (immutable)YesNoNo
Object never half-builtYes: fully ready after newNo: can be missing partsNo: null until Spring sets it
Dependency is requiredYes, enforced by the compilerOptional by natureHidden
Unit test without Springnew OrderService(fakeRepo, fakeSender)Call settersNeeds reflection or Spring test support
Too many dependencies is visibleYes: a long constructor warns youNoNo: ten fields look harmless
Circular dependenciesFail fast at startupCan hide a bad designCan hide a bad design
Needs reflection to injectNoNoYes (sets private fields)

Several beans of the same type

Suppose two classes implement NotificationSender. A constructor parameter of that type matches both, and Spring cannot choose. Three tools solve it.

@Component
@Primary
public class EmailSender implements NotificationSender { /* ... */ }

@Component
public class SmsSender implements NotificationSender { /* ... */ }
@Service
public class OtpService {
    private final NotificationSender sender;

    public OtpService(@Qualifier("smsSender") NotificationSender sender) {
        this.sender = sender;      // bean name: class SmsSender -> "smsSender"
    }
}

A third way: name the parameter like the bean (NotificationSender smsSender); Spring falls back to the parameter name when several beans match. It works but breaks silently when someone renames the parameter, so prefer @Qualifier. An explicit @Qualifier always wins over @Primary.

Injecting all implementations: the strategy pattern

Ask for a List or a Map and Spring injects every bean of the type. This gives you the strategy pattern with no if chains.

public interface PaymentService {
    void pay(long amountInPaise);
}

@Service("upi")  public class UpiPayment  implements PaymentService { /* ... */ }
@Service("card") public class CardPayment implements PaymentService { /* ... */ }

@Service
public class PaymentRouter {
    private final Map<String, PaymentService> byName;   // key = bean name
    private final List<PaymentService> all;

    public PaymentRouter(Map<String, PaymentService> byName,
                         List<PaymentService> all) {
        this.byName = byName;
        this.all = all;
    }

    public void pay(String method, long amountInPaise) {
        PaymentService service = byName.get(method);    // "upi" or "card"
        if (service == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown method: " + method);
        }
        service.pay(amountInPaise);
    }
}

Adding a new payment method means adding one new class; PaymentRouter does not change (open/closed principle). The order inside the List follows @Order or the Ordered interface when present.

Optional dependencies

@Service
public class FeatureService {
    private final Optional<MetricsClient> metrics;
    private final ObjectProvider<AuditLog> audit;

    public FeatureService(Optional<MetricsClient> metrics,
                          ObjectProvider<AuditLog> audit,
                          @Autowired(required = false) Cache cache) {
        this.metrics = metrics;
        this.audit = audit;
    }

    public void run() {
        metrics.ifPresent(m -> m.count("feature.run"));
        audit.ifAvailable(a -> a.record("run"));
    }
}

ObjectProvider<T> is the most flexible: getIfAvailable(), ifAvailable(...), getObject(), stream(), and it also resolves late, which is how you get a new prototype bean each time (see scopes).

@Resource and @Inject

@Autowired is Spring's own annotation (match by type, then name). @Inject (jakarta.inject) behaves almost the same. @Resource matches by name first. In new code use constructor injection and skip all three.

Rules

  • A single constructor is autowired without any annotation; with two or more, annotate exactly one with @Autowired.
  • A required dependency with no matching bean stops startup (NoSuchBeanDefinitionException).
  • Two matching beans with no @Primary or @Qualifier stop startup (NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException).
  • @Autowired works only on beans managed by Spring, never on objects you create with new.

Conventions

  • Constructor injection, private final fields, interface types.
  • Use @Primary for "the usual one" and @Qualifier for the exceptions.
  • If a constructor has more than about five parameters, split the class.

Edge cases

  • A Map<String, T> uses bean names as keys, so keep names meaningful ("upi", not "upiPaymentServiceImpl") when the key matters.
  • An injected List is empty (not an error) when no bean of the type exists, unlike a single required bean.
  • Constructor injection with @Lazy on a parameter injects a lazy proxy; useful to break a cycle, not as a habit.

Mistake: field injection and then new

A class with @Autowired private Repo repo; cannot be unit-tested with new OrderService(): repo stays null and you get a NullPointerException. Constructor injection makes that mistake impossible.

Wrong: field injection

@Service
class OrderService {
    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;
}
// new OrderService().place()  -> NullPointerException

Right: constructor injection

@Service
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
}
// new OrderService(fakeRepo) works in a plain unit test

Interview: "Constructor vs field injection? How do you pick between two beans?"

  • Constructor injection: immutability, required dependencies, easy testing, no reflection, visible class size. Field injection hides all of that.
  • Setter injection for optional dependencies only.
  • Two candidates: @Primary on one, or @Qualifier("name") at the injection point, or inject a Map/List of all.
  • Single constructor needs no @Autowired since Spring 4.3.

Common bean errors and how to read the startup failure report

Most Spring startup failures are a missing bean, two matching beans or a circular dependency; the failure report at the end of the log names the class, the parameter and usually the fix.

When the container cannot build the object graph, the application refuses to start. Do not scroll through the 200-line stack trace. Look for the box that Boot prints at the bottom.

***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

Parameter 0 of constructor in com.example.shop.order.OrderService
required a bean of type 'com.example.shop.order.OrderRepository'
that could not be found.

Action:

Consider defining a bean of type 'com.example.shop.order.OrderRepository'
in your configuration.

The Description says what went wrong and where; the Action suggests a fix. Read those two first. If you see only a long stack trace, scroll to the last Caused by:: the deepest cause is the real problem; the BeanCreationException lines above are wrappers.

1. NoSuchBeanDefinitionException (the bean is missing)

Cause: nothing in the container matches the required type or name.

CheckFix
Class has no stereotype annotationAdd @Service, @Component or a @Bean method
Class is outside the scanned packagesMove it under the main class's package (scanning)
You asked for the implementation, but the bean is a proxy of the interfaceInject the interface type
The bean is excluded by @Profile or a conditionActivate the profile or fix the condition
A starter is missing (no DataSource bean)Add the dependency; check with the conditions report
Test with a slice (@WebMvcTest)Mock the missing collaborator or @Import it

2. NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException (too many beans)

Parameter 0 of constructor in com.example.shop.OtpService required a
single bean, but 2 were found:
    - emailSender: defined in file [.../EmailSender.class]
    - smsSender: defined in file [.../SmsSender.class]

Action: Consider marking one of the beans as @Primary, updating the
consumer to accept multiple beans, or using @Qualifier to identify the
bean that should be consumed

Fix by one of: @Primary on the usual bean; @Qualifier("smsSender") at the injection point; accept List/Map of all; or a bean-name-matching parameter name. Another cause is two @Bean methods that both return the same type.

3. UnsatisfiedDependencyException

This is a wrapper. Spring says "I could not satisfy a dependency of bean X" and the reason is in the nested exception: usually one of the two above, or an exception thrown by another bean's constructor. Always read the last Caused by.

4. Circular dependencies

A needs B and B needs A. With constructors neither can be created first.

@Service
class OrderService {
    OrderService(CustomerService customers) { }
}

@Service
class CustomerService {
    CustomerService(OrderService orders) { }
}
The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context
form a cycle:

┌─────┐
|  orderService defined in file [.../OrderService.class]
↑     ↓
|  customerService defined in file [.../CustomerService.class]
└─────┘

Action: Despite circular references being allowed by default in Spring
Framework, they are prohibited by Spring Boot by default...

Since Spring Boot 2.6 cycles are prohibited by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references is false). Treat a cycle as a design smell and fix the design, in this order of preference:

  1. Extract the shared logic into a third class that both use. Often A and B both really need "customer lookup", which belongs in its own service.
  2. Move one direction to events: A publishes an event, B listens (events).
  3. Pass data, not services: give the method the values it needs instead of the whole bean.
  4. Last resort: @Lazy on one constructor parameter, which injects a lazy proxy that resolves on first call. It hides the problem; document why.

Setting spring.main.allow-circular-references=true brings the old behaviour back for setter and field injection. Do not do that; it only postpones the design fix.

5. Other errors you will meet

MessageMeaning and fix
Failed to configure a DataSource: 'url' attribute is not specifiedA JDBC starter is on the classpath but spring.datasource.* is not set. Add the properties, or exclude the auto-configuration if the app has no database.
Web server failed to start. Port 8080 was already in useAnother process uses the port. Stop it or set server.port.
ConflictingBeanDefinitionExceptionTwo beans with the same name. Rename one or give an explicit name.
BeanCurrentlyInCreationExceptionCircular reference found while creating a bean (see above).
BeanInstantiationExceptionThe constructor threw, or there is no usable constructor. Read the cause.
Could not resolve placeholder 'app.name'A @Value("${app.name}") property does not exist. Add it, or give a default.
Binding to target ... failedA @ConfigurationProperties value has the wrong type or fails validation.
BeanNotOfRequiredTypeExceptionThe bean is a JDK proxy, so it cannot be cast to the class. Use the interface.

A debugging routine

  1. Read the "Description" and "Action" of the failure report.
  2. Find the last Caused by: in the stack trace if no report was printed.
  3. Check the three basics: annotation present, package scanned, profile active.
  4. Run with --debug to print the conditions report, and list beans with ctx.getBeanDefinitionNames() if needed.
  5. Fix the root cause, never by switching injection style or allowing cycles.

Rule: fail fast is good

These errors appear at startup, because singletons are created eagerly. That is the container protecting you; never hide them with lazy tricks unless you understand why.

Edge cases

  • Field-injected cycles used to "work" before Boot 2.6 because Spring injected a half-built object. Upgrading old projects shows these cycles suddenly.
  • A @Lazy constructor parameter breaks a startup cycle but not a cycle in real method calls: infinite recursion causes a StackOverflowError at runtime.
  • An exception inside a @PostConstruct method also aborts startup, reported as BeanCreationException: Invocation of init method failed.

Mistake: fixing a cycle with allow-circular-references

It silences the error and leaves two classes that know too much about each other. Extract a third class or use an event instead.

Interview: "What is a circular dependency and how do you fix it?"

  • A needs B and B needs A; constructor injection cannot create either first. Since Boot 2.6 it fails at startup by default.
  • Fix by redesign: extract a third class, use events, pass data instead of beans. @Lazy on one parameter or setter injection are last resorts.
  • Also be able to name NoSuchBeanDefinitionException (missing bean) and NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException (several candidates) with causes and fixes.

Bean scopes: singleton, prototype and web scopes

The scope decides how many instances of a bean exist and how long they live; the default singleton scope gives one shared instance per container, so singleton beans must be stateless or thread-safe.

A scope answers: "when someone asks the container for this bean, does it give the same object or a new one?"

ScopeInstancesLives forUse for
singleton (default)One per containerWhole applicationServices, repositories, controllers, clients
prototypeA new one for every injection or getBeanUntil garbage collected; Spring does not destroy itStateful helper objects
requestOne per HTTP requestThe requestPer-request data (a request id, tenant)
sessionOne per HTTP sessionThe user sessionShopping cart in a server-side session
applicationOne per ServletContextWhole web applicationRare; usually a singleton does the same

The web scopes (request, session, application) exist only in a web application. There is also websocket, which is rare.

Singleton: shared, so keep it stateless

"Singleton" here means one instance per container, not the classic Gang-of-Four pattern with a private constructor. Because every request thread uses the same instance at the same time, a singleton bean must hold no per-request mutable state.

Wrong: per-user state in a singleton

@Service
public class CartService {
    private List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();   // shared by ALL users!

    public void add(Item item) { items.add(item); }
}

Right: state passed in or stored per user

@Service
public class CartService {
    private final CartRepository carts;           // stateless; state lives in the DB
    public CartService(CartRepository carts) { this.carts = carts; }

    public void add(long userId, Item item) { carts.addItem(userId, item); }
}

Fields that are final collaborators are fine. Mutable counters, caches and lists are not, unless you use thread-safe types (AtomicLong, ConcurrentHashMap); see Core Java · Module 6.

Prototype

@Component
@Scope("prototype")          // or ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE
public class ReportBuilder {
    private final List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    public void add(String line) { lines.add(line); }
}

Spring creates and injects a prototype, then forgets it: destroy callbacks like @PreDestroy are not called. Releasing resources is your job.

The classic trap: a prototype inside a singleton

A singleton is built once, so its dependencies are injected once. If one of them is a prototype, the singleton keeps that single instance forever, and the "new instance every time" behaviour is lost.

@Service
public class ReportService {
    private final ReportBuilder builder;          // injected ONCE

    public ReportService(ReportBuilder builder) { this.builder = builder; }

    public String build() { return builder.toString(); }   // shared, grows forever
}

Ask the container for a fresh one each time, with ObjectProvider:

@Service
public class ReportService {
    private final ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> builders;

    public ReportService(ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> builders) {
        this.builders = builders;
    }

    public String build() {
        ReportBuilder builder = builders.getObject();    // a NEW instance
        builder.add("Total: 1500");
        return builder.toString();
    }
}

Alternatives: @Scope(value = "prototype", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) (a proxy that gets a new target per call), or a @Lookup method. ObjectProvider is the clearest. Often the best answer is simpler still: create the helper with new inside the method, since it is not really a bean.

Web scopes

@Component
@RequestScope                       // = @Scope(value = "request", proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS)
public class RequestContext {
    private String requestId;
    // getters and setters
}

@Service
public class AuditService {
    private final RequestContext context;     // a proxy, safe to inject here
    public AuditService(RequestContext context) { this.context = context; }

    public void log(String action) {
        System.out.println(context.getRequestId() + " " + action);
    }
}

The singleton AuditService is created at startup, when there is no request. So Spring injects a scoped proxy instead of the real bean. On each call the proxy finds the real RequestContext of the current request and forwards the call. @RequestScope and @SessionScope set up that proxy for you; with plain @Scope("request") you must add proxyMode yourself. Using the bean outside a request (a scheduled job, a new thread) throws IllegalStateException: No thread-bound request found.

Server-side sessions fit badly with REST APIs, which should be stateless (Module 2). So in API projects request scope is the only web scope you may use, and rarely.

Rules

  • Default is singleton; keep singleton beans free of mutable per-request state.
  • Spring calls @PreDestroy for singletons (and other long-lived scopes), not for prototypes.
  • A longer-lived bean (singleton) that needs a shorter-lived one (prototype, request) must get it through a provider or a scoped proxy.

Conventions

  • Over 95 percent of beans are singletons; do not add @Scope without a clear reason.
  • Put request data (the user, a tenant, a trace id) in method parameters, a ThreadLocal-backed context, or the security context, not in a mutable singleton field.

Edge cases

  • Singleton beans are shared across threads, but created eagerly in one thread at startup; that does not make their later use thread-safe.
  • A prototype injected into a prototype is a new instance each time; the trap exists only when a longer-lived bean holds it.
  • Two @Bean methods returning the same class give two different singletons, because the scope is per bean definition, not per class.

Interview: "What are bean scopes? Is a singleton bean thread-safe?"

  • Singleton (default), prototype, request, session, application (and websocket). Singleton is one per container, not per JVM and not the GoF pattern.
  • A singleton is not automatically thread-safe: keep it stateless or use thread-safe state.
  • Prototype into singleton: injected once; fix with ObjectProvider, a scoped proxy, or @Lookup. Prototype beans are not destroyed by Spring.

The bean lifecycle: from construction to destruction

The container creates a bean, injects its dependencies, calls the Aware and post-processor callbacks, runs your init methods, keeps it in use, and calls destroy methods at shutdown; AOP proxies are created right after initialization.

Knowing the order helps you decide where code belongs: dependencies are not available in the constructor of a field-injected bean, a proxy appears only after init, and cleanup runs at shutdown. This is a favourite interview topic.

The steps, in order

  1. Instantiate — the constructor runs. With constructor injection all dependencies are already passed in.
  2. Populate properties — setter and field injection happen now (and @Value fields are set).
  3. Aware callbacks — if the bean implements BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware or ApplicationContextAware, Spring passes in the name, factory or context.
  4. BeanPostProcessor, before init — every registered postProcessBeforeInitialization runs. This is where the handling of @PostConstruct itself happens.
  5. @PostConstruct — your method runs; everything is injected.
  6. InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() — the interface-based alternative.
  7. Custom init method — @Bean(initMethod = "start").
  8. BeanPostProcessor, after init — postProcessAfterInitialization may return a replacement. This is where Spring wraps the bean in an AOP proxy for @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Async. What other beans receive may be the proxy, not your object.
  9. In use — the bean serves calls until the context closes.
  10. @PreDestroy, then DisposableBean.destroy(), then a custom destroyMethod — cleanup at shutdown. Singletons only.

Watching the order yourself

import jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct;
import jakarta.annotation.PreDestroy;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanNameAware;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.InitializingBean;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class LifecycleDemo implements BeanNameAware, InitializingBean {

    public LifecycleDemo() {
        System.out.println("1 constructor");
    }

    @Override
    public void setBeanName(String name) {
        System.out.println("3 BeanNameAware: " + name);
    }

    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        System.out.println("5 @PostConstruct");
    }

    @Override
    public void afterPropertiesSet() {
        System.out.println("6 afterPropertiesSet");
    }

    @PreDestroy
    public void cleanup() {
        System.out.println("10 @PreDestroy");
    }
}
1 constructor
3 BeanNameAware: lifecycleDemo
5 @PostConstruct
6 afterPropertiesSet
... application runs ...
10 @PreDestroy

The package is jakarta.annotation in Boot 3 and 4 (it was javax.annotation in Boot 2). The annotations come from the Jakarta Annotations API, which Boot's starters already include.

@PostConstruct: what to use it for

  • Validating configuration: fail startup if a required value is blank.
  • Warming up: loading a small lookup table or opening a connection once.
  • Setting derived fields that need injected dependencies.

Keep it short and fast. Do not call slow remote services there; a slow @PostConstruct delays application startup, and a failure aborts it. For work that should run once the app is up, use a runner.

CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner

These run after the context is fully built, just before SpringApplication.run returns. They are good for seeding data or one-off start-up tasks.

@Component
@Order(1)
public class SeedData implements CommandLineRunner {

    private final ProductRepository products;
    public SeedData(ProductRepository products) { this.products = products; }

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {          // raw command-line arguments
        if (products.count() == 0) {
            products.save(new Product("MSE-1001", "Wireless Mouse"));
        }
    }
}

@Component
class Warmup implements ApplicationRunner {
    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {        // parsed: --mode=fast
        System.out.println("fast? " + args.containsOption("mode"));
    }
}

ApplicationRunner gives parsed options (--name=value) and non-option arguments; CommandLineRunner gives the raw string array. Order several runners with @Order. An exception in a runner fails startup.

@Lazy and @DependsOn

  • @Lazy on a bean (or class) delays creation until the first request for it. It speeds startup but moves errors to runtime. You can enable it for all beans with spring.main.lazy-initialization=true, a trade-off to use knowingly.
  • @DependsOn("databaseMigrator") forces that bean to be created first even if there is no injection link between them (for example a bean that must exist before this one, as a side effect). Use it sparingly; normally injection already orders things.

Defining callbacks for third-party beans

@Bean(initMethod = "connect", destroyMethod = "disconnect")
public LegacyQueueClient queueClient() {
    return new LegacyQueueClient("amqp://localhost");
}

For @Bean methods Spring also guesses a destroy method named close or shutdown if the class has one (this is called inference). Set destroyMethod = "" to turn that off.

Why the order matters in practice

  • Do not use an injected field in a constructor of a field-injected bean: it is still null. This is another reason to prefer constructor injection.
  • Calling a @Transactional method of the same bean from @PostConstruct does not start a transaction, because the proxy is created in step 8, after the method runs.
  • Cleaning up resources (thread pools, files) belongs in @PreDestroy or a close() method; Spring Boot's graceful shutdown calls it when the JVM gets a stop signal.

Rules

  • @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy methods take no arguments and should return void.
  • Destroy callbacks run for singletons at context close, not for prototypes, and not if the JVM is killed with kill -9.
  • Prefer the annotations over the interfaces InitializingBean and DisposableBean, which tie your class to Spring.

Conventions

  • Constructor: assign fields only. @PostConstruct: light set-up. Runner: start-up tasks that need the running app.
  • Keep seed data and migrations out of production profiles (use profiles).

Edge cases

  • Both @PostConstruct and afterPropertiesSet exist: the annotation runs first. If the same method name is also declared as an init method, Spring runs it once.
  • If the constructor throws, you see BeanInstantiationException; if @PostConstruct throws, BeanCreationException: Invocation of init method failed.
  • A BeanPostProcessor is itself a bean; make its @Bean method static so it is created early and does not force its configuration class to load too soon.

Interview: "Explain the bean lifecycle"

  • Instantiate → populate dependencies → Aware callbacks → post-processor before → @PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet → init-method → post-processor after (proxies) → ready → @PreDestroy → destroy → destroy-method.
  • Name one use for each hook: @PostConstruct to validate config; BeanPostProcessor to wrap beans (AOP); @PreDestroy to release resources.
  • Say prototype beans are not destroyed by Spring, and runners run after the context is ready.

Configuration: application.properties, application.yml and property precedence

Boot reads settings from application.properties or application.yml, and from many other sources; when the same key appears twice, the higher-priority source (command-line arguments, then environment variables, then files) wins.

Code should not contain a database URL, a port or an API key. Those change between your laptop, the test server and production. Externalised configuration means keeping them outside the compiled code, so the same JAR runs everywhere with different settings.

properties vs YAML: the same keys

Boot reads src/main/resources/application.properties or application.yml (or .yaml). Pick one format per project. The keys are identical; YAML nests them by indentation.

server.port=8081
spring.application.name=order-service
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop_user
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
logging.level.com.example.shop=DEBUG
server:
  port: 8081
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
    username: shop_user
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
logging:
  level:
    com.example.shop: DEBUG
.properties.yml
RepetitionFull key on every lineShared prefixes written once
Listsapp.hosts[0]=a, or comma separatedNatural - a list syntax
PitfallFewIndentation errors; use spaces, never tabs; a value like on, no or 08 may change meaning, so quote strings
Per-profile filesapplication-dev.propertiesapplication-dev.yml or multi-document

If both application.properties and application.yml exist, the .properties values win. Do not mix them.

Where Boot looks

In order of increasing priority: the classpath root, then a /config folder on the classpath, then the current directory, then ./config/ and its sub-folders. A file next to the JAR can therefore override the one packed inside it, which is handy on servers. Change the name or the location with spring.config.name and spring.config.location.

Property source precedence (highest first)

Boot gathers settings from many places and merges them. For a given key, the first source in this list that has it wins:

  1. Command-line arguments: java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
  2. Java system properties: -Dserver.port=9090 (SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON sits near here too)
  3. Operating-system environment variables: SERVER_PORT=9090
  4. Profile-specific files: application-prod.yml (outside the JAR beats inside)
  5. application.yml / application.properties: outside the JAR beats inside
  6. @PropertySource files and default properties: the lowest priority, including defaults in your @Value("${x:default}")

The simplified rule to remember: command line > environment > profile files > application.yml > defaults. This gives a clean design: put safe defaults in application.yml, specific values in a profile file, and secrets or per-server overrides in environment variables.

$ java -jar app.jar                               # 8081 from application.yml
$ SERVER_PORT=9000 java -jar app.jar              # environment variable wins
$ java -jar app.jar --server.port=9100            # command line wins over all

Relaxed binding: one setting, many spellings

Boot matches names loosely, so the same setting can be written in different ways depending on where it lives.

WhereFormExample for property app.max-retries
.properties / .ymlkebab-case (recommended)app.max-retries=3
.properties / .ymlcamelCase and underscore also acceptedapp.maxRetries=3
Environment variableUPPER_CASE with underscoresAPP_MAXRETRIES=3 or APP_MAX_RETRIES=3
Java class fieldcamelCaseint maxRetries;

That is why SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD sets spring.datasource.password. Write keys in kebab-case in files.

Secrets

Never commit passwords, API keys or JWT secrets. Use environment variables, a secrets manager, or a file that is not in Git. Reference them with a placeholder so the file stays safe to commit:

spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop}
    username: ${DB_USER:shop_user}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}              # no default: must be provided
app:
  jwt-secret: ${JWT_SECRET}

${NAME:default} reads the environment (or any property) and falls back to the default after the colon. With no default and no value, startup fails with Could not resolve placeholder, which is what you want for a missing secret.

spring.config.import and the Environment

Pull in extra files with spring.config.import. The prefix optional: means "do not fail if it is missing".

spring:
  config:
    import: optional:file:./local-secrets.properties

Inside code, the Environment bean gives programmatic access: env.getProperty("app.name"), env.getActiveProfiles(). Prefer @Value or @ConfigurationProperties in normal code (next articles).

Seeing which value won

With Actuator, /actuator/env lists each property source and each value (expose it only in dev; it can reveal secrets, so Boot masks values by default). In the log, The following 1 profile is active: "dev" tells you the profile.

Rules

  • YAML uses spaces only, a consistent indent (2 spaces), and key: value with a space after the colon.
  • A key set in a higher-priority source completely overrides lower ones; lists are replaced as a whole, not merged.
  • Changing a property file needs a restart (DevTools restarts for you in development).

Conventions

  • Use kebab-case keys, a common prefix for your own settings (app.* or the company name), and YAML for nested data.
  • Defaults for local development live in application.yml; production differences arrive through profile files and environment variables.
  • Secrets only through environment variables or a secret store; never in Git.

Edge cases

  • A password containing # or : in YAML or properties needs quotes in YAML ("p#ss"); in .properties, # inside a value is fine but a leading # starts a comment.
  • A YAML key spring.datasource.url written as one dotted key works, but mixing dotted and nested forms in the same file is confusing.
  • Unknown keys are silently ignored for @Value; @ConfigurationProperties can be told to fail on unknown fields, which catches typos.

Mistake: committing the production password

A password in a file in Git stays in the history forever, even after you delete it. Rotate the secret and move it to an environment variable.

Interview: "How do you externalise configuration? What is the precedence?"

  • Properties/YAML files, environment variables, system properties and command-line arguments; the same JAR works in every environment.
  • Order, highest first: command line, environment, profile-specific files, application.yml, defaults.
  • Relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url. Secrets come from the environment, never from Git.

Profiles: dev, test and prod settings

A profile is a named set of configuration and beans that is switched on with spring.profiles.active, so the same code uses an H2 database and debug logs in dev and PostgreSQL and quiet logs in prod.

You rarely run an application with the same settings everywhere. On your laptop you want a local database and detailed logs; in production a managed database, small logs and real payment keys. Profiles let you describe each environment once and pick one when starting. The build artifact stays the same (one JAR); only the profile changes. This idea is called build once, configure per environment, and it is the base of every Docker or Kubernetes deployment.

Activating a profile

$ java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
$ java -Dspring.profiles.active=prod -jar app.jar
$ SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod java -jar app.jar          # typical in Docker
$ ./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev

You can also set spring.profiles.active=dev in application.yml as a local default, but do not commit a hard-coded prod there. Several profiles are separated by commas (dev,debug). In tests, use @ActiveProfiles("test") (Module 5). If no profile is set, the profile named default is active. IntelliJ users set the same value in the run configuration under "Active profiles".

Boot tells you what it chose in the first lines of the log. Always look at this line when something behaves strangely:

The following 1 profile is active: "prod"
# or, when nothing was set:
No active profile set, falling back to 1 default profile: "default"

Profile-specific files

Boot loads application.yml first, then application-{profile}.yml for every active profile, which overrides the base values. The same naming works for .properties files.

spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
app:
  notification:
    channel: email
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop_dev
    username: dev
    password: dev
logging:
  level:
    com.example.shop: DEBUG
app:
  notification:
    channel: console
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
logging:
  level:
    root: WARN
    com.example.shop: INFO

How Boot decides which value wins

When the same key appears in several places, the more specific source wins. From weakest to strongest, the order that matters in daily work is:

  1. application.yml inside the JAR (the shared defaults).
  2. application-{profile}.yml inside the JAR.
  3. An application.yml and application-{profile}.yml placed outside the JAR (next to it, or in a config/ folder).
  4. Operating-system environment variables (SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL).
  5. Command-line arguments (--server.port=9090).

So a base file gives defaults, the profile file overrides them for one environment, and the deployment can still override a single value without rebuilding. When two profiles are active (dev,debug), the profile listed later overrides the earlier one. The full list of sources is in the configuration files article.

Multi-document YAML in one file

A YAML file can hold several documents separated by ---. Each can be tied to a profile with spring.config.activate.on-profile.

app:
  notification:
    channel: email
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: dev
app:
  notification:
    channel: console
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod
app:
  notification:
    channel: sms

In .properties files use the separate-file naming instead (the multi-document form exists with #--- but is rare). Older tutorials use spring.profiles: dev for this; that key was removed in Boot 2.4, so use spring.config.activate.on-profile.

@Profile: beans that depend on the environment

Put @Profile on a bean or configuration class and it is registered only when the profile is active. Internally it is a condition checked while the container reads bean definitions, so a bean in an inactive profile is never even created (see the container). This is how the notification app chooses its sender.

public interface NotificationSender {
    void send(String to, String text);
}

@Component
@Profile("dev")
public class ConsoleSender implements NotificationSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) {
        System.out.println("[DEV] to " + to + ": " + text);
    }
}

@Component
@Profile("prod")
public class SmsSender implements NotificationSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) { /* call the SMS gateway */ }
}

@Component
@Profile("!dev & !prod")       // every other profile, including 'default'
public class NoOpSender implements NotificationSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) { }
}

Expressions use ! (not), & (and) and | (or); mixing & and | needs parentheses. Without a matching sender the app fails to start with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, so make sure every profile has exactly one implementation, or add a catch-all like the last one. The opposite problem, two matching senders, gives NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException (bean errors).

@Profile also works on a @Bean method and on a whole @Configuration class. You can read the profiles in code when you really need to:

@Component
class ProfileInfo {
    ProfileInfo(Environment env) {
        String[] active = env.getActiveProfiles();           // e.g. ["prod"]
        boolean prod = env.acceptsProfiles(Profiles.of("prod"));
    }
}

Profile, property or condition?

Profiles describe environments; properties describe choices. Pick the smallest tool that fits.

NeedBest toolExample
Different values per environmentProfile file or env varspring.datasource.url
A bean only in some environments@ProfileFake payment gateway in dev
A feature switched on by a setting@ConditionalOnPropertyapp.notification.channel=sms
A bean only if a class or bean exists@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBeanLibrary auto-configuration
 
@Component
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.notification.channel", havingValue = "sms")
public class SmsSender implements NotificationSender {
    public void send(String to, String text) { /* call the SMS gateway */ }
}

Other profile features

  • spring.profiles.include adds profiles unconditionally (for example dev always includes local-db).
  • spring.profiles.group.prod: prod-db,prod-logging activates a group with one name. Starting with prod then activates all three.
  • Environment.getActiveProfiles() returns the active profiles at runtime; the Actuator /actuator/env endpoint shows them too, if you expose it (Actuator).
  • spring.profiles.default changes the name of the fallback profile, which is rarely needed.

Rules

  • Profile-specific files override application.yml, and the active profile list order matters: later profiles override earlier ones.
  • @Profile without a value is invalid; a bean without it exists in every profile.
  • An unknown profile name is not an error: it only means no file matches.
  • spring.profiles.active and spring.profiles.include cannot be set inside a profile-specific file or a document with on-profile. Boot refuses to start with an InvalidConfigDataPropertyException, because the profile would depend on itself. Set them in the base file, an environment variable or an argument.

Conventions

  • Keep profile names few and standard: dev, test, prod (and maybe staging).
  • Do not branch on "prod" inside business code; use properties and let configuration differ.
  • Keep real production values out of application-prod.yml; read them from the environment.
  • Make dev work with one command on a fresh laptop (Docker Compose for the database, Compose), so new team members start without a setup document.

Mistake: secrets and environment checks in the code
