Wrong: password in Git, profile test in code

spring:
  datasource:
    password: Sup3rSecret!      # committed to the repository
if (env.acceptsProfiles(Profiles.of("prod"))) {
    sendRealSms(to, text);
} else {
    log.info("fake sms");
}

Right: placeholder, and two beans

spring:
  datasource:
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}    # injected by the deployment
@Profile("prod")  class SmsSender implements NotificationSender { ... }
@Profile("!prod") class LogSender implements NotificationSender { ... }

A password in Git stays in the history even after you delete it. Branching on the profile name makes the production path impossible to test on your laptop.

Edge cases and errors

  • With no active profile, application-default.yml is loaded if present. Do not rely on this; it confuses people.
  • Too many profiles combine in unexpected ways (dev,debug,local). If you need more than three, use properties.
  • A list in a profile file replaces the whole list from the base file; it is not merged. If application.yml has three app.allowed-origins and the profile file has one, only that one remains. Scalar keys are overridden one by one, maps are merged key by key.
  • A typo in a profile name (SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prd) is silent: the app starts with base settings, often connecting to the dev database. Check the startup log line.
  • A ${DB_URL} placeholder with no value fails at startup with IllegalArgumentException: Could not resolve placeholder 'DB_URL'. That is good: it stops a misconfigured prod start.
  • On Windows PowerShell set an environment variable with $env:SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE="dev"; cmd uses set SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev.
  • Profile-specific files are loaded only for active profiles, so a test that forgets @ActiveProfiles("test") silently uses the base settings.

Real projects

A typical setup: application.yml with local defaults, application-test.yml pointing to Testcontainers or H2, and production values injected by the deployment (Kubernetes or Docker env vars, DevOps · Module 3) with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod. Some teams add a staging profile that equals prod but with a smaller database and test payment keys. Secrets come from a secret store (Kubernetes Secrets, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), never from Git.

Interview: "What are Spring profiles? How do you use them?"

  • Profiles group configuration and beans per environment. Activate with spring.profiles.active (property, argument or env var).
  • Config: application-{profile}.yml or multi-document YAML with spring.config.activate.on-profile. Beans: @Profile, with expressions like !prod.
  • Precedence: command line and environment beat profile files, which beat application.yml; later profiles beat earlier ones.
  • Add that you keep secrets in environment variables, and prefer properties over profile checks for feature choices. A follow-up is often "how do you run tests with a different database?" (@ActiveProfiles("test") and application-test.yml).

@Value and @ConfigurationProperties: reading settings in code

Use @Value("${key:default}") for one simple setting; use @ConfigurationProperties with a record and @Validated for a group of related settings, because it is type-safe, validated and easy to test.

Once a value is in application.yml, your classes need to read it. Spring offers two main ways, and a quick look at the third.

@Value: one value at a time

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final String appName;
    private final int maxItems;
    private final boolean giftWrapEnabled;

    public OrderService(@Value("${spring.application.name}") String appName,
                        @Value("${app.order.max-items:20}") int maxItems,
                        @Value("${app.order.gift-wrap:false}") boolean giftWrapEnabled) {
        this.appName = appName;
        this.maxItems = maxItems;               // 20 if the key is missing
        this.giftWrapEnabled = giftWrapEnabled;
    }
}
  • ${key} reads a property; ${key:default} uses the default after the colon if the key is missing; without a default a missing key fails startup.
  • Spring converts the string to int, boolean, Duration, List and more. A list: @Value("${app.hosts}") List<String> with a,b,c.
  • #{...} is a SpEL expression (Spring Expression Language): @Value("#{2 * 60}"), @Value("#{systemProperties['user.home']}"). Use it rarely.

It is perfect for one value. Its limits show up quickly: the keys are strings spread across many classes (a typo is found only at runtime), there is no grouping, no validation, no IDE help, and testing needs every key set. Relaxed binding is also weaker: @Value wants the exact kebab-case key.

@ConfigurationProperties: a typed group

Bind a whole prefix to an object. With a record the settings become immutable and the object is created through its constructor (constructor binding).

app:
  payment:
    base-url: https://pay.example.com
    api-key: ${PAYMENT_API_KEY}
    timeout: 5s
    max-retries: 3
    allowed-methods:
      - upi
      - card
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Max;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotEmpty;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.DefaultValue;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
@Validated
public record PaymentProperties(
        @NotBlank String baseUrl,
        @NotBlank String apiKey,
        @DefaultValue("5s") Duration timeout,
        @DefaultValue("3") @Min(0) @Max(10) int maxRetries,
        @NotEmpty List<String> allowedMethods) {
}

Register it. The easiest is to scan for such classes on the main class:

@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan          // finds all @ConfigurationProperties classes
public class ShopApplication { /* ... */ }

// or, one by one:
@Configuration
@EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class)
class PaymentConfig { }

Then inject it like any bean:

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    private final PaymentProperties props;

    public PaymentService(PaymentProperties props) {
        this.props = props;
    }

    public void pay(long paise) {
        System.out.println("POST " + props.baseUrl() + " timeout " + props.timeout());
        // retry up to props.maxRetries() times ...
    }
}

What you gain:

  • Type conversion — 5s becomes a Duration, 10MB a DataSize, true a boolean, nested objects and lists work.
  • Validation at startup — a blank api-key stops the app with a clear message:
Binding to target PaymentProperties[...] failed:

    Property: app.payment.apiKey
    Value: ""
    Reason: must not be blank

Action: Update your application's configuration
  • Relaxed binding — base-url, baseUrl and BASE_URL all match the field baseUrl.
  • One place — easy to find, easy to construct in a test with new PaymentProperties(...).

Validation needs the spring-boot-starter-validation dependency. You can also generate IDE auto-complete and documentation for your keys by adding the spring-boot-configuration-processor dependency (optional, annotation-processor only).

Nested records and the class-style alternative

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail")
public record MailProperties(String from, Smtp smtp) {
    public record Smtp(String host, int port, boolean tls) { }
}
// app.mail.from, app.mail.smtp.host, app.mail.smtp.port, app.mail.smtp.tls

Before records, properties were a class with getters and setters (JavaBean binding). That still works and is common in older code. A class with a single constructor and no setters also uses constructor binding. If a class has several constructors, mark the one for binding with @ConstructorBinding.

@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties

@Value@ConfigurationProperties
Best forOne or two simple valuesA group of related settings
BindingBy exact key, per fieldBy prefix, relaxed rules
ValidationNone built in@Validated with Bean Validation
Nested and list dataAwkwardNatural
Defaults${key:default}@DefaultValue or field initialisers
Supports SpELYesNo
Test itNeeds Spring or reflectionPlain new of a record

Rules

  • A @ConfigurationProperties class is a bean only when registered (@ConfigurationPropertiesScan, @EnableConfigurationProperties, or @Component on a mutable class).
  • Validation annotations are checked only when the class also has @Validated.
  • For a prefix use kebab-case lowercase (app.payment), not camelCase.

Conventions

  • Default to @ConfigurationProperties records for anything beyond a single flag; keep @Value for one-off values.
  • Give optional settings sensible defaults and mark required ones with @NotBlank, @NotNull.
  • Never log a properties object that contains secrets; override toString or avoid printing it.

Edge cases

  • @Value is not applied to static fields. And a @Value field is still null in the constructor if you use field injection (use constructor parameters).
  • Unknown keys: by default @ConfigurationProperties ignores unknown properties. Set ignoreUnknownFields = false to make typos fail.
  • Changing a property file does not change a running application; a restart (or Spring Cloud refresh) is needed.
  • @Value("${a.b}") with an empty value gives an empty string, not null; @Value("${a.b:}") gives an empty string when missing.

Mistake: 15 @Value fields scattered everywhere

The same key typed in five classes, with different defaults, is a bug waiting to happen. Group them in one properties record.

Interview: "@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?"

  • @Value injects a single property with optional default and SpEL support. @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole prefix into a typed object.
  • The latter gives relaxed binding, type conversion, nested objects, validation (@Validated) and IDE metadata; it is the recommended style.
  • Constructor binding with records keeps settings immutable.

What @SpringBootApplication does

@SpringBootApplication is three annotations in one: @SpringBootConfiguration (this class is a configuration), @EnableAutoConfiguration (turn on Boot's auto-configuration) and @ComponentScan (scan this package and below).

The annotation on your main class is short but carries the whole Boot idea. It is a meta-annotation: an annotation built from other annotations, so one line on your class has the effect of several. Here is what it contains.

@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@SpringBootConfiguration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = { /* skip some test configurations */ })
public @interface SpringBootApplication {
    // attributes: exclude, excludeName, scanBasePackages, scanBasePackageClasses ...
}

And this is the typical main class it sits on:

package com.example.shop;                 // the ROOT package

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class ShopApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ShopApplication.class, args);
    }
}

The three annotations, one by one

@SpringBootConfiguration
A specialised @Configuration. It marks the class as a source of bean definitions, so you can put @Bean methods directly in the main class. It exists as a separate annotation so that tests can find your main class: @SpringBootTest and the slice tests search upwards from the test package until they find a class with this annotation, and use it as the configuration (Module 5).
@EnableAutoConfiguration
Tells Boot to load all matching auto-configuration classes: beans created for you because of what is on your classpath and in your properties (next article).
@ComponentScan
Scans the main class's package and sub-packages for stereotype annotations (scanning).

You could write the three annotations yourself and get the same behaviour. The combined annotation is just convenient.

Inside @EnableAutoConfiguration

This is the most interesting of the three. It is itself made of two parts:

  • @AutoConfigurationPackage records the package of your main class. Later, JPA auto-configuration uses it as the default place to look for @Entity classes and Spring Data repositories. That is why entities in a package outside your root package are "not found" even though you never configured scanning.
  • @Import(AutoConfigurationImportSelector.class) runs while the context reads configuration. The selector reads the list of auto-configuration class names from the file META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports inside each JAR on the classpath, removes the ones you excluded, and imports the rest. Each of those classes carries @Conditional... rules, so only those that fit your classpath and properties actually create beans.

The same trick is how any library can plug into Boot: it ships a configuration class and lists it in that .imports file. Your own code is never touched.

Inside @ComponentScan on this annotation

The @ComponentScan on @SpringBootApplication has two exclude filters. One (TypeExcludeFilter) lets test slices such as @WebMvcTest remove beans they do not need. The other (AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter) stops the scan from picking up auto-configuration classes as ordinary configuration, because they must go through the conditional import route described above. You normally never think about these filters, but they explain why a sliced test loads only part of your app.

What SpringApplication.run does

The annotation is a description; SpringApplication.run does the work. In simplified order:

  1. Decide the application type from the classpath: servlet web (Spring MVC), reactive web, or none.
  2. Load configuration: application.yml, environment variables, command-line arguments, and set the active profiles (profiles).
  3. Print the banner and create the right ApplicationContext.
  4. Register bean definitions from your classes (component scan, @Bean) and from auto-configuration.
  5. Refresh the context: create all singleton beans; the web context starts the embedded server (embedded server).
  6. Call all CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner beans, then return.

Boot publishes events along the way (ApplicationStartedEvent, ApplicationReadyEvent and more); you can listen to them (events). If anything fails, Boot catches the exception, prints a readable failure analysis ("APPLICATION FAILED TO START", with a Description and an Action) and exits with a non-zero code (bean errors). The run method returns the ConfigurableApplicationContext, which is useful in plain programs and tests; in a web app the JVM stays alive because the server threads keep running.

Running code at startup

A runner is a bean that executes once after the context is ready. Use it for small start-up tasks such as seeding demo data. It is not a place for heavy business logic.

@Component
@Order(1)                                   // lower number runs first
class DemoDataLoader implements CommandLineRunner {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(DemoDataLoader.class);

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {
        log.info("Seeding demo data, args = {}", List.of(args));
    }
}

ApplicationRunner is the same but receives parsed ApplicationArguments (so you can ask args.containsOption("seed") for --seed). A runner that throws an exception stops the application with a failure exit.

Customising startup

public static void main(String[] args) {
    SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(ShopApplication.class);
    app.setBannerMode(Banner.Mode.OFF);
    app.setAdditionalProfiles("local");
    app.run(args);
}

// or the fluent builder:
new SpringApplicationBuilder(ShopApplication.class)
        .profiles("local")
        .run(args);

Most of these switches also exist as properties (spring.main.banner-mode=off, spring.main.web-application-type=none), which is usually better because you do not touch the code. For a command-line tool without a web server, set spring.main.web-application-type=none or leave out the web starter.

Attributes you will use

AttributePurpose
exclude / excludeNameDisable specific auto-configurations (see next article)
scanBasePackagesScan other packages than the default
scanBasePackageClassesA type-safe version: pass a marker class from each package
proxyBeanMethodsWhether the main class is proxied like a @Configuration
 
// do not auto-configure a datasource (for a service that has no database yet)
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)

// scan an extra package that is not below the main class
@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = {"com.example.shop", "com.example.common"})

Comparison: the long form and the short form

You writeYou get
@SpringBootApplicationConfiguration + auto-configuration + scan of the root package
@Configuration @EnableAutoConfiguration @ComponentScanThe same; @Configuration instead of @SpringBootConfiguration works, but tests can no longer find it by that annotation
@SpringBootApplication in the default (no) packageScan of every class on the classpath: slow start and a warning, so always use a named package

Rules

  • Use exactly one @SpringBootApplication per application, in the root package.
  • Keep the main class small: main, annotations, maybe a few shared beans. Put real configuration in separate @Configuration classes.
  • Do not add @EnableAutoConfiguration a second time; it is already there.
  • All your code (controllers, services, entities, repositories) must live in the root package or below, unless you list the extra package in scanBasePackages.

Conventions

  • Name the class after the application, ending in Application (ShopApplication), in the top package of the group id and artifact (com.example.shop).
  • Prefer properties (spring.autoconfigure.exclude) or the exclude attribute over deleting dependencies just to silence one auto-configuration.

Mistake: sprinkling extra annotations on the main class

Adding @EnableJpaRepositories, @EntityScan or @EnableScheduling to the main class changes more than you expect: @EnableJpaRepositories switches off Boot's own repository scanning defaults. This also affects sliced tests, which load the main class. Put such annotations on dedicated configuration classes.

Wrong: main class in a sub-package

com.example.shop.web.ShopApplication   (scans only ...shop.web)
com.example.shop.service.OrderService  (never found)

Right: main class in the root package

com.example.shop.ShopApplication       (scans all of ...shop)
com.example.shop.service.OrderService  (found)

Edge cases and errors

  • In a multi-module project, beans in another module's package are not scanned unless that package is under yours or you list it in scanBasePackages. Libraries should expose their beans through auto-configuration instead.
  • Running a Boot app inside an external Tomcat (WAR) needs a SpringBootServletInitializer; this is the legacy deployment style.
  • Excluding a class that is not an auto-configuration (for example your own @Configuration) fails with IllegalStateException: The following classes could not be excluded because they are not auto-configuration classes. To remove your own bean, use a profile or a condition instead.
  • A class in the default package (no package line) makes the scan cover the whole classpath; Boot warns that the context is unlikely to start. Always declare a package.
  • Two classes with @SpringBootApplication in one module give IllegalStateException: Found multiple @SpringBootConfiguration annotated classes in tests, because the search finds more than one.
  • The main method is not a bean: you cannot inject anything into it. Use a runner or an event listener.

Boot 3 and Boot 4

The annotation and its three parts work the same in both lines. Before Boot 2.7 the auto-configuration list lived in META-INF/spring.factories; modern versions use the .imports file shown above. Boot 4 also splits its large auto-configuration JAR into smaller per-technology modules, which changes dependency names but not how you write your main class.

Interview: "What does @SpringBootApplication do?"

  • It combines @SpringBootConfiguration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan.
  • Scan covers the main class's package and below; auto-configuration creates beans from the classpath and properties, using the imports file and @Conditional rules.
  • SpringApplication.run creates the context, starts the embedded server and calls runners.
  • A strong answer adds why the main class belongs in the root package and how you would exclude one auto-configuration. A common follow-up: "how do you run code at startup?" (CommandLineRunner or ApplicationRunner).

How auto-configuration works

Boot ships hundreds of ordinary @Configuration classes, listed in an .imports file; each is guarded by conditions (is this class on the classpath? is this property set? is a bean of this type already defined?), so only the ones that fit your app apply.

You add spring-boot-starter-web and, with no setup, a DispatcherServlet, a Tomcat server and a JSON converter exist. You add a PostgreSQL driver and a datasource properties, and a pooled DataSource appears. This is auto-configuration: Boot decides what beans you probably want, then creates them, unless you say otherwise.

The mechanism, step by step

  1. @EnableAutoConfiguration triggers an import selector.
  2. The selector reads the file META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports from every JAR on the classpath. It is a plain text file with one fully qualified class name per line. (Before Boot 2.7/3.0 the list lived in spring.factories; that is the old way.)
  3. Each listed class is a normal @AutoConfiguration (a variant of @Configuration) with @Bean methods and conditions.
  4. Conditions are evaluated: a class whose conditions fail contributes nothing.
  5. The surviving classes are processed after your own configuration, so your beans are already known and can win.

A real example, simplified

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)                 // JDBC classes are present
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DataSourceProperties.class)
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)       // you did not define one
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) {
        return props.initializeDataSourceBuilder().build();   // Hikari pool
    }
}

Read it as: "If JDBC is on the classpath and the user has not made their own DataSource, create one from the spring.datasource.* properties." Spring's actual classes are bigger, but the idea is exactly this.

The conditions

ConditionTrue whenExample use
@ConditionalOnClassA class is on the classpathSet up MVC only if DispatcherServlet is present
@ConditionalOnMissingClassA class is absentFallbacks
@ConditionalOnBeanA bean of that type existsAdd a metrics binder if a registry exists
@ConditionalOnMissingBeanNo bean of that type is defined yetBack-off: use my default unless the user made their own
@ConditionalOnPropertyA property has a valueFeature toggles: app.cache.enabled=true
@ConditionalOnWebApplicationThe app is a web appServlet-only beans
@ConditionalOnResourceA file existsOptional config files

You can use the same annotations in your own configuration, for example to create a bean only when a flag is set:

@Configuration
public class SmsConfig {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.sms.enabled", havingValue = "true")
    public SmsSender smsSender() {
        return new SmsSender();
    }
}

Back-off: how you override a default

Because Boot's beans are guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean, defining your own bean replaces the default:

@Configuration
public class JacksonConfig {

    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {         // Boot's ObjectMapper backs off
        return new ObjectMapper()
                .findAndRegisterModules()
                .disable(SerializationFeature.WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS);
    }
}

Note the trade-off: when you replace a Boot bean, you lose Boot's other customisations of it (for example properties like spring.jackson.*). Often a smaller tool is better: a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean, or just a property. Check the reference docs for the right extension point before replacing a whole bean.

Seeing what was applied: the conditions report

Start with --debug (or debug=true in properties) and Boot prints a conditions evaluation report.

$ java -jar app.jar --debug
============================
CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT
============================

Positive matches:
-----------------
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required class 'javax.sql.DataSource'

Negative matches:
-----------------
   MongoAutoConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'com.mongodb.client.MongoClient'

The same data is available live through Actuator: add spring-boot-starter-actuator, set management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=conditions and open /actuator/conditions (only in a safe environment). Module 6 covers Actuator.

Excluding an auto-configuration

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
public class ShopApplication { }
spring:
  autoconfigure:
    exclude:
      - org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration

Typical reason: you added a starter transitively but have no database in this module, and startup fails with Failed to configure a DataSource.

Writing your own auto-configuration (the idea)

Company teams package a shared logging or client library as a starter. The recipe: a @AutoConfiguration class with conditions, a properties class, and one line in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. Not needed for day-to-day work, but it shows there is no magic.

Rules

  • Auto-configuration never overrides a bean you defined (for beans guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean); your configuration is always processed first.
  • Conditions are about the state at startup. They do not react to later changes.
  • Auto-configuration classes must not be found by component scanning; they are loaded only through the imports file.

Conventions

  • Prefer changing a property over replacing a bean, and a customizer over a full replacement.
  • Define your own bean with the same type to take control; do not edit or copy Boot's classes.
  • Use --debug before guessing why a bean does or does not exist.

Edge cases

  • A transitive dependency can trigger an unwanted auto-configuration (a JDBC jar brings DataSource requirements). Exclude it or remove the jar.
  • Defining a bean of the type Boot expects with a different bean name still makes Boot back off, because the condition checks the type.
  • In sliced tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) only a chosen subset of auto-configurations is imported.
  • Boot 4 splits its auto-configuration into smaller modules; the mechanism (conditions, back-off, the .imports file) is unchanged.

Version note: spring.factories vs the imports file

Old tutorials say auto-configurations are listed under EnableAutoConfiguration in META-INF/spring.factories. That was Boot 2.x. From Boot 3.0 the only supported place is the AutoConfiguration.imports file shown above.

Interview: "How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?"

  • @EnableAutoConfiguration loads class names from META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports in every JAR.
  • Each class has conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnProperty and @ConditionalOnMissingBean; only matching ones register beans.
  • "Back-off": if you define your own bean, Boot's default is skipped.
  • Debug with --debug or /actuator/conditions; disable with exclude or spring.autoconfigure.exclude.

Starters and dependency management (the Boot parent and BOM)

A starter is one dependency that pulls in a whole feature with tested, compatible library versions; the Boot parent POM (a BOM) fixes those versions so you never write them yourself.

Without starters you would list Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat, validation and logging separately, and pick versions that work together. A starter is an empty-ish JAR whose only job is to depend on the right libraries. Add spring-boot-starter-web and you get a working web stack in one line.

Common starters

StarterYou getUse it when
spring-boot-starter-webSpring MVC, Jackson (JSON), embedded TomcatBuilding REST APIs or web pages
spring-boot-starter-data-jpaSpring Data JPA, Hibernate, HikariCPRelational database access
spring-boot-starter-jdbcJdbcTemplate, HikariCPPlain SQL
spring-boot-starter-securitySpring SecurityLogin, roles, JWT
spring-boot-starter-validationBean Validation (Hibernate Validator)@Valid, @NotBlank
spring-boot-starter-actuatorHealth, metrics and info endpointsProduction monitoring
spring-boot-starter-testJUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Spring TestAll tests (scope test)
spring-boot-starter-thymeleafThymeleaf templatesServer-rendered HTML
spring-boot-starter-cacheCaching abstraction@Cacheable
spring-boot-starter-aopAspectJ annotation supportYour own @Aspect classes
spring-boot-starter-mailJakarta Mail supportSending email

Starters follow the pattern spring-boot-starter-* for official ones; third-party starters name the other way round (mybatis-spring-boot-starter). Starters are the input; auto-configuration is what turns them into beans (previous article).

Version note: starter names can change between 3.x and 4.x

Boot 4 reorganised some starters and modules. The names above are the long-standing ones; check the names Initializr generates for your Boot version rather than copying from older articles.

No version numbers: the parent and the BOM

Look at the dependency list in a Boot pom.xml: starters have no <version>. The version comes from the parent.

<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.0</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>   <!-- no version -->
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
        <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>      <!-- no version: managed too -->
        <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

A BOM (bill of materials) is a POM that only lists recommended versions of many libraries (dependencyManagement). spring-boot-starter-parent inherits from spring-boot-dependencies, which is that BOM: it fixes hundreds of versions (Hibernate, Jackson, Tomcat, JUnit, the PostgreSQL driver and more) that were tested together. Upgrading Boot upgrades all of them in one step.

The parent also sets Java compiler defaults, UTF-8 encoding, resource filtering and plugin versions for the Boot Maven plugin.

If your company has its own parent POM

You can only extend one parent. Import the Boot BOM instead:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>3.5.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

In Gradle the Spring Boot plugin plus the io.spring.dependency-management plugin does the same. The Maven build part is in Core Java · Module 8.

Overriding a managed version

Sometimes you need a different version (for example a security fix in a library). Set the property the BOM uses:

<properties>
    <jackson-bom.version>2.18.2</jackson-bom.version>   <!-- illustration only -->
</properties>

Property names are listed in the Boot reference documentation (Dependency Versions appendix). Override only with a reason, because you leave the combination that Boot tested. See what is really on the classpath with ./mvnw dependency:tree.

Removing or swapping a transitive dependency

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>

Rules

  • Do not mix Boot versions: all spring-boot-* and spring-* artifacts must come from one BOM.
  • Do not write versions for libraries the BOM already manages.
  • Database drivers use runtime scope; test libraries use test.

Conventions

  • Add only the starters you need; every starter adds startup time and auto-configuration.
  • Upgrade Boot by changing one version number, then read the release notes and run the tests.
  • Keep the Initializr link in your README so a new teammate can regenerate a similar project.

Edge cases

  • Two starters can bring two JSON or logging libraries; Boot's exclusions handle the common cases. A Multiple SLF4J bindings warning means one of your own dependencies adds a second logging backend.
  • spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-webflux together: Boot chooses Spring MVC. Reactive stack is a different style, rarely needed at the beginning.

Interview: "What is a starter? Why no versions in the pom?"

  • A starter is a dependency descriptor that brings a feature's libraries together. Auto-configuration then configures them.
  • The parent spring-boot-starter-parent (via spring-boot-dependencies) is a BOM that manages tested versions.
  • Override a version with a property; exclude a transitive library with <exclusions>.

The embedded server, executable JAR and DevTools

Boot runs Tomcat inside your application, so one executable JAR starts the whole server with java -jar; change it with server.* properties and use DevTools for automatic restarts while you develop.

Before Boot, you built a WAR and deployed it into a separately installed Tomcat. With an embedded server the server is just a library: SpringApplication.run starts it from main. The application owns its server version and settings, which fits Docker and cloud deployment perfectly: the artifact is the whole runtime.

Tomcat by default, Jetty and Undertow as options

spring-boot-starter-web includes spring-boot-starter-tomcat. You can exchange it, as shown in the starters article. Tomcat is the default choice and what almost all companies use; there is rarely a reason to change it.

Server properties you will use

server:
  port: 8081                       # 0 = pick a random free port (useful in tests)
  servlet:
    context-path: /shop            # all URLs start with /shop
  shutdown: graceful               # finish running requests before stopping
  compression:
    enabled: true                  # gzip JSON responses
  error:
    include-message: never         # do not leak exception text to clients
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200                     # request-handling threads (the default)
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s
PropertyPurpose
server.portThe HTTP port (default 8080)
server.servlet.context-pathA URL prefix for the whole app
server.shutdown=gracefulOn stop signal, refuse new requests and let running ones finish
server.tomcat.threads.maxMaximum worker threads; one thread serves one request at a time
server.ssl.*HTTPS directly in the app (usually a proxy does TLS instead)
server.http2.enabledHTTP/2 (needs HTTPS in browsers)

Each incoming request is handled by one thread from Tomcat's pool; this is why singleton beans must be thread-safe (scopes). Since Java 21 you can switch on virtual threads with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true in Boot 3.2 and later; read more in Core Java · Module 6.

The executable (fat) JAR

The spring-boot-maven-plugin repackages the normal JAR into one that contains everything:

A plain Java java -jar cannot read JARs inside a JAR, so Boot adds a small launcher that sets up a class loader for BOOT-INF/lib, and then calls your main. You never see this. For Docker, the layered layout (layers.idx) lets an image keep dependencies in one layer and your code in another, so rebuilds are small (DevOps · Module 3).

Spring Boot DevTools

DevTools makes development faster. Add it as an optional development-only dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>
  • Automatic restart: when a class on the classpath changes, DevTools restarts the application. It uses two class loaders (one for unchanging libraries, one for your code), so a restart is much faster than a cold start.
  • LiveReload: a browser extension can refresh the page after a restart (mostly for server-rendered pages).
  • Development defaults: template caching is switched off, and more debug information is shown.
  • Remote restart: possible, but not recommended.

In IntelliJ you must trigger a compile (Ctrl+F9, or enable "build project automatically") for the restart to start, because DevTools reacts to changed class files, not to saved sources. DevTools is automatically disabled when the app runs from a packaged JAR (java -jar), and it is excluded from repackaged JARs by default, so it does not reach production.

Rules

  • Never run DevTools in production; mark it optional or runtime as shown.
  • The embedded server's context-path and port come only from properties of the app; an external server's WAR deployment ignores server.port.
  • Secure real deployments with HTTPS, normally terminated by a reverse proxy or load balancer in front of the app.

Conventions

  • Package as a JAR; use the same JAR in every environment, configured by profile and environment variables.
  • Enable graceful shutdown so a deployment does not cut requests in half.
  • Turn on compression only if no proxy already does it.

Edge cases

  • Port 0 chooses a random port; read it from the local.server.port property in tests (@LocalServerPort).
  • Behind a proxy, set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework or native so redirects and links use the public scheme and host.
  • A WAR build for an external Tomcat is still possible (extend SpringBootServletInitializer, mark Tomcat provided), but it is the legacy route.

Interview: "What is an embedded server? How is a Boot app packaged?"

  • The server (Tomcat) is a library started by main; no separate installation, easier containers, per-app server versions.
  • The Boot Maven plugin builds a fat JAR with BOOT-INF/classes, nested BOOT-INF/lib and a launcher; start it with java -jar.
  • Change the port with server.port; swap the server with exclusions; DevTools gives restart for development only.

Spring AOP and proxies: how @Transactional works, and the self-invocation pitfall

Spring wraps beans in proxy objects that run extra code (transactions, caching, security, your aspects) before and after the real method; calling a method on this bypasses the proxy, so the extra behaviour silently does not happen.

Some concerns cut across many classes: open a transaction, log timing, check a role, cache a result. Writing that in every method is repetitive and hides the business logic. Aspect-oriented programming (AOP) moves such code into one place and applies it to many methods without changing them.

Vocabulary in simple words

Aspect
A class holding the cross-cutting code, for example "log how long a service method takes".
Advice
The code itself, plus when it runs: @Before the method, @After it, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, or @Around (wraps the call and decides whether to proceed).
Join point
A point where advice can run. In Spring AOP it is always a method execution on a bean.
Pointcut
An expression that selects which methods get the advice, such as execution(* com.example.shop.service..*(..)).
Proxy
A stand-in object created by Spring that holds the advice and forwards calls to the real bean (the target).

A small aspect

import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Aspect
@Component
public class TimingAspect {

    // every public method of every class in a package named "service"
    @Around("execution(public * com.example.shop..service..*(..))")
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();                     // call the real method
        } finally {
            long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
            System.out.println(pjp.getSignature().toShortString() + " took " + ms + " ms");
        }
    }
}
OrderService.placeOrder(..) took 12 ms

OrderService has no logging code. Spring noticed that the pointcut matches it, and when the bean was created it gave out a proxy instead of the original object.

How the proxy works

The proxy is created in the "after initialization" step of the bean lifecycle (lifecycle). Everything that injects OrderService receives the proxy. Annotations that work through proxies include @Transactional (Module 3), @Cacheable, @Async, @Retryable and method security such as @PreAuthorize (Module 4).

JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB

JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB proxy
Built onjava.lang.reflect.ProxyA generated subclass of your class
NeedsThe bean to implement an interfaceA non-final class with non-final methods
Proxy typeImplements the interface; is not your classExtends your class
Boot defaultOnly if you set spring.aop.proxy-target-class=falseYes: spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true is Boot's default

Spring Framework itself uses a JDK proxy when the class has an interface; Spring Boot changes the default to CGLIB so injecting the concrete class works. In both cases the proxy sits in front of the real object.

The self-invocation pitfall

A call from outside goes through the proxy. A call from inside the same object goes straight to this, which is the real object, so no advice runs.

@Service
public class OrderService {

    public void checkout(Cart cart) {
        // ... some work ...
        saveOrder(cart);            // really this.saveOrder(cart): NOT via proxy
    }

    @Transactional
    public void saveOrder(Cart cart) {
        // runs WITHOUT a transaction when called from checkout()
    }
}

The same applies to @Cacheable, @Async and @PreAuthorize: they silently do nothing. There is no error, which makes this a famous bug and a favourite interview question. Fixes, best first:

  1. Move the method to another bean, and inject that bean. This is clean and obvious.
  2. Put the annotation on the entry method (checkout) so the whole operation is covered.
  3. Inject the bean into itself (self-injection with @Lazy) or use AopContext.currentProxy() with exposeProxy; these work but are ugly.
  4. Use AspectJ weaving (compile-time or load-time), which changes the bytecode and works for internal calls. Heavy; rarely used.
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderPersister persister;
    public OrderService(OrderPersister persister) { this.persister = persister; }

    public void checkout(Cart cart) {
        persister.saveOrder(cart);      // goes through persister's proxy
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderPersister {
    @Transactional
    public void saveOrder(Cart cart) { /* in a transaction */ }
}

Other proxy limits

  • Only public methods are advised in the default proxy setup for @Transactional; annotating a private or package-private method has no effect (a protected one may work on newer versions, but do not rely on it).
  • CGLIB cannot override final methods or subclass a final class: advice on them is skipped, or startup fails.
  • Objects you create with new have no proxy. @Transactional on such an object does nothing.
  • With a JDK proxy, a field of the concrete type fails with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException. Inject interfaces.
  • An exception inside the advice or a proxy that hides the target changes stack traces; the real method appears deeper in the trace.

Rules

  • Proxy-based annotations work only when the call comes from another bean through the container.
  • Only methods of Spring beans can be advised; only method execution, not field access or constructors.
  • You need spring-boot-starter-aop for your own @Aspect classes (annotations from AspectJ).

Conventions

  • Put @Transactional on service methods, not on controllers or repositories' internals.
  • Use aspects for real cross-cutting needs: audit, timing, rate limiting. Do not hide business rules in aspects.
  • Keep pointcuts narrow. A broad one such as execution(* *(..)) slows startup and surprises people.

Mistake: trusting an annotation that is silently skipped

If a "transactional" method does not roll back, or a cache never hits, check the call path first: is it called through another bean, and is the method public? Turn on logging.level.org.springframework.transaction=DEBUG to see transactions begin and end.

Interview: "How does @Transactional work? Why can it fail on a method called from the same class?"

  • Spring creates a proxy (CGLIB by default in Boot, or JDK when an interface is used) around the bean; the proxy begins and commits or rolls back the transaction around the call.
  • Self-invocation uses this, bypassing the proxy, so no transaction (same for @Cacheable, @Async).
  • Fix by moving the method to another bean, restructuring, or AspectJ weaving. Mention public-method and final-class limits.
  • Define aspect, advice, pointcut and join point in one line each.

Application events: publishing and listening inside the app

With ApplicationEventPublisher a bean announces that something happened and any number of @EventListener methods react, so the publisher does not need to know who is listening.

Placing an order should save it, send a confirmation, update stock and write an audit record. If OrderService calls all of these directly, it knows too many classes. With events, OrderService says "an order was placed" and the other parts subscribe independently. This reduces coupling (and helps break the circular dependencies from the errors article).

Publishing and listening

public record OrderPlacedEvent(long orderId, String customerEmail, long amountInPaise) { }
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;

    public OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher) {
        this.publisher = publisher;
    }

    public void placeOrder(String email, long amountInPaise) {
        long id = 101;                               // ... save the order ...
        System.out.println("Order saved: " + id);
        publisher.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(id, email, amountInPaise));
        System.out.println("placeOrder finished");
    }
}
@Component
public class EmailListener {
    @EventListener
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        System.out.println("Email to " + event.customerEmail());
    }
}

@Component
public class AuditListener {
    @EventListener
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        System.out.println("Audit: order " + event.orderId());
    }
}
Order saved: 101
Email to ravi@example.com
Audit: order 101
placeOrder finished

Since Spring 4.2 an event can be any object; you do not need to extend ApplicationEvent. Listeners are chosen by the parameter type, so a listener for a parent class also receives subclasses.

Key behaviours

  • Synchronous by default. publishEvent calls every listener in the same thread, one after another, before it returns (as the output above shows). An exception in a listener goes back to the publisher, and a slow listener slows the caller.
  • Same transaction. Because it is the same thread, listeners run inside the publisher's transaction, if one is active.
  • Order. Control it with @Order(1) on the listener method.
  • Conditions. @EventListener(condition = "#event.amountInPaise > 100000") filters with SpEL.
  • Chaining. A listener may return a new event object, which Spring then publishes.

Asynchronous listeners

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableAsync
public class ShopApplication { /* ... */ }

@Component
public class EmailListener {
    @Async
    @EventListener
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        // runs on a task-executor thread; the caller does not wait
    }
}

An async listener cannot roll back the publisher's transaction, and exceptions do not reach the publisher; handle them inside the listener. @Async is proxy-based, so the self-invocation rule applies (AOP article).

Publishing only after a successful commit

A frequent bug: you publish an "order placed" event inside a transaction, a listener sends the email, and then the transaction rolls back. The customer gets an email for an order that does not exist. Use @TransactionalEventListener, which waits for the transaction phase (the default is AFTER_COMMIT).

@Component
public class EmailListener {
    @TransactionalEventListener              // phase = AFTER_COMMIT by default
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        // safe to send the email now
    }
}

Without an active transaction this listener is skipped (unless you set fallbackExecution = true). For work that must never be lost even if the app crashes, use a message broker and the outbox pattern from Module 7 instead of in-memory events.

Events Spring Boot publishes itself

EventWhen
ApplicationStartingEventVery early, before the context exists
ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEventEnvironment and properties are ready
ContextRefreshedEventThe context finished creating beans
ApplicationStartedEventContext refreshed, runners not yet called
ApplicationReadyEventRunners done; app ready for traffic
ContextClosedEventShutdown has begun
 
@Component
public class StartupLogger {
    @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)
    public void ready() {
        System.out.println("Application is ready to serve requests");
    }
}

Rules

  • The listener must be a Spring bean; an object created with new receives nothing.
  • A listener method takes one parameter (the event) or none when the type is named in the annotation.
  • Events are in-memory and in one application only; they do not cross services or survive a restart.

Conventions

  • Name events in the past tense: OrderPlacedEvent, UserRegisteredEvent. Make them immutable (records).
  • Use events for side effects (notification, audit, cache refresh), not for the main flow whose result you need.
  • Do not overuse them; a plain method call is easier to read and trace when only one class reacts.

Edge cases

  • An event published while the context is still starting may arrive before some listeners are registered. Use ApplicationReadyEvent for start-up work.
  • Listeners run in a synchronous chain: if the first throws, the later ones never run for that event.
  • If no listener exists, publishEvent does nothing and is not an error.

Interview: "How do Spring events work? Sync or async?"

  • A publisher calls ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent; @EventListener methods that match the type receive it.
  • Synchronous in the same thread and transaction by default; add @Async (with @EnableAsync) for async.
  • Use @TransactionalEventListener to run after commit. For cross-service or durable messaging use a broker, not in-app events.

Interview questions — Spring fundamentals

What is the difference between Spring and Spring Boot?

Spring Framework is the core: the IoC container, AOP, MVC, transactions. Spring Boot is a layer on top that removes setup. It adds starters (feature bundles), auto-configuration, an embedded server, an executable JAR, Actuator and sensible defaults. Boot does not replace Spring; the beans are the same, only created for you.

What are IoC and DI, and what problem do they solve?

Without them a class creates its dependencies with new, which makes it tightly coupled and hard to test. With dependency injection the object receives its dependencies (best via the constructor). Inversion of Control means the framework, not your code, creates and wires objects and controls their life. The result is loose coupling, easy mocking and one place to configure and add proxies.

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?

BeanFactory is the basic container and creates beans lazily. ApplicationContext extends it with events, Environment/property handling, i18n, resource loading and eager singleton creation, so wiring mistakes fail at startup. Applications always use the ApplicationContext.

@Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller?

All register a bean through component scanning. @Service and @Repository are specialisations of @Component that mark the layer; @Repository also translates persistence exceptions into DataAccessException. @Controller marks a web handler, and @RestController adds @ResponseBody so return values become JSON.

@Component vs @Bean?

@Component is placed on your own class and found by scanning. @Bean is placed on a method in a @Configuration class and its return value is registered, so it works for third-party classes and for objects needing custom construction logic. With proxyBeanMethods = true a call from one @Bean method to another returns the same singleton.

Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?

Fields can be final, the object is never half-built, dependencies are visibly required, it needs no reflection, and a unit test can just call new with fakes. A very long constructor also warns you that a class has too many responsibilities. A single constructor needs no @Autowired. Setter injection is for optional dependencies.

Two beans of the same type exist. What happens and how do you fix it?

Startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Mark the usual bean @Primary, name the wanted bean with @Qualifier("name") at the injection point (it beats @Primary), or inject List<T> / Map<String, T> to receive all of them, as in the strategy pattern.

What is a circular dependency, and how do you handle it?

A needs B and B needs A. With constructor injection neither can be built first, and since Boot 2.6 cycles are rejected by default. Fix the design: extract the shared logic into a third bean, publish an event instead of calling directly, or pass values instead of beans. @Lazy on one parameter or enabling spring.main.allow-circular-references are last resorts that hide the problem.

What are the bean scopes? Is a singleton thread-safe?

Singleton (default, one per container), prototype (new each time), and the web scopes request, session and application. A singleton bean is shared by all request threads, so it is not automatically thread-safe: keep it stateless or use thread-safe state. A prototype injected into a singleton is injected once only; use ObjectProvider to get a fresh one each time.

Explain the bean lifecycle.

Instantiate (constructor), inject dependencies, Aware callbacks, BeanPostProcessor before-init, @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, custom init method, BeanPostProcessor after-init (where AOP proxies are made), then the bean is in use. At shutdown: @PreDestroy, destroy(), custom destroy method. Spring does not call destroy callbacks for prototype beans.

How does externalised configuration work, and what is the precedence?

Boot merges settings from files, environment variables, system properties and command-line arguments. From highest to lowest: command line, environment, profile-specific files, application.yml, defaults. Relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url. Secrets come from the environment, not from Git.

@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?

@Value("${key:default}") injects one value and supports SpEL. @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "...") binds a group into a typed object (a record is ideal), with relaxed binding, nested structures, type conversion and validation through @Validated. Use it for anything beyond a single flag, so a typo or blank value fails at startup.

What does @SpringBootApplication do, and how does auto-configuration work?

It is @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan. Auto-configuration reads META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports from all JARs; each listed class has conditions (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnMissingBean) and only matching classes create beans. If you define your own bean, Boot's default backs off. Debug with --debug; disable with exclude.

Why does @Transactional not work when a method calls another method of the same class?

Spring applies transactions through a proxy around the bean. A call from another bean goes through the proxy; a call on this goes straight to the target and skips the advice. The same happens with @Cacheable and @Async. Fix it by moving the method into another bean, annotating the entry method, or using AspectJ weaving. Also remember that the method must be public and the class non-final for CGLIB.

Cheat sheet — Spring fundamentals

  • Spring vs Boot Spring = container + features; Boot = starters, auto-configuration, embedded server, fat JAR, Actuator
  • Initializr start.spring.io: Maven, Java, latest stable Boot, group/artifact, Jar, Java 21, add starters
  • Run ./mvnw spring-boot:run; ./mvnw clean package then java -jar target/app.jar
  • IoC / DI the container creates and wires objects; classes receive dependencies instead of calling new
  • ApplicationContext the container: bean registry, events, environment; creates singletons eagerly
  • Scan rule main class package and sub-packages only; a bean outside gives NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
  • Stereotypes @Component generic, @Service logic, @Repository data + exception translation, @RestController JSON
  • @Bean a method in a @Configuration class; for third-party classes; name = method name
  • Injection constructor (preferred, final fields); setter for optional; avoid field injection
  • Single constructor no @Autowired needed; Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor writes it
  • Many candidates @Primary default, @Qualifier("name") explicit, or inject List/Map
  • Optional bean Optional<T>, ObjectProvider<T>, @Autowired(required = false)
  • Circular dependency rejected since Boot 2.6; extract a class or use an event; @Lazy last resort
  • Failure report read "Description" and "Action"; deepest Caused by is the real error
  • Scopes singleton (default, keep stateless), prototype, request, session, application
  • Prototype in singleton injected once; use ObjectProvider.getObject()
  • Lifecycle constructor → inject → Aware → post-processor → @PostConstruct → init → proxy → use → @PreDestroy
  • Runners CommandLineRunner / ApplicationRunner run after the context is ready
  • Precedence command line > environment > profile files > application.yml > defaults
  • Profiles spring.profiles.active, application-dev.yml, @Profile("dev"), spring.config.activate.on-profile
  • @Value ${key:default} for one value; @ConfigurationProperties record + @Validated for groups
  • Secrets environment variables (SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD), never Git
  • @SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan
  • Auto-configuration AutoConfiguration.imports + @ConditionalOnClass/OnProperty/OnMissingBean; your bean wins; --debug shows the report
  • Starters / BOM one dependency per feature; parent manages versions, so no version in the pom
  • Embedded server Tomcat default; server.port; fat JAR with BOOT-INF; DevTools for dev restarts
  • AOP / proxies CGLIB by default in Boot; self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so @Transactional/@Cacheable/@Async do nothing
  • Events publishEvent + @EventListener; sync by default; @TransactionalEventListener after commit

Practice — Spring fundamentals

  1. First project. Generate a Maven project at start.spring.io with Spring Web and DevTools. Run it with ./mvnw spring-boot:run, then build the JAR and start it with java -jar. Done when: the log shows Tomcat started on 8080 and you can start the JAR with --server.port=9090.
  2. DI by hand, then Spring. In plain Java write NotificationSender, EmailSender, SmsSender and an OrderService that takes the sender in its constructor; wire it in main. Then convert it to Spring beans. Done when: both versions print the same message and you can name which line the container replaced.
  3. Break and fix. Move a @Service to a sibling package and read the failure report; then add a second NotificationSender and cause NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Fix with @Primary and then with @Qualifier. Done when: you can explain each report's "Description" and "Action".
  4. Notification app (roadmap exercise). Build an app with NotificationSender, EmailSender, SmsSender, ConsoleSender, and an OrderService. Select the sender by profile (dev → console, prod → SMS) using @Profile, with the activation done through spring.profiles.active. Done when: running with each profile prints from a different sender and a CommandLineRunner places a sample order at startup.
  5. Strategy map. Add three PaymentService beans named upi, card and netbanking, and a router that injects Map<String, PaymentService>. Done when: adding a fourth class needs no change to the router.
  6. Typed configuration. Create app.notification.* settings (sender name, retries, timeout, allowed channels) as a @ConfigurationProperties record with @Validated. Supply the secret API key from an environment variable. Done when: a blank key stops startup with a clear binding error, and --app.notification.max-retries=5 on the command line overrides the file.
  7. Scopes and lifecycle. Create a singleton service with a prototype dependency; show the bug, then fix it with ObjectProvider. Add a bean printing each lifecycle step. Done when: the console shows the exact order from the lifecycle diagram, with @PreDestroy at shutdown.
  8. See auto-configuration. Run with --debug and find one positive and one negative match. Define your own ObjectMapper bean (or Clock) and prove Boot's default backs off by listing bean names. Then exclude DataSourceAutoConfiguration in an app that has a JDBC starter but no database. Done when: the app starts and you can explain each condition that decided the result.
  9. Self-invocation. Write a timing aspect (add spring-boot-starter-aop) on a service. Call the advised method from outside and from another method of the same class, and compare the output. Fix it with a second bean. Done when: you can show, with logs, that the internal call skips the aspect, and that the fixed version runs it.
  10. Events. Replace the direct email and audit calls in OrderService by an OrderPlacedEvent with two listeners. Make one async and one @TransactionalEventListener. Done when: you can show which listener runs in which thread and that a rolled-back order sends no email.
2

Module 2·Weeks 3–4Must

REST APIs

23 topics · about 3 h of reading

Almost every Spring Boot job is about one thing: building REST APIs — HTTP endpoints that a React app, a mobile app or another service calls to read and change data, usually as JSON. This module takes you from the raw text of an HTTP request all the way to a layered, validated, documented CRUD API with clean error responses and pagination.

It builds on Spring fundamentals (Module 1: beans, dependency injection, configuration). The repository layer uses Spring Data JPA, which Module 3 explains in depth; Module 4 secures the API and Module 5 tests it. The React app in Frontend · Module 6 is the client that consumes what you build here. Examples work on Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x; where the two differ, a version note says so.

After this module you will be able to:

  • read and write raw HTTP requests and responses, and choose the right method, status code and headers;
  • design resource URLs, version an API, and explain what makes an API RESTful;
  • build controllers with the mapping annotations and explain how a request travels through Spring MVC;
  • split an application into controller, service and repository layers, and map entities to DTOs by hand or with MapStruct;
  • validate input with Bean Validation and return consistent error JSON with ProblemDetail;
  • add pagination, sorting and filtering, document the API with Swagger UI, and test it with curl, Postman or Bruno.

HTTP basics: how a request and a response look

HTTP is a text-based request–response protocol: the client sends a method, a URL, headers and an optional body, and the server answers with a status code, headers and an optional body.

Every REST API runs on HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol). Your React app, Postman, curl and a mobile app all do the same thing: open a connection, send one request, and read one response. Spring annotations only make sense when you can read the raw messages, because that is what your controller methods really work with.

The five words you need first

Client
The program that sends the request: a browser, a React app, a mobile app, curl, or another service.
Server
The program that listens and answers. For you, that is your Spring Boot application running inside an embedded Tomcat.
Resource
A "thing" the API exposes, named by a URL: a product, an order, a user.
Request
One message from client to server that says "do this method on that URL".
Response
The server's single reply to a request: a status code, headers and, usually, a body.

A request, line by line

This is exactly what travels over the network when a client creates a product. Nothing is hidden: it is plain text.

POST /api/v1/products HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Content-Length: 68

{"sku":"MSE-1001","name":"Wireless Mouse","price":799.00,"stock":25}
  1. Request line — three parts: the method (POST), the request target (path plus query string: /api/v1/products) and the protocol version (HTTP/1.1).
  2. Headers — one Name: value pair per line. They describe the request: which host, what format the body is in, what format the client wants back, how long the body is.
  3. An empty line — this blank line is the signal "headers are over".
  4. Body (optional) — the data. A GET normally has none; a POST or PUT usually carries JSON.

A response, line by line

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/1
Content-Length: 75
Date: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 04:45:30 GMT

{"id":1,"sku":"MSE-1001","name":"Wireless Mouse","price":799.00,"stock":25}

The first line is the status line: protocol version, a three-digit status code (201) and a short reason phrase (Created). The reason phrase is optional and clients ignore it — Spring Boot's Tomcat usually sends just HTTP/1.1 201. Then come the response headers, a blank line and the body. Code decides everything; the phrase is only for humans.

The parts of a URL

A URL tells the client where the resource lives. Take this one:

https://shop.example.com:8443/api/v1/products/42?category=books&sort=price#reviews
PartIn the exampleWhat it does
SchemehttpsThe protocol. https is HTTP inside an encrypted TLS connection.
Hostshop.example.comWhich machine to talk to (looked up through DNS).
Port8443Which program on that machine. Defaults: 80 for http, 443 for https. Spring Boot listens on 8080 unless you set server.port.
Path/api/v1/products/42Which resource. This is where @PathVariable values come from.
Query stringcategory=books&sort=priceExtra options as name=value pairs joined by &. This is where @RequestParam values come from.
Fragment#reviewsA position inside the page. The browser keeps it; it is never sent to the server.

Seeing real HTTP yourself

Do not guess what is on the wire — look. Two tools show it. First, curl -v prints the request lines (starting with >) and the response lines (starting with <). Second, the browser: press F12, open the Network tab, click any request and read its Headers, Payload and Response tabs.

$ curl -v http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/1
> GET /api/v1/products/1 HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:8080
> User-Agent: curl/8.x
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 200
< Content-Type: application/json
< Content-Length: 75
< Date: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 04:46:02 GMT
<
{"id":1,"sku":"MSE-1001","name":"Wireless Mouse","price":799.00,"stock":25}

Use curl -i when you want only the response headers followed by the body, without the request lines.

HTTP is stateless

The server treats every request as a brand-new conversation. It does not remember that you called it a second ago. That is called being stateless. To stay "logged in", the client must send proof with every request: either a session cookie (Cookie: JSESSIONID=…) or a token (Authorization: Bearer …). REST APIs prefer tokens, because any server instance can verify a token without shared memory — you will build this in Module 4.

HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

VersionHow it travelsWhat changes for you
HTTP/1.1Plain text messages; one request at a time per connection (the connection can be reused)This is what you see in curl. It is the default for Tomcat.
HTTP/2Binary frames; many requests in parallel on one connection; compressed headersSame methods, status codes and headers. Spring Boot can enable it with server.http2.enabled=true; browsers use it only over HTTPS.
HTTP/3Same meaning as HTTP/2, but over QUIC (UDP) instead of TCPUsually handled by a CDN or load balancer, not by your Spring app.

The important point: the meaning (methods, status codes, headers, bodies) is the same in all versions. Learn the semantics once.

Rules of the message format

  • A message is: start line, headers, an empty line, optional body — in that order.
  • Header names are case-insensitive (content-type equals Content-Type). Header values and URL paths are normally case-sensitive.
  • HTTP/1.1 requires a Host header.
  • If there is a body, the sender says how long it is (Content-Length) or sends it in chunks (Transfer-Encoding: chunked).

Edge cases

  • A GET request can carry a body, but its meaning is undefined and many proxies and servers drop it. Do not design APIs that depend on it.
  • Some responses never have a body: replies to HEAD, 204 No Content and 304 Not Modified.
  • Very long URLs get rejected. Servers usually limit the request line plus headers to a few KB (Tomcat's default is 8 KB), so never pack big data into the query string.
  • Local development uses plain http://localhost:8080. In production, HTTPS is mandatory; it is usually terminated by a reverse proxy or load balancer in front of your app (see DevOps · Module 2).

Mistake: putting secrets in the URL

Everything in the URL ends up in server logs, browser history, proxy logs and the Referer header. Passwords and tokens belong in the body or in the Authorization header, and always over HTTPS.

Wrong: credentials in the query string

GET /login?user=ravi&password=Secret@123 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com

Right: credentials in the body, over HTTPS

POST /api/v1/auth/login HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"email":"ravi@example.com","password":"Secret@123"}

Interview: "What is HTTP? What does stateless mean?"

  • HTTP is an application-layer request–response protocol over TCP (or QUIC for HTTP/3). The client always starts; the server only replies.
  • A request has a method, a target, headers and an optional body. A response has a status code, headers and an optional body.
  • Stateless means the server keeps no memory of earlier requests; each request carries everything needed, such as a token. This lets you run many identical server instances behind a load balancer.
  • HTTPS is HTTP over TLS: it encrypts the traffic and proves the server's identity with a certificate. The HTTP messages themselves are unchanged.

HTTP methods: purpose, safe and idempotent

The method says what you want to do with a resource; safe methods never change server state, and idempotent methods leave the server in the same state whether you call them once or ten times.

An HTTP method (also called a verb) is the first word of a request. It tells the server the intent: read, create, replace, change, delete. The URL names the resource, and the method says what to do with it. If you pick methods correctly, clients, proxies, caches and browsers all behave correctly without extra work.

The methods at a glance

MethodPurposeRequest bodySafeIdempotent
GETRead a resource or a collectionNoYesYes
POSTCreate a resource, or trigger an actionYesNoNo
PUTReplace a resource completelyYesNoYes
PATCHChange part of a resourceYesNoNot guaranteed
DELETERemove a resourceUsually noNoYes
HEADSame as GET, but only the headers come backNoYesYes
OPTIONSAsk which methods a URL supports (also used for CORS preflight)NoYesYes

Safe and idempotent — two different ideas

Safe
The method only reads. It must not change anything the user cares about on the server. Because GET is safe, browsers can prefetch it, search-engine crawlers can follow it, and caches can store its response.
Idempotent
Sending the same request many times has the same effect on the server as sending it once. This is what makes a request safe to retry after a network timeout, when the client does not know whether the first attempt worked.

Every safe method is idempotent, but not the other way round: DELETE changes state, yet deleting the same product twice leaves the same final state — the product is gone. The response may differ (first call 204, second call 404); idempotency is about server state, not about identical responses.

Idempotency is a promise that you keep in your code. HTTP does not enforce it. If you write a PUT handler that appends to a list each time, it is no longer idempotent, and clients that retry will create damage.

POST vs PUT vs PATCH

These three cause the most confusion. Use the same product to compare them.

POST /api/v1/products HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"sku":"MSE-1001","name":"Wireless Mouse","price":799.00,"stock":25}
PUT /api/v1/products/1 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"name":"Wireless Mouse","description":"Silent click","price":749.00,"stock":25}
PATCH /api/v1/products/1 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"price":749.00}
QuestionPOSTPUTPATCH
Target URLA collection (/products)One resource (/products/1)One resource (/products/1)
Body means"Create something from this""This is the new full state""Apply these changes"
Fields you leave outServer uses defaultsReset to null or defaultLeft unchanged
Repeat 3 timesThree productsSame final stateDepends on the change
Typical success201 + Location200 or 204200

Why PATCH is "not guaranteed" idempotent: it depends on what the patch says. {"status":"SHIPPED"} sets a value, so repeating it changes nothing — idempotent. {"stockDelta":-1} subtracts one each time — not idempotent. The method itself does not decide; your design does.

PUT can also create. If the client chooses the id and the resource does not exist yet, PUT /users/ravi may create it (return 201); if it exists, replace it (return 200 or 204). Most Spring APIs use PUT only for replacing an existing resource and generate ids on the server with POST.

Which method for which job?

You want to…Use
Fetch one item or a listGET
Create an item and let the server choose its idPOST to the collection
Replace the whole item with a new versionPUT
Change one or two fieldsPATCH
Remove an itemDELETE
Check that a URL exists without downloading the bodyHEAD
Run something that is not CRUD (cancel an order, send an OTP)POST to an action URL such as /orders/5/cancel

Making a POST safe to retry: the Idempotency-Key pattern

Creating a payment with POST is the classic danger: the client times out, retries, and the customer is charged twice. Payment APIs such as Stripe solve this with an idempotency key: the client generates a unique value (a UUID) and sends it in a header. Spring has no built-in feature for this; you implement it in a filter or in the service.

  1. The client sends POST /payments with Idempotency-Key: 7c9e6679-….
  2. The server looks the key up in a table. If the key is new, it processes the payment and stores the key together with the response it produced.
  3. If the client retries with the same key, the server does not process again. It returns the stored response.
  4. Keys expire after some time (for example 24 hours), and the same key with a different body is rejected with 422 or 409.

What Spring does for you

In Spring MVC each method has a mapping annotation (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping; see the mapping annotations article). Two things happen automatically: a GET mapping also answers HEAD (the body is dropped), and OPTIONS on a mapped path returns an Allow header that lists the supported methods.

$ curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products
HTTP/1.1 200
Allow: GET,HEAD,POST,OPTIONS
Content-Length: 0

Rules

  • GET, HEAD and OPTIONS must never change data. No "delete" or "cancel" behind a GET.
  • PUT and DELETE must be idempotent. Design them so that a retry is harmless.
  • Only GET and HEAD responses are normally cached.
  • A wrong method on a known URL must give 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header. Spring does this for you (HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException).

Conventions

  • One URL, several methods: /products supports GET and POST; /products/{id} supports GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
  • Prefer PATCH for partial updates and keep PUT for full replacement. If you only offer one update endpoint, PUT with the full body is the simplest and safest.
  • Return the updated resource (200) or nothing (204) from PUT/PATCH — pick one style for the whole API.

Edge cases

  • The second DELETE of the same id: return 404 (honest) or 204 (idempotent outcome). Both are valid; stay consistent.
  • DELETE with a body is allowed but unreliable; some proxies strip it. Put the identifier in the URL.
  • Plain HTML forms can only send GET and POST. That limit does not apply to fetch/axios in a React app.
  • Firewalls and old proxies sometimes block PUT, PATCH and DELETE. If a client behind such a network fails, this is the first thing to check.
  • TRACE and CONNECT exist but are not used for APIs; TRACE is normally disabled.

Mistake: using GET for actions

A link, a browser prefetch or a crawler can call any GET URL. If that URL deletes data, the data disappears without anyone clicking "delete".

Wrong: a state change behind GET

@GetMapping("/products/{id}/delete")
public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    service.delete(id);
}

Right: DELETE on the resource

@DeleteMapping("/products/{id}")
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    service.delete(id);
}

Interview: "PUT vs PATCH vs POST?" and "Is DELETE idempotent?"

  • POST creates under a collection and is not idempotent. PUT replaces a whole resource at a known URL and is idempotent. PATCH changes part of a resource and is idempotent only if the change itself is.
  • Safe = read-only (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). Idempotent = same server state after one or many identical calls (safe methods plus PUT and DELETE).
  • DELETE is idempotent because the end state is the same ("not there") even though the second call may answer 404.
