  • Mention retries: idempotency is why clients and gateways can retry PUT and DELETE automatically, and why POST needs an idempotency key for payments.

HTTP status codes and which one to return

The first digit of a status code tells the class — 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error — and a good API returns the most specific code so clients can react without reading the body.

A status code is the three-digit number at the start of every response. Clients, browsers, load balancers and monitoring dashboards all make decisions from it alone: retry or not, show an error or not, count it as a failure or not. Returning 200 for everything and hiding the real outcome in the body breaks all of that.

The five classes

ClassMeaningWho should act
1xxInformational (for example 100 Continue)Handled by the HTTP stack; you rarely see them.
2xxSuccess — the request workedNobody; carry on.
3xxRedirection — look somewhere else, or use your cached copyThe client follows the Location header.
4xxClient error — the request is wrongThe caller must fix the request. Retrying the same request will not help (exceptions: 408, 429).
5xxServer error — the server failedYou must fix it. The client may retry later.

The codes you will actually use

CodeNameReturn it whenNotes
200OKA read or an update succeeded and you return a bodyAlso for an empty search result (with [])
201CreatedA POST created a resourceAdd a Location header; the body is usually the new resource
202AcceptedYou accepted the request but processing is not finished (report, email, video encoding)Return a status URL the client can poll
204No ContentSuccess with nothing to returnTypical for DELETE; must have no body
301 / 302Moved Permanently / FoundThe URL moved for good / temporarilyRare in JSON APIs; 307 and 308 keep the method
304Not ModifiedA conditional GET found the client's cached copy still validNo body; see ETag in the headers article
400Bad RequestMalformed JSON, a missing or invalid parameter, a failed validationThe catch-all for "your request is wrong"
401UnauthorizedThe caller is not authenticated: no token, bad token, expired tokenSend WWW-Authenticate; the name is historical
403ForbiddenThe caller is authenticated but not allowed to do thisLogging in again will not help
404Not FoundThe resource does not existAlso used to hide that a resource exists
405Method Not AllowedThe URL exists but not for this methodSend an Allow header
409ConflictThe request clashes with the current state: duplicate unique value, version conflict, resource still in useThe most useful "business rule failed" code
415Unsupported Media TypeThe request body's Content-Type is not supportedExample: XML sent to a JSON-only endpoint
422Unprocessable ContentThe JSON is well-formed but its content breaks a ruleAlternative to 400 for validation errors
429Too Many RequestsThe caller hit a rate limitSend Retry-After
500Internal Server ErrorAn unexpected bug or failure in your codeNever use it for bad client input
502Bad GatewayA gateway or proxy got an invalid reply from the service behind itSeen from nginx or an API gateway
503Service UnavailableThe server is overloaded, starting up or in maintenanceAdd Retry-After if you can
504Gateway TimeoutA gateway waited too long for the service behind itSlow downstream call or database

Also good to know: 406 Not Acceptable (the server cannot produce what the Accept header asks for), 410 Gone (existed once, removed on purpose), 412 Precondition Failed (an If-Match check failed) and 413 (the upload is too large).

Which code for which operation?

OperationSuccessTypical failures
GET /products200 (empty list is still 200)400 bad filter, 401, 403
GET /products/{id}200404, 401, 403
POST /products201 + Location400/422 invalid, 409 duplicate, 415
PUT /products/{id}200 or 204400, 404, 409
PATCH /products/{id}200400, 404, 409
DELETE /products/{id}204404, 409 (still referenced)

Choosing a code: a quick decision path

In Spring the order is slightly different in one place: the request body is validated before your method runs. So a bad body sent to a missing id gives 400, not 404.

401 vs 403

401 Unauthorized403 Forbidden
Real meaningI do not know who you are (unauthenticated)I know who you are, and you may not do this
ExampleNo Authorization header, or an expired JWTA normal user calls DELETE /users/7, which needs the ADMIN role
Client reactionLog in (again) and retryShow "access denied"; do not retry

400 vs 422 for validation errors

Both are used in real APIs. 400 means "I cannot understand or accept this request" and is what Spring returns by default for malformed JSON and failed @Valid checks. 422 means "I understood the JSON, but the values break rules". Pick one for validation, document it, and use it everywhere. These notes use 400 because it is Spring's default.

How Spring maps its own exceptions

ExceptionStatusCaused by
HttpMessageNotReadableException400Missing body, malformed JSON, wrong field type
MethodArgumentNotValidException400@Valid on a request body failed
MissingServletRequestParameterException400A required @RequestParam is absent
MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException400/products/abc where a number is expected
NoResourceFoundException404No controller and no static file matches (Spring 6.1+, Boot 3.2+)
HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException405Wrong method for a known path
HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException406The Accept header cannot be satisfied
HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException415Unsupported Content-Type on the request
any uncaught exception500A bug in your code

In your own code, pick codes with the HttpStatus enum (HttpStatus.CREATED) or by number (ResponseEntity.status(409)). Spring 6 also has the HttpStatusCode interface, which covers any number, including codes that are not in the enum.

Rules

  • A 201 response should carry a Location header; a 204 response must not have a body.
  • A 401 response should carry WWW-Authenticate; a 405 response must carry Allow.
  • The error body must match the status. Never send 200 with {"error": ...}.
  • 4xx means "the caller can fix it"; 5xx means "we have a bug or an outage". Use them honestly so monitoring works.

Conventions

  • An empty collection is 200 with [], not 404. The collection exists; it is just empty.
  • To hide that something exists (another user's order), answer 404 instead of 403.
  • Use 409 for business-rule clashes (duplicate SKU, insufficient stock), and put the explanation in the error body.
  • Return a consistent error body for every 4xx and 5xx (the ProblemDetail articles in this module).

Edge cases

  • A search with no matches is 200 and [], but GET /products/9999 for a missing id is 404.
  • Redirects (301, 302) may change a POST into a GET in some clients. 307 and 308 keep the method and body.
  • Behind a gateway, 502, 503 and 504 usually come from the gateway, not from your Spring app. Check the gateway logs first.
  • If an exception is thrown after the response has started streaming, the status is already sent and cannot change.

Mistake: success status with an error inside

Clients, caches and dashboards read the status code first. A 200 that contains "success": false looks like a success everywhere except in your own front-end code.

Wrong: HTTP 200 for a missing product

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public Map<String, Object> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    Optional<Product> product = repository.findById(id);
    if (product.isEmpty()) {
        return Map.of("success", false, "message", "Product not found");
    }
    return Map.of("success", true, "data", product.get());
}

Right: throw, and let the handler answer 404

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    // throws ResourceNotFoundException, which the global
    // handler turns into a 404 response
    return service.findById(id);
}

Interview: "401 vs 403? 200 vs 201 vs 204? When 409?"

  • 401 = not authenticated (no or bad credentials). 403 = authenticated but not authorised.
  • 200 = success with a body, 201 = something was created (with Location), 204 = success with no body.
  • 409 = the request conflicts with the current state: a duplicate email, an optimistic-locking version clash, deleting a record that others still use.
  • 400 = malformed or invalid input; 422 = well-formed but semantically invalid; 404 = no such resource; 405 = wrong method; 415 = wrong Content-Type.
  • 502, 503 and 504 are gateway-side failures: bad reply, unavailable, and timeout. 500 is an unexpected bug in the service itself.

HTTP headers that matter for APIs

Headers are name–value metadata on a request or response; Content-Type, Accept, Authorization, Location, Cache-Control and ETag do most of the work in a REST API.

A header is one line of the form Name: value placed before the body. Headers carry information about the message: what format the body is in, who is calling, how long the answer may be cached. Your JSON stays clean because this extra information travels beside it.

The headers you will meet every day

HeaderSent inMeaningExample
Content-TypeRequest and responseThe format of the body being sentapplication/json
AcceptRequestThe formats the client is willing to receiveapplication/json
AuthorizationRequestCredentials for the callerBearer eyJhbGciOi…
LocationResponseURL of the newly created resource (201) or the redirect target (3xx)/api/v1/products/42
Cache-ControlResponse (and request)Rules for storing and reusing the responsemax-age=60
ETagResponseA version label for the representation"3"
If-None-MatchRequest"Send the body only if the ETag changed""3"
If-MatchRequest"Apply my update only if the ETag still matches""3"
AllowResponseMethods the URL supports (sent with 405)GET, POST
WWW-AuthenticateResponseHow to authenticate (sent with 401)Bearer
Retry-AfterResponseWhen to retry (sent with 429/503)30 (seconds)
OriginRequestThe website that started a browser call (CORS)http://localhost:5173
X-Request-IdBothA correlation id to trace one request across servicesb4f1c2…

Header names are case-insensitive. You can invent custom headers; the old habit of prefixing them with X- is discouraged for new ones, but X-Request-Id and similar names are everywhere. Use hyphens, not underscores: nginx drops headers with underscores by default.

Content-Type vs Accept

These two are confused all the time. Content-Type describes the data I am sending. Accept describes the data I want back.

HeaderDirectionIf it is wrong, Spring answers…
Content-Type on the requestDescribes the request body415 Unsupported Media Type when no converter can read that type
Accept on the requestAsks for a response format406 Not Acceptable when no converter can produce it
Content-Type on the responseDescribes the response bodySet by Spring from the converter it used

A very common surprise: curl -d '{"name":"x"}' sends Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded by default, so your JSON endpoint answers 415. Always add -H "Content-Type: application/json", or use curl --json '…' (curl 7.82 and newer), which sets both Content-Type and Accept for you.

Authorization

The caller proves who it is with Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>. Two schemes matter. Basic sends username:password encoded in Base64 — encoded, not encrypted, so it is only acceptable over HTTPS. Bearer sends a token, usually a JWT: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi…. "Bearer" means whoever holds the token is let in, so treat tokens like passwords. Module 4 builds the JWT flow. Never send credentials in the URL.

Caching with Cache-Control

Cache-Control tells browsers and proxies whether and how long they may reuse a response.

  • max-age=60 — the response is fresh for 60 seconds; reuse it without asking the server.
  • no-cache — you may store it, but you must revalidate with the server before every reuse.
  • no-store — do not store it at all. Use it for sensitive data such as account details.
  • public / private — shared caches (CDNs) may store it / only the user's own browser may.

ETag and conditional requests

An ETag is a label for one version of a representation, such as a hash or a version number. The client stores it and sends it back, and the server can reply "nothing changed" instead of resending the body.

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    ProductResponse product = service.findById(id);
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .eTag(String.valueOf(product.version()))   // quotes are added for you
            .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofSeconds(60)).cachePublic())
            .body(product);
}
GET /api/v1/products/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
If-None-Match: "3"

HTTP/1.1 304
ETag: "3"
Cache-Control: max-age=60, public

When a ResponseEntity carries an ETag and the request has a matching If-None-Match, Spring turns the reply into 304 for you. If you do not want to compute ETags yourself, register Spring's ShallowEtagHeaderFilter: it hashes each response body and adds the ETag. It saves bandwidth, not server work, because the handler still runs.

If-Match solves a different problem: the lost update. Two users load product 1 (ETag "3"). User A saves; the ETag becomes "4". User B then sends PUT with If-Match: "3", the server sees the mismatch and answers 412 Precondition Failed instead of silently overwriting A's change. In a JPA application the ETag is usually the @Version column (Module 3).

Reading and setting headers in Spring

  • Read a header with @RequestHeader (details in the request body and headers article).
  • Set response headers with ResponseEntity builders (the ResponseEntity article), with HttpHeaders, or on the HttpServletResponse parameter.
  • CORS headers (Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, …) are covered in the CORS article; Spring Security also adds protective headers such as X-Content-Type-Options (Module 4).

Rules

  • Send Content-Type: application/json whenever the request has a JSON body.
  • Every 201 Created response needs a Location header; every 405 needs Allow.
  • Never put tokens or passwords in URLs; use Authorization.
  • Weak validators, W/"abc", mean "semantically the same"; strong ones mean "byte-for-byte the same". If-Match needs strong ETags.

Edge cases

  • Some headers repeat or hold a comma-separated list (Accept: application/json, text/plain;q=0.5). The q value is a preference weight from 0 to 1.
  • Oversized headers (huge cookies or tokens) can be rejected by Tomcat or a proxy with a 400 or 431 before your code runs.
  • Behind a reverse proxy, the original client IP and scheme arrive in X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto. Without server.forward-headers-strategy set, Spring may build wrong absolute URLs (for example in Location).
  • Browsers hide most response headers from JavaScript on cross-origin calls unless the server lists them in Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

Mistake: forgetting Content-Type on a JSON POST

Without Content-Type: application/json your @RequestBody endpoint cannot choose a converter and returns 415. Testing tools set the header for you only if you pick "JSON" as the body type.

Wrong: curl sends a form content type

$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products \
    -d '{"name":"Mouse"}'
HTTP/1.1 415

Right: declare the body as JSON

$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"name":"Mouse"}'

Real projects

In a typical service you read Authorization in Spring Security (not by hand), add a X-Request-Id or traceparent header in a filter so logs from several services line up, set Cache-Control: no-store on anything personal, and add ETags only to read-heavy endpoints that really benefit, such as product details or reference data.

Interview: "Content-Type vs Accept? How does ETag caching work? no-cache vs no-store?"

  • Content-Type labels the body you send; Accept lists the formats you want back. Wrong values give 415 and 406.
  • ETag: the server labels a version; the client sends it back in If-None-Match; if unchanged, the server returns 304 with no body. With If-Match the same label protects updates from lost writes (412).
  • no-cache means "revalidate before reuse"; no-store means "never keep a copy".
  • Tokens go in Authorization: Bearer …, never in the URL. Basic auth is only Base64, not encryption.

JSON and Jackson basics

JSON is the text format APIs speak; Jackson converts Java objects to JSON (serialization) and JSON back to Java objects (deserialization), and Spring Boot configures it for you.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the body format of almost every REST API: easy to read, light, and understood by every language. In a Spring Boot app, a library called Jackson does the conversion between Java objects and JSON. You rarely call Jackson yourself — Spring's message converters call it for @RequestBody parameters and for return values — but every surprise about dates, nulls and field names comes from Jackson's rules, so you need to know them.

JSON in one minute

{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Wireless Mouse",
  "price": 799.00,
  "inStock": true,
  "tags": ["wireless", "usb"],
  "dimensions": { "widthMm": 60, "heightMm": 35 },
  "discount": null
}

JSON has only six kinds of value: object ({…} with named members), array ([…]), string, number, boolean and null. The rules are strict: keys and strings use double quotes only, there are no comments, no trailing commas, and the text is UTF-8. A single misplaced comma makes the whole document invalid.

JSON valueUsually maps to this Java type
objecta record, a class, or Map<String, Object>
arrayList<T>, Set<T>, T[]
stringString, an enum, LocalDate, UUID, …
numberint, long, double, BigDecimal
booleanboolean / Boolean
nullnull

Serialization and deserialization

Serialization
Java object → JSON text. It happens when your controller returns an object. Jackson reads the object through its getters (or the accessors of a record).
Deserialization
JSON text → Java object. It happens for @RequestBody. Jackson creates the object through a constructor, or through the no-argument constructor plus setters.

Returning a record from a controller is all you need; Spring Boot's auto-configured ObjectMapper does the rest.

public record ProductResponse(
        Long id,
        String name,
        BigDecimal price,
        boolean inStock,
        List<String> tags,
        LocalDate launchDate) {}
{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Wireless Mouse",
  "price": 799.00,
  "inStock": true,
  "tags": ["wireless", "usb"],
  "launchDate": "2026-08-15"
}

You can also use the mapper by hand, for example in a test, in a Kafka consumer, or when you store JSON in a column:

// objectMapper is the auto-configured bean; inject it through the constructor
String json = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(response);                 // Java → JSON
ProductResponse back = objectMapper.readValue(json, ProductResponse.class);  // JSON → Java

// Generic types need a TypeReference because of type erasure
List<ProductResponse> list = objectMapper.readValue(
        listJson, new TypeReference<List<ProductResponse>>() {});

// No class available? Read a tree
JsonNode tree = objectMapper.readTree(json);
String name = tree.get("name").asText();

What Spring Boot configures for you

BehaviourSpring Boot defaultWhy it matters
Dates and timesWritten as ISO-8601 strings, not numbers"2026-10-21" is readable and unambiguous
java.time typesSupported out of the boxLocalDate, Instant and friends just work
Unknown JSON propertiesIgnored (plain Jackson would fail)Clients can send extra fields without a 400
Constructor parameter namesRecognisedClasses with an all-args constructor can be deserialized
Property namesUsed as they are (camelCase)Matches what JavaScript expects
NullsWritten as nullStable JSON shape

Change the defaults with spring.jackson.* properties — for example spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null or spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE — or per class with annotations.

The annotations you use most

AnnotationEffectExample
@JsonPropertyRename a JSON key; or make it write-only@JsonProperty("product_name")
@JsonIgnoreLeave the field out, both waysinternal codes
@JsonIgnorePropertiesIgnore listed names, or ignoreUnknown = trueon a class
@JsonIncludeOmit nulls (NON_NULL) or empties (NON_EMPTY)on a class or field
@JsonFormatCustom date pattern or shape@JsonFormat(pattern = "dd-MM-yyyy")
@JsonAliasAccept other names when reading@JsonAlias({"qty", "count"})
@JsonCreatorChoose the constructor or factory for readingimmutable classes
@JsonNamingChange the naming style of a whole classsnake_case
@JsonValueUse one method's result as the JSON valueenum codes
 
@JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)
public record ProductView(
        Long id,
        @JsonProperty("product_name") String name,
        BigDecimal price,
        @JsonFormat(pattern = "dd-MM-yyyy") LocalDate launchDate,
        String note,                      // null, so it is left out
        @JsonIgnore String internalCode) {}   // never sent
{"id":42,"product_name":"Wireless Mouse","price":799.00,"launchDate":"15-08-2026"}

Dates and times

Java typeJSON valueUse it for
LocalDate"2026-10-21"A calendar date with no time or zone: birthday, due date
LocalDateTime"2026-10-21T10:15:30"Wall-clock time with no zone (ambiguous; avoid for events)
Instant"2026-10-21T04:45:30Z"A precise moment in time: createdAt, updatedAt
OffsetDateTime"2026-10-21T10:15:30+05:30"A moment plus the offset the user saw (+05:30 is India)

The professional habit: send timestamps as UTC Instant values (they end with Z), store them in UTC, and convert to the user's time zone only when you display them, in the React app. Do not use java.util.Date in new code. A LocalDateTime without a zone is the usual source of "the time is off by 5½ hours" bugs.

Nulls and missing fields

  • Writing: nulls are written as null. Omit them per class with @JsonInclude(NON_NULL) or for the whole app with spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null. Omitting shrinks the payload; always writing keys gives a stable shape that is easier to type in TypeScript. Choose one policy for the whole API.
  • Reading: a missing field becomes null for objects, but 0 or false for primitives. You cannot tell "missing" from "zero". Use wrapper types (Integer, Boolean) together with @NotNull for required numbers.
  • A plain DTO also cannot tell "field absent" from "field explicitly null". That matters for PATCH; see the partial-update section of the DTO article.

Unknown properties

Because Boot ignores unknown properties, a client that sends "prcie": 500 (a typo) gets no error — the field is silently dropped. That is friendly to clients that add fields later, but it hides mistakes. To be strict, set spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true; unknown fields then produce a 400. Public APIs usually stay tolerant; internal APIs often go strict.

Enums, money and big numbers

  • Enums are written by name ("status": "ACTIVE"). An unknown name on input fails with a 400. If the API value must differ from the constant name, use @JsonValue and @JsonCreator.
  • Money: never double (0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3). Use BigDecimal, which becomes a JSON number like 799.00. Some teams send an integer in paise (79900) or a string to avoid any rounding in JavaScript.
  • Big numbers: JavaScript reads JSON numbers as 64-bit floating point, which is exact only up to 9,007,199,254,740,991 (253 − 1). A Long id larger than that loses digits in the browser; send such ids as strings.

Records, classes and constructors

Records work without any annotations (Jackson 2.12 and newer). For a normal class, Jackson needs either a no-argument constructor plus setters, or a constructor whose parameter names it can see (Spring Boot compiles with -parameters and registers the right module), or an explicit @JsonCreator. If none exists you get InvalidDefinitionException: Cannot construct instance of … (no Creators, like default constructor, exist). Spring reports this as a 500, not a 400, because the fault is in your class definition and not in the client's JSON.

Spring Boot 3.x uses Jackson 2; Spring Boot 4 uses Jackson 3

Boot 3.x ships Jackson 2 (com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper). Spring Boot 4 uses Jackson 3 by default. Jackson 3 moved its core and databind classes to a new package, tools.jackson (for example tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper), and its exceptions are unchecked. The annotations in this article (@JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonInclude, @JsonFormat and the rest) still live in com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation. Everything above about annotations, dates and null policy applies to both versions; only the imports and the direct ObjectMapper calls differ. If you upgrade an existing app, read the Boot 4 migration guide for its Jackson section.

Rules

  • JSON must be valid: double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas.
  • Jackson derives property names from getters: getName() gives name, and isActive() on a boolean gives active (not isActive).
  • For reading, Jackson needs a way to create the object: a record, a no-arg constructor with setters, or a constructor it can map.
  • Generic collections read by hand need a TypeReference.

Conventions

  • Use camelCase keys, ISO-8601 dates, UTC Instant for timestamps, and one consistent null policy.
  • Serialize DTOs, not JPA entities (DTO article).
  • Do not hand-write JSON with string concatenation. Build objects and let Jackson write them.

Edge cases and the exceptions you will see

  • Infinite recursion: an entity graph where Order points to OrderItem and back fails with JsonMappingException: Infinite recursion (StackOverflowError); Spring wraps it in HttpMessageNotWritableException and the client gets a 500.
  • Hibernate proxies: serializing a lazy entity can fail with No serializer found for class org.hibernate.proxy.pojo.bytebuddy.ByteBuddyInterceptor. Another reason to use DTOs.
  • Input errors (bad JSON syntax, wrong type, unknown enum name) arrive as HttpMessageNotReadableException and become a 400.
  • @JsonIgnore on a field also blocks reading it. A write-only password field needs @JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.WRITE_ONLY) instead.

Mistake: hiding a password with @JsonIgnore on a two-way class

The client must be able to send the password when registering but must never receive it back. @JsonIgnore blocks both directions, so registration silently stores a null password.

Wrong: the password can no longer be read from the request

public class UserDto {
    private String email;
    @JsonIgnore
    private String password;
    // getters and setters
}

Right: accepted on input, never written to output

public class UserDto {
    private String email;
    @JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.WRITE_ONLY)
    private String password;
    // getters and setters
}

Interview: "How does Spring convert JSON to objects? How do you handle dates and nulls?"

  • An HttpMessageConverter backed by Jackson's ObjectMapper reads the body for @RequestBody and writes return values, chosen by Content-Type and Accept.
  • Serialization = object to JSON (getters); deserialization = JSON to object (constructor or setters).
  • Dates: ISO-8601 strings, Instant in UTC for timestamps, @JsonFormat only when a contract demands another pattern.
  • Nulls: @JsonInclude(NON_NULL) or spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion; use wrapper types and @NotNull to detect missing input.
  • Common annotations: @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonIgnoreProperties, @JsonInclude, @JsonFormat, @JsonCreator.

What makes an API RESTful

REST is an architectural style in which resources are identified by URLs and handled through representations with standard HTTP methods, one stateless request at a time; most real-world "REST APIs" follow it only partly, at level 2 of the Richardson model.

REST stands for Representational State Transfer. Roy Fielding described it in his 2000 PhD dissertation as a set of design rules for networked systems, taken from how the web itself works. REST is a style, not a protocol, a library or a standard. An API that follows the rules is called RESTful. In daily work, "REST API" usually means "JSON over HTTP with sensible URLs, methods and status codes".

The key ideas

Resource
Anything the API can name: a product, an order, a user, "the cart of user 7". A resource is a noun with a URL. It is not a database table and not a Java class; one resource may combine data from several tables.
Representation
A snapshot of a resource's state in some format, usually JSON. The same resource could have a JSON and an XML representation. The client never touches the database row; it exchanges representations.
Statelessness
Every request contains everything the server needs (token, parameters, body). The server keeps no conversation memory between requests.
Uniform interface
Every resource is handled the same way: identified by a URL, changed through representations, with standard methods and status codes, in self-descriptive messages (the method, status and Content-Type tell you what is going on).
Client–server
The UI and the data store are separate. The React app can change without touching the backend, and the other way round.
Cacheable
Responses say whether they may be reused (Cache-Control, ETag), so repeated reads can be cheap.
Layered system
A client cannot tell whether it talks to your server or to a proxy, CDN or load balancer in front of it.

Fielding also lists "code on demand" (the server sends executable code, like JavaScript) as an optional constraint. The uniform interface includes one more rule, HATEOAS, which is explained below.

Statelessness: why it matters

Imagine an e-commerce site on three server instances behind a load balancer. If server A kept your login in its own memory, your next request could land on server B, which would not know you. With a stateless design, you send a token every time and any instance can check it. The benefits are real:

  • Scaling: add or remove instances freely.
  • Reliability: if one instance dies, nothing is lost with it.
  • Simplicity: a request can be understood on its own, logged, replayed and retried.

The cost is that the token travels with every request and the server must verify it every time. This is why JWT-based security (Module 4) is configured as stateless in Spring Security. The client's UI state (which page you are on) may still be remembered by the client — "stateless" is about the server.

Richardson Maturity Model

Leonard Richardson's model grades how much of REST an API uses. It is a favourite interview topic.

LevelIdeaLooks like
0One URL, one method; HTTP is only a tunnel (RPC style)POST /api with {"action":"getProduct","id":42}
1Separate resources, each with its own URLPOST /products/42 for everything
2Proper HTTP methods and status codesGET /products/42 → 200 or 404
3Hypermedia: responses contain links to the next possible actions (HATEOAS)An order with cancel and pay links

Most production APIs, including the ones you will write, sit at level 2. That is a good, practical target.

HATEOAS in one paragraph

HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) means a response tells the client what it can do next by including links, the way a web page has links. The client follows links instead of building URLs from documentation. For an order that can still be cancelled, the response could carry a cancel link; once the order ships, that link disappears. Spring has a library for this (spring-boot-starter-hateoas) and a common format called HAL. In practice, JSON APIs for single-page apps rarely go to level 3, because the front-end developers already know the URLs. Know the idea for interviews; do not feel bad about not using it.

{
  "id": 5,
  "status": "PLACED",
  "total": 1598.00,
  "_links": {
    "self":   { "href": "/api/v1/orders/5" },
    "cancel": { "href": "/api/v1/orders/5/cancel" }
  }
}

REST compared with other API styles

StyleFormatBest forWatch out for
RESTJSON over HTTP, many URLsPublic and web/mobile APIs; cacheable readsOver- or under-fetching of fields
GraphQLOne endpoint, client writes the queryApps that need flexible data shapesCaching and rate limiting are harder
gRPCBinary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2Fast, strongly typed service-to-service callsBrowsers need extra tooling
SOAPXML envelopesLegacy enterprise and banking integrationsVerbose; heavy tooling

Rules of a RESTful API

  • Identify things with nouns in URLs (/orders/5), and let the HTTP method be the verb.
  • Keep requests self-contained: no server-side session needed to understand them.
  • Use standard status codes and media types so that clients and proxies understand the messages.
  • Do not let a read change data: GET must be safe.

Conventions: a practical checklist

  • Plural nouns, lowercase, consistent naming (URL design).
  • JSON in and out; camelCase keys; ISO-8601 dates.
  • Correct status codes and one error format everywhere.
  • Pagination for every list; a version in the URL when you must break clients.
  • Token-based authentication in the Authorization header.

Edge cases: where pure REST bends

  • Some operations do not map to CRUD: "cancel an order", "send an OTP", "transfer money". Model them as sub-resources or action URLs and use POST (see URL design).
  • A "session" or "cart" is state, but you can store it on the server as a resource (/carts/{id}) that the client refers to by id. That is still stateless communication.
  • Long-running work does not fit request–response; answer 202 Accepted and give a status resource to poll.

Mistake: RPC in disguise

Endpoints named after methods (/getUser, /createOrder, /deleteProduct) with everything sent as POST are level 0 or 1. Caches, monitoring and developers lose all the meaning that HTTP already provides.

Wrong: verbs in URLs, POST for everything

POST /api/getUser        {"id": 7}
POST /api/createOrder    {"userId": 7, "items": [...]}
POST /api/deleteProduct  {"id": 42}

Right: resources and methods

GET    /api/v1/users/7
POST   /api/v1/orders          {"items": [...]}
DELETE /api/v1/products/42

Interview: "What is REST? What are its constraints? What does stateless mean?"

  • An architectural style from Fielding's dissertation: client–server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system, optional code on demand.
  • Resources are named by URLs; clients exchange representations (JSON) using standard methods and status codes.
  • Stateless: each request is complete on its own, so any server instance can serve it; this makes horizontal scaling easy.
  • Richardson levels 0–3: single endpoint, resources, HTTP verbs and codes, then HATEOAS. Say that most APIs are level 2.
  • Be ready for "REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC": REST is simple and cacheable, GraphQL gives flexible queries, gRPC is binary and fast for internal calls.

Designing resource URLs

Name resources with plural lowercase nouns, let the HTTP method be the verb, nest at most one or two levels, and use query parameters for filtering, sorting and paging.

URLs are the user interface of your API. A consistent scheme means a developer who has seen /products can guess /orders without reading any documentation. The rules below are the common agreement of the industry; follow them unless your team has a written reason not to.

The standard shape for one resource

OperationMethod and URLSuccessNotes
ListGET /products200Filter, sort and page with query parameters
Read oneGET /products/{id}200404 if missing
CreatePOST /products201Location header with the new URL
ReplacePUT /products/{id}200 / 204Whole representation in the body
Update partPATCH /products/{id}200Only changed fields in the body
DeleteDELETE /products/{id}204404 if missing

The rules

  1. Use nouns, not verbs. The method already says what to do. POST /products, not /createProduct.
  2. Use plural for collections. /products and /products/42, always plural, even for the single item. A mix of /product and /products is confusing.
  3. Lowercase letters with hyphens. Paths are case-sensitive, so /Products and /products would be different URLs. Hyphens are readable: /order-items, not /order_items or /orderItems.
  4. No trailing slash, no file extension. Not /products/ and not /products.json; the format is chosen by the Accept header. (Spring 6 and later already treats /products/ as a different, unmapped URL.)
  5. Identity goes in the path; options go in the query. /products/42 says which product; ?sort=price says how to show the list.
  6. Nest only when a resource belongs to another. /orders/9/items is fine, because an item cannot exist without its order. Go at most two levels deep. For anything deeper, expose the child directly: /order-items/3/reviews.
  7. Start with a stable prefix and a version. /api/v1/... separates the API from the React app's own routes and leaves room to evolve.
  8. Use ids that you can keep stable. Do not use names or database internals. Sequential numeric ids are easy to guess, so never rely on "nobody knows the id" for security; always check permissions. UUIDs make guessing harder but are not a security control either.

Good and bad URLs

BadProblemBetter
GET /getAllProductsVerb in the URL; GET already says "read"GET /products
POST /createProductVerb in the URLPOST /products
GET /product/42Singular; inconsistent with the collectionGET /products/42
GET /Products/42/Capital letter and trailing slashGET /products/42
DELETE /products?id=42Identity belongs in the pathDELETE /products/42
GET /products/search?name=mouse"search" is not a resource; it is a filterGET /products?name=mouse
GET /order_itemsUnderscoreGET /order-items
GET /users/7/orders/9/items/3/reviewsToo deeply nestedGET /order-items/3/reviews
GET /products.jsonFormat in the URLGET /products with Accept: application/json
GET /tbl_prod_mstLeaks database namingGET /products

Actions that are not CRUD

Some things are not "create, read, update, delete": cancel an order, send an OTP, transfer money, log in. You have three honest choices, in order of preference.

  1. Model the result as a noun: POST /orders/5/cancellation, POST /payments/9/refunds, POST /accounts/3/transfers. Each call creates something (a cancellation, a refund, a transfer) that you can later read with GET.
  2. Use an action sub-path with POST: POST /orders/5/cancel. This is pragmatic, very common, and acceptable. It breaks the "nouns only" rule on purpose, because there is no good noun.
  3. Top-level action endpoints for things that are not tied to a resource: POST /auth/login, POST /auth/logout, POST /search.

Whichever you choose, use POST, never GET, and say in the docs whether it is idempotent.

@PostMapping("/{id}/cancel")
public OrderResponse cancel(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return orderService.cancel(id);   // 200 with the updated order, or 409 if already shipped
}

Query parameters: what belongs there

PurposeExample
Filtering/products?category=books&inStock=true&maxPrice=500
Free-text search/products?q=wireless+mouse
Sorting/products?sort=price,desc
Paging/products?page=0&size=20
Choosing fields/products?fields=id,name,price
Including related data/products/42?expand=category

All of these are optional and never change which resource you mean. A list URL such as /products?name=mouse always answers with a list (possibly empty); /products/mouse would claim there is one resource named "mouse".

A worked example: a job portal API

The Project 2 job portal fits the rules directly:

RequestPurpose
GET /api/v1/jobs?title=java&location=pune&minSalary=800000&page=0&size=10Search jobs
POST /api/v1/jobsA recruiter posts a job
GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}Job details
POST /api/v1/jobs/{jobId}/applicationsA candidate applies
GET /api/v1/jobs/{jobId}/applicationsA recruiter lists the applications for one job
GET /api/v1/applications/{id}One application (deeper nesting avoided)
POST /api/v1/applications/{id}/withdrawAction that is not CRUD
GET /api/v1/users/meThe logged-in user (a "singleton" resource)

Rules for responses that go with the URLs

  • A list endpoint always returns a JSON object or array of the same item shape every time; an empty result is [] or an empty content, not an error.
  • Wrap paged lists in an object ({"content": [...], "page": 0, ...}). A bare array has no room for paging metadata, so adding it later would break every client.
  • Keep the same field names for the same concept across endpoints (id, createdAt).

Conventions

  • One controller class per resource, with the base path on the class (@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")).
  • Query parameter names are camelCase (minPrice) and match the JSON field names.
  • Boolean fields read as adjectives: active, inStock, not isActive (Jackson turns isActive() into active anyway).
  • Irregular plurals are fine (/people); just be consistent.

Edge cases

  • A path variable cannot contain a slash. An encoded slash (%2F) is rejected by Tomcat by default. Use a query parameter for values such as file paths.
  • Words with special characters in the path must be URL-encoded (/search/c%2B%2B); clients' HTTP libraries usually do it for you.
  • Verbs are acceptable for real actions: /login, /logout, /orders/{id}/cancel, /search.
  • Bulk operations (create 100 items) do not have a standard URL. POST /products/bulk or a POST of an array to the collection are both used; document which one you choose.

Mistake: using the query string to identify a resource

GET /products?id=42 works, but it reads like a filter and returns a list in the minds of most developers. If the URL points to exactly one thing, put the id in the path.

Wrong: id and verb in the query

@GetMapping("/getProduct")
public ProductResponse get(@RequestParam Long id) {
    return service.findById(id);
}

Right: id in the path

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return service.findById(id);
}

Interview: "Design the URLs for a library / e-commerce system" and "Path variable or query parameter?"

  • Name the resources first (books, members, loans), then give each the collection and item URLs with the standard methods.
  • Show nesting for owned data (/members/{id}/loans), keep it shallow, and put filters, sorting and paging in the query string.
  • Path = identifies a resource; query = refines the view. Query parameters are optional; path variables are not.
  • For actions, explain the trade-off: a noun sub-resource if you can (/loans/{id}/return or /returns), otherwise a clearly named action with POST.

API versioning strategies

Version an API so existing clients keep working while you make breaking changes; the most common way is a version in the URL path (/api/v1/…), with header, media-type and query-parameter versioning as alternatives.

Once other people depend on your API, you cannot change it freely. A mobile app installed on a million phones cannot be updated the day you rename a JSON field. Versioning lets you publish a new, incompatible shape (v2) while the old one (v1) keeps working until its clients have moved.

Breaking and non-breaking changes

You only need a new version for a breaking change. Everything else you can add to the current version.

Breaking — needs a new versionNon-breaking — safe in the same version
Removing or renaming a fieldAdding a new optional response field
Changing a field's type or meaning (price from number to object)Adding a new endpoint
Making an optional request field requiredAdding an optional request field or query parameter
Changing a URL, a status code or the error formatMaking a validation rule more lenient
Tightening validation so that old requests failFixing a bug so the API matches its documentation

This works only if clients are tolerant readers: they ignore response fields they do not know. Tell your API consumers this in the docs. Adding a new value to an enum is a grey area: clients that switch over the values may break, so announce it.

The four strategies

StrategyExampleGoodBad
URI pathGET /api/v2/products/42Visible, easy to test in a browser, easy to route and cache, simple docsPurists say a URL should identify a resource, not a version; every client URL changes
Custom headerX-API-Version: 2Clean URLs; one URL per resourceHidden; harder to try in a browser; caches need Vary; easy to forget
Media typeAccept: application/vnd.shop.v2+jsonMost "pure" REST; versions each representationComplex; weaker tool support; hard to explore
Query parameterGET /products/42?version=2Easy to try; easy to defaultClutters URLs and cache keys; optional parameter that is easy to omit

Some public APIs, such as Stripe's, use date-based versions sent in a header, so each client stays on the behaviour of the day it integrated. For most teams, the URI path is the right default: it is boring, visible and works with every tool.

Implementing path versioning in Spring MVC

Keep one service layer and version only the web layer: the controller and its DTOs. Suppose v2 changes price from a plain number into an object with a currency.

public record ProductResponseV1(Long id, String name, BigDecimal price) {}

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {}

public record ProductResponseV2(Long id, String name, Money price, Instant createdAt) {}
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
public class ProductControllerV1 {
    private final ProductService service;

    public ProductControllerV1(ProductService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponseV1 get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        ProductDetails d = service.getDetails(id);          // shared business logic
        return new ProductResponseV1(d.id(), d.name(), d.price());
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v2/products")
public class ProductControllerV2 {
    private final ProductService service;

    public ProductControllerV2(ProductService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponseV2 get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        ProductDetails d = service.getDetails(id);          // the same service call
        return new ProductResponseV2(d.id(), d.name(),
                new Money(d.price(), "INR"), d.createdAt());
    }
}

The other strategies are variations on the mapping attributes you will meet in the mapping annotations article:

// Header versioning: the request must contain "X-API-Version: 2"
@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", headers = "X-API-Version=2")

// Media-type versioning: the request must send Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json
@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", produces = "application/vnd.shop.v2+json")

// Query-parameter versioning: the request must end with ?version=2
@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", params = "version=2")

Spring Framework 7 / Spring Boot 4: built-in API versioning

Spring Framework 7, the base of Spring Boot 4, adds first-class support for API versioning. The mapping annotations get a version attribute (for example @GetMapping(path = "/{id}", version = "2")), and you configure once, in the MVC configuration, where the version is read from: a request header, a path segment, a query parameter or a media-type parameter. That replaces the hand-written headers, params and produces tricks above. The configuration API is new, so follow the Spring Framework 7 reference for your exact release. The strategies and trade-offs in this article stay the same, and on Boot 3.x you still use the manual approach.

The lifecycle of a version

  1. Release v2 with documentation of what changed and why.
  2. Keep v1 stable. Fix bugs and security problems only; add nothing new.
  3. Announce deprecation with a date, in the docs and by email. You can also send the Sunset response header (RFC 8594) with the planned end date.
  4. Measure usage per version (a metric tagged with the version). When nobody calls v1 any more, remove it.
  5. Return 410 Gone or a clear error from the removed version for a while instead of a mysterious 404.

Rules

  • Never change an existing version's behaviour in a breaking way. That is the whole point of a version.
  • Version the whole API together (/api/v1/...), not one resource at a time. Mixed versions per resource are painful to document and use.
  • Use whole-number major versions (v1, v2). Minor versions in URLs (v1.1) only multiply the paths.

Conventions

  • Start with /api/v1 from day one, even if v2 never comes; adding a prefix later is itself a breaking change.
  • Support at most two versions at a time. Each live version doubles testing and support.
  • Share services and the database; version controllers and DTOs only.
  • Publish one OpenAPI group per version (OpenAPI article).

Edge cases

  • Missing version with header or parameter versioning: decide the default. Serving the oldest stable version protects old clients; requiring an explicit version avoids guessing.
  • Evolve without versioning where you can: add optional fields, deprecate old ones, and migrate in the "expand then contract" way (add the new field, let clients move, remove the old one later).
  • Internal APIs that you control end to end (one team owns client and server, deployed together) often need no versioning at all.

Mistake: copying the whole stack for every version

Duplicating services and repositories for v2 doubles every bug fix. Put business rules in one service; let each controller only translate between that service and its own DTOs.

Interview: "How do you version a REST API? What counts as a breaking change?"

  • Four options: URI path (most common), custom header, media type (vnd.…+json) and query parameter. Give one pro and one con of each.
  • Breaking: removing or renaming fields, changing types or status codes, adding required inputs. Non-breaking: adding optional fields or endpoints.
  • Version only the web layer; keep one service layer. Deprecate with a timeline, a Sunset header, and usage metrics.
  • Mention that clients should be tolerant readers, and that Spring Framework 7 adds built-in versioning support.

How a request flows through Spring MVC

Every HTTP request enters the embedded Tomcat, passes the filters, reaches the single DispatcherServlet, which finds your controller method, calls it, and turns the return value into a response through an HttpMessageConverter such as Jackson.

When you write @GetMapping("/products/{id}") you never write code that opens a socket, parses text or sets headers. Spring Web MVC does all of that around your method. If you understand the path a request takes, errors like "404 for a URL that exists", "415 Unsupported Media Type" or "my filter runs but my interceptor does not" stop being mysteries. This article is the map for the rest of module 2.

The big picture

Step by step

  1. Embedded Tomcat. Spring Boot starts Tomcat inside your JAR (default port 8080). Tomcat accepts the TCP connection, parses the HTTP text and builds an HttpServletRequest and an empty HttpServletResponse. One thread from Tomcat's pool handles the request from start to end (the classic "thread per request" model).
  2. Servlet filters. The request passes through a chain of jakarta.servlet.Filter objects: character encoding, CORS, request logging, and later Spring Security's filter chain. Filters see raw requests and responses and know nothing about controllers. A filter can stop the request, for example by returning 401.
  3. DispatcherServlet. This is the front controller: the one servlet mapped to /, so every URL that no other servlet handles comes to it. It does no business work; it coordinates the other pieces below.
  4. HandlerMapping. The dispatcher asks "which handler matches this method, path, Content-Type and Accept?". For annotated controllers the answer comes from RequestMappingHandlerMapping, which built a lookup table at startup from every @RequestMapping-style annotation. The result is a handler execution chain: your controller method plus any interceptors. If nothing matches you get 404 (or 405 if the path matches but the method does not).
  5. HandlerInterceptor.preHandle. Interceptors are Spring MVC's own, lighter hooks. They know the matched handler, so they suit things like auditing or per-endpoint timing. preHandle can return false to stop.
  6. HandlerAdapter. The adapter (RequestMappingHandlerAdapter) knows how to call your method. It resolves every parameter: path variables, query parameters, headers and the body. For @RequestBody it picks an HttpMessageConverter using the request's Content-Type; Jackson reads the JSON into your DTO. If the parameter has @Valid, Bean Validation runs here, before your method starts.
  7. Your controller method runs. It calls a service and returns an object, a ResponseEntity, or nothing.
  8. Return value handling. The adapter chooses a converter using the Accept header and the return type, writes the body (JSON by Jackson, String as text) and sets the status and headers.
  9. Back out. Interceptor postHandle / afterCompletion run, the response travels back through the filters in reverse order, and Tomcat sends it to the client.
  10. Exceptions. If anything throws, the dispatcher hands the exception to HandlerExceptionResolver beans. Your @RestControllerAdvice is one of them; see global error handling.

Key components

ComponentJobYou touch it when…
FilterWork on every request before Spring MVCsecurity, CORS, request-id logging
DispatcherServletCoordinates the whole flowalmost never (debug logging)
HandlerMappingURL + method → handleryou debug a 404 or 405
HandlerAdapterResolves arguments, calls the methodcustom argument resolvers (rare)
HttpMessageConverterBody bytes ↔ Java objectscustom formats (CSV, XML)
HandlerInterceptorHooks around a matched handleraudit, per-endpoint rules
HandlerExceptionResolverException → responsevia @RestControllerAdvice

Filter vs interceptor

Servlet FilterHandlerInterceptor
Belongs toServlet API (Tomcat)Spring MVC
RunsBefore the DispatcherServletAfter the handler is chosen
Knows the controller methodNoYes
Sees requests for static files and 404sYesOnly for matched handlers
Typical useSecurity, CORS, loggingAuditing, rate rules per endpoint

Spring Security (module 4) is built from filters for this reason: it must reject a request before any controller code is even chosen.

See the flow yourself

Turn on debug logging for web requests and read what Spring decides:

logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG
# very detailed: parameters and headers of each request
spring.mvc.log-request-details=true
DispatcherServlet : POST "/api/v1/products", parameters={}
RequestMappingHandlerMapping : Mapped to ProductController#create(CreateProductRequest)
RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor : Read "application/json;charset=UTF-8" to [...]
RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor : Writing [ProductResponse[id=1, ...]]
DispatcherServlet : Completed 201 CREATED

Where the common errors come from

  • 404: HandlerMapping found nothing for the path. Check the class-level and method-level paths together and the context path.
  • 405 Method Not Allowed: the path matches but not the HTTP method (HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException).
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type: no converter can read the request's Content-Type, or your method's consumes does not allow it (HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException).
  • 406 Not Acceptable: no converter can produce what Accept asks for (HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException).
  • 400 Bad Request: broken JSON (HttpMessageNotReadableException), a missing required parameter, or a path variable that cannot be converted (MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException), or a validation failure.
  • A 401/403 before your controller: a security filter answered; the DispatcherServlet never ran.

Servlet stack vs reactive stack

This flow is Spring MVC (servlet stack, blocking, Tomcat by default), which this module uses. Spring WebFlux is a separate reactive stack with DispatcherHandler instead of DispatcherServlet. Since Java 21 you can also run MVC on virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) and keep the same simple code. The flow above stays the same in Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x.

Interview angle

"Explain what happens when a request hits a Spring Boot application." Strong answer: Tomcat → filter chain → DispatcherServlet (front controller) → HandlerMapping finds the controller method → HandlerAdapter resolves arguments (message converter reads the JSON, validation runs) → controller → return value written by a message converter → response back through the filters. Add one failure case (exception resolver and @RestControllerAdvice) and the filter vs interceptor difference.

@Controller vs @RestController

@RestController is @Controller plus @ResponseBody: every method's return value is written straight into the HTTP response body (as JSON), instead of being treated as the name of a view to render.

Spring MVC supports two styles of web app. In the older server-rendered style, a controller returns the name of an HTML template (Thymeleaf, JSP) and a view resolver renders it. In the REST style, the controller returns data and a message converter writes it as JSON. The annotation you choose on the class selects the style.

The two annotations

@Controller
public class PageController {

    @GetMapping("/welcome")
    public String welcome(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("user", "Asha");
        return "welcome";          // a VIEW name: templates/welcome.html
    }
}
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductService productService;

    public ProductController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return productService.findById(id);   // written as JSON
    }
}
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":42,"name":"Wireless Mouse","sku":"MS-100","price":799.00,"stock":25}

@RestController is a composed annotation: its source is just @Controller + @ResponseBody. @Controller itself is a @Component stereotype, so component scanning registers the class as a bean (see scanning). @ResponseBody tells Spring: "do not look up a view; hand the return value to an HttpMessageConverter".

@Controller@RestController
Return value meansView name ("welcome")Response body
Equivalent to—@Controller + @ResponseBody
OutputHTML pageJSON (or text, XML)
Needs a template engineYesNo
Used forServer-rendered web appsREST APIs for React, mobile, other services

How it works inside

After DispatcherServlet finds your method (request flow), the RequestMappingHandlerAdapter calls it and then hands the return value to the first return value handler that supports it. This choice is the real difference between the two annotations:

  • For a @Controller method returning String, a view-name handler takes the value, and the ViewResolver turns it into a template.
  • For a method with @ResponseBody (or any method of a @RestController), a body handler (RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor) takes the value. It looks at the request's Accept header, goes through the registered HttpMessageConverter list, and uses the first converter that can write that Java type as an acceptable media type.
  • For a ResponseEntity return type, another handler writes the status and headers first and then the body in the same way (ResponseEntity).

Boot registers the usual converters for you. A String is written as-is by the string converter. A byte[] or Resource is written as raw bytes. Records, classes, lists and maps are written by Jackson as JSON (Jackson basics). The same list also reads request bodies for @RequestBody (next article).

What the return value becomes

Method returnsResponse
A record or classJSON object, status 200
List<ProductResponse>JSON array, status 200
StringThe text as it is (not quoted JSON); content type depends on the request's Accept
voidEmpty body, status 200 (use @ResponseStatus for 204)
ResponseEntity<T>Body and status and headers that you choose
nullEmpty body, status 200 (often a bug; prefer an explicit 404)
Optional<T>Not unwrapped to 404; Jackson writes it as the value or null. Unwrap in the service

A small trap with String: return "ok" sends the three characters ok, not "ok" with quotes. A client that parses the response as JSON then fails. If the client expects JSON, return a record such as new StatusResponse("ok").

Mixing both styles

You can have both kinds in one app: a @Controller serving an HTML landing page and several @RestController classes serving /api/**. You can also keep @Controller and put @ResponseBody on single methods, but when everything in the class is an API method, @RestController is cleaner. In a React plus Spring Boot project, nearly every controller is a @RestController, because React is a separate app that only asks for data (Frontend · Module 6). The same split exists for global error handlers: @ControllerAdvice versus @RestControllerAdvice (error handling).

@Controller
public class MixedController {

    @GetMapping("/")
    public String home() {
        return "index";                       // view name
    }

    @GetMapping("/ping")
    @ResponseBody                              // this one method is an API method
    public Map<String, String> ping() {
        return Map.of("status", "up");
    }
}

Rules for controllers

Rules

  • Controllers are singletons shared by all threads: keep them stateless. No mutable instance fields.
  • Use constructor injection for the service (one constructor needs no @Autowired).
  • Put the common path prefix on the class with @RequestMapping; put method and sub-path on each method.
  • Keep controllers thin: bind the request, call one service method, shape the response. See layers.
  • Return DTOs (records), never JPA entities. Lazy relations can break serialization and you may leak fields (DTOs).

Convention: one controller per resource

Name it after the resource: ProductController, OrderController, in a web or controller package. One class handles one noun and its sub-resources. A class with forty endpoints is a design smell. Version the prefix (/api/v1/..., see versioning) and use plural nouns (URL design).

Mistake: @Controller on an API class

With @Controller and no @ResponseBody, a method that returns a String or object is treated as a view name. With no view found you see a Whitelabel error page or an error like Circular view path, and the JSON never appears. If your API "returns a 404 HTML page" for a URL that exists, check the class annotation first.

Wrong: view lookup for a DTO

@Controller
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
public class ProductController {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }
}

Right: body is written as JSON

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
public class ProductController {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }
}

Edge cases and errors you can meet

  • HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException (406): the client's Accept header asks for a type no converter can produce, for example Accept: application/xml with no XML library.
  • HttpMessageNotWritableException (500): Jackson cannot write the object, for example a lazy JPA relation closed after the transaction, or a bean with no properties.
  • A @Controller whose URL equals the returned view name gives Circular view path [welcome]: would dispatch back to the current handler URL (common with JSP). With Thymeleaf a missing template gives TemplateInputException and a 500 page.
  • Two methods with the same path and HTTP method give IllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping at startup.
  • A controller bean that is not scanned (outside the root package) simply produces 404 for its URLs, with no error at startup.

Boot 3 and Boot 4

The controller annotations are unchanged. What does change is the JSON library behind the converter: Boot 3 uses Jackson 2, while Boot 4 moves to Jackson 3 by default (different package names for custom modules and serializers). If you only write controllers and records, you do not notice. Check the Boot 4 release notes before porting custom serializers.

Interview angle

Question: "Difference between @Controller and @RestController?" Answer in three points: @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody; the return value goes through HttpMessageConverter instead of the view resolver; use @Controller for server-rendered HTML and @RestController for APIs. Then show depth: the converter is chosen by Accept and the Java type, and Jackson is the JSON one. A follow-up: "How do you return 201 or set a header?" → ResponseEntity (below). Another: "Is a controller thread-safe?" It is a singleton, so it is safe only while it holds no mutable state.

Mapping annotations: @RequestMapping, @PathVariable, @RequestParam

@RequestMapping and its shortcuts (@GetMapping, @PostMapping and so on) connect an HTTP method and path to a Java method; @PathVariable reads values from the path and @RequestParam reads them from the query string or form.

Mapping annotations answer two questions: which requests reach this method, and how do the parts of the request become Java parameters. This article covers the routing side and the two parameter styles you use most. The body, headers and status come next in the following article.

@RequestMapping and the shortcuts

@RequestMapping is the general annotation. On a class it sets a shared prefix; on a method it can set the HTTP method, the path, and conditions on headers and media types. Because writing method = RequestMethod.GET everywhere is noisy, Spring gives one shortcut per method.

AnnotationSame asTypical use
@GetMapping@RequestMapping(method = GET)Read one or many
@PostMappingmethod = POSTCreate; actions
@PutMappingmethod = PUTReplace a whole resource
@PatchMappingmethod = PATCHPartial update
@DeleteMappingmethod = DELETEDelete
 
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")            // prefix for every method
public class ProductController {

    @GetMapping                                // GET    /api/v1/products
    public List<ProductResponse> list() { ... }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")                       // GET    /api/v1/products/42
    public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

    @PostMapping                               // POST   /api/v1/products
    public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(...) { ... }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")                       // PUT    /api/v1/products/42
    public ProductResponse replace(@PathVariable Long id, ...) { ... }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")                    // DELETE /api/v1/products/42
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }
}

consumes and produces

Besides method and path, a mapping can be narrowed by media type. consumes matches the request's Content-Type; produces matches the request's Accept and sets the response Content-Type. A mismatch gives 415 or 406.

@PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
             produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
public ProductResponse create(@RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) { ... }

// same endpoint path, two representations
@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", produces = "application/json")
public ProductResponse json(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", produces = "text/csv")
public String csv(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

Most of the time you do not set them: JSON in and out is the default for REST controllers. Set them when one URL really serves two formats, or when you want a clear 415 for anything but JSON. More in content negotiation.

Path patterns

  • /products/{id} — one segment, captured as a variable.
  • /products/{id:[0-9]+} — a regex after the colon; only digits match. Anything else falls through to 404.
  • /files/* — one segment of anything; /files/** — any number of segments (only as the last part of the pattern).
  • Static paths win over variables: with both /products/featured and /products/{id}, the request /products/featured goes to the first, because the more specific pattern wins.
  • Two methods with the identical method + path + media types cause an IllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping at startup, so the error shows up early.

@PathVariable

A path variable is part of the URL path that identifies a resource. Use it for ids: /products/42.

// Name matches the placeholder: works when compiled with -parameters (Boot default)
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

// Different name: say it explicitly
@GetMapping("/{productId}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable("productId") Long id) { ... }

// Several variables (nested resource)
@GetMapping("/{productId}/reviews/{reviewId}")
public ReviewResponse review(@PathVariable Long productId,
                             @PathVariable Long reviewId) { ... }

// Regex limits the match
@GetMapping("/{code:[A-Z]{3}-\\d{4}}")
public ProductResponse byCode(@PathVariable String code) { ... }
  • A path variable is required by nature. @PathVariable(required = false) exists but is awkward; define two methods instead.
  • Spring converts the text to your parameter type (Long, UUID, LocalDate, an enum). If conversion fails — /products/abc for a Long — you get MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException and a 400.
  • A dot in the last variable (/files/report.pdf) is safe in current Spring versions; suffix-based content negotiation was removed.

@RequestParam

A request parameter is a key in the query string (?category=mouse&page=2) or in a form body. Use it for filtering, sorting and paging, not for identifying a resource.

// GET /api/v1/products?category=mouse
@GetMapping
public List<ProductResponse> list(
        @RequestParam String category) { ... }                  // required: 400 if missing

// optional, with a default
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size                     // ?size absent → 20
@RequestParam(required = false) String category                 // absent → null
@RequestParam Optional<BigDecimal> maxPrice                    // absent → Optional.empty()

// different name in the URL
@RequestParam("q") String searchText

// repeated or comma-separated values: ?tag=usb&tag=wireless  or  ?tag=usb,wireless
@RequestParam List<String> tag

// every parameter as a map (rarely a good idea)
@RequestParam Map<String, String> all
AttributeMeaning
name / valueThe key in the query string; defaults to the parameter name
requiredDefault true. Missing → MissingServletRequestParameterException → 400
defaultValueUsed when missing or empty; also makes the parameter not required

@PathVariable vs @RequestParam

@PathVariable@RequestParam
Lives inThe path: /products/42The query: ?category=mouse
MeaningWhich resourceHow to filter, sort, page
RequiredAlways (part of the URL)Optional by choice
Cache and bookmarkEach id is its own URLSame path, many variations

Binding many parameters to one object

When the list of filters grows, group them in a plain object without any annotation. Spring binds query parameters to its properties (a record works too).

public record ProductFilter(String category, BigDecimal minPrice, BigDecimal maxPrice) {}

// GET /api/v1/products?category=mouse&minPrice=500
@GetMapping
public List<ProductResponse> list(ProductFilter filter) { ... }

Do not add @RequestBody here: a GET request should not carry a body.

Mistake: primitive types for optional parameters

@RequestParam(required = false) int size fails with IllegalStateException when the parameter is absent, because null cannot become an int. Use Integer, Optional<Integer> or defaultValue.

Conventions

  • Version the prefix on the class: /api/v1/... (see API versioning).
  • Use the shortcut annotations, never bare @RequestMapping for a method.
  • Name query parameters in camelCase or lowercase and keep the style the same across the API (minPrice).
  • Do not trust path or query values: validate them (Bean Validation) and put a maximum on size.

@RequestBody, @RequestHeader and @ResponseStatus

@RequestBody turns the JSON body into a Java object, @RequestHeader reads a header, and @ResponseStatus sets a fixed status code for a method or an exception class.

@RequestBody

@RequestBody asks Spring to read the whole request body and convert it into the parameter type. The converter is chosen by the request's Content-Type; for application/json it is Jackson. Use it with POST, PUT and PATCH.

public record CreateProductRequest(
        String name,
        String sku,
        BigDecimal price,
        int stock) {}
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) {
    ProductResponse created = productService.create(request);
    ...
}
POST /api/v1/products HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{ "name": "Wireless Mouse", "sku": "MS-100", "price": 799.00, "stock": 25 }

How the body is converted

Spring keeps a list of HttpMessageConverter objects. For a parameter with @RequestBody, it asks them in order: "can you read this Java type from this Content-Type?" The first one that says yes does the work. Boot's list contains converters for byte[], String, form data, and Jackson for JSON.

  1. The request arrives with Content-Type: application/json and a body.
  2. The argument resolver for @RequestBody picks the Jackson converter, because it can read JSON into your type.
  3. Jackson builds the record or class from the JSON. A record uses its constructor; a class needs a default constructor and setters or a suitable constructor.
  4. If the parameter has @Valid, the validator then checks the constraints (validation).
  5. The object is passed into your method. If any step fails, your method is never called.

Because the converter works from the declared type, you can also bind to a List<CreateProductRequest> (a JSON array), a Map<String, Object> (any JSON object), a plain String (the raw text), a byte[], or a record with nested records. Prefer a specific record: the contract is then visible in code and in the OpenAPI document (OpenAPI).

@PostMapping("/bulk")
public List<ProductResponse> bulk(@RequestBody List<CreateProductRequest> items) { ... }

@PostMapping("/webhook")
public void webhook(@RequestBody String rawJson) { ... }   // needed to verify a signature

@PutMapping("/{id}/note")
public void note(@PathVariable Long id,
        @RequestBody(required = false) NoteRequest note) { ... }  // body may be absent

What can go wrong, and the status you get (before you add your own handler):

ProblemExceptionStatus
Body missing (required = true is the default)HttpMessageNotReadableException400
Invalid JSON (a trailing comma, a missing quote)HttpMessageNotReadableException400
Wrong type: "price": "abc" for a BigDecimalHttpMessageNotReadableException400
Content-Type is not JSON (for example text/plain)HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException415
@Valid constraint failsMethodArgumentNotValidException400
Class cannot be built by JacksonInvalidDefinitionException (your bug)500
  • Only one @RequestBody per method — the body stream can be read once. Wrap several parts in one DTO.
  • A JSON field the DTO does not have is ignored by Spring Boot (see Jackson basics).
  • A missing JSON field becomes null (or 0 for a primitive). Required fields must be enforced with validation.
  • Never bind a JPA entity directly: see DTOs.

A bad request body shows up in the log as a warning, and the client sees a 400. With the default Boot error body, the reason is hidden; a global handler can return a helpful message (error handling).

HTTP/1.1 400
Content-Type: application/json

{"timestamp":"2026-11-11T09:30:12.411+00:00","status":400,
 "error":"Bad Request","path":"/api/v1/products"}

@RequestHeader

Reads one HTTP header. Header names are case-insensitive. Use it for things that describe the request rather than the resource: a correlation id, a client version, an idempotency key, a conditional-request If-Match.

// required: missing header → 400 (MissingRequestHeaderException)
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id,
        @RequestHeader("X-Request-Id") String requestId) { ... }

// optional with a default
@RequestHeader(value = "Accept-Language", defaultValue = "en") String lang

// all headers
@RequestHeader HttpHeaders headers

// idempotency key for a safe retry of POST
@PostMapping("/orders")
public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> place(
        @RequestHeader(value = "Idempotency-Key", required = false) String key,
        @Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrderRequest request) { ... }

Spring converts the header text to the parameter type: @RequestHeader("X-Page-Size") int size works, and a value like abc gives MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException (400). A header that is sent several times can be bound to a List<String>. For the standard headers in more detail, see HTTP headers.

Do not read Authorization by hand

You can write @RequestHeader("Authorization"), but once Spring Security is in place the filter already parsed the token. Take the user from @AuthenticationPrincipal or Authentication instead (module 4). The same applies to cookies: @CookieValue("name") reads one.

@ResponseStatus

The default status for a successful response is 200. @ResponseStatus changes it to a fixed value, on a controller method or on an exception class.

@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)       // 204, empty body
public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    productService.delete(id);
}

@PostMapping("/{id}/archive")
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.ACCEPTED)         // 202
public void archive(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
public class ProductNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ProductNotFoundException(Long id) {
        super("Product " + id + " not found");
    }
}
// throwing it anywhere in a request gives a 404 response

Inside, the status on an exception is applied by ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, one of the resolvers that DispatcherServlet asks when a controller throws. It calls response.sendError(404), and Boot's /error endpoint then builds the JSON error body. Note that by default Boot does not put the exception message into that body (the property server.error.include-message defaults to never), so the client sees status 404 and a generic body unless you set the property or write your own handler.

The limits of @ResponseStatus: the status is fixed at compile time (no choice by data), it cannot add headers such as Location, and on an exception it gives you no control over the JSON shape. For those cases use ResponseEntity and @RestControllerAdvice. Also, if a method with @ResponseStatus throws an exception, the exception's own status wins.

Three ways to choose a status

WayWhereGood for
@ResponseStatus on a methodControllerA fixed success status such as 204 or 202
@ResponseStatus on an exception classExceptionQuick prototypes; one fixed status per exception
ResponseStatusExceptionThrown in codeOne-off errors without a new class
@ExceptionHandler in adviceGlobalUniform JSON errors (recommended)
 
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return productService.findOptional(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(
                    HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Product " + id + " not found"));
}

Other parameter annotations (short list)

Annotation or typeReads
@CookieValueOne cookie
@RequestPart / MultipartFileA part of a multipart/form-data upload (module 6 has file storage notes)
@MatrixVariablePath parameters with ; — rare
HttpServletRequestThe raw request; avoid, it couples you to the servlet API
HttpEntity<T> / RequestEntity<T>Body and headers together in one object
PageablePaging and sorting (pagination)
