Principal / AuthenticationThe logged-in user

Comparison: where each input comes from

AnnotationSourceMissing means
@PathVariableURL path segment404 (no route matches)
@RequestParamQuery string or form field400 MissingServletRequestParameterException
@RequestHeaderHTTP header400 MissingRequestHeaderException
@RequestBodyRequest body (JSON)400 HttpMessageNotReadableException

See mapping annotations for the first two.

Rules

  • Add @Valid next to @RequestBody; without it, constraint annotations on the record are not checked.
  • The client must send Content-Type: application/json for a JSON body, or it gets 415.
  • A 204 response has no body, so a @ResponseStatus(NO_CONTENT) method must return void.

Mistake: using the entity or reading the body twice

Wrong: entity as body, two bodies

@PostMapping
public Product create(@RequestBody Product entity,
                      @RequestBody Audit audit) { ... }

Right: one request DTO

@PostMapping
public ProductResponse create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) { ... }

An entity as the body lets a client set fields like id or role (mass assignment). Reading the stream twice, for example in a filter and again in the controller, gives an empty body the second time.

Conventions

  • Name request bodies CreateXRequest and UpdateXRequest, and make them records.
  • Use custom headers sparingly; if a value belongs to the resource, put it in the body or the path. Older code prefixes custom headers with X-; newer standards do not require it.
  • Prefer one global error handler over @ResponseStatus on many exceptions once the API grows.

In real projects

Teams give every request a correlation id: a filter reads X-Request-Id (or makes one), puts it in the logging context (MDC), and echoes it back in the response so a user's bug report can be traced across services. Payment-style POST endpoints take an Idempotency-Key header so a client can retry after a timeout without charging twice. Webhook endpoints (a payment gateway calling you) bind the body as a String first, because the signature in a header is calculated over the exact raw bytes.

Interview angle

"How does @RequestBody work?" It reads the body through an HttpMessageConverter selected by Content-Type (Jackson for JSON) and passes the object to the method; errors are 400 or 415. "What if the JSON has extra fields?" Boot ignores them. "@ResponseStatus vs ResponseEntity?" The first is a fixed status, the second can vary status and add headers. A strong answer also names MethodArgumentNotValidException for @Valid failures and says why you never bind entities.

ResponseEntity and the Location header

ResponseEntity lets a method choose the status code, headers and body of a response, which you need for 201 Created with a Location header, 204 No Content, conditional 404s and cache headers.

Returning a plain object always means status 200. A real API needs more: 201 after creating, 204 after deleting, 404 when nothing exists, Location pointing to the new resource, ETag for caching. ResponseEntity<T> is the whole HTTP response as a Java object: status + headers + body. T is the body type, written by the message converter.

How it works inside

ResponseEntity extends HttpEntity, a small class that holds headers and a body, and adds a status. When a controller method returns it, a dedicated return value handler (HttpEntityMethodProcessor) does three things in order: it copies the status to the response, copies your headers, and then writes the body through the same HttpMessageConverter chain used for a plain @ResponseBody (controller article). A null body is allowed and produces an empty body. Because the handler is chosen by the return type, ResponseEntity works in a @RestController and also in a plain @Controller, with no @ResponseBody needed.

The builders you use

BuilderStatusUse for
ResponseEntity.ok(body)200Successful read or update
ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(body)201 + LocationPOST that created a resource
ResponseEntity.accepted().build()202Work queued, not finished
ResponseEntity.noContent().build()204Delete, or update without a body
ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(e)400Rarely by hand; use the exception handler
ResponseEntity.notFound().build()404Missing resource (body-less)
ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).body(e)anyAny other status
ResponseEntity.of(optional)200 or 404Optional present → 200, empty → 404

All builders end with .build() (no body) or .body(x). Between them you can chain .header(name, value), .headers(...), .contentType(...), .eTag(...), .lastModified(...) and .cacheControl(...). You can also call the constructor new ResponseEntity<>(body, headers, status), which older code uses; the builder style is easier to read. For the meaning of each status, see status codes.

Create with 201 and Location

After POST creates something, the correct answer is 201 Created, a Location header with the URL of the new resource, and normally the created resource in the body. Build the URL from the current request so it is right on every host, port and context path. Never hard-code http://localhost:8080.

import org.springframework.web.servlet.support.ServletUriComponentsBuilder;

@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) {

    ProductResponse created = productService.create(request);

    URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder
            .fromCurrentRequest()          // http://host/api/v1/products
            .path("/{id}")                 // .../products/{id}
            .buildAndExpand(created.id())  // .../products/42
            .toUri();

    return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(created);
}
HTTP/1.1 201
Location: http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/42
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":42,"name":"Wireless Mouse","sku":"MS-100","price":799.00,"stock":25}

A shorter alternative is MvcUriComponentsBuilder.fromMethodName(...), but fromCurrentRequest() is the simplest and works well for the create-then-fetch pattern. You can also let Spring inject a UriComponentsBuilder as a method parameter; it is already initialised from the current request:

@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request,
        UriComponentsBuilder uriBuilder) {

    ProductResponse created = productService.create(request);
    URI location = uriBuilder.path("/api/v1/products/{id}")
            .buildAndExpand(created.id()).toUri();
    return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(created);
}

Behind a reverse proxy, make sure Boot honours X-Forwarded-* headers (server.forward-headers-strategy=framework), or the host in Location will be the internal one.

Why bother? A client that gets Location can fetch the new resource without guessing its id, and a browser-based client can follow it. It is also a REST rule that a response to a create should point to the new resource (REST principles).

Read: 200 or 404

// 1. Throw. The exception handler produces a 404 body. (Preferred in services.)
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return productService.findById(id);          // throws ProductNotFoundException
}

// 2. Decide in the controller with ResponseEntity
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return productService.findOptional(id)       // Optional<ProductResponse>
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
}

The first style keeps controllers short and gives every 404 the same JSON error body from the global handler (error handling). The second gives a 404 with no body. In a big project choose the first.

Delete, headers and caching

// 204 No Content
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    productService.delete(id);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}

// Custom headers and cache control
@GetMapping("/{id}/image-meta")
public ResponseEntity<ImageMeta> meta(@PathVariable Long id) {
    ImageMeta meta = productService.imageMeta(id);
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(10)).cachePublic())
            .eTag("\"" + meta.version() + "\"")
            .header("X-Total-Images", String.valueOf(meta.count()))
            .body(meta);
}

// Download a file
@GetMapping("/export")
public ResponseEntity<byte[]> export() {
    byte[] csv = productService.exportCsv();
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, "attachment; filename=\"products.csv\"")
            .contentType(MediaType.parseMediaType("text/csv"))
            .body(csv);
}

For large files, do not load everything into a byte[]. Return a ResponseEntity<Resource> (for example an InputStreamResource) or use a streaming body, so memory stays small (file download).

Conditional requests with ETag

An ETag is a version label for a response. The client sends it back in If-None-Match; if nothing changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, saving bandwidth. Spring can do this check for you with WebRequest.checkNotModified:

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> get(@PathVariable Long id, WebRequest request) {
    ProductResponse p = productService.findById(id);
    String etag = "\"" + p.version() + "\"";
    if (request.checkNotModified(etag)) {
        return null;                     // Spring already wrote 304
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(etag).body(p);
}

Returning null here is the documented pattern, because checkNotModified has already written the 304 response. This is the one case where null from a controller is correct. The same ETag idea is reused for optimistic updates with If-Match (locking).

ResponseEntity vs @ResponseStatus vs a plain return

Plain return@ResponseStatusResponseEntity
Status200 alwaysOne fixed statusAny, can depend on data
HeadersNoNoYes
Code sizeSmallestSmallA little more
Best forSimple GET, PUTDelete → 204Create → 201 + Location, caching

Rules

  • The status code must match the result: 201 only for a created resource, 204 only with no body, 4xx for client errors.
  • ResponseEntity.created(uri) needs a non-null URI; it sets the Location header for you.
  • Set the status and headers before the body is written; with ResponseEntity this is automatic because the whole response is built first.

Convention

Return the DTO directly for plain reads and updates. Use ResponseEntity only where you need to control status or headers: create (201 + Location), delete (204), caching and downloads. Always use a specific generic type (ResponseEntity<ProductResponse>), not ResponseEntity<?> or a raw type, so tools like springdoc can read the schema.

Mistakes

  • Returning 200 with {"error": "not found"} in the body. Clients and monitoring tools rely on the status code.
  • Returning ResponseEntity.created(...) with no Location, or hard-coding the host in the URI.
  • Returning 204 with a body. A 204 must have no body.
  • Returning null from a controller for "not found" (gives 200 and an empty body).

Wrong: success status with an error body

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<?> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    var p = productService.findOptional(id);
    if (p.isEmpty()) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of("error", "not found"));
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok(p.get());
}

Right: real 404 and a typed result

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return ResponseEntity.of(productService.findOptional(id));
}

Edge cases and errors

  • Using ResponseEntity.ok(null) or .build() on a method declared ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> is fine: the body is just empty.
  • If the body cannot be written (for example Jackson fails on a lazy collection), you get HttpMessageNotWritableException and a 500, after the status was chosen but before it was sent.
  • If the client's Accept header cannot be satisfied, the result is 406 (HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException) even though you built a 200 entity.
  • A HEAD request to a GET method returns the headers of your ResponseEntity without the body.
  • A relative Location such as /api/v1/products/42 is allowed by HTTP, but absolute URLs are safer for simple clients.

In real projects

Most teams use ResponseEntity in three places only: create endpoints (201 + Location), file downloads (Content-Disposition), and cache-friendly reads (ETag, Cache-Control). Everything else returns a record, and errors go through one @RestControllerAdvice. Integration tests then assert the status and the Location header with MockMvc (controller tests).

Interview angle

"How do you return 201 with the URL of the new object?" Use ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto) with the URI built by ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest().path("/{id}").buildAndExpand(id).toUri(). Then explain why Location matters (the client can fetch the new resource), and when you prefer throwing an exception for 404 (one consistent error format). Be ready for "difference between ResponseEntity and @ResponseBody": the first carries status, headers and body; the second only marks the return value as the body.

Layers: controller, service, repository

A Spring Boot API is split into three layers: the controller handles HTTP, the service holds business rules and transactions, and the repository talks to the database; each layer calls only the one below it.

A layered architecture gives every class one reason to change. If the JSON format changes, only the controller changes. If a business rule changes (for example "an order over ₹50,000 needs approval"), only the service changes. If you switch from PostgreSQL to MongoDB, only the repository changes. It also makes testing easy: you can test the service without HTTP and the controller without a database.

What each layer does

LayerAnnotationResponsible forMust not
Controller@RestControllerPaths, binding, validation trigger, status codes, calling one service methodContain business logic, call repositories, open transactions
Service@ServiceBusiness rules, orchestration, @Transactional, mapping entity ↔ DTOKnow about HTTP (ResponseEntity, HttpServletRequest, status codes)
Repository@Repository / Spring Data interfaceQueries and persistence of entitiesContain business rules; return DTOs of the web layer

Next to the three layers sit two kinds of classes that cross them: the entity (the database row as an object, used by service and repository) and the DTO (the shape of the JSON, used by controller and service). See DTOs.

What goes where: a worked example

Requirement: "Create a product. The SKU must be unique. Price must be positive. Save it and return it."

  • Controller: receives the JSON, triggers format checks (@Valid: price not null, name not blank), calls service.create(request), returns 201 and Location.
  • Service: checks the business rule "SKU is not already used" (existsBySku), throws DuplicateResourceException if it is, builds the entity, calls save, maps the result to a response DTO.
  • Repository: save(entity) and existsBySku(sku). Nothing else.

Note the split in validation: format rules (not blank, positive, an email shape) belong to Bean Validation at the edge; business rules that need data (unique SKU, enough stock, user may cancel only own order) belong to the service.

Transactions live in the service

A transaction groups several database operations into one all-or-nothing unit. One business action usually touches several repositories (reduce stock, create order, create payment record), so the service method is the unit of work. Put @Transactional there, not on controllers or repositories. Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) on read methods. Full details are in module 3.

Dependency direction and wiring

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductService productService;       // depends on the service only

    public ProductController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }
}

@Service
public class ProductService {

    private final ProductRepository productRepository; // depends on the repository only

    public ProductService(ProductRepository productRepository) {
        this.productRepository = productRepository;
    }
}

Depending on an interface for the service (ProductService + ProductServiceImpl) is optional. With one implementation it adds files and no value. Introduce an interface when you truly have two implementations or need a clean seam for a test double; Mockito can mock concrete classes anyway.

Package structure

StyleLayoutGood for
By layercontroller/, service/, repository/, dto/, entity/Small apps, learning
By featureproduct/ (controller, service, repository, dto…), order/, user/Growing apps; microservice splits later

Package-by-feature keeps everything about one resource together, lets you make classes package-private, and is what most teams move to after the first few months. Both work; pick one and keep it.

Rules of the layers

  • Controller → service → repository. Never skip a layer (a controller calling a repository), never call upwards.
  • No HTTP types in services: no ResponseEntity, HttpStatus, HttpServletRequest. A service throws domain exceptions; the web layer maps them to status codes.
  • No entities in controller signatures. Controllers speak DTOs.
  • No business logic in controllers or repositories.
  • Do not put @Transactional on a controller; do not call a @Transactional method from another method of the same class and expect a new transaction (self-invocation bypasses the proxy; see module 3).

Mistake: the fat controller

Wrong: logic and database in the controller

@PostMapping
public Product create(@RequestBody Product p) {
    if (repo.existsBySku(p.getSku())) {
        throw new RuntimeException("dup");
    }
    p.setCreatedAt(Instant.now());
    return repo.save(p);
}

Right: controller delegates

@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest r) {
    ProductResponse created = service.create(r);
    return ResponseEntity.created(location(created)).body(created);
}

The wrong version cannot be tested without a database, repeats its rules in every controller that needs them, and exposes the entity.

Exception: simple lookups

For a trivial read-only app, a service that only forwards to the repository is "pass-through" code. Some teams still keep it so there is one place to add rules and transactions later. Pick the discipline early; moving it into a project later is harder than starting with it.

Interview angle

"Why not call the repository from the controller?" Strong points: separation of concerns, one place for business rules and transactions, easier unit tests (mock the repository, no HTTP needed), reuse of the service from other entry points (scheduled jobs, message listeners), and the controller stays a thin translation layer between HTTP and your domain. Also name @Component, @Service, @Repository as stereotypes of the same idea (module 1).

Complete CRUD example: Product API

One resource through every layer: entity, repository, DTO records, mapper, service, controller and exception handler, with curl requests and the JSON they return.

This is the pattern you will repeat for every resource in a job project. Pieces that need a later topic are marked: validation details are in Bean Validation, the full error handler in error handling, and JPA in module 3. The example uses PostgreSQL and Spring Data JPA.

Setup

Start from Spring Initializr with: Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, Validation, PostgreSQL Driver. Package-by-feature under com.example.shop.product.

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop_user
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
# schema comes from Flyway/Liquibase or SQL scripts
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
CREATE TABLE product (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name        VARCHAR(120)   NOT NULL,
    sku         VARCHAR(40)    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    price       NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (price > 0),
    stock       INTEGER        NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL
);

While learning you can use spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update to let Hibernate create the table; real projects use migrations (module 3).

1. Entity

package com.example.shop.product;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;

@Entity
@Table(name = "product")
public class Product {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 120)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 40)
    private String sku;

    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal price;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private int stock;

    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private Instant createdAt;

    protected Product() { }                       // required by JPA

    public Product(String name, String sku, BigDecimal price, int stock) {
        this.name = name;
        this.sku = sku;
        this.price = price;
        this.stock = stock;
    }

    @PrePersist
    void onCreate() { this.createdAt = Instant.now(); }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public String getSku() { return sku; }
    public BigDecimal getPrice() { return price; }
    public int getStock() { return stock; }
    public Instant getCreatedAt() { return createdAt; }

    public void update(String name, BigDecimal price, int stock) {
        this.name = name;
        this.price = price;
        this.stock = stock;
    }
}

2. Repository

package com.example.shop.product;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {

    boolean existsBySku(String sku);
}

Spring Data creates the implementation at startup; existsBySku becomes SQL from the method name.

3. DTOs (records)

public record CreateProductRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 120) String name,
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 40) String sku,
        @NotNull @Positive @Digits(integer = 8, fraction = 2) BigDecimal price,
        @PositiveOrZero int stock) {}

public record UpdateProductRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 120) String name,
        @NotNull @Positive @Digits(integer = 8, fraction = 2) BigDecimal price,
        @PositiveOrZero int stock) {}

public record ProductResponse(
        Long id, String name, String sku, BigDecimal price, int stock, Instant createdAt) {}

The update request has no sku: the SKU cannot change, so the API does not accept it.

4. Mapper (by hand)

@Component
public class ProductMapper {

    public Product toEntity(CreateProductRequest r) {
        return new Product(r.name(), r.sku(), r.price(), r.stock());
    }

    public ProductResponse toResponse(Product p) {
        return new ProductResponse(p.getId(), p.getName(), p.getSku(),
                p.getPrice(), p.getStock(), p.getCreatedAt());
    }
}

5. Exceptions

public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String resource, Object id) {
        super(resource + " with id " + id + " not found");
    }
}

public class DuplicateResourceException extends RuntimeException {
    public DuplicateResourceException(String message) { super(message); }
}

6. Service

@Service
public class ProductService {

    private final ProductRepository repository;
    private final ProductMapper mapper;

    public ProductService(ProductRepository repository, ProductMapper mapper) {
        this.repository = repository;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<ProductResponse> findAll() {
        return repository.findAll().stream().map(mapper::toResponse).toList();
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public ProductResponse findById(Long id) {
        return mapper.toResponse(getOrThrow(id));
    }

    @Transactional
    public ProductResponse create(CreateProductRequest request) {
        if (repository.existsBySku(request.sku())) {
            throw new DuplicateResourceException(
                    "Product with SKU " + request.sku() + " already exists");
        }
        Product saved = repository.save(mapper.toEntity(request));
        return mapper.toResponse(saved);
    }

    @Transactional
    public ProductResponse update(Long id, UpdateProductRequest request) {
        Product product = getOrThrow(id);
        product.update(request.name(), request.price(), request.stock());
        return mapper.toResponse(product);          // dirty checking saves it at commit
    }

    @Transactional
    public void delete(Long id) {
        Product product = getOrThrow(id);
        repository.delete(product);
    }

    private Product getOrThrow(Long id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Product", id));
    }
}

7. Controller

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductService service;

    public ProductController(ProductService service) { this.service = service; }

    @GetMapping
    public List<ProductResponse> list() {
        return service.findAll();
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return service.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(
            @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) {
        ProductResponse created = service.create(request);
        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}").buildAndExpand(created.id()).toUri();
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(created);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponse update(@PathVariable Long id,
            @Valid @RequestBody UpdateProductRequest request) {
        return service.update(id, request);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
        service.delete(id);
    }
}

8. Exception handler (minimal)

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(DuplicateResourceException.class)
    ProblemDetail conflict(DuplicateResourceException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, ex.getMessage());
    }
}

Try it with curl

Run the app (./mvnw spring-boot:run), then:

Without a handler for MethodArgumentNotValidException you only get a generic 400 body. The validation and error-handling articles turn it into a clean list of field errors.

What to notice

  • The entity never leaves the service. The controller sees only records.
  • The service has no ResponseEntity; it throws domain exceptions that the advice maps to 404 and 409.
  • update loads the entity and changes it inside a transaction; Hibernate's dirty checking writes the UPDATE. No save call is needed.
  • The check existsBySku is not race-proof: two concurrent requests can both pass it. The database UNIQUE constraint is the real guard; handle DataIntegrityViolationException as 409 too (see error handling).
  • PUT replaces the writable fields; that is why UpdateProductRequest requires all of them. For a partial update, use PATCH with an optional-field DTO.

Edge cases you should think about

  • Delete of an already deleted product: this code returns 404 the second time. Some APIs return 204 again to make DELETE strictly idempotent in outcome; both are accepted, be consistent.
  • findAll() on a big table is a performance bug. Real list endpoints are paged: pagination.
  • Concurrent updates overwrite each other (lost update). Add a @Version field for optimistic locking (module 3).

In real projects

Reviewers check this checklist on every endpoint: correct verb and status, DTO in and out, @Valid on bodies, no logic in the controller, transaction on the service, domain exceptions mapped centrally, a test for the happy path and for 400/404/409, and documentation in Swagger. You will use this same skeleton for the job-portal project in the practice article.

DTOs and mapping (manual, MapStruct)

A DTO is a small class or record that defines exactly what goes into and out of your API; you map entities to DTOs in the service so internal fields and database details never leak, either by hand or with MapStruct.

A DTO (Data Transfer Object) carries data across a boundary. On the web edge, your API contract is the set of request and response DTOs. Your entity is a different thing: it describes a database table and may hold lazy relationships, password hashes, audit columns and internal flags. Mixing the two is the most common beginner mistake in Spring Boot APIs.

Why you should never expose entities

  1. Leaking data. Return a User entity and the JSON includes passwordHash, roles, deleted, internal ids. Adding a column to the table silently adds it to the public API.
  2. Over-posting (mass assignment). If @RequestBody is an entity, a client can send {"id": 1, "role": "ADMIN", "price": 1} and set fields you never meant to expose. A request DTO has only the fields a client may set.
  3. Lazy-loading errors. A JPA relationship such as order.getItems() is loaded on demand. Jackson touches it after the transaction is closed and you get LazyInitializationException; with open-session-in-view it silently fires extra queries per row (the N+1 problem).
  4. Infinite recursion. A bidirectional relationship (Order ↔ OrderItem) makes Jackson loop until StackOverflowError or a "Document nesting depth" failure.
  5. Tight coupling. A database refactoring (rename a column, split a table) breaks every client. With DTOs the API stays the same and only the mapper changes.
  6. Different shapes for different needs. A list view needs three fields, a detail view fifteen, a create request needs no id and no timestamps. One entity cannot be all of these.
  7. Validation fits the request. Constraints like @NotBlank on a create request differ from the update request; the entity should hold database rules.

Wrong: entity as the API

@PostMapping
public User register(@RequestBody User user) {   // client can set role, id, ...
    return userRepository.save(user);            // response includes passwordHash
}

Right: DTOs in and out

@PostMapping
public UserResponse register(@Valid @RequestBody RegisterRequest request) {
    return userService.register(request);        // service hashes the password
}

Request DTO vs response DTO

Use separate types for input and output and often one per operation. Java records are ideal: immutable, no boilerplate, and Jackson supports them.

public record RegisterRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 80) String name,
        @NotBlank @Email String email,
        @NotBlank @Size(min = 8, max = 72) String password) {}

public record UserResponse(Long id, String name, String email, Instant createdAt) {}
// no password, no roles, no internal flags

public record UserSummary(Long id, String name) {}   // for lists and nested use
DTO kindContainsDoes not contain
Create requestFields the client may setid, timestamps, computed fields
Update requestChangeable fieldsImmutable fields (SKU, owner)
Patch requestOptional fieldsAnything required
ResponseWhat the client needs to displaySecrets, internal flags, lazy collections
Summary / list itemA few fieldsLarge nested data

Mapping by hand

Hand-written mapping is plain Java: no magic, easy to debug, the compiler tells you when you add a field and forget it somewhere. Keep it in a mapper class or as a static factory on the DTO.

// Style 1: a static factory method on the response record
public record ProductResponse(Long id, String name, BigDecimal price) {
    public static ProductResponse from(Product p) {
        return new ProductResponse(p.getId(), p.getName(), p.getPrice());
    }
}
List<ProductResponse> list = products.stream().map(ProductResponse::from).toList();

// Style 2: a @Component mapper (see the CRUD article)
@Component
public class ProductMapper {
    public ProductResponse toResponse(Product p) { ... }
    public Product toEntity(CreateProductRequest r) { ... }
}

It is boring code, and that is fine for apps with up to a few dozen DTOs. When you have hundreds of mappings, a generator saves time and typos.

MapStruct

MapStruct is an annotation processor: at compile time it generates a plain Java implementation of your mapper interface. There is no reflection at runtime, so it is fast, and the generated source is readable in target/generated-sources. If a target property has no source, the compiler warns you (set unmappedTargetPolicy = ReportingPolicy.ERROR to fail the build).

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.mapstruct</groupId>
    <artifactId>mapstruct</artifactId>
    <version>${mapstruct.version}</version>
</dependency>

<!-- inside maven-compiler-plugin configuration -->
<annotationProcessorPaths>
    <path>
        <groupId>org.mapstruct</groupId>
        <artifactId>mapstruct-processor</artifactId>
        <version>${mapstruct.version}</version>
    </path>
</annotationProcessorPaths>

Use the current stable MapStruct version from its website for mapstruct.version. If you also use Lombok, add Lombok and the lombok-mapstruct-binding artifact to the same processor-path list, with Lombok listed first, or mappers will not see Lombok-generated getters.

import org.mapstruct.*;

@Mapper(componentModel = "spring")          // generated class is a Spring bean
public interface ProductMapper {

    ProductResponse toResponse(Product product);       // same names: automatic

    List<ProductResponse> toResponses(List<Product> products);

    @Mapping(target = "id", ignore = true)
    @Mapping(target = "createdAt", ignore = true)
    Product toEntity(CreateProductRequest request);

    // different names and a small conversion
    @Mapping(source = "title", target = "name")
    @Mapping(target = "slug", expression = "java(request.title().toLowerCase())")
    Product fromLegacy(LegacyRequest request);

    // update an existing entity in place
    @Mapping(target = "id", ignore = true)
    @Mapping(target = "sku", ignore = true)
    void updateEntity(UpdateProductRequest request, @MappingTarget Product product);
}
MapStruct featureUse
@Mapper(componentModel = "spring")Generated implementation is a bean you inject
@Mapping(source, target)Rename a property
@Mapping(target, ignore = true)Do not fill this property
@Mapping(target, expression) / constantSmall computed values
@MappingTargetUpdate an existing object
uses = OtherMapper.classReuse a mapper for nested types
@BeanMapping(nullValuePropertyMappingStrategy = IGNORE)Skip nulls on update (simple PATCH)

With a mapper bean, the service is the same as before: ProductResponse r = mapper.toResponse(entity). MapStruct works with records and with classes.

ModelMapper and other reflection mappers

Libraries like ModelMapper map by guessing at runtime: modelMapper.map(entity, ProductResponse.class). It saves typing but has real costs: errors show up at runtime (or silently as nulls) instead of compile time, a rename in one class quietly breaks a mapping, reflection is slower, and refactoring tools cannot follow it. Most teams, and most interviewers, prefer MapStruct or hand-written mapping.

By handMapStructModelMapper
Checked atCompile timeCompile timeRuntime
SpeedFastestFast (plain code)Slower (reflection)
BoilerplateHighLowLowest
DebuggingEasyEasy (generated source)Hard
RecommendedSmall and medium appsLarge appsAvoid

Nested DTOs and partial updates

  • Nested objects: map a relationship to a small summary record, not the full entity: OrderResponse(Long id, UserSummary customer, List<OrderItemResponse> items). Load the data you need in the service (a fetch join or an entity graph, module 3) so no lazy load happens outside the transaction.
  • Partial update (PATCH): use a request record with wrapper types, where null means "do not change": PatchProductRequest(String name, BigDecimal price). A plain DTO cannot tell "not sent" from "sent as null". If you must support "set to null", use JSON Merge Patch or JsonNullable-style wrappers; for most APIs "null means unchanged" is enough.
  • Projections: for read-heavy lists, Spring Data can return interface or record projections straight from the query, skipping the entity (module 3).

Rules

  • No entity in a controller method signature, as parameter or return type, not even inside List or ResponseEntity.
  • Map inside the service transaction, before lazy data is out of reach.
  • Response DTOs never hold secrets; request DTOs never hold server-controlled fields (id, role, createdAt).

Naming

Common names: CreateProductRequest, UpdateProductRequest, ProductResponse, ProductSummary. The suffix Dto alone (ProductDto) is also widely used, but it hides whether the type is for input or output. Nest the records inside a single ProductDtos class only for tiny projects.

Mistakes

  • One ProductDto used for create, update and response, so the client must send an id and the response has null fields.
  • Using @JsonIgnore on entity fields to "hide" them. It is easy to forget and couples the database model to the API. Separate types are safer.
  • A mapper that calls entity.getItems() outside a transaction, giving LazyInitializationException.
  • Putting JPA annotations on DTOs, or validation annotations only on the entity.

Interview angle

"Why use DTOs instead of returning entities?" Give at least four reasons: security (hide fields, stop over-posting), stability (API independent of the schema), lazy loading and recursion problems, and different shapes per use case. Then "How do you map?" Hand-written or MapStruct (compile-time, generated, fast); explain why you avoid reflection-based mappers.

Bean Validation: @Valid, @NotBlank, @Email, @Size and custom constraints

Bean Validation lets you declare rules with annotations on DTO fields; adding @Valid to a @RequestBody makes Spring check them before your method runs and throw an exception, which you turn into a clean 400.

Never trust data from outside. A client can send an empty name, a negative price, an email without @ or a 10 MB string. Bean Validation (the Jakarta Validation standard; Hibernate Validator is the implementation Spring Boot uses) lets you write these rules once, as annotations, next to the fields. Add the starter and you are ready:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
</dependency>

The annotations live in the package jakarta.validation.constraints (older Boot 2 projects used javax.validation).

The first example

import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

public record CreateProductRequest(

        @NotBlank(message = "name is required")
        @Size(max = 120, message = "name must be at most 120 characters")
        String name,

        @NotBlank @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]{2}-\\d{3,6}", message = "sku looks like MS-100")
        String sku,

        @NotNull @Positive @Digits(integer = 8, fraction = 2)
        BigDecimal price,

        @PositiveOrZero
        int stock) {}
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(
        @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) {   // @Valid starts the check
    ...
}

With @Valid, Spring validates the object right after Jackson builds it. If any rule fails, the method is not called; a MethodArgumentNotValidException is thrown and the response is 400. Without @Valid the annotations are simply ignored. That is the number-one "my validation does nothing" cause.

The annotation table

AnnotationRuleApplies to
@NotNullNot null (empty is fine)any type
@NotEmptyNot null and length/size > 0String, collection, map, array
@NotBlankNot null and at least one non-whitespace characterString only
@Size(min, max)Length of a string or size of a collectionString, collection, map, array
@Min / @MaxNumeric lower / upper bound (inclusive)integers, BigDecimal
@DecimalMin / @DecimalMaxSame, with a decimal string; can be exclusivenumbers, BigDecimal
@Positive / @PositiveOrZero> 0 / ≥ 0numbers
@Negative / @NegativeOrZero< 0 / ≤ 0numbers
@Digits(integer, fraction)At most that many digitsnumber types, numeric strings
@EmailLooks like an email addressString
@Pattern(regexp)Matches a regular expressionString
@Past / @PastOrPresentDate is in the pastjava.time types
@Future / @FutureOrPresentDate is in the futurejava.time types
@AssertTrue / @AssertFalseA boolean must be true / falseboolean (often on a helper method)

Hibernate Validator adds extras such as @Length, @Range and @URL; they are not part of the standard and may be deprecated, so prefer the standard ones.

@NotNull vs @NotEmpty vs @NotBlank

Input@NotNull@NotEmpty@NotBlank
nullfailsfailsfails
"" (empty)passesfailsfails
" " (spaces)passespassesfails
"Mouse"passespassespasses

Use @NotBlank for text, @NotEmpty for lists that must have an element, @NotNull for numbers, dates and objects.

Most annotations treat null as valid

Only the three Not… annotations (and @AssertTrue in some cases) reject null. @Size(min = 3), @Email, @Pattern and @Positive all pass a null value, because "absent" and "invalid" are different questions. So a required email is @NotBlank @Email, and a required price is @NotNull @Positive. A primitive int can never be null: a missing JSON field becomes 0, which @Positive would reject. Use Integer with @NotNull if you must tell "missing" from "zero".

Custom messages

Every annotation has a message. Write messages a user can read: not "must not be blank" but "name is required". You can use placeholders from the annotation: @Size(max = 120, message = "at most {max} characters"). For many messages or for translation, put keys in messages.properties (or ValidationMessages.properties) and write message = "{product.name.required}".

Nested objects and lists

Validation does not go into nested objects automatically. Mark the field with @Valid to cascade.

public record PlaceOrderRequest(
        @NotNull @Valid Address shippingAddress,           // cascade into Address

        @NotEmpty @Size(max = 50)
        List<@Valid OrderLine> lines) {}                    // each element is checked

public record Address(
        @NotBlank String line1,
        @NotBlank @Pattern(regexp = "\\d{6}", message = "PIN code must have 6 digits")
        String pin) {}

public record OrderLine(@NotNull Long productId, @Positive int quantity) {}

Errors from nested objects get a path such as lines[1].quantity or shippingAddress.pin, so the client can show the message at the right input.

@Valid vs @Validated

@Valid (Jakarta)@Validated (Spring)
Packagejakarta.validationorg.springframework.validation.annotation
StandardYes, part of the specSpring-specific
Validation groupsNoYes: @Validated(OnCreate.class)
Cascade into nested fieldYes (put it on the field)No
On a classNoYes: enables method validation for the class's beans
Use for@RequestBody parameters and nested fieldsGroups; class-level validation of parameters

Validation groups

Sometimes one DTO is used in two situations with different rules: id must be null on create but required on update. Groups are marker interfaces that select a subset of rules. Often separate request records (create vs update) are simpler, but you should know groups for interviews and legacy code.

public interface OnCreate {}
public interface OnUpdate {}

public record ProductRequest(
        @Null(groups = OnCreate.class) @NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class) Long id,
        @NotBlank(groups = {OnCreate.class, OnUpdate.class}) String name) {}

@PostMapping
public ... create(@Validated(OnCreate.class) @RequestBody ProductRequest r) { ... }

@PutMapping("/{id}")
public ... update(@Validated(OnUpdate.class) @RequestBody ProductRequest r) { ... }

A constraint without groups belongs to the Default group. Once you use @Validated(OnCreate.class), only that group runs, not Default, unless OnCreate extends Default.

Validating @PathVariable and @RequestParam

Constraints can sit directly on controller method parameters. This is method validation.

@GetMapping("/{id}")
public ProductResponse get(@PathVariable @Positive Long id) { ... }

@GetMapping
public Page<ProductResponse> search(
        @RequestParam @Size(min = 2, max = 50) String q,
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Min(1) @Max(100) int size) { ... }
  • Since Spring Framework 6.1 (Boot 3.2+) the framework validates these parameters itself and throws HandlerMethodValidationException (a 400). You do not need @Validated on the class.
  • If the controller class has @Validated (older style, a proxy-based check), a failure throws jakarta.validation.ConstraintViolationException instead, which you must handle yourself or you get a 500. Do not mix: pick the built-in 6.1+ approach and leave @Validated off controller classes.
  • On services, @Validated on the class still enables validation of method arguments (ConstraintViolationException) for non-web callers.

A custom constraint

When the built-in set is not enough, write your own annotation plus a validator. Example: a SKU must match the company's format and must not be a reserved word.

import jakarta.validation.*;
import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Documented
@Constraint(validatedBy = SkuValidator.class)       // which class does the check
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER, ElementType.RECORD_COMPONENT})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface ValidSku {
    String message() default "invalid SKU";          // the three required attributes
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}
public class SkuValidator implements ConstraintValidator<ValidSku, String> {

    private static final Pattern FORMAT = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{2}-\\d{3,6}");
    private static final Set<String> RESERVED = Set.of("XX-000");

    @Override
    public boolean isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext context) {
        if (value == null) {
            return true;                  // convention: null is handled by @NotNull
        }
        return FORMAT.matcher(value).matches() && !RESERVED.contains(value);
    }
}

// usage
public record CreateProductRequest(@NotBlank @ValidSku String sku, ...) {}

Validators are created as Spring-aware objects, so a validator can have injected dependencies (for example a repository for a "unique email" check). Be careful: a uniqueness check in a validator is a convenience for good error messages only. The database unique constraint is still the real guard (two requests can race).

For a rule across several fields (startDate before endDate), either put the custom constraint on the class (@Target(TYPE)), or add a boolean helper to the record with @AssertTrue:

public record DateRange(@NotNull LocalDate start, @NotNull LocalDate end) {
    @AssertTrue(message = "end must not be before start")
    public boolean isValidRange() {
        return start == null || end == null || !end.isBefore(start);
    }
}

What exception is thrown, and what the client sees

Where the rule isExceptionHandled by default?
@Valid @RequestBody objectMethodArgumentNotValidException400, but a thin body
Constraint on a controller parameter (Spring 6.1+)HandlerMethodValidationException400, thin body
Constraint with class-level @ValidatedConstraintViolationExceptionNo: 500 unless you handle it
Bean in a service with @ValidatedConstraintViolationExceptionNo: 500 unless you handle it
JPA entity breaks a constraint at saveConstraintViolationException (wrapped)No: 500

The default 400 is not useful to a React form. Map each of these exceptions to one consistent JSON shape with a field-error list. The full code is in global error handling; the target looks like this:

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "One or more fields are invalid",
  "instance": "/api/v1/products",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "name",  "message": "name is required" },
    { "field": "price", "message": "must be greater than 0" }
  ]
}

Rules

  • No @Valid, no validation. Put it on every @RequestBody that has constraints, and on nested fields to cascade.
  • Most constraints accept null; combine with @NotNull/@NotBlank for required fields.
  • Constraints on a record go on the components (the parameters in the header); they are copied to the right places.
  • The server must validate even if the React form already did. Client-side checks are only for convenience.

Conventions

  • Validate format (shape, range, size) at the edge with annotations; validate business rules that need data in the service.
  • Always limit sizes (@Size(max=…)) on strings and lists. Unbounded input is a denial-of-service risk and may overflow your column.
  • Keep messages short, specific and user-readable.
  • Put the same limits in the database schema (VARCHAR(120), NOT NULL). Two lines of defence.

Mistakes

  • Forgetting @Valid (the rules never run) or forgetting the starter dependency (the annotations compile but nothing is enforced on some setups, or the classes are missing).
  • Using @NotNull on a string and expecting blank strings to be rejected.
  • Using @Size on an Integer (it is for length); use @Min/@Max.
  • Adding @Valid on a nested object field without validating the outer object, or the reverse.
  • Validating the JPA entity instead of the request DTO, then getting a 500 at save time.

Boot 3.x and 4.x

Everything here works the same in Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x (Jakarta Validation, Hibernate Validator, built-in method validation since Spring 6.1). The thing to remember from older tutorials: the package is jakarta.validation, not javax.validation.

Interview angle

Typical questions: "Difference between @NotNull, @NotEmpty, @NotBlank", "What does @Valid do and what is thrown on failure?", "@Valid vs @Validated", "How do you validate a path variable?" and "How do you write a custom validator?" Name the pieces: constraint annotation with @Constraint(validatedBy), a ConstraintValidator<A, T>, and the exception mapped by @RestControllerAdvice.

Global error handling: @RestControllerAdvice and ProblemDetail

Throw domain exceptions from your services and map them in one @RestControllerAdvice class to a consistent error JSON (ProblemDetail, RFC 9457) with the right status code, never a stack trace.

When something goes wrong, the client needs three things: the right status code, a machine-readable shape it can parse the same way for every error, and a human message. It must never get a Java stack trace, a SQL error or a framework page. Spring lets you do this in one central place instead of try/catch in every controller.

What Spring Boot does by default

An uncaught exception ends at Boot's /error endpoint and produces this body:

{
  "timestamp": "2026-11-10T08:15:30.123+00:00",
  "status": 500,
  "error": "Internal Server Error",
  "path": "/api/v1/products/7"
}

Messages and stack traces are hidden by default (server.error.include-message and include-stacktrace are never). Do not turn them on in production. The default is safe but not helpful, and it is a different shape from your own errors. Fix both with an advice class.

Step 1: domain exceptions

Services throw exceptions that describe what went wrong in business terms, not HTTP. Make them unchecked (RuntimeException) so they pass through without throws clutter and, with @Transactional, roll back by default.

public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String resource, Object id) {
        super(resource + " with id " + id + " not found");
    }
}

public class DuplicateResourceException extends RuntimeException {
    public DuplicateResourceException(String message) { super(message); }
}

public class BusinessRuleException extends RuntimeException {   // 422
    public BusinessRuleException(String message) { super(message); }
}

Step 2: @RestControllerAdvice and @ExceptionHandler

@RestControllerAdvice = @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody: a bean whose @ExceptionHandler methods apply to all controllers. Each handler names the exception type it handles; Spring picks the closest match in the class hierarchy. You can narrow an advice to some controllers with @RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "...").

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setTitle("Resource not found");
        return pd;
    }
}

ProblemDetail (RFC 9457)

Instead of inventing an error format for each project, use the standard Problem Details format (RFC 9457, which replaced RFC 7807). Spring has the class ProblemDetail and serves it as Content-Type: application/problem+json. Frontend developers and API tools understand it.

MemberMeaningExample
typeURI that identifies the kind of problem (default about:blank)https://api.example.com/errors/duplicate
titleShort, the same for every case of this typeConflict
statusHTTP status code409
detailExplanation for this one occurrenceSKU MS-100 already exists
instanceURI of this occurrence (Spring fills it with the request path)/api/v1/products
extra membersYour own fields, via setPropertyerrors, traceId
 
ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
        "Product with SKU MS-100 already exists");
pd.setTitle("Duplicate resource");
pd.setType(URI.create("https://api.example.com/errors/duplicate"));
pd.setProperty("sku", "MS-100");          // extra member, shown at top level of the JSON
pd.setProperty("timestamp", Instant.now());
return pd;
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/duplicate",
  "title": "Duplicate resource",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Product with SKU MS-100 already exists",
  "instance": "/api/v1/products",
  "sku": "MS-100",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-10T08:15:30.123Z"
}

When a handler returns a ProblemDetail, the HTTP status of the response is taken from its status field.

Step 3: the complete advice class

Extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler gives you handlers for all the standard Spring MVC exceptions (400 malformed JSON, 405, 406, 415, 404 for no handler, missing parameter, type mismatch …) already in ProblemDetail format. You override only what you want to customise and add your own exceptions.

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(GlobalExceptionHandler.class);

    // --- your domain exceptions ---------------------------------------------

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
        return problem(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Resource not found", ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(DuplicateResourceException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleDuplicate(DuplicateResourceException ex) {
        return problem(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Duplicate resource", ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(BusinessRuleException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleRule(BusinessRuleException ex) {
        return problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "Business rule violated",
                ex.getMessage());
    }

    // --- database constraint that slipped past the service check ------------

    @ExceptionHandler(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleIntegrity(DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
        log.warn("Data integrity violation", ex);                  // details only in the log
        return problem(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Data conflict",
                "The request conflicts with existing data");
    }

    // --- validation: @Valid @RequestBody -------------------------------------

    @Override
    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(
            MethodArgumentNotValidException ex, HttpHeaders headers,
            HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {

        List<Map<String, String>> errors = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(fe -> Map.of("field", fe.getField(),
                        "message", String.valueOf(fe.getDefaultMessage())))
                .toList();

        ProblemDetail pd = problem(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Validation failed",
                "One or more fields are invalid");
        pd.setProperty("errors", errors);
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(pd);
    }

    // --- validation: constraints on path / query parameters (Spring 6.1+) ----

    @Override
    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleHandlerMethodValidationException(
            HandlerMethodValidationException ex, HttpHeaders headers,
            HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {

        List<Map<String, String>> errors = new ArrayList<>();
        ex.getParameterValidationResults().forEach(result ->
                result.getResolvableErrors().forEach(error ->
                        errors.add(Map.of(
                                "field", String.valueOf(
                                        result.getMethodParameter().getParameterName()),
                                "message", String.valueOf(error.getDefaultMessage())))));

        ProblemDetail pd = problem(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Validation failed",
                "One or more parameters are invalid");
        pd.setProperty("errors", errors);
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(pd);
    }

    // --- validation: class-level @Validated on service or controller ---------

    @ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)
    ProblemDetail handleConstraintViolation(ConstraintViolationException ex) {
        List<Map<String, String>> errors = ex.getConstraintViolations().stream()
                .map(v -> Map.of("field", v.getPropertyPath().toString(),
                        "message", v.getMessage()))
                .toList();
        ProblemDetail pd = problem(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Validation failed",
                "One or more values are invalid");
        pd.setProperty("errors", errors);
        return pd;
    }

    // --- last resort: never leak internals -----------------------------------

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    ProblemDetail handleUnexpected(Exception ex) {
        String errorId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        log.error("Unexpected error, id={}", errorId, ex);          // full stack trace here
        ProblemDetail pd = problem(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Internal error",
                "Something went wrong. Quote this id to support: " + errorId);
        pd.setProperty("errorId", errorId);
        return pd;
    }

    private static ProblemDetail problem(HttpStatus status, String title, String detail) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(status, detail);
        pd.setTitle(title);
        return pd;
    }
}
  • The imports you need: org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, org.springframework.web.method.annotation.HandlerMethodValidationException, org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException, org.springframework.dao.DataIntegrityViolationException and jakarta.validation.ConstraintViolationException.
  • The catch-all Exception handler is safe because Spring chooses the most specific matching handler. The standard MVC exceptions are caught by the parent class handler first, so a malformed JSON stays a 400.
  • Log the stack trace on the server (with an id the client can quote); return only a generic message.
  • The catch-all should not swallow Spring Security's AccessDeniedException or AuthenticationException in a way that turns 403 into 500. See module 4 for the Security handlers; a common pattern is to rethrow them or add specific handlers.

The built-in alternative: spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled

If you do not want to extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, one property gives you ProblemDetail output for the standard MVC exceptions:

spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true

Boot then registers a built-in advice that extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. Do not turn it on and define your own advice that extends the same class: you would have two such beans and an ambiguity. Either use the property and add a plain advice with only your own @ExceptionHandler methods, or extend the class yourself (as above) and leave the property off.

Custom exceptions that carry their status: ErrorResponseException

ErrorResponseException is an exception that already contains a status and a ProblemDetail. Spring handles it automatically without any @ExceptionHandler (with the standard handler class active). Handy for exceptions that need their own title and type.

public class ProductNotFoundException extends ErrorResponseException {
    public ProductNotFoundException(Long id) {
        super(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND,
              ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND,
                      "Product " + id + " not found"),
              null);
        getBody().setTitle("Product not found");
    }
}

The trade-off: the exception now knows about HTTP, which goes against the "no HTTP in services" rule. Many teams accept it for convenience; stricter teams keep plain exceptions and map them in the advice.

ResponseStatusException: when it is fine

return repository.findById(id).orElseThrow(() ->
        new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Product " + id + " not found"));

It is a one-liner that needs no custom class. It is fine for prototypes and for small, one-off cases in the controller. For anything reused, a named domain exception is better: it is searchable, testable and keeps HTTP out of the service.

Which exception gives which status

ProblemExceptionStatus
Malformed JSONHttpMessageNotReadableException400
Missing query parameterMissingServletRequestParameterException400
Wrong type in path or queryMethodArgumentTypeMismatchException400
Bean Validation failedMethodArgumentNotValidException400
Unknown URLNoResourceFoundException / NoHandlerFoundException404
Wrong HTTP methodHttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException405
Cannot produce requested typeHttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException406
Unsupported body typeHttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException415
Your ResourceNotFoundExceptionyour handler404
Unique key brokenDataIntegrityViolationException409
Optimistic lock clashObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException409
Anything elseException500

A consistent error shape for the frontend

The goal: React reads status, shows detail, and puts each item of errors next to its field, for every error in the API. Decide the shape once, put it in this one class, and test it. With ProblemDetail you already have it:

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "One or more fields are invalid",
  "instance": "/api/v1/products",
  "errors": [ { "field": "price", "message": "must be greater than 0" } ]
}

If your team already has its own error class (ApiError(timestamp, status, error, message, path, fieldErrors)), that works as well; what matters is that it is the same everywhere. Authentication and authorization errors from Spring Security filters should use the same shape (module 4).

Rules

  • Never return a stack trace, SQL text, class names or file paths to a client. Log them.
  • The status code must match the error: not 200 with an error body, not 500 for client mistakes.
  • Handlers should be as specific as possible; the catch-all Exception is the last resort only.
  • The advice must be in a package covered by component scanning (the same or a sub-package of your @SpringBootApplication class).

Edge cases

  • Controller-local handlers win: an @ExceptionHandler inside a controller overrides the global one for that controller only.
  • Errors in filters (such as Spring Security) happen before the DispatcherServlet, so @RestControllerAdvice never sees them. Handle those in the security configuration.
  • A rolled-back transaction: a @Transactional method rolls back on unchecked exceptions, so throwing your domain exception also undoes the database changes. Checked exceptions do not roll back by default (module 3).
  • A 404 for an unknown URL comes from the framework (NoResourceFoundException in recent versions), not from your code. With the standard handler active it becomes a ProblemDetail as well.

Mistakes

  • try { ... } catch (Exception e) { return null; } in controllers. It hides errors and returns 200.
  • e.printStackTrace() instead of a logger, or returning e.getMessage() from a catch-all (it may include SQL or paths).
  • Using @ControllerAdvice without @ResponseBody semantics and getting a view-name lookup. @RestControllerAdvice avoids this.
  • Handling Exception in a controller class and accidentally hiding the validation 400s.

Spring versions

ProblemDetail, ErrorResponseException and the spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled property arrived with Spring Framework 6 / Boot 3.0 and work the same in Boot 4. HandlerMethodValidationException needs 6.1+ (Boot 3.2+). If you target an older Boot 2.x codebase, none of these exist; teams there use their own ApiError class.

Interview angle

"How do you handle exceptions in a Spring Boot REST API?" Strong answer: domain exceptions thrown by services; one @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods that map them to status codes; a consistent body using ProblemDetail (RFC 9457); validation errors as a field list; a catch-all that logs and returns a generic 500; and no stack traces to clients. Bonus: the difference between @ControllerAdvice and @RestControllerAdvice, and why filter-level errors are not caught.

Pagination, sorting and filtering

Never return a whole table: accept page, size and sort parameters through Spring's Pageable, cap the page size, filter with optional query parameters, and return your own page DTO instead of the raw Page.

A findAll() that works with 20 rows in development will freeze the server and the browser with 2 million rows in production. Pagination returns one slice of the data at a time. Sorting decides the order of rows, which a page needs to be stable. Filtering narrows the rows. Together they make every list endpoint safe and fast. Spring Data and Spring MVC support all three with very little code.

The Pageable parameter

Declare a Pageable parameter on a controller method. Spring MVC fills it from the query string.

@GetMapping
public PageResponse<ProductResponse> list(
        @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "name") Pageable pageable) {
    return service.findAll(pageable);
}
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products?page=0&size=10"
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products?page=2&size=10&sort=price,desc"
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products?sort=category,asc&sort=name,desc"
ParameterMeaningDefault
pagePage number, zero-based (first page is 0)0
sizeRows per page20
sortproperty,direction; repeat for several fieldsunsorted

Defaults and limits are set in properties. The default maximum page size is large (2000), so lower it yourself:

spring.data.web.pageable.default-page-size=20
spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size=100
# set to true if the client counts pages from 1 (not recommended: confusing)
spring.data.web.pageable.one-indexed-parameters=false

A request with size=100000 is then reduced to the maximum instead of loading everything. This protects the database and memory: always set a maximum.

Repository side: Page and Slice

A Spring Data repository method that takes a Pageable can return a Page or a Slice. JpaRepository already has findAll(Pageable).

public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {

    Page<Product> findByCategory(String category, Pageable pageable);

    Slice<Product> findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(String text, Pageable pageable);
}
Pageable p = PageRequest.of(0, 20);                                  // page 0, 20 rows
Pageable sorted = PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("price").descending());
Pageable multi = PageRequest.of(1, 10,
        Sort.by(Sort.Order.asc("category"), Sort.Order.desc("name")));
Page<T>Slice<T>
Extra count queryYes: select count(*)No
Knows total elements and pagesYesNo
Knows if there is a next pageYesYes (fetches one extra row)
Cost on a big tableHigher (count can be slow)Lower
Good forAdmin tables with "page 3 of 40"Infinite scroll, "Load more"

Useful methods: getContent(), getTotalElements(), getTotalPages(), getNumber() (current page), getSize(), hasNext(), isFirst(), isLast(), and map(function), which converts each element (entity → DTO) and keeps the paging data.

Return a page DTO, not the raw Page

If you return Spring Data's Page from a controller, Jackson serializes the implementation class PageImpl with many internal fields (pageable, sort, numberOfElements, …). Spring Data logs a warning that serializing PageImpl as-is gives no guarantee about the stability of the JSON structure: a library upgrade can change what your clients receive. It also exposes entities if you forgot to map. Define your own small record:

public record PageResponse<T>(
        List<T> content,
        int page,
        int size,
        long totalElements,
        int totalPages,
        boolean last) {

    public static <E, T> PageResponse<T> from(Page<E> page, Function<E, T> mapper) {
        return new PageResponse<>(
                page.getContent().stream().map(mapper).toList(),
                page.getNumber(), page.getSize(),
                page.getTotalElements(), page.getTotalPages(), page.isLast());
    }
}

// service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public PageResponse<ProductResponse> findAll(Pageable pageable) {
    return PageResponse.from(repository.findAll(pageable), mapper::toResponse);
}
{
  "content": [
    { "id": 7, "name": "Mechanical Keyboard", "price": 3499.00 },
    { "id": 3, "name": "Wireless Mouse", "price": 799.00 }
  ],
  "page": 0,
  "size": 2,
  "totalElements": 23,
  "totalPages": 12,
  "last": false
}

Spring Data's own DTO mode

Since Spring Data 3.3 you can opt in to a stable, documented JSON shape (PagedModel) with @EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = EnableSpringDataWebSupport.PageSerializationMode.VIA_DTO). It outputs content and a page object with size, number, totalElements and totalPages. It is a fine choice if you want less code; a hand-written record gives you full control over the names, so many teams keep their own. Both exist in Boot 3.3+ and 4.x.

Sorting safely

Sort names from the URL go straight to the query. An unknown property (sort=salary on Product) throws PropertyReferenceException, which becomes a 500 unless you handle it. A property that is not indexed makes the query slow. Two protections:

  • Whitelist the allowed fields and map public names to entity fields:
private static final Set<String> SORTABLE = Set.of("name", "price", "createdAt");

private Pageable safe(Pageable in) {
    for (Sort.Order o : in.getSort()) {
        if (!SORTABLE.contains(o.getProperty())) {
            throw new BadRequestException("Cannot sort by " + o.getProperty());
        }
    }
    return in;
}
  • Always add a stable tiebreaker such as id. If you sort by price and many rows have the same price, rows can jump between pages. @PageableDefault(sort = {"createdAt", "id"}) or Sort.by("price").and(Sort.by("id")) fixes it.

Filtering with optional query parameters

curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products?category=mouse&maxPrice=1000&q=wire&page=0&size=10"

For one or two fixed filters, derived query methods are enough (findByCategory, findByPriceBetween). When filters are optional and combine freely, use the Specification API: each filter is a small reusable object, and you add only those that were sent. The repository must extend JpaSpecificationExecutor.

public interface ProductRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Product, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Product> { }

public final class ProductSpecs {
    public static Specification<Product> categoryIs(String category) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("category"), category);
    }
    public static Specification<Product> priceAtMost(BigDecimal max) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> cb.lessThanOrEqualTo(root.get("price"), max);
    }
    public static Specification<Product> nameContains(String text) {
        return (root, query, cb) ->
                cb.like(cb.lower(root.get("name")), "%" + text.toLowerCase() + "%");
    }
}

// service: combine only the filters that were provided
Specification<Product> spec = Specification.where(null);
if (filter.category() != null) spec = spec.and(ProductSpecs.categoryIs(filter.category()));
if (filter.maxPrice() != null) spec = spec.and(ProductSpecs.priceAtMost(filter.maxPrice()));
if (filter.q() != null)        spec = spec.and(ProductSpecs.nameContains(filter.q()));
Page<Product> page = repository.findAll(spec, pageable);

Specifications, JPQL and the Criteria API are explained in module 3. In the controller, bind filters with a plain record (mapping annotations) plus the Pageable:

@GetMapping
public PageResponse<ProductResponse> search(
        ProductFilter filter,
        @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = {"name", "id"}) Pageable pageable) {
    return service.search(filter, pageable);
}

Offset paging and its limits; keyset (cursor) paging

The page/size style is offset pagination: SQL LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40000. The database must walk past the first 40,000 rows before returning 20, so deep pages get slower. Also, if rows are inserted while the user browses, items shift and the user sees duplicates or misses some.

Keyset (cursor) pagination asks for "the 20 rows after the last one I saw", using an indexed column:

SELECT * FROM product
WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId)     -- the cursor from the previous page
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

The API returns a nextCursor token (often a Base64 string with the last created_at and id) and the client sends it back as ?cursor=…. It stays fast on any depth and is stable under inserts, but you cannot jump to "page 37". It suits feeds, logs and infinite scroll. Spring Data has a Scroll API for this (Window and ScrollPosition, Spring Data 3.1+). Offset paging is correct for most business apps; mention keyset when the interviewer asks about millions of rows.

Rules

  • Every list endpoint that can grow is paged, with a maximum page size.
  • Pages are zero-based in Spring: page=0 is the first.
  • Sorting must be deterministic: add a unique tiebreaker.
  • Return your own page DTO, map entities to response DTOs inside the transaction (Page.map).

Mistakes

  • Returning List<Product> from findAll() with no limit.
  • Returning Page<Product> (entities) directly: JSON instability and entity exposure.
  • Letting the client sort by any column, or using LIKE '%text%' on a huge table and wondering about speed (a leading wildcard cannot use a normal index).
  • A Page query with a heavy join fetch: the count query repeats it, or Hibernate pages in memory (warning HHH90003004). Page the parent ids first; see module 3.

Interview angle

"How do you implement pagination in Spring Boot?" Pageable in the controller, Page from the repository, map to a page DTO, cap the size. Then: "Page vs Slice" (count query), "problem with large offsets" (use keyset), and "how do you filter?" (derived queries for simple cases, Specifications for optional combinations).

API documentation with springdoc-openapi and Swagger UI

Add the springdoc starter and your controllers produce an OpenAPI document at /v3/api-docs and an interactive Swagger UI page where anyone can read and try every endpoint.

An API without documentation is a guessing game for the React developer, the mobile team and your future self. OpenAPI (formerly "Swagger spec") is the standard, machine-readable description of a REST API: paths, parameters, request and response schemas, status codes and security. Swagger UI turns that description into a web page with a "Try it out" button. springdoc-openapi is the library that builds the OpenAPI document from your Spring annotations at runtime, so the docs match the code.

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
    <version>${springdoc.version}</version>
</dependency>

Match springdoc to your Spring Boot version

springdoc releases follow Spring Boot: the 2.x line is for Spring Boot 3.x, and Spring Boot 4 needs the newer springdoc line built for it. Check the version table in the springdoc documentation (springdoc.org) before choosing springdoc.version; a mismatched version fails at startup with confusing NoSuchMethodError or ClassNotFoundException errors. Use springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui for Spring MVC (the webflux variant is for WebFlux).

Start the app and open:

URLWhat you get
http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.htmlInteractive UI (redirects to /swagger-ui/index.html)
http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docsThe OpenAPI document as JSON
http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs.yamlThe same as YAML

With no annotations at all, springdoc already lists every endpoint, the parameters and the DTO schemas, including @Valid constraints such as @NotBlank and @Size. Annotations add the human explanation.

Describe the API once

import io.swagger.v3.oas.models.OpenAPI;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.models.info.Info;

@Configuration
public class OpenApiConfig {

    @Bean
    public OpenAPI shopOpenApi() {
        return new OpenAPI().info(new Info()
                .title("Shop API")
                .version("v1")
                .description("Products, orders and customers"));
    }
}

The annotations you use

AnnotationOnPurpose
@Tag(name, description)controllerGroup endpoints in the UI
@Operation(summary, description)methodTitle and explanation of an endpoint
@ApiResponse(responseCode, description, content)methodDocument a status code and its body
@Parameter(description, example)parameterDescribe a path or query parameter
@Schema(description, example, requiredMode)DTO field or classDescribe a model and its fields
@Hiddenmethod, classLeave out of the docs
@SecurityRequirement(name)method, classMark an endpoint as needing the named scheme
 
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.*;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.media.*;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.responses.ApiResponse;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.tags.Tag;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
@Tag(name = "Products", description = "Create, read, update and delete products")
public class ProductController {

    @Operation(summary = "Get a product by id",
               description = "Returns one product or 404 when the id does not exist")
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", description = "Product found")
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "No product with this id",
            content = @Content(mediaType = "application/problem+json",
                    schema = @Schema(implementation = ProblemDetail.class)))
