    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ProductResponse get(
            @Parameter(description = "Product id", example = "42")
            @PathVariable Long id) {
        return service.findById(id);
    }
}
public record CreateProductRequest(
        @Schema(description = "Display name", example = "Wireless Mouse")
        @NotBlank String name,

        @Schema(description = "Unique stock keeping unit", example = "MS-100")
        @NotBlank String sku,

        @Schema(description = "Price in rupees", example = "799.00")
        @NotNull @Positive BigDecimal price,

        @Schema(example = "25") @PositiveOrZero int stock) {}

Do not repeat the status codes of every endpoint by hand if your global error handler produces them. A common trick is to document the shared 400/404/500 once in a custom OperationCustomizer or on a base annotation. For a small API, annotating the main responses is enough.

Documenting JWT authentication

Once the API is secured with a JWT (module 4), Swagger needs an "Authorize" button that sends the Authorization: Bearer … header. Declare a security scheme and require it:

import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.security.SecurityScheme;
import io.swagger.v3.oas.annotations.enums.SecuritySchemeType;

@Configuration
@SecurityScheme(
        name = "bearerAuth",
        type = SecuritySchemeType.HTTP,
        scheme = "bearer",
        bearerFormat = "JWT")
public class OpenApiConfig { /* the OpenAPI bean from above */ }

// on a controller or method that needs a token
@SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth")
@RestController
public class OrderController { ... }

In the UI, click Authorize, paste the token (without the word "Bearer"), and "Try it out" sends it. Remember to allow the docs URLs in your Spring Security configuration (/swagger-ui.html, /swagger-ui/**, /v3/api-docs/**) or Swagger itself gets a 401.

Grouping and versions

For larger APIs, split the documentation by path or package: one group per API version or per audience (public vs admin).

@Bean
GroupedOpenApi publicApi() {
    return GroupedOpenApi.builder().group("public").pathsToMatch("/api/v1/**").build();
}

@Bean
GroupedOpenApi adminApi() {
    return GroupedOpenApi.builder().group("admin").pathsToMatch("/api/admin/**").build();
}

Swagger UI then shows a dropdown with the groups; each has its own /v3/api-docs/{group}.

Useful properties and turning it off in production

springdoc.swagger-ui.path=/swagger-ui.html
springdoc.swagger-ui.operations-sorter=method
springdoc.swagger-ui.tags-sorter=alpha
springdoc.packages-to-scan=com.example.shop
springdoc.paths-to-match=/api/**
springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false
springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false

Public Swagger on an internet-facing production service shows attackers a complete map of your API. Disable it in the prod profile (profiles in module 1), or put it behind authentication. Internal tools and staging are fine.

Code-first vs contract-first

Code-first (springdoc)Contract-first
You writeControllers, then generate the specThe OpenAPI YAML first, then code
Good forOne team owns client and server; fast startSeveral teams agree on the API before coding; public APIs
RiskThe API shape changes by accident with a code changeSpec and code drift unless generated or tested
Toolsspringdoc, annotationsOpenAPI Generator (server stubs and client SDKs), contract tests

Most Spring Boot job projects are code-first. Even so, you can export /v3/api-docs as a file, import it into Postman or Bruno, or generate a typed TypeScript client for the React app from it (Frontend · Module 6).

Rules

  • The starter version must match your Spring Boot line.
  • Documentation must describe DTOs, not entities (another reason for DTOs).
  • Do not leave Swagger UI open on a public production server.

Common problems

  • Swagger page shows "Failed to load API definition" or a 401: security rules block /v3/api-docs.
  • Every endpoint returns 200 in the docs even though you return 201: add @ApiResponse(responseCode = "201"), or return ResponseEntity with a status the library can see.
  • Returning ResponseEntity<?> or Object: the schema is empty. Use concrete types.

Interview angle

"How do you document a REST API?" OpenAPI with springdoc: one dependency, /swagger-ui.html and /v3/api-docs, annotate with @Operation, @ApiResponse, @Schema, add the bearer security scheme for JWT, disable it in production. Mention contract-first as the alternative.

Testing endpoints: curl, Postman, Bruno and .http files

Use curl for quick checks and copy-pasteable bug reports, and Postman or Bruno for saved collections with environments, auth and test scripts that your whole team can share.

You test an endpoint by hand while you build it, long before you write automated tests (module 5). A good tool lets you save requests, switch between local and staging, reuse an auth token and check the response automatically. Learn curl first, because it works on every server and in every CI log; then use a GUI client for daily work.

curl

OptionMeaning
-X POSTHTTP method (GET is the default)
-H "Name: value"Add a header
-d '{...}' / --data-binary @file.jsonRequest body, inline or from a file
-iShow response status and headers
-vVerbose: request and response details
-sSilent (no progress meter)
-o fileWrite the body to a file
-w "%{http_code}"Print the status code only
-u user:passBasic authentication
 
# login, keep the token in a variable (jq extracts JSON fields)
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"asha@example.com","password":"secret123"}' | jq -r .accessToken)

# call a protected endpoint
curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# create with a body from a file
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --data-binary @product.json

# only the status code
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/999
404

Windows quoting

In Windows cmd.exe single quotes do not group text, and JSON quotes need escaping (-d "{\"name\":\"Mouse\"}"). In PowerShell, call curl.exe (plain curl is an alias for Invoke-WebRequest) or use Git Bash, where the Linux examples work unchanged. Putting the JSON in a file and using --data-binary @file.json avoids most quoting trouble.

Postman

Postman is a GUI client with collections, environments and scripts. The concepts you need:

Request
Method + URL + headers + body, saved with a name.
Collection
A folder of requests, for example "Shop API", grouped into folders (Auth, Products, Orders). One collection per project.
Environment
A named set of variables: local, staging, prod. Each has its own values for the same names.
Variable
Written {{name}} in URLs, headers and bodies. Example: {{baseUrl}}/api/v1/products. Keep secrets in "current value" fields, which are not shared when you export.
Scripts
JavaScript that runs before a request (pre-request) or after the response (tests).

The usual setup: environment local with baseUrl = http://localhost:8080 and an empty token. The login request has a test script that saves the token. Every other request uses Authorization: Bearer {{token}} (or the collection's Authorization tab, type Bearer Token, value {{token}}, inherited by all requests).

pm.test("login returns 200", function () {
  pm.response.to.have.status(200);
});

const body = pm.response.json();
pm.test("token is present", function () {
  pm.expect(body.accessToken).to.be.a("string");
});

pm.environment.set("token", body.accessToken);   // reused as {{token}}
pm.test("created with Location", function () {
  pm.response.to.have.status(201);
  pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("Location")).to.include("/api/v1/products/");
});
pm.environment.set("productId", pm.response.json().id);   // next request: /{{productId}}

Run the whole collection with the Collection Runner to smoke-test the API in order. Postman also has a command-line tool (the Postman CLI) that runs a collection in a script or CI job, so the same requests can guard a deployment. You can import an OpenAPI file (/v3/api-docs) to create a collection automatically (springdoc). For your project's README, export the collection (and the environment without secrets) as JSON files and commit them in a docs/ folder.

Bruno

Bruno is an open-source API client that saves each request as a plain-text file (a .bru file) in a folder on your disk. Because collections are ordinary files, they live in your Git repository next to the code, reviews show readable diffs, and there is no cloud account needed. It has the same concepts: collections, environments (files in an environments folder), {{variables}}, pre-request scripts and tests (JavaScript with a Postman-like expect style), and a command-line runner for CI.

PostmanBrunocurl
StorageCloud workspace or export filesPlain files in your repoShell history, scripts
Team sharingWorkspaces (account)GitCopy and paste
Scripts and testsYes (JavaScript)Yes (JavaScript)Shell
Learning curveMediumLowMedium
Best forLarge teams, mock servers, monitorsGit-centred teams, small projectsServers, CI, bug reports

IntelliJ HTTP client (.http files)

IntelliJ IDEA (and VS Code with an extension) can run requests written in a plain .http file inside the editor. They are easy to commit and review.

### variables for the file
@baseUrl = http://localhost:8080

### list
GET {{baseUrl}}/api/v1/products?page=0&size=5
Accept: application/json

### create
POST {{baseUrl}}/api/v1/products
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "Wireless Mouse",
  "sku": "MS-100",
  "price": 799.00,
  "stock": 25
}

Conventions

  • Keep one environment per target (local, staging); never put production tokens or passwords in an exported file or in Git.
  • Name requests like the operation: "Create product", "Get product by id".
  • Test the failure cases too: invalid body (400), unknown id (404), duplicate (409), no token (401), wrong role (403).
  • When you report a bug, attach the curl command and the response with status and headers.

Lombok basics

Lombok is a compile-time tool whose annotations generate getters, setters, constructors, equals, hashCode, toString, builders and loggers, so you write less boilerplate; use it carefully, and not with @Data on JPA entities.

Java classes carry a lot of repeated code: fields, getters, setters, constructors, toString. Lombok is an annotation processor: while javac compiles your class, Lombok adds the methods to the compiled .class file. The source stays short. Many Spring Boot projects use it, so you must be able to read it, even if you prefer records.

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
    <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

Spring Boot manages the Lombok version, and its Maven plugin keeps Lombok out of the final jar. In the IDE, enable annotation processing (IntelliJ: Settings → Build, Execution, Deployment → Compiler → Annotation Processors → Enable). Current IntelliJ versions include Lombok support; in Eclipse or VS Code install the Lombok plugin or agent. If the code compiles with Maven but the IDE shows "cannot find symbol getName()", annotation processing or the plugin is the cause.

The annotations

AnnotationGenerates
@Getter / @SetterGetters / setters for all fields (or one field)
@ToStringtoString(); @ToString.Exclude removes a field
@EqualsAndHashCodeequals and hashCode from fields (choose with onlyExplicitlyIncluded)
@NoArgsConstructorConstructor with no parameters
@AllArgsConstructorConstructor with every field
@RequiredArgsConstructorConstructor for final and @NonNull fields
@DataGetter + setter + toString + equals/hashCode + required-args constructor
@ValueImmutable class: all fields private final, getters only
@BuilderBuilder pattern: Product.builder().name("x").build()
@Slf4jA private static final Logger log field
@NonNullNull check on the parameter or field
 
public class CustomerDto {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    public CustomerDto() { }
    public CustomerDto(Long id, String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public void setId(Long id) { this.id = id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
    // plus equals, hashCode, toString ...
}
@Getter @Setter
@NoArgsConstructor @AllArgsConstructor
@ToString
public class CustomerDto {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
}

The Spring Boot favourites

@Slf4j
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor                  // constructor for all final fields
public class ProductService {

    private final ProductRepository repository;   // injected through that constructor
    private final ProductMapper mapper;

    public ProductResponse findById(Long id) {
        log.info("Loading product {}", id);        // log comes from @Slf4j
        return mapper.toResponse(repository.findById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Product", id)));
    }
}

This pair removes the constructor and logger boilerplate from every service and controller. Spring uses the single generated constructor for injection.

@Builder
public record SearchCriteria(String text, BigDecimal minPrice, BigDecimal maxPrice) {}

SearchCriteria c = SearchCriteria.builder().text("mouse").maxPrice(new BigDecimal("1000")).build();

@Data and JPA entities: avoid

Do not put @Data (or @EqualsAndHashCode / @ToString) on JPA entities

  • equals/hashCode on all fields: the generated version includes the id (null until saved) and mutable fields. An entity put in a HashSet and then saved is "lost", because its hash code changed. Hibernate proxies and lazy collections break comparison too.
  • toString touching relationships: it calls getOrders() on a lazy collection (extra queries or LazyInitializationException), and two entities that point to each other cause infinite recursion and StackOverflowError.
  • Setters everywhere let any code put an entity in an invalid state.

Instead use @Getter with a protected no-args constructor (@NoArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PROTECTED)), write equals/hashCode on the id (or a business key) by hand as described in module 3, and exclude relationships from toString.

Lombok vs records

Java recordLombok
Part ofThe language (Java 16+)A library plus compiler plugin
ImmutableAlwaysWith @Value or final fields
Best forDTOs, value objects, request/response typesClasses that need to be mutable or extended: entities, config classes, services (@RequiredArgsConstructor, @Slf4j)
Tool supportEverything worksNeeds plugin; can conflict with other processors

A practical split: records for DTOs, Lombok for the repetitive bits of services and entities (and some teams skip Lombok entirely, which is also fine). Since the modern IDE can generate constructors and getters in a click, Lombok's value is mostly in keeping files short and diffs small.

Conventions

  • Check the team's rules: some codebases ban Lombok or limit it to a few annotations.
  • Prefer specific annotations (@Getter, @RequiredArgsConstructor) over @Data.
  • With MapStruct, add the lombok-mapstruct-binding processor and list Lombok first (DTOs).
  • Use delombok if you ever need to see the generated source.

Interview angle

"What is Lombok and how does it work?" An annotation processor that modifies the compiled classes to add methods; no runtime cost. "Why is @Data dangerous on entities?" Equals/hashCode on mutable or lazy state, toString loops on relationships. Show you know @RequiredArgsConstructor for constructor injection.

Content negotiation, CORS and file uploads (pointers)

Content negotiation lets the client ask for a format through the Accept header; CORS is a browser rule that you configure on the server so a React app on another origin may call your API; file uploads arrive as multipart requests.

Content negotiation

The same resource can have several representations: JSON, XML, CSV. The client states what it can read in the Accept header, and says what it sends in Content-Type. Spring MVC picks an HttpMessageConverter that fits both (request flow). Spring Boot REST apps normally have only the JSON converter, so the result is always JSON.

  • Accept: application/json → JSON. Accept: */* → the default (JSON).
  • Accept: application/xml with no XML converter on the classpath → 406 Not Acceptable (HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException).
  • Body sent as text/plain to a JSON-only @RequestBody → 415 Unsupported Media Type.
  • To offer XML too, add jackson-dataformat-xml to the classpath; the converter is registered and clients can ask for either.
  • You can pin a method to one format with produces and consumes (mapping annotations), or give one URL two methods that differ only in produces.
  • Do not use file extensions (/products.json) or a ?format= parameter for negotiation in new APIs; use the headers. Recent Spring versions have removed suffix matching.
curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/1 -H "Accept: application/xml"
HTTP/1.1 406

See the header tables in HTTP headers and the versioning-by-media-type idea in API versioning.

CORS in one paragraph

A browser lets a page call another origin (scheme + host + port) only if that server says so. Your React dev server runs on http://localhost:5173 and your API on http://localhost:8080: different ports, so different origins, and the browser blocks the response unless your API sends CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin and friends), after a preflight OPTIONS request for non-simple calls. CORS is enforced by browsers only; curl and Postman never see it. Configure it on the server, and list exact origins, never * together with credentials. The quick way is @CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:5173") on a controller; the right way for a whole API is one global configuration, and with Spring Security it must be wired into the security filter chain so the preflight is not rejected with 401. The full explanation, the Java configuration and the React side are in Frontend · Module 6; the security wiring is in module 4.

File upload pointer

A file arrives as a multipart/form-data request, and a controller reads it with @RequestPart or a MultipartFile parameter:

@PostMapping(value = "/{id}/image", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
public ResponseEntity<Void> uploadImage(@PathVariable Long id,
                                        @RequestPart("file") MultipartFile file) {
    // check size and content type, store the file, save its URL or key
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=5MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=10MB
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/1/image -F "file=@mouse.png"

Rules for real uploads: limit the size, check the content type and extension against an allow-list, never trust the original file name (path traversal), and store files in object storage such as S3 instead of the app server's disk. Storage choices are covered in module 6. Too-large files give MaxUploadSizeExceededException (a 413 response with a handler).

Interview questions — REST APIs with Spring Boot

What is REST, and what makes an API RESTful?

REST is an architectural style for APIs over HTTP. Resources (products, orders) are identified by URLs, the client works with representations of them (usually JSON), and the HTTP method says what to do with them. Key constraints: client-server, stateless requests (each request carries everything the server needs, such as the token), a uniform interface (standard methods and status codes), cacheable responses and a layered system. In practice a good REST API uses nouns in plural URLs, the right verb for each action, and correct status codes.

PUT vs PATCH vs POST: what is the difference, and which are idempotent?

POST creates a resource (or runs an action); sending it twice creates two resources, so it is not idempotent. PUT replaces the whole resource at a known URL; repeating it leaves the same state, so it is idempotent. PATCH changes some fields; whether it is idempotent depends on the change ("set price to 500" is, "increase price by 10" is not). GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; GET and HEAD are also safe (no state change).

Which status codes do you return for create, update, delete, validation error, missing resource and duplicate?

Create: 201 Created with a Location header. Read/update: 200 OK. Delete: 204 No Content. Invalid input: 400 Bad Request (some teams use 422 for business-rule failures). Not found: 404. Duplicate or version conflict: 409 Conflict. Not logged in: 401; logged in but not allowed: 403. Unexpected server error: 500, with no stack trace in the body.

Explain what happens when a request reaches a Spring Boot application.

Embedded Tomcat accepts the connection and builds a servlet request. It passes through the filter chain (CORS, security, logging). The DispatcherServlet, the front controller, asks HandlerMapping which controller method matches the method, path and media types. The HandlerAdapter resolves the arguments: path variables, query parameters, and the body through an HttpMessageConverter (Jackson), running @Valid validation. Your method runs; its return value is written by a message converter as JSON. If an exception is thrown, @RestControllerAdvice turns it into an error response.

What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?

@RestController is @Controller plus @ResponseBody. With @Controller the returned String is a view name for a template engine; with @RestController every return value is serialized into the response body, normally as JSON. Use @RestController for APIs.

@PathVariable vs @RequestParam: when do you use each?

A path variable identifies a resource (/products/42) and is always required. A request parameter is a query-string value for filtering, sorting and paging (?category=mouse&page=1) and can be optional with required = false, defaultValue or Optional. A path variable that cannot be converted (/products/abc for a Long) causes a 400 through MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException.

How do you return 201 with the URL of the new resource?

Return a ResponseEntity:

URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
        .path("/{id}").buildAndExpand(created.id()).toUri();
return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(created);

The URI is built from the current request, so it is right in every environment. The client can follow Location to fetch the new resource.

Why should you never return JPA entities from a controller?

Because it leaks fields (password hash, internal flags), lets clients over-post fields you did not intend to expose, ties the API to the database schema, and causes LazyInitializationException and infinite recursion on bidirectional relationships. Use request and response DTOs (records) and map in the service, by hand or with MapStruct.

MapStruct vs ModelMapper: which do you choose and why?

MapStruct generates plain mapping code at compile time. It is fast, errors appear at build time, and the generated code can be read and debugged. ModelMapper maps by reflection at runtime: slower, and a renamed field can silently map to nothing. Hand-written mapping is also fine for small projects. Configure MapStruct with @Mapper(componentModel = "spring") so the mapper is injectable.

Explain @NotNull, @NotEmpty and @NotBlank. What do @Valid and @Validated do?

@NotNull rejects null only. @NotEmpty also rejects empty strings and collections. @NotBlank (strings only) also rejects text made of spaces. The other constraints (@Size, @Email, @Positive) accept null, so combine them with a Not-annotation for required fields.

@Valid (Jakarta) triggers validation of a @RequestBody and cascades into nested objects. @Validated (Spring) supports validation groups and enables method-level validation on a class. A failed @Valid @RequestBody throws MethodArgumentNotValidException and the method is never called.

How do you handle exceptions globally and return a consistent error body?

Services throw domain exceptions (ResourceNotFoundException, DuplicateResourceException). One @RestControllerAdvice class has @ExceptionHandler methods mapping them to 404, 409 and so on, and returns a ProblemDetail (RFC 9457) with type, title, status, detail, instance and extra properties such as the list of field errors. Extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler covers the framework's own exceptions. A catch-all Exception handler logs the stack trace and returns a generic 500. Errors raised in security filters are not seen by the advice and are handled in the security configuration.

How do you implement pagination and sorting? What is the difference between Page and Slice?

Add a Pageable parameter to the controller (?page=0&size=20&sort=name,asc), pass it to a repository method returning Page<T>, map to a page DTO and cap the size with spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size. Page runs an extra count query to know the total elements and pages; Slice skips it and only knows whether a next page exists, which is cheaper for infinite scroll. Return your own page record instead of the raw PageImpl, because its JSON shape is not guaranteed to be stable. For huge tables, offset paging gets slow; use keyset (cursor) pagination.

How do you version a REST API? What are the options?

Options: URI (/api/v1/products, the simplest and most common), a custom request header, a media type (Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json), or a query parameter. URI versioning is easy to see, cache and test; header and media-type versioning keep URLs clean but are harder to use from a browser. Whatever you choose, avoid breaking changes inside a version: adding fields is safe; removing or renaming fields needs a new version.

What is the difference between 401 and 403? Between 400, 404 and 422?

401 Unauthorized really means "unauthenticated": no valid credentials. 403 Forbidden means the user is known but not allowed. 400 means the request is malformed or fails validation, 404 means the resource does not exist, and 422 (used by some APIs) means the request is well-formed but breaks a business rule.

How do you document an API, and how do you test an endpoint manually?

Add springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui (a version matching your Boot line). It exposes /v3/api-docs and Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html; annotate with @Tag, @Operation, @ApiResponse and @Schema, declare a bearer security scheme for JWT, and disable it in production. For manual testing use curl for quick checks and Postman or Bruno for collections with environments ({{baseUrl}}, {{token}}) and test scripts.

Cheat sheet — REST APIs with Spring Boot

  • GET / POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE read / create or action / replace / partial change / remove; GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; GET and HEAD are safe.
  • Status codes 200 OK, 201 Created (+ Location), 204 No Content, 400 bad input, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 422 rule broken, 500 server bug.
  • @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody; return values become JSON.
  • Request path Tomcat → filters → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → HandlerAdapter → controller → message converter.
  • @RequestMapping("/api/v1/products") on the class; @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping on methods.
  • @PathVariable identifies a resource (/{id}); @RequestParam filters, sorts and pages (?q=).
  • @RequestParam options required, defaultValue, Optional<T>; never a primitive for an optional value.
  • @RequestBody JSON → object; invalid JSON gives HttpMessageNotReadableException → 400; wrong Content-Type gives 415.
  • ResponseEntity status + headers + body: ok, created(uri), noContent, notFound, status(...).
  • Location URI ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest().path("/{id}").buildAndExpand(id).toUri().
  • @ResponseStatus fixed status on a method or exception class (e.g. NO_CONTENT for delete).
  • Layers controller (HTTP) → service (rules, @Transactional, mapping) → repository (data); no HTTP types in services.
  • DTOs records for request and response; never expose entities (leaks, over-posting, lazy loading, recursion).
  • MapStruct @Mapper(componentModel = "spring"), @Mapping, @MappingTarget; avoid reflection mappers.
  • Validation @NotBlank (text), @NotEmpty (lists), @NotNull (everything else), @Size, @Positive, @Email, @Pattern; @Valid on bodies and nested fields.
  • Validation exceptions MethodArgumentNotValidException (body), HandlerMethodValidationException (parameters, Spring 6.1+), ConstraintViolationException (class-level @Validated).
  • Error handling @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler; return ProblemDetail (application/problem+json); catch-all logs and returns a generic 500.
  • Exception to status not found → 404, duplicate or DataIntegrityViolationException → 409, business rule → 422, validation → 400.
  • Paging Pageable (page from 0, size, sort=field,dir); cap spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size; return your own page record.
  • Page vs Slice Page runs a count query; Slice only knows if there is a next page.
  • Filtering optional query parameters bound to a record; Specifications for combinable filters; keyset paging for deep pages.
  • springdoc springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui; /swagger-ui.html, /v3/api-docs; turn off in prod.
  • Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor, @Slf4j, @Getter, @Builder; no @Data on JPA entities.
  • Tools curl for quick checks; Postman or Bruno with {{baseUrl}} and {{token}} variables for collections.

Practice — REST APIs with Spring Boot

  1. Hello API (easy). Create a project on start.spring.io (Web, Validation). Add GET /api/v1/hello?name=Asha returning {"message":"Hello, Asha"} from a record. Use defaultValue = "world". Done when curl returns the JSON and the response header Content-Type is application/json.
  2. Status code drill (easy). Build an in-memory Map based CRUD for a Note resource (no database). Return 201 + Location on create, 200 on read and update, 204 on delete, and 404 for an unknown id. Done when all five curl calls show the right status and the Location header opens the new note.
  3. Product CRUD with layers (medium). Copy the Product API from the CRUD article with PostgreSQL and Spring Data JPA. Write it yourself without looking, then compare. Done when create, list, get, update and delete all work, and the entity never appears in a controller signature.
  4. Validation and global errors (medium). Add Bean Validation to the request records (@NotBlank, @Positive, @Size, a custom @ValidSku). Write a @RestControllerAdvice returning ProblemDetail with a field-error list for 400, plus 404, 409 and a safe 500. Done when invalid input, an unknown id, a duplicate SKU and a forced RuntimeException each return the same JSON shape and no stack trace.
  5. Validate parameters (medium). Add @Positive on the {id} path variable and @Min(1) @Max(100) on a size query parameter. Handle HandlerMethodValidationException. Done when /products/-1 returns a 400 with the parameter name in errors.
  6. Search, paging and sorting (medium). Add GET /api/v1/products?q=&category=&maxPrice=&page=&size=&sort= using a filter record, a Pageable, a Specification, and a PageResponse record. Cap the size at 50 and whitelist the sort fields. Done when 30 seeded products page correctly and sort=salary gives a clean 400, not a 500.
  7. Project 2 — job-portal API (hard). Follow the roadmap's Project 2 steps for this module:
    • Create a new project from Spring Initializr with Web, JPA, Validation, the PostgreSQL driver and Security (you will use Security properly in module 4).
    • Build CRUD endpoints for jobs (and companies) with request and response DTOs and Bean Validation.
    • Add a global error handler that returns consistent JSON errors (ProblemDetail with a field-error list).
    • Add job search by title, location and salary with pagination and sorting.
    • Document every endpoint in Swagger UI with springdoc: tags, summaries, example values and the 400/404 responses.
    Done when a stranger can open Swagger UI, try every endpoint, and get sensible errors for bad input.
  8. Collection and README (hard). Create a Postman or Bruno collection with a local environment (baseUrl, token) and test scripts that check the status code and the Location header. Export it into docs/ and add the curl equivalent of three requests to the README. Done when a teammate can clone the repo, import the collection, and run it end to end.
3

Module 3·Weeks 5–6Must

Data access with Spring Data JPA

15 topics · about 2 h of reading

Almost every backend job means reading and writing a relational database. In Spring Boot you do this with Spring Data JPA, which sits on top of JPA and Hibernate. This module explains the layers from the bottom up: what JDBC does, what an ORM adds, how Hibernate tracks your objects, how entities and relationships are mapped, and how to stop the classic performance traps (the N+1 problem, lazy-loading errors, wrong transaction boundaries).

It builds on module 1 (beans, proxies, AOP — @Transactional is a proxy) and module 2 (the layered Product CRUD API, DTOs, pagination). The SQL itself — indexes, isolation levels, locking, how a database works inside — is in SQL · Module 4, Module 5 and Module 6. Here we use that knowledge from Java. The running example is the job-portal project: User, Company, Job and Application.

After this module you will be able to:

  • Explain ORM, JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA and how they relate.
  • Describe the persistence context, entity states, dirty checking and flush.
  • Map entities correctly (ids, columns, enums, embeddables) and write safe equals/hashCode.
  • Write repositories, derived queries, @Query, projections and Specifications.
  • Model one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many and one-to-one with the right owning side and cascade.
  • Find and fix N+1 queries and LazyInitializationException.
  • Use @Transactional with correct propagation and rollback rules, and avoid the self-invocation trap.
  • Protect data with optimistic and pessimistic locking, add audit fields, and manage the schema with Flyway.
  • Configure the datasource, HikariCP, SQL logging and batch inserts for PostgreSQL or MySQL.

ORM, JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data: how they relate

An ORM maps Java objects to database rows; JPA is the standard API for that, Hibernate is the engine that implements it, and Spring Data JPA is a thin layer on top that writes repository code for you.

The problem: the object–relational mismatch

Java stores data as objects: nested, linked by references, with inheritance and collections. A relational database stores rows in tables: flat, linked by foreign keys, with no inheritance and no collections inside a row. Moving data between the two is tedious and full of small differences. This gap is called the object–relational impedance mismatch.

Object worldRelational worldWhat goes wrong by hand
Reference to another objectForeign key columnYou write joins and rebuild the graph yourself
A List<Job> inside CompanyRows in job with company_idOne-to-many is not a column
InheritanceNo such thingYou must choose a table layout
Identity: == / equalsPrimary keyTwo objects, one row
camelCase, Instant, enumssnake_case, timestamptz, text/intConversion code in every query

The layers, from bottom to top

JDBC
The low-level Java API: open a Connection, prepare a statement, set parameters, loop over a ResultSet, map columns to fields, close everything. Reliable, but 20 lines for one query.
JdbcTemplate / JdbcClient
Spring helpers over JDBC. They manage connections, close resources and convert exceptions; you still write the SQL and the row mapping.
ORM (Object-Relational Mapping)
A technique and a kind of library that maps classes to tables and objects to rows, and generates SQL for you.
JPA (Jakarta Persistence API)
A specification: the annotations (@Entity, @Id, @OneToMany), the EntityManager interface and the JPQL query language. It is only interfaces and rules, no code that runs. Packages start with jakarta.persistence (older code uses javax.persistence).
Hibernate
The most-used JPA implementation (also called a provider). It does the real work: tracks changes, generates SQL, caches, lazy-loads. Spring Boot uses it by default. It also has features beyond JPA (@BatchSize, @CreationTimestamp, statistics).
Spring Data JPA
A Spring module that generates repository implementations from interfaces, so findByEmail(String email) becomes a query. It does not replace Hibernate; it calls the EntityManager for you.

Analogy: JPA is like the JDBC idea of "a standard"; Hibernate is like the PostgreSQL driver — one of several implementations (EclipseLink is another). You write to the standard, and run on the implementation.

One query at three levels

// 1. Plain JDBC (about 20 lines in real code)
try (Connection c = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
             "SELECT id, name, email FROM app_user WHERE email = ?")) {
    ps.setString(1, email);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        if (rs.next()) {
            return Optional.of(new User(rs.getLong("id"),
                    rs.getString("name"), rs.getString("email")));
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }
}

// 2. Spring JdbcClient (Spring Framework 6.1+): SQL stays, plumbing goes
Optional<User> user = jdbcClient
        .sql("SELECT id, name, email FROM app_user WHERE email = :email")
        .param("email", email)
        .query(User.class)
        .optional();

// 3. Spring Data JPA: no SQL, no mapping
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);
}

When JdbcTemplate / JdbcClient is the better tool

JPA is excellent for loading and saving object graphs with business rules. It is a poor fit for some jobs. Use JdbcTemplate or JdbcClient (they live in spring-boot-starter-jdbc, which JPA already pulls in) when:

  • You run reports and analytics with window functions, CTEs, many joins and aggregations. Plain SQL is clearer than JPQL.
  • You do bulk operations on millions of rows (INSERT ... SELECT, big updates).
  • The data has no useful object model: a read-only dashboard row, an export file.
  • You need database-specific features (PostgreSQL jsonb operators, full-text search) and want full control.

Mixing is normal: JPA for the write model, JdbcClient for a few heavy read queries. Both can join the same @Transactional transaction because they share one DataSource connection.

JDBC / JdbcClientSpring Data JPA (Hibernate)
You writeSQL and row mappingEntities and repository interfaces
StrengthFull control, predictable SQL, fast for reportsProductivity, change tracking, relationships
WeaknessBoilerplate, no object graphHidden SQL, N+1, learning curve
Best forReporting, bulk, simple tablesBusiness entities with rules and relations

What the starter gives you

Add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and a database driver. Boot then auto-configures a DataSource (with HikariCP), a JPA EntityManagerFactory built by Hibernate, a transaction manager, and repository scanning. You write no XML and no persistence.xml. Setup details are in datasource and HikariCP.

Boot 3.x vs 4.x

Spring Boot 3.x uses Hibernate ORM 6.x and Jakarta Persistence 3.1; Spring Boot 4.x moves to Hibernate ORM 7.x. The annotations in these notes (@Entity, @ManyToOne, @Version, @Transactional) and the Spring Data repository style are the same in both. Where something differs, a version note says so. Always keep jakarta.persistence.* imports; javax.persistence stops working from Boot 3.

Mistake: thinking JPA hides the database

JPA hides the syntax, not the database. Every repository call becomes SQL, and bad mappings give slow SQL. Learn to read the SQL log (SQL logging) from day one, and keep your SQL skills sharp (SQL · Module 4).

Interview angle

"What is the difference between JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA?" Strong answer: JPA is the specification (interfaces and annotations); Hibernate is an implementation that generates SQL and manages entities; Spring Data JPA is an abstraction on top that creates repository implementations from interfaces and uses JPA underneath. Add one sentence on the mismatch problem and one on when you would pick JdbcTemplate instead.

Persistence context, entity states and dirty checking

The persistence context is Hibernate's per-transaction workspace that tracks every loaded entity; entities in it are "managed", and any change to them is written to the database at flush time without a save() call.

Hibernate does not run SQL the moment you call a setter or persist. It keeps a persistence context (also called the first-level cache or session): a map from (entity type, id) to the entity object, plus a snapshot of the data as it was loaded. Within one transaction there is one EntityManager and one persistence context. In a Spring Boot app, this context lives as long as the transaction (see @Transactional).

The four entity states

Transient (new)
Created with new, not known to any persistence context, no row in the database (yet).
Managed (persistent)
Attached to the persistence context. Hibernate watches it. Entities returned by find or by a query are managed. Anything you change is saved at flush.
Detached
Has an id and may have a row, but the persistence context that loaded it is closed or cleared. Changes are not tracked. This is the state of an entity after the service method returns.
Removed
Managed entity scheduled for deletion; the DELETE is sent at flush.

Dirty checking: no save() needed

When Hibernate loads an entity, it keeps a copy of the loaded values. At flush it compares each managed entity with its snapshot. If a field differs, the entity is dirty and Hibernate issues an UPDATE. This is automatic dirty checking.

@Transactional
public void changeSalary(Long jobId, BigDecimal newMax) {
    Job job = jobRepository.findById(jobId).orElseThrow();   // managed
    job.setSalaryMax(newMax);                                // just a setter
    // no save() call. At commit Hibernate sees the difference and runs:
    // update job set salary_max=?, ... where id=?
}

Calling save() here is harmless (the entity is already managed) but useless. The same code without @Transactional does nothing: findById returns a detached entity once the repository's own tiny transaction ends, and no one flushes the change.

Flush: when SQL is really sent

Flush means "synchronise the persistence context with the database": send the pending INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements. It does not commit. With the default FlushModeType.AUTO, a flush happens:

  • before the transaction commits;
  • before a query that could be affected by pending changes (so the query sees them);
  • when you call flush() / saveAndFlush() yourself.

So SQL runs late. A constraint violation (duplicate email) often appears at commit, outside the line that caused it. Call saveAndFlush or flush() when you need the error right there. Exception: with GenerationType.IDENTITY, persist runs the INSERT immediately, because the database must generate the id (see ID strategies).

The first-level cache

@Transactional
public void demo() {
    Job a = jobRepository.findById(1L).get();   // SELECT ... where id=1
    Job b = jobRepository.findById(1L).get();   // no SQL: served from the context
    System.out.println(a == b);                 // true: the very same object
}

Within one persistence context, one row is one object. This guarantees identity (a == b) and saves queries, but only for lookups by id. A JPQL or derived query always goes to the database (it then returns the already-managed instance for rows it has seen). The cache lives and dies with the transaction; it is not shared between requests.

EntityManager basics

The EntityManager is the JPA API behind every repository. You rarely use it directly, but you should know its methods, and you can inject it with @PersistenceContext (or constructor injection) for custom code.

MethodWhat it does
persist(e)Makes a new entity managed; INSERT at flush (or now for IDENTITY). Returns void; e itself becomes managed.
find(Class, id)Loads by id (SELECT unless cached); null if missing.
getReference(Class, id)Returns a lazy proxy with the id, no SELECT; fails later if the row is missing.
merge(e)Copies state of a detached/new object onto a managed copy and returns that copy.
remove(e)Schedules DELETE of a managed entity.
flush()Sends pending SQL now.
detach(e) / clear()Stops tracking one entity / all entities.
refresh(e)Reloads the entity from the database, discarding in-memory changes.

persist vs merge, and how save() chooses

persistmerge
InputA transient entityA detached or transient entity
Your object becomes managed?Yes, the same instanceNo: the returned copy is managed
SQLINSERTSELECT first (to load the current state), then INSERT or UPDATE
UseNew dataRe-attaching changed data

repository.save(entity) in SimpleJpaRepository is basically:

@Transactional
public <S extends T> S save(S entity) {
    if (entityInformation.isNew(entity)) {
        em.persist(entity);
        return entity;
    } else {
        return em.merge(entity);      // extra SELECT, returns a different object
    }
}

isNew is true when the entity has a @Version attribute of a wrapper type that is null, otherwise when the @Id is null (or 0 for a primitive id). Consequences:

  • With a generated id, new Job() has id null → persist → one INSERT. Good.
  • With an id you assign (a UUID you made, a business code), the id is never null, so save thinks the entity is old and calls merge: a useless SELECT before every insert. Fix: add a @Version Long version field, or implement Persistable<ID> with an isNew() method.
  • Always use the return value of save: job = repo.save(job). After a merge, your original object is not the managed one.

findById vs getReferenceById

@Transactional
public void apply(Long jobId, Long userId, String coverLetter) {
    Application app = new Application();
    app.setJob(jobRepository.getReferenceById(jobId));    // proxy, no SELECT
    app.setApplicant(userRepository.getReferenceById(userId));
    app.setCoverLetter(coverLetter);
    applicationRepository.save(app);   // insert into application (job_id, user_id, ...)
}

findById returns Optional and runs a SELECT (unless cached). getReferenceById (the new name for the old getById) returns a proxy holding only the id, so you can set a foreign key without loading the whole row. If the row does not exist you get an EntityNotFoundException later, when the proxy is first used, or a foreign-key error at flush. Use it when you only need the id; use findById when you must validate existence or read data.

Rules

  • Changes to a managed entity are saved at flush; changes to a detached entity are lost unless you merge/save it.
  • Entity state is only tracked inside a transaction (an open persistence context). Put @Transactional on the service method that changes entities.
  • Use the object returned by save/merge, not the one you passed in.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • PersistentObjectException: detached entity passed to persist — you called persist on an object that already has an id. Use merge (or let save decide).
  • EntityNotFoundException — a getReference proxy points to a missing row.
  • TransientObjectException / TransientPropertyValueException — a managed entity references a transient one that is not persisted and has no cascade.
  • A big loop that loads thousands of entities grows the persistence context (memory + slow dirty checking). For batch jobs, process in chunks and call flush() then clear().
  • Setting a managed field and then throwing a checked exception: the change is still flushed on commit if the transaction does not roll back (see rollback rules).

Mistake: expecting an update without a transaction

Wrong: entity is detached, change is lost

public void rename(Long id, String name) {      // no @Transactional
    Company c = companyRepository.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    c.setName(name);                             // nothing saves this
}

Right: transaction + dirty checking

@Transactional
public void rename(Long id, String name) {
    Company c = companyRepository.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    c.setName(name);                             // UPDATE at commit
}

Interview angle

"What is dirty checking?" At flush Hibernate compares each managed entity with the snapshot taken at load time and issues UPDATEs for changed ones. Follow-ups: "Why does my change not save?" (not in a transaction, entity detached), "When does Hibernate send SQL?" (flush: commit, before queries, explicit flush), "What is the first-level cache?" (per-transaction identity map, only for lookups by id), "persist vs merge?" (see the table).

Entities and mappings: @Entity, @Id, @Column and friends

An entity is a plain Java class marked @Entity with an @Id and a protected no-arg constructor; annotations such as @Table, @Column, @Enumerated and @Embedded describe how fields map to columns.

The rules for an entity class

Rules for entities (JPA spec)

  • Annotate the class with @Entity (jakarta.persistence.Entity).
  • It needs an @Id field (or @EmbeddedId/@IdClass for composite keys).
  • It needs a no-argument constructor, public or protected. protected is the professional choice: Hibernate can use it, your code cannot create half-built objects.
  • The class must not be final, and persistent methods must not be final, because Hibernate creates proxy subclasses for lazy loading.
  • Fields (or getters) must not be final/static to be persisted. Java records cannot be entities (they are final and immutable); records are good as DTOs and embeddables.

A first complete entity

package com.example.jobs.user;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.Instant;

@Entity
@Table(name = "app_user",                       // "user" is a reserved word in PostgreSQL
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_user_email", columnNames = "email"))
public class User {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 80)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 150)
    private String email;

    @Column(name = "password_hash", nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String passwordHash;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private Role role;                           // enum Role { CANDIDATE, RECRUITER, ADMIN }

    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private Instant createdAt;

    protected User() { }                         // for JPA only

    public User(String name, String email, String passwordHash, Role role) {
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
        this.passwordHash = passwordHash;
        this.role = role;
    }

    // getters; setters only where the business needs to change the field
}

Mapping annotations

AnnotationPurposeNotes
@EntityMarks a persistent classEntity name defaults to the class name; used in JPQL
@Table(name, schema, uniqueConstraints, indexes)Table name and constraintsDefault: class name converted by the naming strategy (JobPosting → job_posting in Boot)
@IdPrimary keyUse a wrapper type (Long) so "new" can be null
@ColumnColumn detailsname, nullable, unique, length (strings, default 255), precision/scale (decimals), updatable, insertable, columnDefinition
@EnumeratedHow an enum is storedAlways EnumType.STRING
@TransientField is not persistedFor computed or cached values
@LobLarge object (CLOB/BLOB)For big text or bytes; avoid loading it by default
@Embedded / @EmbeddableValue object stored in the owner's tableSee below
@TemporalOnly for java.util.DateNot needed for Instant, LocalDate, LocalDateTime
@VersionOptimistic locking columnLocking

Naming. Spring Boot's default naming strategy turns createdAt into created_at and JobPosting into job_posting, so @Column(name = "created_at") is optional. Writing it explicitly is still common because it makes the mapping obvious and independent of the strategy.

Length and precision. @Column(length = 80) only affects the DDL that Hibernate generates and gives you no runtime validation. Use Bean Validation (@Size) for the check and keep both in sync with the migration. Money must be BigDecimal with precision and scale, for example @Column(precision = 12, scale = 2); never double.

Enums: STRING, never ORDINAL

Wrong: ORDINAL (the default!)

@Enumerated            // same as EnumType.ORDINAL
private Role role;     // stores 0, 1, 2
// Insert a new constant in the middle of the enum
// and every stored number now means a different role.

Right: STRING

@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
@Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
private Role role;     // stores 'CANDIDATE', 'RECRUITER'

Renaming a constant still breaks stored data, so treat enum names as part of your schema. A database CHECK constraint or native enum type can protect the values.

Embedded value objects

A value object has no identity of its own, only values (an address, a money amount, a salary range). Mark the class @Embeddable and use it with @Embedded: its fields become columns of the owner's table.

@Embeddable
public class SalaryRange {
    @Column(name = "salary_min", precision = 12, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal min;
    @Column(name = "salary_max", precision = 12, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal max;

    protected SalaryRange() { }
    public SalaryRange(BigDecimal min, BigDecimal max) { this.min = min; this.max = max; }
    // getters; equals/hashCode on both fields
}

@Entity
public class Job {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Embedded
    private SalaryRange salary;          // columns salary_min, salary_max in table job
}

If you embed the same type twice (home and office address), rename columns with @AttributeOverride. If all embedded columns are null, Hibernate loads the embedded field as null, so guard for that.

equals and hashCode for entities

Entities go into Sets and maps, and Hibernate compares them, so equals/hashCode matter. The three obvious choices all have a catch:

ChoiceProblem
Do not override (identity)Fine inside one persistence context. Breaks when the same row is loaded in two contexts, or compared with a detached copy.
All fields (Lombok @Data)Hash changes when a field changes; touches lazy collections; can loop forever on bidirectional links.
Generated idThe id is null before the first save, so the hash changes when the entity is persisted. An entity inside a HashSet gets "lost".
Business key (email, ISBN)Best when you have a stable unique natural key; not always available.

A safe, widely used pattern: equal only when both ids are non-null and equal; hash code constant per class. A constant hash code is fine because it only costs performance in huge sets of entities, which you rarely keep.

import org.hibernate.Hibernate;

@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (o == null || Hibernate.getClass(this) != Hibernate.getClass(o)) return false;
    Job other = (Job) o;
    return id != null && id.equals(other.id);   // two new objects are never equal
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Hibernate.getClass(this).hashCode();     // same for all Job instances
}

Hibernate.getClass unwraps a lazy proxy, so proxy.equals(real) works. Never use getClass() != o.getClass() with proxies, and never read fields directly on the other object (other.id on a proxy is null; use other.getId() when the other side may be a proxy). If your entity has a real business key, use it in both methods instead.

Lombok and entities

Lombok is popular but dangerous on entities. @Data generates equals/hashCode/toString over all fields, which causes the problems above plus StackOverflowError when Company.toString() prints its jobs and each Job.toString() prints its company. Use @Getter (and selective @Setter), @NoArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PROTECTED), and if you want toString, exclude relationships: @ToString(exclude = {"jobs"}) or write it by hand with only basic fields.

Design habits that pay off

  • Keep setters out where a method with a business name is clearer: job.close(), user.changeEmail(...).
  • Use Instant (UTC) for timestamps, LocalDate for dates, BigDecimal for money.
  • Keep entities separate from DTOs (module 2).
  • Table names: avoid reserved words (user, order, group); use app_user, orders, etc.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • InstantiationException: No default constructor for entity / HibernateException — the entity has no no-arg constructor.
  • org.hibernate.AnnotationException or MappingException at startup — missing @Id, bad mappedBy, unknown column type.
  • A field holding a lazy proxy compares unequal with ==; use equals as above.
  • Inheritance (@Inheritance, @MappedSuperclass) exists; for a shared base with id and audit columns use @MappedSuperclass (see auditing).

Interview angle

"Why does an entity need a no-arg constructor and why can't it be final?" Hibernate instantiates entities by reflection and creates subclass proxies for lazy loading. "Why EnumType.STRING?" Ordinal values shift when the enum changes. "How do you write equals/hashCode for an entity?" Explain why all-field equals and generated-id hash codes are unsafe, then show the id-null-safe pattern or a business key.

ID generation strategies and ddl-auto

IDENTITY, SEQUENCE and UUID decide who creates primary keys and whether JDBC batching works; spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto decides whether Hibernate touches your schema, and in production it should be validate or none.

@GeneratedValue strategies

@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "job_seq")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "job_seq", sequenceName = "job_seq", allocationSize = 50)
private Long id;
IDENTITY
Uses an auto-increment column (BIGSERIAL / GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY in PostgreSQL, AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL). The database creates the id during INSERT, so Hibernate must run the INSERT immediately on persist to learn the id. Result: simple, but JDBC insert batching is disabled.
SEQUENCE
Uses a database sequence object. Hibernate asks the sequence for a number before the INSERT, so it can delay and batch inserts. Supported by PostgreSQL, Oracle, H2, SQL Server and MariaDB; not by MySQL, where Hibernate falls back to a table-like emulation or you use IDENTITY.
UUID
GenerationType.UUID (JPA 3.1) generates a random UUID in Java; the field type is java.util.UUID. No database round trip, ids are globally unique and safe to expose, but they are 16 bytes and random, so B-tree indexes fragment and are bigger than a bigint.
AUTO
Lets the provider choose. In Hibernate 6+ it picks SEQUENCE for numeric ids on databases that support sequences, UUID for UUID fields, and IDENTITY or a table emulation elsewhere. Convenient for demos, but explicit is better in real code.
TABLE
Keeps ids in a helper table. Slow because of locking; almost never used.

allocationSize: why SEQUENCE is faster

With allocationSize = 50 (the default for sequence generators), Hibernate calls the sequence once, gets a value like 1000, and hands out the next 50 ids (951–1000 or 1000–1049, depending on the optimizer) from memory. One sequence call per 50 inserts. The database sequence must use the same increment (INCREMENT BY 50); if they differ, Hibernate warns or generates duplicates. A Flyway migration should create it:

CREATE SEQUENCE job_seq START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 50;

Side effect: ids have gaps after restarts (unused ids of a block are lost). That is normal; never rely on gap-free ids.

Comparison

IDENTITYSEQUENCEUUID
Who makes the idDatabase, at INSERTSequence, before INSERTJava, at persist
Insert batchingNoYesYes
Round trips1 per insert1 per 50 idsNone
MySQL supportYes (default choice)NoYes
Index size / order8 bytes, ordered8 bytes, ordered16 bytes, random
Safe to expose in URLsGuessableGuessableNot guessable

Practical guidance: PostgreSQL + heavy inserts → SEQUENCE; MySQL → IDENTITY; distributed or public ids → UUID (or a time-ordered UUID/ULID if index locality matters). For small CRUD apps like the Product example in module 2, IDENTITY is perfectly fine.

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto

Hibernate can read your entities and create or change tables. The property spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto controls it:

ValueWhat Hibernate does at startupUse
noneNothingProduction (schema from Flyway)
validateCompares entities with the schema; fails startup on a mismatch (missing table/column, wrong type). Changes nothing.Production, staging, CI
updateAdds missing tables/columns. Never drops or renames, never migrates data.Quick learning only
createDrops and recreates the schema on every startThrowaway local runs
create-dropLike create, and drops the schema when the app stopsTests with an in-memory DB

Boot's default is create-drop for an embedded database (H2) with no schema manager, and none for a real database. Do not rely on defaults: set the value explicitly in each profile.

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.flyway.enabled=true

Mistake: update (or create) in production

  • update cannot rename a column (it adds a new empty one), cannot change a type safely, never removes anything, and gives you no history or review of what changed.
  • create or create-drop on a production URL deletes every row at startup. This has happened to real companies.
  • Use versioned migrations instead (Flyway) and let Hibernate only validate. Hibernate-generated DDL is also not tuned: no indexes beyond keys and uniques you declared, default varchar(255).

Tip: see the DDL without running it

For a first draft of a migration, run once with ddl-auto=create on a throwaway local database and copy the SQL from the log, or use Hibernate's schema generation properties. Then review it by hand, add indexes and constraint names, and commit it as V1__init.sql.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • SchemaManagementException: Schema-validation: missing column [x] in table [y] — validate found an entity field with no column.
  • Schema-validation: wrong column type — for example entity String versus text, or Long versus integer. Fix the migration or the mapping.
  • IDENTITY inserts with hibernate.jdbc.batch_size set: Hibernate silently does not batch them.
  • Sequence increment mismatch: duplicate-key errors or a warning about allocationSize.

Interview angle

"IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE?" Mention who generates the id, the early INSERT, and that only SEQUENCE allows batch inserts; mention allocationSize and gaps. "What ddl-auto do you use in production?" validate or none with Flyway, and explain why update is unsafe.

Spring Data repositories and derived queries

You declare an interface that extends JpaRepository; Spring Data creates the implementation, gives you CRUD and paging for free, and turns method names such as findByEmail into queries.

The repository hierarchy

InterfaceAdds
Repository<T, ID>Nothing: a marker. Extend it to expose only the methods you choose.
CrudRepositorysave, saveAll, findById, existsById, findAll, count, deleteById, delete, deleteAll
ListCrudRepositorySame as above but returns List instead of Iterable
PagingAndSortingRepositoryfindAll(Sort), findAll(Pageable)
JpaRepositoryJPA extras: flush, saveAndFlush, deleteInBatch-style methods, getReferenceById

In Spring Data 3.x, PagingAndSortingRepository no longer extends CrudRepository, which is why ListCrudRepository and ListPagingAndSortingRepository exist; JpaRepository combines them so you get everything.

Using it

public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);
}

No @Repository annotation is needed; Boot's auto-configuration scans for interfaces that extend a Spring Data repository (starting at the package of your @SpringBootApplication class). At startup Spring creates a proxy that implements the interface, backed by SimpleJpaRepository. Exceptions are translated into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy.

User saved = repo.save(user);                 // insert or update
Optional<User> one = repo.findById(5L);        // SELECT ... where id=?
List<User> all = repo.findAll();              // SELECT all (careful on big tables)
Page<User> page = repo.findAll(PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("name")));
long n = repo.count();
boolean has = repo.existsById(5L);
repo.deleteById(5L);                          // loads the entity, then DELETE
repo.saveAll(users);                          // one persist/merge per element

deleteById loads the entity first (so cascades and lifecycle callbacks work). deleteAllInBatch() and deleteAllByIdInBatch(ids) issue a single bulk DELETE and skip callbacks and cascades. Paging was introduced in module 2; the same Pageable works on every repository method below.

Derived queries: the method name is the query

Spring Data parses the method name. The prefix says what to do (find…By, read…By, get…By, query…By, count…By, exists…By, delete…By), and the part after By is a list of conditions on entity properties, joined by And / Or. A wrong property name fails at startup, not at runtime, which is a big advantage.

KeywordExampleJPQL / SQL idea
And, OrfindByCityAndStatus(c, s)where city=?1 and status=?2
Is, EqualsfindByEmail(e)where email=?1
BetweenfindBySalaryMaxBetween(a, b)between ?1 and ?2
LessThan, LessThanEqualfindByExperienceLessThan(3)< ?1
GreaterThan, GreaterThanEqualfindByCreatedAtGreaterThanEqual(t)>= ?1
After, BeforefindByPostedAtAfter(t)> ?1 / < ?1
IsNull, IsNotNullfindByClosedAtIsNull()is null
Like, NotLikefindByTitleLike("%dev%")like ?1 (you add the %)
ContainingfindByTitleContaining("dev")like %?1% (adds %)
StartingWith, EndingWithfindByNameStartingWith("A")like ?1% / like %?1
IgnoreCasefindByEmailIgnoreCase(e)upper(email)=upper(?1)
In, NotInfindByStatusIn(List.of(...))in (?1)
True, FalsefindByActiveTrue()active = true
OrderBy…Asc/DescfindByCityOrderByCreatedAtDesc(c)order by created_at desc
Top, FirstfindTop5ByOrderBySalaryMaxDesc()limit 5
DistinctfindDistinctByCity()select distinct
existsByexistsByEmail(e)returns boolean
countBycountByStatus(s)returns long
deleteBy, removeBydeleteByStatus(s)loads then deletes each (needs a transaction)
 
public interface JobRepository extends JpaRepository<Job, Long> {

    List<Job> findByStatusOrderByPostedAtDesc(JobStatus status);

    List<Job> findByCityIgnoreCaseAndStatus(String city, JobStatus status);

    List<Job> findTop5ByStatusOrderByPostedAtDesc(JobStatus status);

    long countByCompanyId(Long companyId);          // traverses job.company.id

    boolean existsByCompanyIdAndTitle(Long companyId, String title);

    Page<Job> findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase(String text, Pageable pageable);
}

Property traversal: findByCompanyName(n) joins to company. If a name is ambiguous, separate with an underscore: findByCompany_Name(n). findByCompanyId uses the foreign key without a join.

select j.* from job j
where upper(j.city) = upper(?) and j.status = ?

Return types

Return typeMeaning
TOne result or null; throws IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException if more than one
Optional<T>Zero or one. Use for "find one" methods
List<T>, Set<T>All results, loaded in memory
Page<T>One page + total count (an extra count query)
Slice<T>One page + "has next?" only (fetches size+1 rows, no count query)
Stream<T>Lazy stream; must run in a transaction and be closed (try-with-resources)
long, booleanFor countBy / existsBy

Use Slice for "load more" or infinite scroll when the total count is not shown; the count query on a big table can be slower than the page itself.

Limits of derived queries

Names are checked at startup and are great for one to three conditions. After that they become unreadable: findByStatusAndCityAndExperienceLessThanEqualAndSalaryMaxGreaterThanEqualOrderByPostedAtDesc. Switch to @Query (next article) for long or join-heavy queries, and to Specifications for optional filters. Derived queries also cannot do joins with conditions on collections, aggregations, or group by.

Rules

  • Property names in the method must match entity field names (postedAt, not posted_at).
  • Parameters are bound by position, in the order of the conditions in the name.
  • deleteBy… and modifying queries need a transaction; put @Transactional on the service method.
  • A repository for an aggregate root only. Do not create one repository per table (e.g. no ApplicationItemRepository if items are only reached through their parent).

Mistakes

  • Using List<T> findAll() on a table with millions of rows. Always page.
  • Returning T (not Optional) for a "find one" and then getting null or an exception when it is missing.
  • Using deleteByStatus for a mass delete: it loads every entity and deletes row by row (N+1 deletes). Use a @Modifying @Query instead.
  • Expecting Like to add wildcards. Like uses your string as is; Containing adds them.

Exceptions

  • PropertyReferenceException: No property 'x' found for type 'Job' — typo in a derived method; the app fails to start.
  • IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException — a single-result method found two rows.
  • InvalidDataAccessApiUsageException: no transaction — deleteBy… or a modifying query outside a transaction (TransactionRequiredException inside).
  • DataIntegrityViolationException — unique or foreign-key violation on save; map it to HTTP 409 (module 2).

Interview angle

"How does Spring Data create a repository with no implementation?" At startup it builds a JDK proxy for the interface, backed by SimpleJpaRepository; method names are parsed into queries (PartTree) and validated against the entity. "Page vs Slice?" Page runs an extra count query; Slice does not. "findAll vs findAll(Pageable)?" Memory and speed on large tables.

@Query, projections, Specifications and Query by Example

When a method name is too long, write the query with @Query (JPQL or native SQL); return small DTO projections for reads; use Specifications to build dynamic filters from optional parameters.

JPQL with @Query

JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language) looks like SQL but works on entities and fields, not tables and columns. You write from Job j where j.city = :city, and Hibernate translates it into SQL for your database. That is why JPQL is portable.

public interface JobRepository extends JpaRepository<Job, Long> {

    @Query("""
           select j from Job j
           where j.status = :status
             and (:city is null or lower(j.city) = lower(:city))
             and j.salary.max >= :minSalary
           order by j.postedAt desc
           """)
    List<Job> search(@Param("status") JobStatus status,
                     @Param("city") String city,
                     @Param("minSalary") BigDecimal minSalary);

    @Query("select j from Job j join j.company c where c.name = :company")
    List<Job> findByCompanyName(@Param("company") String company);
}
  • Use the entity name (Job) and field names (j.postedAt), not job and posted_at.
  • Use named parameters :status with @Param("status"). Positional ?1 works but breaks silently when you reorder arguments. (With -parameters compiler flag, which Boot's Maven/Gradle plugins enable, @Param is optional; keeping it is safer.)
  • JPQL is validated at startup, so a typo fails fast.
  • The (:city is null or ...) trick works for a few optional filters; it can hurt index use. For many filters use Specifications.

Native SQL

@Query(value = """
        select * from job
        where to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || description)
              @@ plainto_tsquery('english', :text)
        """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Job> fullTextSearch(@Param("text") String text);

@Query(value = "select * from job where status = :s",
       countQuery = "select count(*) from job where status = :s",
       nativeQuery = true)
Page<Job> findPageNative(@Param("s") String status, Pageable pageable);

Native queries use table and column names and database-specific features, and are not checked at startup. They do not apply Sort from a Pageable reliably; give a countQuery and write the order by yourself. Use them for window functions, full-text search, jsonb and tuned reports.

Sorting and paging with @Query

@Query("select j from Job j where j.company.id = :companyId")
Page<Job> findByCompany(@Param("companyId") Long companyId, Pageable pageable);

// call:
jobRepository.findByCompany(7L,
        PageRequest.of(0, 10, Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "postedAt")));

Spring Data appends order by from the Sort and builds the count query from your query. If the query is complex (joins, distinct, group by), pass your own countQuery. Sort property names are entity fields in JPQL. Never concatenate user input into the query string; sort fields from the client must be checked against an allow-list.

@Modifying: UPDATE and DELETE queries

@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushAutomatically = true)
@Query("update Job j set j.status = 'CLOSED' where j.closingDate < :today")
int closeExpired(@Param("today") LocalDate today);     // returns rows changed

Call it from a @Transactional service method. A bulk statement runs directly in the database and bypasses the persistence context: entities already loaded in memory still show the old values. clearAutomatically = true clears the context after the update so the next read hits the database; flushAutomatically = true flushes pending changes first. Bulk statements also skip @Version, lifecycle callbacks and auditing, unless you handle them yourself. One UPDATE for 100,000 rows beats loading and changing 100,000 entities.

Projections: read only what you need

Loading an entire Job (with description text and relationships) to show a list of titles wastes memory and time. A projection returns only chosen fields.

// 1. Interface-based (closed projection): getters named like entity fields
public interface JobSummary {
    Long getId();
    String getTitle();
    String getCity();
}
List<JobSummary> findByStatus(JobStatus status);   // derived query, selects 3 columns

// 2. Record / DTO-based
public record JobCard(Long id, String title, String companyName) {}

List<JobCard> findCardsByStatus(JobStatus status);   // derived queries can return DTOs too

@Query("""
       select new com.example.jobs.job.JobCard(j.id, j.title, c.name)
       from Job j join j.company c
       where j.status = :status
       """)
List<JobCard> cards(@Param("status") JobStatus status);   // constructor expression
select j.id, j.title, c.name
from job j join company c on c.id = j.company_id
where j.status = ?
KindProsCons
Interface (closed)Little code; Spring selects only the declared fieldsProxy-based; native queries need aliases matching the getters
Interface (open, with @Value("#{...}"))Computed valuesLoads the whole entity; loses the benefit
Record / class DTOPlain, immutable, easy to testNeeds a matching constructor; full class name in a JPQL constructor expression
Dynamic: findBy(..., Class<T>)Same method, many projection typesGeneric parameter at the end of the method

Projections are also a way to dodge the N+1 problem (next module topics): a DTO query with an explicit join reads exactly what the response needs in one SQL statement.

Specifications: dynamic filters

The "search jobs" screen has optional filters: city, minimum salary, keyword, status. Writing one method per combination is impossible. A Specification is a small reusable predicate; you combine the ones you need. Make the repository also extend JpaSpecificationExecutor<Job>.

public interface JobRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Job, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Job> { }

public final class JobSpecs {
    private JobSpecs() { }

    public static Specification<Job> hasStatus(JobStatus status) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("status"), status);
    }
    public static Specification<Job> inCity(String city) {
        return (root, query, cb) ->
                cb.equal(cb.lower(root.get("city")), city.toLowerCase());
    }
    public static Specification<Job> titleContains(String text) {
        return (root, query, cb) ->
                cb.like(cb.lower(root.get("title")), "%" + text.toLowerCase() + "%");
    }
    public static Specification<Job> minSalary(BigDecimal min) {
        return (root, query, cb) ->
                cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(root.get("salary").get("max"), min);
    }
}

// in the service
Specification<Job> spec = Specification.where(JobSpecs.hasStatus(JobStatus.OPEN));
if (city != null && !city.isBlank()) spec = spec.and(JobSpecs.inCity(city));
if (text != null && !text.isBlank()) spec = spec.and(JobSpecs.titleContains(text));
if (min != null) spec = spec.and(JobSpecs.minSalary(min));

Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("postedAt").descending());
Page<Job> page = jobRepository.findAll(spec, pageable);

Each lambda gets root (the entity, like from Job j), query and the CriteriaBuilder cb. The builder produces a type-aware, injection-safe query: user text goes in as a bound parameter. The attribute names are strings, so a typo fails at runtime; the JPA static metamodel (Job_.status) gives compile-time safety if you generate it. Combining with and/or/not reads well.

Query by Example (QBE), briefly

Job probe = new Job();
probe.setCity("Pune");
ExampleMatcher matcher = ExampleMatcher.matching()
        .withIgnoreCase()
        .withStringMatcher(ExampleMatcher.StringMatcher.CONTAINING);
List<Job> jobs = jobRepository.findAll(Example.of(probe, matcher));   // needs QueryByExampleExecutor

QBE builds a query from a filled-in "probe" object. It is quick for simple equality and string matching on non-null fields, but it cannot express ranges, or or nested collections. Most real projects choose Specifications (or QueryDSL / jOOQ for heavy reporting).

NeedUse
One or two simple conditionsDerived query
Fixed, joined, or aggregated query@Query JPQL
Database-specific feature@Query(nativeQuery = true)
List screen with few columnsProjection (interface or record)
Optional filters from a search formSpecifications
Prototype with equality filtersQuery by Example

Mistakes

  • Table names in JPQL: from job works only if it happens to match the entity name. Think entities.
  • Forgetting @Modifying on an update query: an InvalidDataAccessApiUsageException at runtime (the query is run as a SELECT and the DML is rejected).
  • Concatenating user input into a JPQL or native string: SQL/JPQL injection. Always bind parameters.
  • Reading entities after a bulk update without clearAutomatically: you see stale values.
  • Projection getter names that do not match fields: null values, or startup errors for constructor expressions with the wrong signature.

Interview angle

"JPQL vs native?" JPQL is portable and entity-based, validated at startup; native is raw SQL, not portable, for special features. "Why use projections?" Fewer columns, less memory, no lazy loading, avoids N+1. "How do you build a search with optional filters?" Specifications (or Criteria API) combined with and, with paging. "After a bulk update, why are my entities stale?" The persistence context was bypassed; clear it.

Relationships: owning side, mappedBy, cascade and orphanRemoval

A relationship is stored as a foreign key; the entity whose table holds that column is the owning side, mappedBy marks the inverse side, and cascade and orphanRemoval decide what happens to children when the parent changes.

The four relationship types

AnnotationMeaningDatabase shapeExample
