@ManyToOneMany rows point to oneFK column on the "many" tableJob → Company
@OneToManyOne row has many childrenFK on the child table (mirror of ManyToOne)Company → Jobs
@ManyToManyMany to manyA join table with two FKsJob ↔ Tag
@OneToOneOne to oneFK (unique) on one side, or shared primary keyUser → Profile

Every relationship can be unidirectional (only one entity has a field) or bidirectional (both have one). The database has just one foreign key either way. In bidirectional relations, two Java fields describe one FK, so JPA needs to know which field is "the real one".

The owning side and mappedBy

The owning side is the one that controls the foreign key column: when you change it, Hibernate writes the FK. It is always the side whose table contains the foreign key: the @ManyToOne side. The other side is the inverse side, marked with mappedBy = "fieldNameOnTheOwner"; changes made only on the inverse side are ignored when saving.

@Entity
public class Company {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "company", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<Job> jobs = new ArrayList<>();    // inverse side

    public void addJob(Job job) {                       // keep both sides in sync
        jobs.add(job);
        job.setCompany(this);
    }
    public void removeJob(Job job) {
        jobs.remove(job);
        job.setCompany(null);
    }
}

@Entity
public class Job {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "company_id", nullable = false)  // owning side: the FK
    private Company company;
}

@JoinColumn names the FK column (the default would be company_id anyway). Without mappedBy, a @OneToMany becomes its own owning side and Hibernate creates a hidden join table (company_jobs) or, with @JoinColumn on the many side, extra UPDATE statements. Both are usually unwanted.

Helper methods keep both sides in sync

In memory, Java does not update the other side for you. If you only call company.getJobs().add(job), job.getCompany() stays null, and since Job is the owner, the FK is saved as NULL (or the insert fails). Always change both sides in one place, with addJob/removeJob methods, and avoid exposing the raw list for modification (return Collections.unmodifiableList(jobs)).

Unidirectional vs bidirectional

  • Prefer unidirectional @ManyToOne only: Job.company exists, Company.jobs does not. You can still ask jobRepository.findByCompanyId(id) with paging. It is simpler, avoids sync bugs and JSON loops, and avoids loading big collections.
  • Add the @OneToMany side only when the parent really owns a small child list and cascading is useful (an Order with its OrderItems). A company with 50,000 jobs should never be loaded through company.getJobs().
  • Avoid a unidirectional @OneToMany without mappedBy: it generates inefficient SQL.

Cascade types

Cascade says "when I do this to the parent, do it to the children too".

CascadeTypeEffect
PERSISTSaving the parent (persist) saves new children
MERGEMerging the parent merges the children
REMOVEDeleting the parent deletes the children
REFRESH, DETACHPassed to children on refresh / detach
ALLAll of the above

Cascade is for composition: children that cannot exist without the parent and are not shared (an order and its items; a job and its screening questions). Do not cascade across independent aggregates: deleting a Company must not silently delete Users, and an Application must not cascade REMOVE to its Job.

orphanRemoval = true deletes a child when it is removed from the parent's collection (company.getJobs().remove(job) → DELETE), even if the parent itself stays. Use it only for true compositions. Do not replace the collection object (setJobs(newList)) on an orphanRemoval collection: Hibernate throws HibernateException: A collection with cascade="all-delete-orphan" was no longer referenced. Clear and addAll instead.

Never CascadeType.REMOVE (or ALL) on @ManyToMany

Deleting one Job would delete every Tag it links to, although other jobs use those tags. The same for REMOVE on a @ManyToOne: deleting a job would delete its company. Rule: cascade flows from parent to owned children only.

@ManyToMany and the join table

@Entity
public class Job {
    // ...
    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(name = "job_tag",
            joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "job_id"),
            inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "tag_id"))
    private Set<Tag> tags = new HashSet<>();

    public void addTag(Tag tag)    { tags.add(tag);    tag.getJobs().add(this); }
    public void removeTag(Tag tag) { tags.remove(tag); tag.getJobs().remove(this); }
}

@Entity
public class Tag {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;

    @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "tags")          // inverse side
    private Set<Job> jobs = new HashSet<>();
}
create table job_tag (
    job_id bigint not null references job(id),
    tag_id bigint not null references tag(id),
    primary key (job_id, tag_id)
);

Use Set for @ManyToMany: removing from a List makes Hibernate delete all join rows of that owner and re-insert the remaining ones; a Set deletes just one row. For @OneToMany a List without @OrderColumn is a "bag" (unordered, duplicates allowed); a Set avoids the MultipleBagFetchException trap (see fetching pitfalls), but then equals/hashCode must be correct (entities).

Many-to-many with extra columns: an explicit join entity

The moment the link needs data of its own (when did the user apply, with which status, which cover letter), the join table has columns beyond the two FKs. @ManyToMany cannot hold them. Model the link as an entity with two @ManyToOnes. In the job portal, Application is exactly this: User ↔ Job many-to-many, made explicit (see the full example).

Wrong: no place for status

@ManyToMany
@JoinTable(name = "application", ...)
private Set<Job> appliedJobs;       // where do appliedAt and status go?

Right: explicit entity

@Entity
class Application {
    @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) private User applicant;
    @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) private Job job;
    private Instant appliedAt;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) private ApplicationStatus status;
}

@OneToOne and @MapsId

A one-to-one is a foreign key with a unique constraint. The owning side holds the FK (@JoinColumn); the other uses mappedBy. Because Hibernate cannot make the inverse side lazy without extra work (it must query to know whether the row exists), the inverse side of a bidirectional @OneToOne is often loaded eagerly anyway. Prefer unidirectional from the side with the FK.

@MapsId shares the primary key: the child's id is the parent's id, so no separate FK or index is needed.

@Entity
public class UserProfile {
    @Id
    private Long id;                         // same value as user.id

    @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @MapsId                                  // copies user's id into this id
    @JoinColumn(name = "id")
    private User user;

    private String headline;
    private String resumeUrl;
}

@JoinColumn and defaults

  • @JoinColumn(name = "company_id", nullable = false) sets the FK column name and NOT NULL.
  • foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_job_company") names the constraint (useful if Hibernate generates the DDL).
  • optional = false on @ManyToOne tells Hibernate the FK is never null, so it can use inner joins.

Rules

  • The side with the foreign key (@ManyToOne) is the owner; mappedBy goes on the other side and names the owner's field.
  • Only the owning side writes the FK. Update both sides in memory with helper methods.
  • Cascade and orphanRemoval only for owned children (composition).
  • Use Set for @ManyToMany; use an explicit entity when the link has its own data.
  • Do not use entities with bidirectional links in JSON responses; use DTOs (module 2).

Exceptions and edge cases

  • TransientPropertyValueException: object references an unsaved transient instance — you linked to an entity that was never persisted and has no cascade.
  • DataIntegrityViolationException (null value in column "company_id") — set only the inverse side.
  • ConstraintViolationException on delete — a child row still references the parent; delete children first or cascade.
  • StackOverflowError in toString/hashCode/Jackson — bidirectional loop (entities).

Interview angle

"What is the owning side?" The side with the foreign key; the other has mappedBy. "What does mappedBy do?" Tells JPA this side only mirrors a mapping defined on the other entity, so no extra table or column. "Cascade vs orphanRemoval?" Cascade propagates operations; orphanRemoval deletes children that leave the collection. "How to model many-to-many with extra columns?" A join entity with two ManyToOne. "Why Set for ManyToMany?" Efficient removal and no duplicates.

Project 2 model: User, Company, Job, Application

A full set of entities for the job portal: Company 1-n Job, User 1-n Application n-1 Job, with lazy ManyToOne everywhere, a Set-based tag link, the matching Flyway SQL, and the repository methods that read it.

The job portal has recruiters who post jobs for a company, and candidates who apply. The relationships are:

  • Company → Job: one-to-many; Job.company is the owner.
  • Company → User: a recruiter works for one company (User.company, nullable for candidates).
  • User ↔ Job through Application: an explicit join entity with status and date. A candidate may apply to a job only once: a unique constraint on (job_id, user_id).

Base class with the shared id

@MappedSuperclass
public abstract class BaseEntity {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    public Long getId() { return id; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (o == null || Hibernate.getClass(this) != Hibernate.getClass(o)) return false;
        BaseEntity other = (BaseEntity) o;
        return id != null && id.equals(other.getId());
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() { return Hibernate.getClass(this).hashCode(); }
}

A @MappedSuperclass is not an entity itself; its fields become columns in each subclass's table. Audit fields are added to it in the auditing article.

The entities

@Entity
@Table(name = "company")
public class Company extends BaseEntity {

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 120)
    private String name;

    @Column(length = 200)
    private String website;

    protected Company() { }
    public Company(String name, String website) { this.name = name; this.website = website; }
    // getters
    // No Set<Job> jobs on purpose: a company can have thousands of jobs.
}
@Entity
@Table(name = "app_user")
public class User extends BaseEntity {

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 80)  private String name;
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 150) private String email;
    @Column(name = "password_hash", nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String passwordHash;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private Role role;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)           // null for candidates
    @JoinColumn(name = "company_id")
    private Company company;

    protected User() { }
    // constructor, getters
}
@Entity
@Table(name = "job")
public class Job extends BaseEntity {

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 150) private String title;
    @Column(nullable = false, columnDefinition = "text") private String description;
    @Column(length = 80) private String city;

    @Embedded private SalaryRange salary;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private JobStatus status = JobStatus.OPEN;

    @Column(name = "posted_at", nullable = false)
    private Instant postedAt = Instant.now();

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "company_id", nullable = false)
    private Company company;

    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(name = "job_tag",
            joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "job_id"),
            inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "tag_id"))
    private Set<Tag> tags = new HashSet<>();

    protected Job() { }
    public Job(Company company, String title, String description) {
        this.company = company; this.title = title; this.description = description;
    }
    public void close() { this.status = JobStatus.CLOSED; }
}
@Entity
@Table(name = "application",
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(
               name = "uk_application_job_user", columnNames = {"job_id", "user_id"}))
public class Application extends BaseEntity {

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "job_id", nullable = false)
    private Job job;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "user_id", nullable = false)
    private User applicant;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private ApplicationStatus status = ApplicationStatus.SUBMITTED;

    @Column(name = "cover_letter", columnDefinition = "text")
    private String coverLetter;

    @Column(name = "applied_at", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private Instant appliedAt = Instant.now();

    protected Application() { }
    public Application(Job job, User applicant, String coverLetter) {
        this.job = job; this.applicant = applicant; this.coverLetter = coverLetter;
    }
    public void shortlist() { this.status = ApplicationStatus.SHORTLISTED; }
}

Notice the decisions: every @ManyToOne is LAZY; nobody has a List that could grow without limit; the one collection (tags) is a Set and small; Application has behaviour (shortlist()) instead of a public setter.

The matching Flyway migration

CREATE TABLE company (
    id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    website VARCHAR(200)
);

CREATE TABLE app_user (
    id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name          VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL,
    email         VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    password_hash VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    role          VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
    company_id    BIGINT REFERENCES company (id),
    CONSTRAINT uk_user_email UNIQUE (email)
);

CREATE TABLE job (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    company_id  BIGINT       NOT NULL REFERENCES company (id),
    title       VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    description TEXT         NOT NULL,
    city        VARCHAR(80),
    salary_min  NUMERIC(12, 2),
    salary_max  NUMERIC(12, 2),
    status      VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
    posted_at   TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_job_company ON job (company_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_job_status_posted ON job (status, posted_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE application (
    id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    job_id       BIGINT      NOT NULL REFERENCES job (id),
    user_id      BIGINT      NOT NULL REFERENCES app_user (id),
    status       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    cover_letter TEXT,
    applied_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uk_application_job_user UNIQUE (job_id, user_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_application_user ON application (user_id);

PostgreSQL does not index foreign key columns automatically, so add indexes on job.company_id and application.user_id yourself (the unique index on (job_id, user_id) already covers lookups by job_id). See SQL · Module 5 on indexes.

Repositories and a service

public interface ApplicationRepository extends JpaRepository<Application, Long> {

    boolean existsByJobIdAndApplicantId(Long jobId, Long userId);

    Page<Application> findByApplicantId(Long userId, Pageable pageable);

    @Query("select a from Application a join fetch a.applicant where a.job.id = :jobId")
    List<Application> findForJob(@Param("jobId") Long jobId);
}

@Service
public class ApplicationService {
    // constructor injection of repositories omitted

    @Transactional
    public Long apply(Long jobId, Long userId, String coverLetter) {
        if (applicationRepository.existsByJobIdAndApplicantId(jobId, userId)) {
            throw new DuplicateResourceException("Already applied");
        }
        Job job = jobRepository.findById(jobId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Job", jobId));
        if (job.getStatus() != JobStatus.OPEN) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Job is closed");
        }
        User applicant = userRepository.getReferenceById(userId);   // no SELECT
        return applicationRepository.save(
                new Application(job, applicant, coverLetter)).getId();
    }
}
select count(*) > 0 from application where job_id=? and user_id=?
select ... from job where id=?
insert into application (applied_at, cover_letter, job_id, status, user_id)
    values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)

Design notes

  • The database UNIQUE (job_id, user_id) is the real guarantee; the existsBy check only gives a friendly message. Catch DataIntegrityViolationException for the race.
  • Give constraints and indexes explicit names. They appear in error messages and make migrations easier to read.
  • Aggregate boundaries: Application has its own repository because it is queried by user and by job, not only through a parent.

In real projects

Teams often skip bidirectional collections entirely and read children through repositories with paging, which avoids both huge collections and the N+1 traps discussed next. Cascading is used rarely: for an Order with its OrderItems, yes; for anything shared between aggregates, no.

Lazy vs eager loading, proxies and LazyInitializationException

Fetch type decides when a related entity is loaded; make every association LAZY, load what you need explicitly in the service, and turn off Open Session in View so lazy loading cannot leak into the web layer.

Lazy and eager

  • EAGER: the related data is loaded together with the owner, always, whether you need it or not.
  • LAZY: the related data is loaded only when you first touch it (job.getCompany().getName()), with a second query.
AnnotationDefault fetchMeaning of the default
@ManyToOneEAGERLoading a Job also loads its Company
@OneToOneEAGERSame
@OneToManyLAZYChildren loaded on first access
@ManyToManyLAZYJoin rows loaded on first access
@Basic fieldsEAGERColumn loaded with the row (LAZY on a basic field needs bytecode enhancement)

The defaults are historical and dangerous: an eager @ManyToOne on Application.job means "load 20 applications" also loads 20 jobs, and each job eagerly loads its company. With JPQL/derived queries this becomes extra queries per row; with findById it becomes joins you did not ask for. Also, fetch = EAGER cannot be switched off for a single query. LAZY can be switched on per query (join fetch, entity graph), so LAZY is the flexible default.

Rule: make every association LAZY

Write @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) and @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) everywhere. Then decide per use case what to load: JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, batch fetching, or a DTO projection (see the N+1 article).

How lazy loading works: proxies

For a lazy @ManyToOne, Hibernate puts a proxy in the field: a generated subclass of Company that holds only the id. Calling job.getCompany().getId() does not hit the database. The first call to any other method (getName()) makes the proxy run select ... from company where id=? through the open session and fill itself. For a lazy collection, Hibernate puts its own collection class (PersistentBag/PersistentSet) that loads on first iteration or size().

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public String companyOfJob(Long jobId) {
    Job job = jobRepository.findById(jobId).orElseThrow();   // select from job where id=?
    Company c = job.getCompany();                             // proxy, no SQL yet
    return c.getName();                                       // select from company where id=?
}

Consequences of proxies: c.getClass() is not Company but Company$HibernateProxy$...; instanceof and equals need care (Hibernate.getClass, entities); final classes and methods cannot be proxied.

LazyInitializationException

The proxy can only load data while its session is open, that is, inside the transaction. If you touch it after the service method returned, there is no session and you get:

org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy
[com.example.jobs.company.Company#7] - no Session
// service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public Job getJob(Long id) { return jobRepository.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }

// controller (no transaction)
Job job = jobService.getJob(5L);
return job.getCompany().getName();       // BOOM: session already closed

Wrong fixes people copy from the internet: make the association EAGER (slow everywhere), add @Transactional to the controller (wrong layer), or keep Open Session in View. Right fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Map to a DTO inside the service (inside the transaction) and return the DTO. This is the standard in module 2.
  2. Load what you need with the query: join fetch, @EntityGraph, or a DTO/projection query that selects the fields directly.
  3. Initialise explicitly in the service (Hibernate.initialize(job.getTags())) only for rare cases.

Open Session in View (OSIV)

Open Session in View keeps the Hibernate session open for the whole HTTP request, until the response is written. Lazy loading then works in the controller and in JSON serialization. Spring Boot enables it by default (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true) and prints a warning at startup: "spring.jpa.open-in-view is enabled by default... Explicitly configure spring.jpa.open-in-view to disable this warning".

Why it exists

  • No LazyInitializationException in controllers or views.
  • Convenient for quick demos.

Why to switch it off

  • Hides N+1 queries: every row serialised can fire a query, outside any transaction boundary.
  • Holds a database connection for the whole request, including slow JSON writing and calls to other services, so the pool runs out under load.
  • Lets the web layer depend on entity internals; the service stops being the data boundary.
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

With it off, your code must fetch everything the response needs inside the service. That is the discipline you want, and the exceptions will tell you early where a fetch is missing.

Eager loading when you do need it

Do not mark the mapping EAGER. Ask for it in the query instead, so only that screen pays:

@Query("select j from Job j join fetch j.company where j.id = :id")
Optional<Job> findWithCompany(@Param("id") Long id);

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "company")
Optional<Job> findDetailedById(Long id);          // derived query + graph
select j.*, c.* from job j join company c on c.id = j.company_id where j.id = ?

Other lazy-related details

  • getReferenceById gives a proxy on purpose (persistence context).
  • Lazy basic fields and @Lob: to avoid loading a big text column, move it to its own entity or use a projection; true attribute laziness needs Hibernate bytecode enhancement.
  • optional = false helps Hibernate use an inner join instead of a left join for fetches.
  • Serialising entities with Jackson triggers lazy loads on every getter, one more reason for DTOs.

Exceptions

  • LazyInitializationException — lazy association touched with no open session (above).
  • EntityNotFoundException — a proxy tries to load a row that was deleted.
  • HibernateException: Unable to find ... with id — same cause, older style message, from stale foreign keys.

Mistakes

  • Making associations EAGER to silence LazyInitializationException. You trade one error for hidden slowness.
  • Leaving OSIV on because the app "works", then discovering 300 queries per page in production.
  • Calling a lazy getter in a toString() (Lombok) or in logging.

Interview angle

"What is LazyInitializationException and how do you fix it?" Explain proxy + closed session, then give the DTO-in-service and fetch-in-query fixes, and say why not EAGER or OSIV. "What are the default fetch types?" ToOne = EAGER, ToMany = LAZY. "What is Open Session in View and should you use it?" Describe it and its connection and N+1 downsides; recommend false.

The N+1 problem: detect and fix with JOIN FETCH, EntityGraph and batching

N+1 means one query loads N parents and then N more queries load each parent's relation; find it in the SQL log, and fix it with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, batch fetching or a DTO query.

What it is

You load a list of Applications (1 query) and then, for each one, print app.getApplicant().getName(). Because applicant is lazy, Hibernate loads each user separately: N more queries. For 50 applications, that is 51 queries instead of 1 or 2. It looks fine with 5 rows in development and kills the database with 5,000 rows in production.

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<ApplicantRow> applicantsOfJob(Long jobId) {
    List<Application> apps = applicationRepository.findByJobId(jobId);   // 1 query
    return apps.stream()
            .map(a -> new ApplicantRow(a.getId(), a.getApplicant().getName()))  // N queries
            .toList();
}
select a.* from application a where a.job_id=?          -- 1 query, 3 rows
select u.* from app_user u where u.id=?                 -- user 11
select u.* from app_user u where u.id=?                 -- user 12
select u.* from app_user u where u.id=?                 -- user 13

The same happens with a lazy collection: companies.forEach(c -> c.getJobs().size()) runs one extra query per company. And with EAGER associations on a JPQL query: Hibernate loads the parents with your query, then loads each eager relation with separate queries. Eager is not a fix; it is another source of N+1.

Detecting it

  1. Read the SQL log. Turn on logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug in development and look for the same statement repeating with different ids (SQL logging).
  2. Hibernate statistics. spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true plus logging.level.org.hibernate.stat=debug prints, per session, how many statements were prepared. A list page with 100+ statements is a red flag.
  3. Tests that count queries. Libraries such as datasource-proxy or Hypersistence Utils assert "this method runs at most 2 queries". It stops regressions.
  4. APM / slow query logs in production show hundreds of identical short queries per request.

Fix 1: JOIN FETCH

join fetch tells JPQL to load the association in the same SQL statement with a join.

@Query("""
       select a from Application a
       join fetch a.applicant
       where a.job.id = :jobId
       """)
List<Application> findByJobIdWithApplicant(@Param("jobId") Long jobId);
select a.*, u.*
from application a join app_user u on u.id = a.user_id
where a.job_id = ?

Use left join fetch when the association may be null or empty (a company with no jobs). distinct removes duplicate parents when you fetch a collection: select distinct c from Company c left join fetch c.jobs (Hibernate 6 removes duplicate entities automatically, but keeping distinct is harmless and clearer).

Fix 2: @EntityGraph

An entity graph says "load these attributes eagerly for this call", without writing JPQL. It works on derived queries and findAll overrides.

public interface ApplicationRepository extends JpaRepository<Application, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"applicant", "job"})
    List<Application> findByJobId(Long jobId);              // derived query + graph

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"job", "job.company"})   // nested path
    Page<Application> findByApplicantId(Long userId, Pageable pageable);
}

An entity graph is a fetch hint, by default of type "fetch" (the listed attributes are eager, others keep their mapping). It is convenient and keeps method names clean; join fetch gives you more control (filters on the joined rows, aliases).

Fix 3: batch fetching

Instead of one query per parent, Hibernate can load many at once: ... where id in (?, ?, ?, ...). This is configured globally, and it makes lazy loading cheap without changing any query.

spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=16
select a.* from application a where a.job_id=?
select u.* from app_user u where u.id in (?,?,?, ... up to 16 ids)

Per association you can use Hibernate's @BatchSize(size = 16) on the field or class. A value between 10 and 50 is common. It is a good safety net: set it once and many accidental N+1s become 1+1.

Fix 4: DTO projection

If the screen needs only a few fields, do not load entities at all (projections):

public record ApplicantRow(Long applicationId, String name, String email,
                           ApplicationStatus status) {}

@Query("""
       select new com.example.jobs.application.ApplicantRow(
              a.id, u.name, u.email, a.status)
       from Application a join a.applicant u
       where a.job.id = :jobId
       """)
List<ApplicantRow> findApplicantRows(@Param("jobId") Long jobId);

This is the fastest option for read-only lists: no entities, no persistence-context tracking, no lazy loading.

FixBest whenWatch out for
JOIN FETCHYou need the entities and the relation, one-to-one or many-to-oneCollections + pagination; duplicates
@EntityGraphSame, with derived queries or findAllSame limits as join fetch
Batch fetchingMany places; collections; paginationStill extra queries (but few)
DTO projectionRead-only list or report screensNo entity behaviour; one DTO per screen

Pitfall 1: JOIN FETCH of a collection with pagination

SQL pages by rows, but a join with a collection multiplies parent rows (a company with 3 jobs appears 3 times). If you ask for page 0 of size 10 on select c from Company c join fetch c.jobs, Hibernate cannot use limit on the SQL safely. It loads all rows, applies the limit in memory and logs a warning (it mentions applying pagination in memory). On a big table this is an outage waiting to happen.

Wrong: fetch join on a collection + Pageable

@Query("select c from Company c left join fetch c.jobs")
Page<Company> findAllWithJobs(Pageable p);   // pagination in memory

Right: page the parents, then fetch children

Page<Company> page = companyRepository.findAll(pageable);   // limit in SQL
// children: default_batch_fetch_size loads jobs for the page with 1 "in" query
// or: select c from Company c left join fetch c.jobs where c in :companies

Fetch joins on to-one associations (join fetch a.applicant) are safe with pagination because they do not multiply rows.

Pitfall 2: MultipleBagFetchException

Fetching two List (bag) collections in one query, such as join fetch j.tags join fetch j.questions, would produce a Cartesian product and Hibernate refuses: org.hibernate.loader.MultipleBagFetchException: cannot simultaneously fetch multiple bags. Fixes: change the collections to Set, or fetch one collection per query (the second query hits the persistence context and fills the other collection), or use batch fetching. Do not "fix" it with FetchType.EAGER.

Pitfall 3: the Cartesian product

Fetching two collections even as Sets multiplies rows (3 tags × 4 questions = 12 rows per job). Prefer one collection per query plus batch fetching.

A practical routine

  1. Keep everything LAZY.
  2. Set default_batch_fetch_size to a modest number as a net.
  3. For each list endpoint, look at the SQL; use DTO projections or join fetch on to-one relations.
  4. Add a query-count assertion in the integration test of the heavy endpoints.

Edge cases

  • LazyInitializationException remains if you add the relation to the DTO but forget to fetch it and map outside the transaction (fetching).
  • Batch fetching applies to lazy loads by id and to collections; it does not rewrite your JPQL.
  • Two queries are not "bad": fetching the parents then one batch query for the children is often better than one huge join.

Interview angle

One of the most common JPA questions. Strong answer: define it with a number ("1 + N queries"), give the lazy-loop example, say how you detect it (SQL log, statistics, query-count tests), list four fixes (join fetch, entity graph, batch size, DTO projection), and mention the two pitfalls: join fetch of a collection with pagination (in-memory) and MultipleBagFetchException. Add why EAGER does not fix it.

@Transactional in depth: proxies, propagation and rollback

@Transactional wraps your bean in a proxy that begins a transaction before the method and commits or rolls back after it; know the self-invocation trap, the rollback rules for checked exceptions and what each propagation value does.

A transaction is an all-or-nothing group of database operations (ACID; see SQL · Module 5). In Spring you do not write begin/commit; you annotate a method and Spring does it. This works because of the AOP proxies from module 1.

How it works: the proxy

When Spring finds @Transactional, it does not give other beans your object; it gives a proxy (a generated subclass with CGLIB, or a JDK interface proxy) with a TransactionInterceptor. The interceptor asks the PlatformTransactionManager (for JPA, JpaTransactionManager) to start a transaction, binds the connection and the EntityManager to the current thread, calls your method, and then commits or rolls back. Hibernate flushes right before the commit, so most SQL runs at the end of the method (flush). Repository methods are already transactional by themselves (SimpleJpaRepository has @Transactional(readOnly = true) on reads and @Transactional on writes), but each call is its own transaction; the service method joins them into one.

@Service
public class ApplicationService {

    @Transactional
    public void withdraw(Long applicationId, Long userId) {
        Application app = applicationRepository.findById(applicationId).orElseThrow();
        if (!app.getApplicant().getId().equals(userId)) {
            throw new AccessDeniedException("Not your application");  // rolls back
        }
        app.withdraw();                                  // dirty checking: UPDATE
        notificationRepository.save(Notification.of(app));   // INSERT, same transaction
    }                                  // both statements commit, or neither
}

The self-invocation pitfall

Only calls that go through the proxy start a transaction. When a method of the same class calls another method of that class, the call is this.method(), which skips the proxy, so the annotation on the second method is ignored.

Wrong: self-invocation

@Service
public class ReportService {
    public void run() {
        saveAudit();                   // this.saveAudit(): NO new transaction
    }
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void saveAudit() { ... }
}

Right: call through another bean

@Service
public class ReportService {
    private final AuditService auditService;     // separate bean
    public void run() {
        auditService.saveAudit();                // goes through the proxy
    }
}
@Service
public class AuditService {
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void saveAudit() { ... }
}

Alternatives: inject the bean into itself (ugly), use TransactionTemplate for programmatic control, or use AspectJ weaving (rare). Splitting into two beans is the usual fix. The same trap affects @Async, @Cacheable and other proxy-based annotations.

Where it works

  • On public methods of Spring beans called from other beans. Spring 6 also supports protected and package-visible methods with class-based proxies, but public is the safe, portable habit.
  • Not on private methods, final methods (CGLIB cannot override them) or objects created with new.
  • Prefer the service layer: a service method is the business unit of work. Not on controllers (web concerns, longer than needed) and not on every repository call.
  • Class-level @Transactional applies to all public methods; method-level overrides it. Put @Transactional(readOnly = true) on the class and @Transactional on the writing methods.

Rollback rules

By default a transaction rolls back only for unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and subclasses) and Error. A checked exception (IOException, your own extends Exception) does not roll back: the transaction commits whatever was already flushed.

@Transactional                                   // checked exception: COMMITS
public void importJobs(MultipartFile file) throws IOException { ... }

@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)    // rolls back on any exception
public void importJobs(MultipartFile file) throws IOException { ... }

@Transactional(noRollbackFor = DuplicateResourceException.class)
public void tolerateDuplicates() { ... }

Many teams make their domain exceptions unchecked (as in module 2) to avoid this. A catch that swallows the exception also prevents rollback: try { ... } catch (Exception e) { log.error(...); } inside a transactional method means Spring never sees the failure. Rethrow it, or call TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly().

Propagation

Propagation answers: "if a transaction already exists when this method is called, what do I do?"

PropagationExisting transactionNo transactionTypical use
REQUIRED (default)Join itCreate oneAlmost everything
REQUIRES_NEWSuspend it, run in a new independent transactionCreate oneAudit log or outbox write that must survive a rollback of the caller
NESTEDRun inside a savepoint; rolls back aloneCreate oneTry something optional, keep the outer work; needs savepoint support (JDBC with JpaTransactionManager)
SUPPORTSJoin itRun withoutRead helper that works either way
MANDATORYJoin itThrow IllegalTransactionStateExceptionCode that must never run alone
NOT_SUPPORTEDSuspend it, run withoutRun withoutLong non-transactional work, e.g. a call to a slow service
NEVERThrow an exceptionRun withoutAssert "no transaction here"

REQUIRED means inner calls share one transaction, so one failure rolls back everything. REQUIRES_NEW uses a second database connection while the first waits, so overuse can exhaust the pool (a deadlock risk with a pool of 1). With REQUIRES_NEW, the inner transaction cannot see uncommitted data of the outer one.

The "silently rolled back" surprise

With REQUIRED, inner and outer share one transaction. If the inner method throws a runtime exception, Spring marks the whole transaction rollback-only. If the outer method catches that exception and carries on, then at commit Spring throws:

org.springframework.transaction.UnexpectedRollbackException:
Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only
@Transactional
public void outer() {
    try {
        inner.doWork();             // REQUIRED, throws RuntimeException: marks rollback-only
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        log.warn("ignored", e);     // you swallowed it, but the mark stays
    }
    repo.save(x);                   // commit fails: UnexpectedRollbackException
}
// Fix: make inner REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED if its failure is acceptable,
// or let the exception propagate.

readOnly, isolation and timeout

@Transactional(readOnly = true)                              // reads
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.READ_COMMITTED)         // see the SQL notes
@Transactional(timeout = 5)                                  // seconds
@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class, propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED)
  • readOnly = true is a hint. With Hibernate it sets the flush mode to MANUAL (no dirty checking, less memory and CPU), and with some drivers/databases it marks the connection read-only so a replica can be used. It does not stop you from running a write query on every database. Use it on every query-only service method.
  • isolation: default DEFAULT = the database default (PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ). Raise it only when you understand the anomalies (SQL · Module 5).
  • timeout: seconds before the transaction is marked for rollback; it is checked at statement boundaries.

@Transactional in tests

In a Spring test (@SpringBootTest or @DataJpaTest), a test method annotated with @Transactional runs inside a transaction that is rolled back at the end by default, so tests leave no data behind. @DataJpaTest is already transactional. Beware: because nothing commits, flush-time errors (constraint violations) may never appear; call flush() in the test. A real test client (MockMvc in same thread is fine; an HTTP call from another thread is a different transaction) will not see uncommitted data.

Spring's vs Jakarta's annotation

org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactionaljakarta.transaction.Transactional
Attributespropagation, isolation, timeout, readOnly, rollbackFor, transactionManagerOnly value (TxType), rollbackOn, dontRollbackOn
Read-only, timeout, isolationYesNo
RecommendationUse this one in Spring appsWorks, but with fewer features; auto-complete may import it by mistake

Rules

  • Transactions belong on service methods (public, called from another bean).
  • Checked exceptions do not roll back unless you add rollbackFor.
  • Keep transactions short: no HTTP calls, file uploads or Thread.sleep inside; they hold a connection and locks.
  • Do your lazy loading and DTO mapping inside the transaction.

Mistakes

  • Self-invocation: a @Transactional method called from the same class.
  • @Transactional on a private method or on a class that is not a Spring bean: silently ignored.
  • Catching and swallowing the exception, so nothing rolls back.
  • Sending an email or a Kafka message inside the transaction, then the commit fails: the message is already out. Use the outbox pattern or send after commit (@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)).
  • Starting an async thread inside a transaction: the new thread has no transaction (transactions are thread-bound).

Interview angle

"How does @Transactional work?" Proxy + interceptor + transaction manager + thread-bound connection; commit or rollback after the call. "Why did my transaction not start?" Self-invocation, private method, not a bean. "What does it roll back on by default?" Unchecked exceptions and Errors only. "Explain REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW." Join vs suspend-and-new; give the audit-log example. "What is UnexpectedRollbackException?" Rollback-only mark set by an inner participating transaction. "Why readOnly = true?" Skips dirty checking, signals intent, may route to a replica.

Optimistic and pessimistic locking

Use @Version for optimistic locking, which detects lost updates and fails the second writer; use pessimistic locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) only for hot rows where conflicts are frequent and retries are not acceptable.

The problem: lost updates

Two recruiters open the same job. Both read vacancies = 5. One saves 4, the other saves 3 a moment later, based on the stale 5. The first change is silently overwritten: a lost update. Transactions alone do not prevent this at the default isolation level because each user reads and writes in separate requests. Background on isolation and row locks: SQL · Module 5.

Optimistic locking with @Version

Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. It does not lock rows; it checks at write time that nobody changed the row since you read it. Add a version field:

@Entity
public class Job extends BaseEntity {

    @Version
    private Long version;          // wrapper type; managed by Hibernate, no setter

    private int vacancies;
}
update job set vacancies=?, version=?, ... where id=? and version=?
-- version in the WHERE is the value you read. If another transaction
-- already changed the row, 0 rows match.

Hibernate increments version on every update. If the UPDATE affects 0 rows, someone else got there first, and Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException, which Spring translates to ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException (a subclass of OptimisticLockingFailureException). Supported version types: Long, Integer, Short or timestamp types. Add the column in the migration: version BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.

Handling the conflict

  • In a REST API, return 409 Conflict (or 412 Precondition Failed with ETag / If-Match) so the client reloads and retries. Map it in your @RestControllerAdvice (module 2).
  • Expose the version to the client. The sequence above only helps if the version read when the form was opened travels with the update. Put version in the response DTO and in the update request, then compare in the service (if (!request.version().equals(job.getVersion())) throw ...) or set it on the entity before merging. If the DTO does not carry the version, only conflicts within a single request are caught.
  • Server-side retry for automatic operations (a counter): catch the exception outside the transaction and re-run the whole transaction a few times (Spring Retry's @Retryable, or a loop).
@ExceptionHandler(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
ProblemDetail conflict(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException ex) {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
            "The record was changed by someone else. Reload and try again.");
}

Important: a bulk @Modifying query does not touch version unless you write set j.version = j.version + 1 (or use update versioned Job in HQL).

Pessimistic locking

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely: it locks the row in the database while you work, and others wait. In SQL that is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

public interface JobRepository extends JpaRepository<Job, Long> {

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("select j from Job j where j.id = :id")
    Optional<Job> findByIdForUpdate(@Param("id") Long id);

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000"))
    Optional<Job> findWithLockById(Long id);          // waits at most 3 seconds
}

@Transactional
public void reserveVacancy(Long jobId) {
    Job job = jobRepository.findByIdForUpdate(jobId).orElseThrow();   // row locked
    job.decreaseVacancies();
}                                                                      // lock released at commit
select j.* from job j where j.id = ? for update
Lock modeMeaning
PESSIMISTIC_WRITEExclusive lock (FOR UPDATE): others can neither read-for-update nor write until commit
PESSIMISTIC_READShared lock (FOR SHARE where supported): others can read, not write
OPTIMISTIC, OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENTVersion check at commit / force a version bump even without changes

The lock exists only inside a transaction, so @Transactional is required. Possible failures: PessimisticLockingFailureException (including CannotAcquireLockException when the timeout expires) and deadlocks (DeadlockLoserDataAccessException) if two transactions lock rows in opposite orders; always lock in a consistent order.

Optimistic vs pessimistic

Optimistic (@Version)Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE)
Locks heldNoneRow lock until commit
Conflict resultException for the loser, retryOthers wait
ThroughputHigh when conflicts are rareLower; risk of waiting and deadlock
Works across HTTP requestsYes (version travels in the DTO)No (lock ends with the transaction)
Best forMost CRUD, user editsCounters, stock, seat booking with heavy contention

Sometimes neither is needed: an atomic SQL update such as update job set vacancies = vacancies - 1 where id = ? and vacancies > 0 (a @Modifying query) is the simplest and fastest guard for counters.

Mistakes

  • Adding @Version but never sending the version to the client, so the form-edit race is not caught.
  • Making version a primitive long with a manually set id: save may treat the entity as old (isNew).
  • Holding a pessimistic lock while calling an external service.
  • Retrying only the failing line instead of the whole transaction: after the exception the transaction is rollback-only.

Interview angle

"How do you prevent lost updates?" Optimistic locking with @Version: describe the where version=? update, the exception and a 409 response. "When would you choose pessimistic locking?" High contention on the same rows, such as stock or seat booking, plus a lock timeout. Mention the atomic-update alternative for counters.

Auditing fields: createdAt, updatedAt, createdBy

Spring Data JPA auditing fills createdAt, updatedAt and createdBy automatically through an entity listener; put the fields in a @MappedSuperclass so every entity gets them.

Auditing means recording when a row was created or changed and by whom. Writing entity.setCreatedAt(Instant.now()) in every service is repetitive and easy to forget. Two options exist: Spring Data's auditing (portable, supports "who") and Hibernate's own annotations (simpler, time only).

Spring Data JPA auditing

  1. Enable it once with @EnableJpaAuditing on a configuration class.
  2. Add @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class) to the entity (or to a base class).
  3. Annotate fields with @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, @LastModifiedBy.
  4. For the "by" fields, provide an AuditorAware bean that returns the current user.
import org.springframework.data.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.support.AuditingEntityListener;

@MappedSuperclass
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public abstract class AuditableEntity extends BaseEntity {

    @CreatedDate
    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private Instant createdAt;

    @LastModifiedDate
    @Column(name = "updated_at", nullable = false)
    private Instant updatedAt;

    @CreatedBy
    @Column(name = "created_by", updatable = false)
    private Long createdBy;                        // user id

    @LastModifiedBy
    @Column(name = "updated_by")
    private Long updatedBy;

    public Instant getCreatedAt() { return createdAt; }
    public Instant getUpdatedAt() { return updatedAt; }
}
@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditorProvider")
public class AuditConfig {

    @Bean
    AuditorAware<Long> auditorProvider() {
        return () -> {
            Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
            if (auth == null || !auth.isAuthenticated()
                    || auth instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken) {
                return Optional.empty();                // system job or anonymous
            }
            return Optional.of(((AppUserDetails) auth.getPrincipal()).getId());
        };
    }
}

The AuditorAware body above assumes Spring Security (module 4) and a principal class that carries the user id. Until security exists, return a fixed id or Optional.empty(). Now Job extends AuditableEntity, and jobRepository.save(job) sets both timestamps on insert, and only updatedAt/updatedBy on update.

insert into job (created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by, title, ...) values (?,?,?,?,?,...)
update job set updated_at=?, updated_by=?, vacancies=?, ... where id=?

Notes: the listener runs on persist and on flush when the entity is dirty. Entities modified through bulk @Modifying queries are not audited. Add updated_at = now() to those queries by hand. @EnableJpaAuditing must not be on the main application class if you use @WebMvcTest slices (it would need the JPA metamodel); put it in a separate configuration class as shown.

Hibernate's @CreationTimestamp and @UpdateTimestamp

import org.hibernate.annotations.CreationTimestamp;
import org.hibernate.annotations.UpdateTimestamp;

@CreationTimestamp
@Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false, updatable = false)
private Instant createdAt;

@UpdateTimestamp
@Column(name = "updated_at", nullable = false)
private Instant updatedAt;
Spring Data auditingHibernate annotations@PrePersist/@PreUpdate
SetupEnable + listener + base classAnnotation onlyCallback methods
Who (user)Yes (AuditorAware)NoManual
Portable to other JPA providersYesNo (Hibernate only)Yes (standard JPA)
Best forMost apps with usersQuick timestampsCustom logic

The Product example in module 2 used @PrePersist, which is plain JPA and fine for a single field.

Conventions

  • Use Instant (UTC) and TIMESTAMPTZ; convert to a zone only for display.
  • Mark createdAt and createdBy as updatable = false.
  • Put the columns in the migration with NOT NULL; set a default for old rows in the migration that adds them.
  • Never expose audit fields as writable in request DTOs.

Mistakes

  • Forgetting @EnableJpaAuditing or @EntityListeners: the fields stay null and the insert fails on NOT NULL.
  • Expecting history. These columns hold only the latest state. For full history use Hibernate Envers or an audit table.
  • An AuditorAware that throws for system jobs; return Optional.empty() instead.

Interview angle

"How do you add createdAt/updatedAt to all entities?" A @MappedSuperclass with @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class), @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate, and @EnableJpaAuditing; mention AuditorAware for "who" and Hibernate's timestamps as a lighter alternative.

Schema migrations with Flyway in Spring Boot

Flyway runs versioned SQL files (V1__init.sql, V2__...) in order at application startup, records them in flyway_schema_history, and refuses to change a migration that was already applied.

A database schema changes over time: new columns, new tables, new indexes. A migration tool keeps the schema in version control like code, so every environment (your laptop, test, production) reaches the same state by running the same ordered scripts. Without it, teams run SQL by hand and drift apart. Flyway is the simplest and most common choice with Spring Boot (Liquibase is the other popular one). Basics of schema design are in SQL · Module 4.

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>   <!-- PostgreSQL support module -->
</dependency>

Recent Flyway versions put database support in separate modules: flyway-database-postgresql for PostgreSQL, flyway-mysql for MySQL and MariaDB. Without it you get an error such as "Unsupported Database: PostgreSQL 17".

Boot 3.x vs 4.x

In Boot 3.x, having flyway-core on the classpath is enough to turn on the auto-configuration. Boot 4 split its auto-configuration into smaller modules; the supported way there is the spring-boot-starter-flyway starter (plus the database module above). Check the Boot 4 migration notes for your exact version.

Where files go and how they are named

db/migration/
    V1__init.sql
    V2__add_tags.sql
    V3__add_job_version_column.sql
    R__job_search_view.sql
TypeName patternBehaviour
VersionedV<version>__<description>.sql (two underscores)Runs once, in version order
RepeatableR__<description>.sqlRe-runs whenever its checksum changes (views, functions)
Java-basedclass implementing JavaMigration / BaseJavaMigrationFor data fixes that SQL cannot express

Versions sort numerically (V2 before V10), and may contain dots: V1_1__... or V2.1__.... In teams, many use timestamps like V20261110_1430__add_tags.sql to avoid two developers both creating V7.

What happens at startup

  1. Boot creates the DataSource; the Flyway auto-configuration runs before JPA's EntityManagerFactory is created (Boot orders this for you).
  2. Flyway creates the table flyway_schema_history if it does not exist.
  3. It scans classpath:db/migration, compares file names and checksums with the history table.
  4. It validates already applied migrations (checksum unchanged) and runs the pending ones in order, each in a transaction where the database supports transactional DDL (PostgreSQL does; MySQL does not roll back DDL).
  5. Hibernate starts; with ddl-auto=validate it checks that entities match the schema Flyway built.
Flyway Community Edition ... by Redgate
Database: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/jobs (PostgreSQL 17.x)
Successfully validated 3 migrations (execution time 00:00.015s)
Creating Schema History table "public"."flyway_schema_history" ...
Migrating schema "public" to version "1 - init"
Migrating schema "public" to version "2 - add tags"
Successfully applied 2 migrations to schema "public", now at version v2

The full V1__init.sql for the job portal is in the relationships example. A follow-up migration:

CREATE TABLE tag (
    id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE job_tag (
    job_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES job (id),
    tag_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES tag (id),
    PRIMARY KEY (job_id, tag_id)
);

ALTER TABLE job ADD COLUMN version BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

Settings (spring.flyway.*)

PropertyPurpose
spring.flyway.enabledTurn Flyway on/off (default true when on the classpath)
spring.flyway.locationsWhere scripts are (default classpath:db/migration); can add a vendor folder such as classpath:db/migration/postgres
spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrateBaseline an existing, non-empty database on first run (see below)
spring.flyway.baseline-versionVersion assigned to the baseline (default 1)
spring.flyway.validate-on-migrateValidate checksums before migrating (default true; keep it)
spring.flyway.out-of-orderAllow a lower version to run after a higher one was applied (default false)
spring.flyway.url, user, passwordUse a separate DB account with DDL rights; by default Flyway uses the app's datasource
spring.flyway.clean-disabledFlyway's clean drops everything; it is disabled by default in current versions. Never enable in production.
 
spring.flyway.enabled=true
spring.flyway.locations=classpath:db/migration
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

Baseline: adding Flyway to an existing database

If the database already has tables created by hand or by Hibernate, V1__init.sql would fail with "table already exists". A baseline tells Flyway "treat the current state as version N; only run migrations above N". Dump the current schema into V1__init.sql (for new environments), then on the existing database set spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrate=true and spring.flyway.baseline-version=1. Flyway records version 1 as already applied and runs V2 onwards. Turn the baseline option off afterwards, because on an empty database it would skip V1.

The golden rule: never edit an applied migration

Rule: applied migrations are immutable

Flyway stores a checksum of every applied script. If you edit it later, the next startup fails with FlywayValidateException: Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 2 (the app refuses to start). To change the schema, add a new migration (V4__fix_...sql). Fix a migration freely only while it exists on your branch and has never run anywhere shared. On a dev database you may delete the database and start again. flyway repair fixes checksums but should be a conscious choice, not a habit.

Migrations that are safe in production

  • Add, do not rename. To rename a column on a running system: add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release (expand and contract).
  • Adding a NOT NULL column to a big table needs a default or a backfill first; check lock time.
  • Build large indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in PostgreSQL (it cannot run inside a transaction; use the per-script non-transactional setting) to avoid blocking writes.
  • Keep one logical change per file, and give constraints and indexes explicit names.
  • Run the whole migration chain on an empty database in CI so mistakes surface before release.

Flyway + ddl-auto=validate

The pairing means: Flyway owns the schema, Hibernate only checks it. If a developer adds a field to an entity and forgets the migration, the app fails at startup with Schema-validation: missing column in dev and CI instead of failing in production on the first query. For tests with Testcontainers PostgreSQL, run the same migrations; avoid H2 with different SQL.

Mistakes

  • Single underscore in V1_init.sql (needs two): the file is ignored or rejected.
  • Putting migrations outside the scanned folder, or in src/test/resources only.
  • Keeping ddl-auto=update next to Flyway: two tools changing the schema.
  • Merging two branches that both created V5__...; rename one before merging.
  • Using application credentials with DDL rights in production; use a separate migration user via spring.flyway.user.

Exceptions

  • FlywayValidateException — checksum mismatch, or a migration missing from the folder that is in the history.
  • FlywayException: Found non-empty schema ... without schema history table — existing database, no baseline.
  • FlywayException: Detected resolved migration not applied to database — an older version appeared after a newer one ran (out-of-order).
  • SQLException in a script — the migration is marked failed. On PostgreSQL it rolls back; on MySQL part of it may remain, requiring manual cleanup.

Interview angle

"How do you manage database changes?" Versioned migrations in source control, run automatically at startup (or in the CI/CD pipeline), history table, checksums, never edit applied scripts, validate in Hibernate. Follow-up: "How to rename a column with zero downtime?" Expand and contract over two releases.

Datasource, HikariCP, SQL logging, batching and PostgreSQL in Docker

Configure the JDBC URL, user and password (from environment variables), tune the HikariCP pool, log SQL with parameters via logger levels, and enable JDBC batching with an id strategy that allows it.

PostgreSQL and MySQL connection

Add the driver as a runtime dependency (org.postgresql:postgresql or com.mysql:mysql-connector-j). Boot reads spring.datasource.* and builds a pooled DataSource. The driver class is detected from the URL; setting driver-class-name is optional.

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/jobs
spring.datasource.username=${DB_USER:jobs_user}
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/jobs?serverTimezone=UTC
spring.datasource.username=${DB_USER:jobs_user}
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
  • ${DB_PASSWORD} reads an environment variable; ${DB_USER:jobs_user} uses a default when it is missing. Never commit real passwords. Because of Boot's relaxed binding, setting the environment variable SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD overrides the property with no file change, which is how containers and cloud platforms inject secrets.
  • Use one profile file per environment (application-dev.properties, application-prod.properties); see module 1.
  • MySQL differences to remember: no sequences (use IDENTITY), DDL is not transactional, default isolation is REPEATABLE READ, identifiers are case-sensitive on Linux, and the dialect is detected automatically in current Hibernate (older code set hibernate.dialect by hand; you rarely need it now).

HikariCP: the connection pool

Opening a database connection costs milliseconds (TCP, authentication). A connection pool opens a fixed set once and lends them to requests. Spring Boot uses HikariCP by default. A request borrows a connection when its transaction starts and returns it at the end, so the transaction length decides how long the connection is busy.

spring.datasource.hikari.pool-name=jobs-pool
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=10
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=30000
spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=600000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000
SettingDefaultMeaning and advice
maximum-pool-size10Max connections. Bigger is not faster; see below
minimum-idlesame as maxIdle connections kept ready. Leave at default (fixed-size pool)
connection-timeout30000 msHow long a caller waits for a free connection before SQLTransientConnectionException
idle-timeout600000 msIdle connections above minimum-idle are retired
max-lifetime1800000 msRetire connections after this age; keep it a few minutes shorter than any database/firewall limit
leak-detection-threshold0 (off)Logs a warning with a stack trace if a connection is held longer than this

Sizing. A database can only do so much in parallel; a small pool (often 10–20 per application instance) usually gives better throughput than a huge one, because extra connections just queue inside the database. Remember the total: instances × pool size must stay below the database's max_connections (PostgreSQL default 100). Many teams tune from monitoring: pool wait time and active connections (see module 1 and the actuator metrics in module 6).

Symptoms of pool problems: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms means all connections are busy, usually because of long transactions, OSIV, a leak, or a slow query, not a pool that is "too small". Fix the cause first.

SQL logging done right

logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug
logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=trace
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
select a1_0.id,a1_0.status from application a1_0 where a1_0.job_id=?
binding parameter (1:BIGINT) <- [7]
  • org.hibernate.SQL=debug logs each statement through your logging framework (so levels, timestamps and files work). Add the bind logger to see parameter values; in Hibernate 5 and older this logger was org.hibernate.type.descriptor.sql.BasicBinder=trace.
  • spring.jpa.show-sql=true prints with System.out: no log levels, no parameters, no routing to log files. Avoid it, and never use either option in production (volume, performance, and bound values can include personal data).
  • Counting statements: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true and logging.level.org.hibernate.stat=debug help to spot N+1 (N+1).
  • For a production-friendly view use APM tools or pg_stat_statements on PostgreSQL instead of application logs.

Batch inserts and updates

Saving 1,000 jobs normally sends 1,000 INSERT statements, each a network round trip. With JDBC batching Hibernate groups them into a few batches.

spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_updates=true
  • jdbc.batch_size is the number of statements per batch.
  • order_inserts / order_updates sort statements by entity type so identical statements sit together; without them, saving a parent and its children alternately breaks the batch.
  • The id strategy must allow it: IDENTITY disables insert batching (ID strategies). Use SEQUENCE on PostgreSQL.
  • For PostgreSQL you can add the driver option reWriteBatchedInserts=true to the JDBC URL (multi-row inserts); for MySQL, rewriteBatchedStatements=true.
@Transactional
public void importJobs(List<Job> jobs) {
    int i = 0;
    for (Job job : jobs) {
        em.persist(job);
        if (++i % 50 == 0) {
            em.flush();        // send the batch
            em.clear();        // free memory, stop dirty checking old entities
        }
    }
}

Without clear() the persistence context keeps every entity and the job slows down and may run out of memory. For millions of rows, think about JdbcClient batch updates or the database's bulk loader (COPY) instead.

Running PostgreSQL in Docker for development

docker run --name jobs-db -d -p 5432:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=jobs -e POSTGRES_USER=jobs_user -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev_password \
  -v jobs-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:17
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: jobs
      POSTGRES_USER: jobs_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev_password
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - jobs-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  jobs-data:

Then set DB_PASSWORD=dev_password in your run configuration. The named volume keeps data across container restarts; docker rm -v or removing the volume resets the database. Boot also offers Docker Compose support (spring-boot-docker-compose dependency) that starts the compose.yaml services with the app and wires the connection details automatically in development. Docker itself is covered in the DevOps page.

Mistakes

  • Committing application.properties with a real password.
  • Raising maximum-pool-size to 200 to fix timeouts that come from long transactions.
  • Leaving show-sql or bind=trace on in production.
  • Setting batch_size but using IDENTITY: no batching happens, and no error tells you.
  • Connecting to localhost from inside a container; use the service name (db) as host.

Exceptions

  • CannotCreateTransactionException / PSQLException: Connection refused — database not running or wrong host/port.
  • PSQLException: FATAL: password authentication failed — wrong credentials (check the environment variable is set in the run configuration).
  • Failed to determine a suitable driver class — no URL, or the driver dependency is missing.
  • HikariPool ... Connection is not available — pool exhausted (above).

Interview angle

"What is connection pooling and which pool does Boot use?" Reuse of expensive connections; HikariCP; mention maximum-pool-size and why bigger is not better. "How do you see the SQL Hibernate runs?" The org.hibernate.SQL and bind loggers, not show-sql in production. "How do you speed up bulk inserts?" JDBC batching, SEQUENCE ids, ordered inserts, flush-and-clear.

Interview questions — Data access with Spring Data JPA

What are JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA, and how do they relate?

JPA is a specification: annotations, the EntityManager interface and JPQL. Hibernate is an implementation of that specification; it tracks entities and generates SQL. Spring Data JPA is a layer on top that creates repository implementations from interfaces and calls the EntityManager underneath. You code against Spring Data and JPA; Hibernate does the work.

What is the persistence context, and what are the entity states?

It is the per-transaction first-level cache and identity map that tracks managed entities. States: transient (new, unknown to JPA), managed (tracked; changes saved at flush), detached (has an id, but the context is closed), removed (scheduled for deletion). Within one context a given row is always the same Java object.

What is dirty checking? Why does my update work without calling save()?

Hibernate keeps a snapshot of each managed entity. At flush (before commit) it compares the entity with the snapshot and issues an UPDATE for changes. So inside @Transactional, loading an entity and calling a setter is enough. Without a transaction the entity is detached and the change is lost.

How does save() decide between INSERT and UPDATE?

It calls isNew: a null id (or a null wrapper @Version) means new, so persist; otherwise merge, which first runs a SELECT. With ids that you assign yourself, the id is never null, so every save does a needless SELECT; add a @Version field or implement Persistable.

IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE vs UUID?

IDENTITY lets the database auto-increment; Hibernate must INSERT immediately to learn the id, which disables batching. SEQUENCE asks a database sequence in blocks (allocationSize, default 50), so inserts can be delayed and batched; MySQL lacks sequences. UUID is generated in Java, needs no round trip and is not guessable, but it is larger and random, which hurts index locality.

What does ddl-auto do and what should production use?

It controls schema generation at startup: none, validate, update, create, create-drop. Production uses validate (or none) with Flyway migrations. update cannot rename or drop and leaves no history; create drops all data.

Explain the owning side and mappedBy.

In a bidirectional relationship the owning side is the entity whose table holds the foreign key (the @ManyToOne side). Only changes on the owning side write the FK. The inverse side uses mappedBy = "fieldOnOwner" and is a read-only mirror. So you must set both sides in memory; use helper methods like addJob.

What are the default fetch types and what do you recommend?

ToOne (@ManyToOne, @OneToOne) is EAGER; ToMany is LAZY. Recommendation: make everything LAZY, and load needed data per use case with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, batch fetching or DTO projections. Eager mappings cannot be turned off per query and cause hidden extra queries.

What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it?

One query loads N parents, then lazy loading fires one query for each parent's relation: 1 + N queries. Detect it with the SQL log, Hibernate statistics or query-count tests. Fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size (turns N into N/size), or a DTO projection. Beware of join-fetching a collection with pagination (done in memory) and MultipleBagFetchException.

What causes LazyInitializationException and how do you solve it properly?

A lazy association is read after the session closed, usually in the controller or during JSON serialization. Solve it by mapping to a DTO inside the service transaction, or by fetching the data in the query. Do not make it EAGER and do not rely on Open Session in View; set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.

How does @Transactional work, and why might it not apply?

Spring wraps the bean in a proxy; the interceptor starts a transaction through the transaction manager, binds the connection to the thread, calls the method and commits or rolls back. It does nothing on self-invocation (this.method() skips the proxy), on private or final methods, or on objects not managed by Spring. It rolls back only for unchecked exceptions and errors unless rollbackFor says otherwise.

REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED?

REQUIRED joins the existing transaction or creates one; a failure anywhere marks the whole thing rollback-only. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer transaction and runs independently on another connection (use it for an audit record that must persist even if the caller rolls back). NESTED runs in a savepoint inside the outer transaction, so only the inner part rolls back.

What is UnexpectedRollbackException?

An inner method taking part in the outer transaction threw a runtime exception, which marked the transaction rollback-only. The outer code caught the exception and continued, then tried to commit; Spring throws because the transaction can only roll back. Let the exception propagate, or run the inner call in REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED.

Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?

Optimistic: add a @Version column; the UPDATE includes where version=?, and the loser gets ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException (return 409, reload, retry). No locks are held. Pessimistic: @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) issues SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and others wait; use for heavy contention like stock or seats, with a timeout. For simple counters an atomic update ... set n = n - 1 where n > 0 is enough.

How do you manage schema changes in a Spring Boot project?

Flyway migrations in db/migration (V1__init.sql, V2__...), applied at startup and recorded in flyway_schema_history with checksums. Applied files are never edited; a change is a new file. Hibernate runs with ddl-auto=validate so a missing migration fails fast. Existing databases are adopted with a baseline.

Cheat sheet — Data access with Spring Data JPA

  • JPA / Hibernate / Spring Data specification / implementation / generated repositories on top
  • Entity rules @Entity, @Id, protected no-arg constructor, not final
  • Enums always @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
  • Money BigDecimal with precision and scale; time as Instant
  • equals/hashCode id non-null and equal; constant hashCode; never Lombok @Data on entities
  • Entity states transient → managed → detached / removed
  • Dirty checking changed managed entities are UPDATEd at flush; no save() needed in a transaction
  • Flush before commit, before queries, on flush(); it is not a commit
  • save() new → persist, else merge (extra SELECT); use the returned object
  • getReferenceById lazy proxy with the id only; findById runs a SELECT
  • IDENTITY no insert batching; SEQUENCE allocationSize 50, batching; UUID no round trip
  • ddl-auto production: validate or none + Flyway
  • Derived queries findBy, And, Or, Between, Containing, In, OrderBy…Desc, Top5, existsBy, countBy
  • Return types Optional (one), List, Page (with count), Slice (no count), Stream
  • @Query JPQL uses entity and field names; bind with :name + @Param; nativeQuery = true for SQL
  • @Modifying bulk update/delete in a transaction; clearAutomatically = true
  • Projections interface or record; selects only needed columns
  • Specifications JpaSpecificationExecutor, combine with and/or for optional filters
  • Owning side the side with the FK (@ManyToOne); mappedBy on the other; sync both sides
  • Cascade only parent → owned children; never REMOVE on ManyToMany or ManyToOne
  • ManyToMany use Set; extra columns → explicit join entity
  • Fetching make all associations LAZY; spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
  • N+1 fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, default_batch_fetch_size, DTO projection
  • Fetch pitfalls collection join fetch + paging = in memory; two bags = MultipleBagFetchException
  • @Transactional proxy-based; service layer; public methods; no self-invocation
  • Rollback unchecked and Error only; rollbackFor = Exception.class for checked
  • Propagation REQUIRED (default), REQUIRES_NEW (independent), NESTED (savepoint), MANDATORY, NEVER, SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED
  • readOnly = true on query-only service methods
  • Locking @Version → 409 on conflict; @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) → FOR UPDATE
  • Auditing @EnableJpaAuditing + AuditingEntityListener + @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate
  • Flyway db/migration/V1__init.sql; never edit applied files; baseline for existing DBs
  • HikariCP maximum-pool-size default 10; keep pools small; watch long transactions
  • SQL logging org.hibernate.SQL=debug + org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=trace in dev only
  • Batching hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, order_inserts, SEQUENCE ids, flush and clear

Practice — Data access with Spring Data JPA

  1. Local database (easy). Start PostgreSQL in Docker, connect the Product API from module 2 with environment-variable credentials, and set ddl-auto=validate. Done when the app starts and the Product endpoints still work against the Docker database.
  2. First migration (easy). Write V1__init.sql for company, app_user, job and application (use the SQL in the relationships example as a starting point), add Flyway, and start the app. Done when flyway_schema_history has one row. Then edit V1 on purpose, restart, and read the checksum error.
  3. Project 2 entities (medium). Map User, Company, Job and Application with all ManyToOne relations LAZY, enums as STRING, BaseEntity with safe equals/hashCode, and a unique constraint on (job, user). Done when Hibernate validate passes and an integration test saves one of each.
  4. Repositories and pagination (medium). Add derived queries (findByEmail, existsByJobIdAndApplicantId), a paged findByStatus, and a Specification-based search (city, text, minimum salary) returning Page<JobCard>. Done when a controller serves GET /api/v1/jobs?city=Pune&page=0&size=10 with correct totals.
  5. Fourth related entity (medium). Add Tag with a many-to-many to Job using Set and helper methods, in a new migration V2. Done when assigning tags creates rows only in job_tag, and removing one deletes exactly one row (check the SQL log).
  6. Auditing and versioning (medium). Create AuditableEntity with createdAt/updatedAt, enable auditing, and add @Version to Job. Done when two parallel updates of the same job make the second fail with ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException, returned as HTTP 409.
  7. Find and fix an N+1 (hard). Write an endpoint "applicants of a job" that returns applicant name per application, with open-in-view=false and lazy mappings. First write it badly, enable SQL logging and count the queries for 20 applications.
