Then fix it with JOIN FETCH, then with @EntityGraph, then with a DTO projection, and finally set default_batch_fetch_size. Done when you can show the query counts before (21) and after (1 or 2) for each fix.
  8. Transaction experiments (hard). (a) Call a REQUIRES_NEW method from the same class and show with logging that it does not start a new transaction; fix it with a second bean. (b) Throw a checked exception from a @Transactional method, show the commit, then add rollbackFor. (c) Reproduce UnexpectedRollbackException. Done when each behaviour is visible in the SQL log or the exception output.
  9. Batch import (hard). Import 10,000 jobs with SEQUENCE ids, batch_size=50 and order_inserts=true; compare statement counts and time with IDENTITY. Done when the log shows batched inserts for SEQUENCE and single inserts for IDENTITY.
4

Module 4·Weeks 7–8Must

Security

16 topics · about 1.5 h of reading

Almost every real API has users, and almost every user-facing bug that hurts a company is a security bug: a recruiter editing another recruiter's job, a candidate reading all applications, a leaked password table. Spring Security is the standard framework that protects Spring Boot applications. It is big, and the old tutorials are mostly out of date, so this module teaches the current style (the lambda DSL, no WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter) from first principles.

You will first understand what happens when you add the security starter, how the filter chain works and where the Authentication object lives. Then you build the full login system for Project 2: users in the database, BCrypt password hashing, stateless JWT tokens (two ways: a custom filter and the OAuth2 Resource Server support), roles CANDIDATE, RECRUITER and ADMIN, owner-only edits, clean JSON error responses, CORS and CSRF. It builds on the REST layer from module 2 and the entities from module 3. How to test all of this is in module 5, and how a React app uses the token is in Frontend · Module 6.

After this module you will be able to:

  • Explain authentication vs authorization, 401 vs 403, and sessions vs tokens.
  • Describe the Spring Security filter chain and write a modern SecurityFilterChain bean.
  • Load users from a database and hash passwords with BCrypt.
  • Issue and validate JWTs with a custom filter or with the OAuth2 Resource Server support.
  • Protect URLs and methods by role, and enforce "only the owner can edit".
  • Configure CORS correctly, and decide when CSRF protection can be off.
  • Design refresh tokens, understand OAuth2 login, and apply a security checklist.

Authentication vs authorization, 401 vs 403, sessions vs tokens

Authentication asks "who are you?", authorization asks "what may you do?"; a failed login is 401, a known user without permission is 403, and a stateless API proves identity on every request with a signed token instead of a server-side session.

Two different questions

Authentication (AuthN) is proving who you are: a username and password, a fingerprint, a one-time code, a signed token. Authorization (AuthZ) is deciding what an already-identified user is allowed to do: "a RECRUITER may post a job, a CANDIDATE may not". Authentication always comes first; you cannot authorize someone you cannot identify. Think of an airport: the passport check is authentication, the boarding pass that lets you into the business lounge is authorization.

AuthenticationAuthorization
QuestionWho are you?What are you allowed to do?
InputCredentials (password, token, certificate)The identity plus roles, permissions, resource owner
Failure status401 Unauthorized403 Forbidden
Spring Security typeAuthenticationManager, AuthenticationAuthorizationManager, @PreAuthorize
ExampleLogin with email and passwordOnly ADMIN can delete users

In practice authorization has two levels. Role-based rules look only at the user ("RECRUITER may post jobs"). Ownership (resource-level) rules also look at the data ("a recruiter may edit only their own jobs"). Roles are checked by Spring Security rules; ownership is usually checked in the service layer (authorization).

How Spring Security models "who you are"

Spring Security represents the current user as an Authentication object. It holds the principal (who: usually your UserDetails), the credentials (the password or token, erased after login), and the authorities (what: a list of strings such as ROLE_RECRUITER). A flag says whether it is authenticated. A filter puts it into the SecurityContext, stored in SecurityContextHolder, which keeps it in a thread-local for the length of the request. Your code reads it from there, or gets it as a controller parameter:

@GetMapping("/api/me")
public Map<String, Object> me(Authentication auth) {
    return Map.of(
            "name", auth.getName(),
            "authorities", auth.getAuthorities().toString());
}
{"name":"asha@example.com","authorities":"[ROLE_RECRUITER]"}

A request with no login is not "empty": Spring Security fills the context with an anonymous authentication (principal anonymousUser, role ROLE_ANONYMOUS). That lets rules like permitAll() and authenticated() work with one uniform check. How the filters build this object is shown in the filter chain article.

401 vs 403

The name of status 401 is misleading: it means "unauthenticated". The server does not know who you are, or your credentials are missing, wrong or expired. Status 403 means "I know who you are, and you may not do this".

  • 401: no token, bad password, expired or tampered JWT. The client should log in (or refresh the token) and retry.
  • 403: a valid CANDIDATE token calls POST /api/jobs. Logging in again changes nothing.
  • 404 instead of 403: sometimes you hide that a resource exists at all (a candidate asking for another candidate's application). Both are acceptable; choose one rule and keep it.
POST /api/jobs                               (no Authorization header)
HTTP/1.1 401

POST /api/jobs   Authorization: Bearer eyJ... (valid token, role CANDIDATE)
HTTP/1.1 403

POST /api/jobs   Authorization: Bearer eyJ... (valid token, role RECRUITER)
HTTP/1.1 201

Inside Spring Security, one filter decides between the two. ExceptionTranslationFilter catches the exceptions thrown further down the chain. If it catches an AuthenticationException, or an AccessDeniedException for an anonymous user, it calls the AuthenticationEntryPoint (response 401, or a redirect to a login page for browsers). If it catches an AccessDeniedException for a logged-in user, it calls the AccessDeniedHandler (response 403). Both can be replaced to return your JSON (JSON error responses).

Strictly, a 401 response should carry a WWW-Authenticate header that names the scheme (Bearer or Basic). The resource server support in Spring Security adds it; hand-written entry points often forget it.

Sessions (stateful) vs tokens (stateless)

HTTP has no memory: each request stands alone. After login the server must recognise you again on the next request. There are two classic ways.

Server-side session. The server stores your login state in memory (or Redis) under a random session id and sends the id in a JSESSIONID cookie. The browser returns the cookie automatically on every request; the server looks the session up. Spring Security can store the SecurityContext in that session. Token-based (stateless). The server stores nothing. After login it gives the client a signed token (usually a JWT, see the JWT article) containing the user id and roles. The client sends it in the Authorization: Bearer ... header, and the server only verifies the signature.

Session + cookieStateless token (JWT)
Server storesSession data for each userNothing (only the signing key)
ScalingNeeds sticky sessions or shared store (Redis)Any instance can verify; easy to scale
Logout / revokeEasy: delete the sessionHard: token is valid until it expires (see refresh tokens)
Sent byCookie, automaticallyHeader, by your JavaScript code
CSRF riskYes, must protectNo, if not kept in a cookie (CSRF)
FitsServer-rendered web appsREST APIs, SPAs, mobile apps, microservices

Neither is "better". A server-rendered site with Thymeleaf is happy with sessions. A React app plus a Spring Boot REST API, plus a future mobile app and several services, is usually happier with tokens. Project 2 uses tokens.

Security details that decide which one is safer

  • Session cookies should be HttpOnly (JavaScript cannot read them, which limits XSS theft), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite (limits CSRF). Spring Security also changes the session id at login (session fixation protection), so an attacker cannot plant a known id before the victim logs in.
  • Tokens in localStorage are easy to use but any XSS bug can read them. A token in an HttpOnly cookie is safer against XSS but brings back CSRF protection duties. Many apps keep a short-lived access token in memory and a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie (refresh tokens).
  • Sessions can scale too: with Spring Session the session data lives in Redis and every instance reads it. Stateless is simpler, not the only way.
  • A JWT cannot be "logged out" by the server alone. Keep access tokens short (minutes), or keep a deny list of revoked token ids.

Other ways to prove identity

MethodHow it worksTypical use
HTTP BasicBase64 of user:password in every requestQuick internal tools; only over HTTPS
Form login + sessionHTML form, then JSESSIONIDServer-rendered apps
Bearer JWTSigned token in the Authorization headerSPAs, mobile apps, APIs
API keyLong random key in a headerServer-to-server calls
OAuth2 / OpenID ConnectLogin delegated to Google, GitHub or a company IdP"Login with Google" (OAuth2 login)

Rules

  • Check authentication first, then authorization; never decide permissions for an anonymous user.
  • Return 401 for "who are you?" problems and 403 for "not allowed". Do not mix them.
  • Do the authorization check on the server for every request. Hiding a button in React is not security.
  • Never trust a role or user id sent by the client in a body or query string; take it from the verified token or session.

Conventions

  • Roles are named in upper case; Spring stores them as authorities with the prefix ROLE_ (ROLE_ADMIN), and hasRole("ADMIN") adds the prefix for you. Fine-grained permissions (job:write) are authorities without the prefix.
  • Use one generic message for failed logins ("Invalid email or password"), so attackers cannot tell which emails exist.

Common mistakes

Wrong: wrong status for the wrong problem

// token missing:
return ResponseEntity.status(403).build();
// logged-in CANDIDATE calling a RECRUITER endpoint:
return ResponseEntity.status(401).build();

Right: 401 = identity, 403 = permission

// token missing or invalid:
return ResponseEntity.status(401).build();
// logged-in CANDIDATE calling a RECRUITER endpoint:
return ResponseEntity.status(403).build();
  • Putting secrets (a password, a card number) inside a JWT payload. A JWT is signed, not encrypted; anyone can read it.
  • Trusting the front end: checking the role only in React.
  • Treating "logged in" as "allowed": forgetting the ownership check, so any user can read another user's order by changing the id (broken access control, the top item of the OWASP list, best practices).

Edge cases and exceptions

  • BadCredentialsException (wrong password), DisabledException, LockedException and UsernameNotFoundException are all AuthenticationExceptions: they lead to 401.
  • AccessDeniedException comes from failed authorization: it leads to 403 (or to 401 if the user is anonymous).
  • With default settings and no custom entry point, an API that disables form login and Basic may answer anonymous requests with 403 instead of 401 (see security configuration).
  • A browser-oriented app redirects (302) to /login instead of returning 401. Fine for HTML pages, wrong for a JSON API.
  • With @PreAuthorize on a service method, the denial happens inside the call and is translated in the same way, but an unhandled AccessDeniedException thrown after the security filters ran is caught by your @ExceptionHandler if you have one for Exception, and may turn into a 500. Handle it explicitly or rethrow.

Real projects

A React + Spring Boot job portal usually works like this: POST /api/auth/login returns an access token (about 15 minutes) and sets a refresh token cookie; React sends the access token as a Bearer header; the API has stateless security with role rules for RECRUITER and CANDIDATE, plus ownership checks in services. An admin web UI built with Thymeleaf in the same company may still use sessions.

Interview angle

"Difference between authentication and authorization?" Give the one-line definitions plus the airport or login-vs-role example. "401 vs 403?" 401 = not authenticated (who are you?), 403 = authenticated but not allowed. "Why JWT instead of sessions?" Stateless, scales across instances, works for SPAs and mobile; the price is that revocation is harder. Strong answers also mention where the token is stored (memory or HttpOnly cookie versus localStorage), that sessions can scale with Redis, and that authorization must be checked on the server.

What happens when you add spring-boot-starter-security

Adding the starter secures every endpoint at once with a generated password and a default login page; you take control by defining your own SecurityFilterChain bean.

Add one dependency and nothing else:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

Restart the application. Spring Boot's auto-configuration now does the following without any code from you:

  1. Every endpoint requires authentication, including your existing REST controllers, static files and the error page. GET /api/jobs now returns 401.
  2. A default user named user is created with a random password printed in the log at startup.
  3. Form login and HTTP Basic are enabled. A browser is redirected to a generated /login page; a client such as Postman can send Basic credentials.
  4. CSRF protection is on: POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE without a CSRF token get 403.
  5. A session is created after login, and the browser keeps the JSESSIONID cookie.
  6. Default security headers are added (X-Content-Type-Options, Cache-Control: no-cache for secured responses, X-Frame-Options and others).
Using generated security password: 8e557245-73e2-4286-969b-1e0e1c1d4a5f

This generated password is for development use only. Your security
configuration must be updated before running your application in production.
$ curl -i localhost:8080/api/jobs
HTTP/1.1 401
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Realm"

$ curl -u user:8e557245-73e2-4286-969b-1e0e1c1d4a5f localhost:8080/api/jobs
HTTP/1.1 200

Taking control

This default is a safe starting point, not a design. You change it in three steps: (1) define your own SecurityFilterChain bean (once Spring Boot sees one, it backs off its default chain, see the configuration article), (2) define a UserDetailsService bean that loads real users, and (3) define a PasswordEncoder bean.

For quick experiments you can set the default user in application.properties:

spring.security.user.name=admin
spring.security.user.password=admin123
spring.security.user.roles=ADMIN

Common mistakes

  • Adding the starter late and thinking "my controllers broke". They did not; the whole app is now secured. Read the 401/403 as a feature.
  • Disabling security with http.csrf(c -> c.disable()) and permitAll() on everything "to make Postman work". Fix the configuration instead.
  • Following a tutorial that extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter. That class was removed in Spring Security 6 (Spring Boot 3), so the code will not compile.

Versions

Spring Boot 3.x uses Spring Security 6.x; Spring Boot 4.x uses Spring Security 7.x. The lambda DSL shown in this module works in both. In Security 7 the old non-lambda style (http.csrf().disable(), chained .and()) is gone, so always write http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()).

The Spring Security architecture: the filter chain and the Authentication object

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters in front of your controllers; filters authenticate the request, store an Authentication in the SecurityContext, and the last filters decide whether the request may continue.

Why filters

Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet and your controllers sit at the end of the request path. A servlet filter is code that runs before the servlet and can read the request, change it, or stop it and write a response itself. Security must run before any controller, so Spring Security is built from filters.

DelegatingFilterProxy
A normal servlet filter registered with the container. It does no security itself; it hands over to a Spring bean. (Spring Boot registers an equivalent for you.)
FilterChainProxy
The bean it delegates to. It holds a list of SecurityFilterChains and picks the first one whose request matcher matches the URL.
SecurityFilterChain
An ordered list of security filters for a group of URLs. This is what you configure with HttpSecurity.

The important filters, in order

FilterWhat it does
SecurityContextHolderFilterLoads the SecurityContext for the request (from the session, if any) and clears it at the end
CorsFilterAnswers CORS preflight requests and adds CORS headers (CORS)
CsrfFilterRejects state-changing requests without a valid CSRF token (CSRF)
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilterHandles form login (POST /login); not used by a JWT API
BasicAuthenticationFilterReads the Authorization: Basic header
BearerTokenAuthenticationFilterReads Authorization: Bearer ... and validates the JWT (added by the OAuth2 Resource Server support)
AnonymousAuthenticationFilterIf nobody logged in, sets an "anonymous" Authentication so later code never sees null
ExceptionTranslationFilterCatches AuthenticationException and AccessDeniedException thrown below it and turns them into 401 / 403 responses
AuthorizationFilterThe last one: checks the URL rules (authorizeHttpRequests) and throws if the user may not continue

Order matters: your own filter must be placed relative to these (for JWT, before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter). To see the real chain of your app, set logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG; at the first request it prints "Will secure any request with [filter1, filter2, ...]".

What is stored: SecurityContext and Authentication

After a successful authentication a filter puts an Authentication object into the SecurityContext, which is kept in the SecurityContextHolder, a thread-local holder (one value per request thread). Any code on that thread can read it.

Authentication
The "who" object. Before authentication it carries credentials (isAuthenticated() == false); after, it carries the principal and authorities.
Principal
The identity. Often a UserDetails (form login / Basic) or a Jwt (resource server). getName() returns the username.
Credentials
The proof (password or token). Erased after a successful login.
GrantedAuthority
One permission as a string, e.g. ROLE_RECRUITER or jobs:write.
Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
String name = auth.getName();                              // e.g. "asha@example.com"
Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> roles = auth.getAuthorities();
boolean loggedIn = auth.isAuthenticated()
        && !(auth instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken);

How a username and password is checked

When some filter or your login controller has credentials, it calls the AuthenticationManager. The standard implementation, ProviderManager, asks a list of AuthenticationProviders whether one supports this kind of credential. For username and password the provider is DaoAuthenticationProvider, which uses two collaborators you supply.

  1. DaoAuthenticationProvider calls userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(name) and receives a UserDetails (name, hashed password, authorities, status flags).
  2. It checks the account flags (enabled, not locked, not expired). A bad flag throws DisabledException, LockedException and so on.
  3. It calls passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, storedHash). A mismatch throws BadCredentialsException.
  4. On success it returns a fully authenticated Authentication with authorities.

All exceptions here extend AuthenticationException, and ExceptionTranslationFilter turns them into 401. A missing user also gives BadCredentialsException by default (so attackers cannot tell "unknown email" from "wrong password").

Rule: the SecurityContext is per thread and per request

The context lives in a thread-local. In a stateless app it is empty at the start of every request and filled again by your token filter. Code that starts another thread (@Async, a manual executor) does not automatically see it; Spring offers DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor and MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL for those rare cases.

Interview angle

"Explain the Spring Security architecture." Filters in front of the DispatcherServlet; FilterChainProxy picks a SecurityFilterChain; an authentication filter builds an Authentication and stores it in the SecurityContextHolder; AuthorizationFilter checks the rules; ExceptionTranslationFilter maps failures to 401/403. Then draw the AuthenticationManager to DaoAuthenticationProvider to UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder path.

Writing a SecurityFilterChain with the lambda DSL

Declare a SecurityFilterChain bean that sets the URL rules, switches off form login and Basic for an API, makes sessions stateless, and plugs in your authentication; matcher order matters, the first match wins.

In the architecture article you saw that Spring Security is a list of servlet filters. The SecurityFilterChain bean is how you choose and configure those filters. You describe what you want with HttpSecurity, a builder, and call http.build(); the result is the list of filters for one group of URLs.

A complete configuration for a stateless REST API

import static org.springframework.security.config.Customizer.withDefaults;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .cors(withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(s ->
                    s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .httpBasic(basic -> basic.disable())
            .formLogin(form -> form.disable())
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/jobs/**", "/api/companies/**")
                        .permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/jobs").hasRole("RECRUITER")
                .anyRequest().authenticated());
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean
    PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
}

(Authentication of tokens is added later: one more line in the chain, shown in the JWT articles.) Line by line:

@EnableWebSecurity
Switches on web security. Optional in Spring Boot (auto-configured), but it states the intent.
@EnableMethodSecurity
Allows @PreAuthorize on methods (authorization).
csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
Turns off CSRF checks. Correct only for token-in-header APIs (CSRF).
cors(withDefaults())
Uses your CorsConfigurationSource bean (CORS).
sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS)
Spring Security never creates or uses an HTTP session to store the SecurityContext. Every request must carry its own token.
httpBasic / formLogin disabled
An API has no HTML login page and does not use Basic. Disabling them removes the default login page and the redirect-to-login behaviour (you get a clean 401).
authorizeHttpRequests
The URL rules, evaluated by AuthorizationFilter.
permitAll()
Anyone, including anonymous users.
authenticated()
Any logged-in user.
hasRole("ADMIN")
Needs authority ROLE_ADMIN.
anyRequest().authenticated()
The safety net: everything not listed above needs a login. Always end with it (deny by default).

What the DSL does inside

The "lambda DSL" is the style where every feature gets its own lambda: .csrf(csrf -> ...). Each call configures one configurer, and each configurer adds one or more filters to the chain. So .csrf(...) adds CsrfFilter, .cors(...) adds CorsFilter, .sessionManagement(...) adds session-related filters, and .authorizeHttpRequests(...) adds AuthorizationFilter near the end. A configurer you disable (or never call) adds nothing. When you call http.build(), Spring Security sorts the filters into their fixed order, so the order of your DSL calls does not change the filter order.

At runtime Boot registers one servlet filter, FilterChainProxy (under the name springSecurityFilterChain), which holds all your SecurityFilterChain beans. For each request it picks the first chain whose request matcher matches, and runs only that chain's filters. A simplified view of a typical API chain:

Two other defaults come with the chain. First, HeaderWriterFilter adds security response headers such as X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and X-Frame-Options: DENY; change them with .headers(h -> ...). Second, the chain needs an AuthenticationManager; Boot builds one from your UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder beans, or from the JWT decoder when you use the resource server (users from the database).

Plugging in your own authentication filter

A custom filter is placed relative to a known one with addFilterBefore or addFilterAfter. This is the "one more line" used by the custom JWT approach (JWT custom filter).

http.addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);

// or, for the resource server approach, a single line:
http.oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(withDefaults()));

Matcher order matters

Rules are checked from top to bottom and the first matching rule wins. Put specific rules first, general ones last.

Wrong: the general rule hides the specific one

.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
    .requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated()          // matches everything
    .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()         // never reached
    .anyRequest().denyAll())

Right: specific first

.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
    .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
    .requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated()
    .anyRequest().denyAll())

Spring Security even throws an error at startup if a rule after anyRequest() is added (IllegalStateException: Can't configure requestMatchers after anyRequest), because it could never match.

Request matchers

  • requestMatchers("/api/jobs/**"): Ant-style paths. * = one segment, ** = any depth.
  • requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/jobs/**"): path plus HTTP method. Use methods to make reads public and writes protected.
  • requestMatchers("/h2-console/**") and similar for tools. In the old API this was antMatchers / mvcMatchers; both were replaced by requestMatchers in Spring Security 6.
RulePasses whenFailure
permitAll()AlwaysNever
denyAll()Never403 (or 401 for anonymous)
authenticated()User is logged in (not anonymous)401
hasRole("ADMIN")Has ROLE_ADMIN403
hasAnyRole("ADMIN", "RECRUITER")Has at least one of them403
hasAuthority("job:write")Has exactly that authority string403

More than one filter chain

You may define several SecurityFilterChain beans for different URL groups, each with @Order and a securityMatcher, for example one stateless chain for /api/** and one session-based chain for an admin web UI. The first chain whose matcher matches the request handles it.

@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain apiChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .csrf(c -> c.disable());
    return http.build();
}

@Bean
@Order(2)
SecurityFilterChain webChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .formLogin(withDefaults());
    return http.build();
}

The last chain has no securityMatcher, so it matches everything and must come last. If a chain that matches every request comes before another one, the later chain can never run; Spring Security 6 detects this and fails at startup with an UnreachableFilterChainException.

Ignoring static resources

Do not use web.ignoring() for URLs that need security headers; use permitAll() instead, so the filters (and headers) still run. Common Spring Boot static locations are already handled by PathRequest.toStaticResources() if you serve a UI from the same app.

Try it: what the client sees

$ curl -i localhost:8080/api/jobs                     # GET, public
HTTP/1.1 200
$ curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/api/jobs -d '{}'     # needs login
HTTP/1.1 401
$ curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/api/jobs -H "Authorization: Bearer $CANDIDATE" ...
HTTP/1.1 403
$ curl -i localhost:8080/api/unknown-thing            # anyRequest().authenticated()
HTTP/1.1 401

Rule: deny by default

End every authorizeHttpRequests block with anyRequest().authenticated() (or denyAll()), and list public URLs explicitly. A forgotten endpoint is then protected, not exposed.

Conventions

  • Keep the chain in one SecurityConfig class; keep filters and handlers as separate classes and inject them.
  • Expose PasswordEncoder as its own bean; services (registration) need it too.
  • Write one test per rule with MockMvc and @WithMockUser (controller tests). A rule nobody tests breaks silently when someone reorders the lines.

Common mistakes

  • Putting permitAll() for /api/auth/** after a broader rule (see the Wrong example).
  • Using hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN"). Spring adds the prefix itself, so use hasRole("ADMIN") (or hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")).
  • Returning the HttpSecurity without calling http.build().
  • Forgetting that the servlet context-path or a trailing slash can change matching; test your rules (module 5).
  • Disabling CSRF on an app that uses session cookies. That is only right for token-in-header APIs.
  • Calling permitAll() on /actuator/** in production. Expose only health, or secure the rest (Actuator).

Edge case: 403 instead of 401 for missing credentials

If you disable httpBasic and formLogin and add no other authentication mechanism, there is no AuthenticationEntryPoint to say "401, please log in", and Spring Security falls back to a plain 403 for anonymous requests. Fix it by configuring an entry point (JSON errors), or by using the resource server support, which sets one.

More edge cases and startup errors

  • The /error trap. When a controller throws an exception, the servlet container forwards to /error, and in Spring Security 6 the authorization rules also apply to that forward. A real 404 or 500 can then appear as 401 or 403. Add .requestMatchers("/error").permitAll() if you see this.
  • IllegalArgumentException: This method cannot decide whether these patterns are Spring MVC patterns or not appears when a second servlet is registered (for example the H2 console) and you pass a string to requestMatchers. Use PathRequest.toH2Console() for that one.
  • Defining your own SecurityFilterChain makes Boot back off from its default chain (starter defaults): the generated password and default form login are gone.
  • A path with a different case or a trailing slash (/API/jobs) is not matched by /api/jobs; with deny-by-default it is still protected.

Spring Security 6 and 7

Spring Boot 3.x uses Spring Security 6; Boot 4.x uses Spring Security 7. The lambda style shown here is the supported style in both. The older chained style (http.csrf().disable().and()...) was deprecated in 6.x and is removed in 7, and WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was already removed in Security 6. Write every new configuration in lambda style.

Interview angle

"How do you configure security in Spring Boot 3?" Expose a SecurityFilterChain bean using HttpSecurity and the lambda DSL; mention that WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was removed. Explain stateless sessions, why CSRF is disabled for token APIs, rule order, and "deny by default". A deeper answer adds that FilterChainProxy picks the first matching chain, that each DSL call configures filters, and where a custom JWT filter goes (addFilterBefore).

Loading users from the database: User, UserDetailsService and registration

Store users with a hashed password and a role, implement UserDetailsService to load them by email, wrap them in a UserDetails with the account-status flags, and offer a registration endpoint that hashes the password before saving.

Spring Security does not know your User table. You teach it in two small steps: a class that describes a user in Security's terms (UserDetails), and a service that fetches that class from your database (UserDetailsService). Registration is the other half: how users get into the table with a safe password hash.

The User entity and roles

Project 2 already has a User entity from module 3. For security it needs three things: a unique login name (we use the email), a password hash (never the password), and a role. Roles are an enum stored as text.

public enum Role {
    CANDIDATE, RECRUITER, ADMIN
}
@Entity
@Table(name = "app_user")
public class User extends BaseEntity {

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;

    @Column(name = "password_hash", nullable = false)
    private String passwordHash;           // BCrypt hash, 60 characters

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)           // never ORDINAL: reordering would break data
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private Role role;

    private boolean enabled = true;
    private boolean locked = false;

    // constructor, getters; no setter for passwordHash except changePassword(hash)
}
alter table app_user add column password_hash varchar(100) not null;
alter table app_user add column role varchar(20) not null default 'CANDIDATE';
alter table app_user add column enabled boolean not null default true;
alter table app_user add column locked boolean not null default false;
create unique index uq_app_user_email on app_user (lower(email));

One role or many?

One role per user keeps Project 2 simple and covers most apps. If a user can hold several, map Set<Role> with @ElementCollection and @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING); the rest of this module (authorities as a list) works unchanged. Load the roles together with the user (@EntityGraph), because login happens outside any long transaction.

UserDetails and UserDetailsService

UserDetails is Spring Security's view of a user: name, password hash, authorities, and four status flags. UserDetailsService has one method, loadUserByUsername(String), and is how DaoAuthenticationProvider finds the user. "Username" is just the login identifier; here it is the email.

public class AppUserDetails implements UserDetails {

    private final Long id;
    private final String email;
    private final String passwordHash;
    private final Role role;
    private final boolean enabled;
    private final boolean accountNonLocked;

    public AppUserDetails(User u) {
        this.id = u.getId();
        this.email = u.getEmail();
        this.passwordHash = u.getPasswordHash();
        this.role = u.getRole();
        this.enabled = u.isEnabled();
        this.accountNonLocked = !u.isLocked();
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public Role getRole() { return role; }

    @Override public Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities() {
        return List.of(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + role.name()));
    }
    @Override public String getPassword() { return passwordHash; }
    @Override public String getUsername() { return email; }
    @Override public boolean isAccountNonExpired() { return true; }
    @Override public boolean isAccountNonLocked() { return accountNonLocked; }
    @Override public boolean isCredentialsNonExpired() { return true; }
    @Override public boolean isEnabled() { return enabled; }
}
@Service
public class DbUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public DbUserDetailsService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String email) {
        return userRepository.findByEmailIgnoreCase(email)
                .map(AppUserDetails::new)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found"));
    }
}

The repository method is a derived query: Optional<User> findByEmailIgnoreCase(String email);. With a UserDetailsService bean and a PasswordEncoder bean in the context, Spring Boot wires DaoAuthenticationProvider for you, and the generated default user disappears.

For a small app you can skip the custom UserDetails class and return Spring's own builder instead. The catch is that you then lose extra fields like the user id, and you must use the full class name because it clashes with your entity:

return org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User
        .withUsername(u.getEmail())
        .password(u.getPasswordHash())
        .roles(u.getRole().name())          // adds the ROLE_ prefix itself
        .disabled(!u.isEnabled())
        .accountLocked(u.isLocked())
        .build();

How DaoAuthenticationProvider uses them

When a login request reaches the AuthenticationManager, it delegates to DaoAuthenticationProvider. This is the exact order of work, and it explains every exception you will see:

  1. It receives a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken holding the email and the raw password the user typed.
  2. It calls userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(email). If your service throws UsernameNotFoundException, the provider by default converts it into BadCredentialsException ("Bad credentials") so the caller cannot tell a wrong email from a wrong password. When the user is not found it still runs one password hash comparison against a dummy hash, so the response time does not reveal which emails exist (a protection against timing attacks).
  3. Pre-checks: it rejects a locked, disabled or expired account (LockedException, DisabledException, AccountExpiredException) before checking the password.
  4. It calls passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, user.getPassword()). A mismatch is a BadCredentialsException.
  5. Post-check: expired credentials give CredentialsExpiredException.
  6. On success it builds a new, authenticated Authentication with the UserDetails as principal and its authorities. The raw password is not kept.

Your login endpoint calls the manager directly. The result is an authenticated principal whose id and role you put into the JWT (JWT basics). The matching of the hash itself is explained in password hashing.

public AppUserDetails login(String email, String password) {
    Authentication auth = authenticationManager.authenticate(
            new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(email, password));
    return (AppUserDetails) auth.getPrincipal();     // then create the token from it
}

The AuthenticationManager bean is not created by default. Expose it from the configuration:

@Bean
AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration config)
        throws Exception {
    return config.getAuthenticationManager();
}

The account-status flags

FlagMeaningException on failure
isEnabled()Account is active (email verified, not deleted)DisabledException
isAccountNonLocked()Not locked, e.g. after too many failed loginsLockedException
isAccountNonExpired()Account validity not over (trial accounts)AccountExpiredException
isCredentialsNonExpired()Password not too oldCredentialsExpiredException

All of them extend AccountStatusException or AuthenticationException, so a login failure becomes a 401. Returning one generic message ("Invalid email or password") for all of them is safer than telling an attacker which accounts exist. One caution: DisabledException and LockedException are thrown only after the user was found, so a different message for them does reveal that the email exists. Map all of them to the same public message in your error handler.

Registration endpoint

Registration creates a user and hashes the password. The caller may choose CANDIDATE or RECRUITER; ADMIN accounts are created by seed data or by another admin, never by the public endpoint. Otherwise anyone could register as ADMIN, a classic privilege-escalation bug.

public record RegisterRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 100) String name,
        @NotBlank @Email String email,
        @NotBlank @Size(min = 8, max = 72) String password,
        @NotNull Role role) {}
@Service
public class AuthService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;

    public AuthService(UserRepository userRepository, PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }

    @Transactional
    public UserResponse register(RegisterRequest req) {
        if (req.role() == Role.ADMIN) {
            throw new AccessDeniedException("Cannot self-register as ADMIN");
        }
        if (userRepository.existsByEmailIgnoreCase(req.email())) {
            throw new DuplicateResourceException("Email already registered");
        }
        User user = new User(req.name(), req.email().toLowerCase(),
                passwordEncoder.encode(req.password()), req.role());
        return UserResponse.from(userRepository.save(user));
    }
}
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/auth")
public class AuthController {
    // fields + constructor omitted

    @PostMapping("/register")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    public UserResponse register(@Valid @RequestBody RegisterRequest req) {
        return authService.register(req);
    }
}
POST /api/auth/register
Content-Type: application/json

{"name":"Asha Rao","email":"Asha@Example.com","password":"S3cure-pass!","role":"RECRUITER"}

HTTP/1.1 201
{"id":7,"name":"Asha Rao","email":"asha@example.com","role":"RECRUITER"}

# the same email again
HTTP/1.1 409
{"status":409,"detail":"Email already registered"}

Never return the entity or its hash: UserResponse is a record with id, name, email and role only (DTOs). The same email check also needs the unique index shown above, because two simultaneous requests can both pass existsBy...; map DataIntegrityViolationException to 409. Registration returning 201 with a Location header is an even better fit (ResponseEntity).

Seeding the first ADMIN

Because the public endpoint refuses ADMIN, the first admin comes from a one-time seed. A runner that reads the password from the environment is a simple option (never hard-code it):

@Component
class AdminSeeder implements CommandLineRunner {

    private final UserRepository users;
    private final PasswordEncoder encoder;
    private final String adminPassword;

    AdminSeeder(UserRepository users, PasswordEncoder encoder,
                @Value("${app.admin.password:}") String adminPassword) {
        this.users = users;
        this.encoder = encoder;
        this.adminPassword = adminPassword;
    }

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {
        if (!adminPassword.isBlank() && !users.existsByEmailIgnoreCase("admin@example.com")) {
            users.save(new User("Admin", "admin@example.com",
                    encoder.encode(adminPassword), Role.ADMIN));
        }
    }
}

Comparison: where users can come from

SourceHowUse for
In-memoryInMemoryUserDetailsManagerDemos and tests only
JDBC tablesJdbcUserDetailsManager (fixed schema)Quick start with Security's own tables
Your JPA entityCustom UserDetailsService (this article)Real applications
External identity providerOAuth2 / OIDC (OAuth2 login)Login with Google, company SSO

Rules

  • Store only a hash made by a PasswordEncoder; the same encoder bean must be used for registration and for login.
  • loadUserByUsername must never return null; throw UsernameNotFoundException when the user is missing.
  • The role stored in the database is the plain name (RECRUITER); the authority is ROLE_RECRUITER.
  • The public registration endpoint must not accept ADMIN.

Conventions

  • Keep the entity free of Spring Security types; wrap it in a separate UserDetails class, as above.
  • Normalise the email (lower case, trimmed) once, in the service, and query case-insensitively.
  • Add a unique index on the normalised email; it is the real protection against duplicates.
  • Put registration and login in an AuthService, not in the controller.

Common mistakes

  • Letting the request body set the role without a whitelist (mass assignment).
  • Case-sensitive email lookup: Asha@x.com and asha@x.com become two accounts. Normalise to lower case.
  • Returning the User entity from a controller: the hash leaks into JSON.
  • Throwing a different message for "unknown email" and "wrong password" (user enumeration).

Wrong: plain password saved, role from the client

User u = new User(req.name(), req.email(), req.password(), req.role());
userRepository.save(u);        // plain text; ADMIN accepted

Right: hash it, restrict the role

if (req.role() == Role.ADMIN) throw new AccessDeniedException("no");
String hash = passwordEncoder.encode(req.password());
userRepository.save(new User(req.name(), email, hash, req.role()));

Edge cases and exceptions

  • UsernameNotFoundException is hidden as BadCredentialsException by default. If you set hideUserNotFoundExceptions to false yourself, the real reason leaks.
  • LazyInitializationException in getAuthorities(): you read a lazy role collection outside a transaction. Copy the data in the constructor of AppUserDetails, inside the transactional loadUserByUsername, as above.
  • IllegalArgumentException: There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id "null" means the stored value has no {bcrypt} prefix while you use a delegating encoder. Use a plain BCryptPasswordEncoder bean (as in the config article) or store the prefix.
  • DataIntegrityViolationException on save: duplicate email under a race; return 409.
  • A user who is deleted or disabled after receiving a JWT keeps a valid token until it expires, because stateless checks do not call the database. Keep access tokens short (refresh tokens).

Real projects

Real systems add email verification (the user starts with enabled = false and a verification link flips it), a failed-login counter that sets locked for 15 minutes, password reset by a one-time token mailed to the user, and a rule that the first ADMIN comes from a deployment seed or a migration script. Many teams also record createdAt and lastLoginAt (auditing).

Interview angle

"How does Spring Security load a user?" DaoAuthenticationProvider calls your UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername, gets a UserDetails, checks the flags, then compares the password with PasswordEncoder.matches. Follow-up: "What does UsernameNotFoundException become?" By default BadCredentialsException, to hide which part was wrong. Another favourite: "How do you stop a user registering as ADMIN?" Whitelist the role in the service; admins are created by seed or by another admin. And: "Why store a hash, not the password?" See password hashing.

Password hashing with BCrypt

Never store passwords or encrypt them; store a salted, deliberately slow hash such as BCrypt, check logins with PasswordEncoder.matches, and use DelegatingPasswordEncoder so the algorithm can change later.

Why hash, and why not encrypt

If your database leaks (it happens to big companies), the attacker must not get passwords. Plain text is the worst choice. Encryption is reversible: whoever has the key (and the key is usually on the same server) gets every password back. A hash is a one-way function: you can turn a password into a hash, but not a hash back into the password. At login you hash the typed password and compare hashes.

Encryption (AES)Fast hash (SHA-256)Password hash (BCrypt)
ReversibleYes, with keyNoNo
Saltedn/aOnly if you add oneYes, automatically
SpeedFastBillions per second on a GPUDeliberately slow, tunable
Use for passwordsNoNoYes

Two problems remain with a plain hash. First, equal passwords give equal hashes, and attackers keep huge tables of common passwords and their hashes (rainbow tables). A salt fixes this: a random value added to each password before hashing, so two users with password123 get different hashes and precomputed tables are useless. Second, SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so an attacker can try billions of guesses per second. A password hash must be slow on purpose: a work factor makes each guess expensive, and you can raise it as computers get faster.

BCrypt

BCrypt generates its own random 16-byte salt, applies a slow key-derivation, and writes everything into one 60-character string:

$2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy
 |  |  |                     |
 |  |  |                     +-- 31 characters of hash
 |  |  +-- 22 characters of salt
 |  +-- cost factor (work factor): 2^10 rounds
 +-- algorithm version

Because salt and cost are inside the string, you store just this one column and need no separate salt column. The cost factor is the exponent: strength 10 means 210 = 1,024 rounds; every +1 doubles the time. The default of BCryptPasswordEncoder is 10 (allowed 4 to 31). Choose a value so that one hash takes roughly 100–300 ms on your production hardware; raising it to 12 is common today. Too high and a login burst becomes a denial-of-service on your own CPU.

PasswordEncoder in Spring

PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder();          // strength 10
// PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);     // stronger

String hash1 = encoder.encode("S3cret#2026");
String hash2 = encoder.encode("S3cret#2026");
System.out.println(hash1.equals(hash2));                        // false (random salt)
System.out.println(encoder.matches("S3cret#2026", hash1));      // true
System.out.println(encoder.matches("wrong", hash1));            // false
false
true
false
  • encode(raw) returns a new hash every time, so you can never compare hashes with equals.
  • matches(raw, stored) reads the salt and cost from stored, hashes raw the same way and compares in constant time.
  • upgradeEncoding(stored) says whether the hash should be recomputed with a newer setting (used by DaoAuthenticationProvider to upgrade hashes at login).

DelegatingPasswordEncoder and the {bcrypt} prefix

Algorithms age. PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() returns an encoder that writes an id in front of the hash and uses that id to pick the algorithm at check time:

{bcrypt}$2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy
{argon2@SpringSecurity_v5_8}...   (another algorithm; different prefix)
@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}

New passwords use the current default (bcrypt); old rows with another prefix still work; you migrate users gradually. If a stored value has no prefix you get IllegalArgumentException: There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id "null". Either add the prefix to old data, or use a plain BCryptPasswordEncoder bean. For a new app that will never change algorithm, a plain BCryptPasswordEncoder is fine; the delegating form is the framework default and the safer long-term choice. Spring also provides Argon2PasswordEncoder (needs the Bouncy Castle library), SCryptPasswordEncoder and Pbkdf2PasswordEncoder.

Limits and good habits

  • 72-byte limit. BCrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of the password, so the rest is ignored (some library versions reject longer input with an exception instead). Limit the password length in validation (@Size(max = 72), as in the DTO above). Do not pre-hash with SHA-256 unless you know exactly why.
  • Never log or return a password or a hash. Check toString() of request records (a record prints all its fields), Lombok @Data classes, and request-logging filters.
  • Do not invent your own scheme ("MD5 twice with a pepper"). Use the framework.
  • Password rules: minimum length matters more than odd character rules; check against a list of leaked passwords if you can.
  • Hashing is slow. That is the point, but it means the login endpoint needs rate limiting (checklist).

Rule: compare with matches, never equals

A salted hash differs every time. Always call passwordEncoder.matches(raw, stored).

Common mistakes

  • Saving request.password() directly, so the database holds plain text.
  • Hashing the password twice: once in the controller and once in the service, so login can never match.
  • Using MD5 or SHA-1 because "it is hashing too".
  • Seeding test users with a plain password in SQL, then wondering why login fails (generate the BCrypt hash first).

Interview angle

"How do you store passwords?" Salted adaptive hash (BCrypt/Argon2), one-way, work factor tunable; never encryption, never plain SHA. "What is a salt?" Random per-user value stored with the hash, defeats rainbow tables and makes equal passwords differ. "Why is BCrypt slow on purpose?" To make brute force expensive. "What is the {bcrypt} prefix?" DelegatingPasswordEncoder id, used to support several algorithms and migrate.

JWT in depth: structure, claims, signing and the login flow

A JWT is a signed JSON document (header.payload.signature) that proves who the user is without server-side storage; anyone can read it but nobody can change it without the key, and it is valid until it expires.

What and why

A JSON Web Token (JWT, pronounced "jot") is a compact string that carries claims about a user and a signature that proves the server issued it. After login the server gives one to the client; the client sends it with each request; the server verifies the signature and trusts the claims inside, with no database or session lookup. That is what makes the API stateless (see sessions vs tokens).

Structure

A JWT has three parts separated by dots, each encoded with base64url (base64 with - and _ instead of + and /, no padding):

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsInJvbGVzIjpbIlJFQ1JVSVRFUiJdfQ.Sx3...k9A
{
  "alg": "HS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}
{
  "iss": "jobportal-api",
  "sub": "42",
  "roles": ["RECRUITER"],
  "iat": 1790000000,
  "exp": 1790003600
}

The signature (part 3) is computed over base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload) with the secret key (or private key). If anybody changes one character of the payload, the signature no longer matches and verification fails.

Rule: the payload is readable by everyone

Base64url is encoding, not encryption. Paste any JWT into a decoder and you see the claims. Never put passwords, card numbers, or secrets in a JWT. Put identifiers and roles only. (An encrypted token format, JWE, exists but is rarely needed.)

Claims

ClaimNameMeaning
subSubjectWho the token is about: the user id (or email)
issIssuerWho created it, e.g. jobportal-api; check it on validation
audAudienceWho it is meant for (which API); check it when several services exist
iatIssued atCreation time (seconds since 1970)
expExpirationAfter this time the token is invalid
nbfNot beforeNot valid before this time
jtiJWT IDUnique id, useful for revocation lists
roles, scopeCustomYour own claims (keep them small)

Times are numbers in seconds, not milliseconds, a frequent source of "token expired in 1970" bugs when you mix them up.

Signing: HS256 vs RS256

HS256 (HMAC-SHA256)RS256 (RSA + SHA-256)
Key typeOne shared secretKey pair: private signs, public verifies
Who can create tokensAnyone who has the secret (every verifier)Only the holder of the private key
Who can verifyAnyone who has the secretAnyone with the public key (can be published, e.g. JWKS)
SpeedVery fastSlower signing
UseOne application issuing and verifying its own tokensSeparate auth server and many resource servers; microservices; third-party login

Project 2 has one application, so HS256 is enough. The HS256 secret must be long and random (at least 256 bits = 32 bytes) and come from an environment variable or secret store, never from the Git repository. Moving to RS256 later is a configuration change when you use the Spring support.

The login flow

  1. The client sends the email and password once to the public login endpoint (over HTTPS).
  2. The controller calls AuthenticationManager.authenticate, which runs the DaoAuthenticationProvider path from the architecture article. A wrong password throws and becomes 401.
  3. On success the server builds a JWT with the user id, roles and an expiry (for example 15–60 minutes) and signs it.
  4. The client keeps the token and sends Authorization: Bearer <token> on each call.
  5. A filter verifies signature, expiry (and issuer), creates an Authentication from the claims, and stores it in the SecurityContext for this request.
  6. URL rules, method security and your controller now see the current user.

Expiry and what JWT cannot do

The server holds no record of issued tokens, so it cannot "log out" a token: until exp passes, any holder is accepted. That is why access tokens are short-lived and paired with a refresh token (refresh tokens). Roles inside the token are also a snapshot: if an admin removes a user's role, the old token still carries it until it expires. Keep the lifetime short, or look the user up on each request when you need immediate effect.

Common mistakes

  • A weak or hard-coded secret ("secret", "mykey") committed to GitHub. Anyone can then forge an ADMIN token.
  • Putting personal or sensitive data in the payload.
  • Accepting tokens without checking expiry, or setting a lifetime of months.
  • Trusting the alg header from the token (the old "alg: none" attack). Libraries today reject it; always configure the expected algorithm yourself.
  • Treating JWT as a replacement for authorization: the token says who the user is, your code must still check ownership.

Interview angle

"What is a JWT and how is it verified?" Three base64url parts; the server recomputes the signature with the key and checks exp/iss. "Is the payload secret?" No, only tamper-proof. "HS256 vs RS256?" Shared secret vs key pair. "How do you invalidate a JWT?" You mostly cannot; use short expiry, refresh-token rotation, or a deny list keyed by jti.

JWT way 1: a custom OncePerRequestFilter with the jjwt library

Write a TokenService that signs and parses tokens with jjwt, a OncePerRequestFilter that turns a valid Bearer token into an Authentication, and register it before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.

This approach gives you full control and shows exactly what happens. The next article shows the shorter Spring-supported way, which is recommended for new code. Both versions use the same login controller, so read this one for understanding even if you ship the other.

Dependencies and configuration

The jjwt library (io.jsonwebtoken) is split into an API jar and two runtime jars. The code below uses the 0.12.x API (parseSignedClaims, verifyWith, subject); older 0.11 tutorials use parseClaimsJws and setSubject, which differ.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId>
    <artifactId>jjwt-api</artifactId>
    <version>0.12.6</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId>
    <artifactId>jjwt-impl</artifactId>
    <version>0.12.6</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId>
    <artifactId>jjwt-jackson</artifactId>
    <version>0.12.6</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
app:
  jwt:
    secret: ${JWT_SECRET}          # Base64 text of at least 32 random bytes
    issuer: jobportal-api
    access-ttl-minutes: 30
$ openssl rand -base64 32
q3L0x1m...(44 characters)...=
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.jwt")
public record JwtProperties(String secret, String issuer, long accessTtlMinutes) {}

Register it with @EnableConfigurationProperties(JwtProperties.class) on any configuration class (or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the application class).

The TokenService contract

The login controller depends on a small interface, so you can swap the implementation (this one, or the Nimbus one) without touching the controller.

public interface TokenService {
    String issueAccessToken(AppUserDetails user);
}

JjwtService: create and parse tokens

import io.jsonwebtoken.Claims;
import io.jsonwebtoken.Jwts;
import io.jsonwebtoken.io.Decoders;
import io.jsonwebtoken.security.Keys;
import javax.crypto.SecretKey;

@Service
public class JjwtService implements TokenService {

    private final SecretKey key;
    private final String issuer;
    private final Duration ttl;

    public JjwtService(JwtProperties props) {
        this.key = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(Decoders.BASE64.decode(props.secret()));
        this.issuer = props.issuer();
        this.ttl = Duration.ofMinutes(props.accessTtlMinutes());
    }

    @Override
    public String issueAccessToken(AppUserDetails user) {
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        return Jwts.builder()
                .issuer(issuer)
                .subject(String.valueOf(user.getId()))
                .claim("email", user.getUsername())
                .claim("roles", List.of(user.getRole().name()))
                .issuedAt(Date.from(now))
                .expiration(Date.from(now.plus(ttl)))
                .signWith(key)                 // HS256 chosen from the key size
                .compact();
    }

    /** Verifies signature, expiry and issuer. Throws JwtException if invalid. */
    public Claims parse(String token) {
        return Jwts.parser()
                .verifyWith(key)
                .requireIssuer(issuer)
                .build()
                .parseSignedClaims(token)
                .getPayload();
    }
}

Keys.hmacShaKeyFor throws WeakKeyException if the key is shorter than 256 bits for HS256, which is a useful safety net. parseSignedClaims only accepts a signed token (an unsigned or "alg: none" token fails). The parser checks exp and nbf itself.

What the parser can throw

ExceptionMeaning
ExpiredJwtExceptionexp is in the past
SignatureExceptionSignature does not match (tampered or wrong key)
MalformedJwtExceptionNot a valid JWT structure
UnsupportedJwtExceptionUnexpected token type (e.g. unsigned)
IncorrectClaimException / MissingClaimExceptionThe issuer you require is wrong or missing
IllegalArgumentExceptionToken is null or empty

All JWT-specific ones extend io.jsonwebtoken.JwtException, so one catch is enough.

The filter

OncePerRequestFilter guarantees one execution per request. The filter's job: read the header, validate the token, and store an Authentication. It does not write error responses itself; if the token is missing or bad it simply leaves the context empty and lets the rest of the chain decide (a protected URL then triggers the authentication entry point, which returns 401).

public class JwtAuthenticationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private static final String PREFIX = "Bearer ";
    private final JjwtService jwtService;

    public JwtAuthenticationFilter(JjwtService jwtService) {
        this.jwtService = jwtService;
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
                                    HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {

        String header = request.getHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION);
        if (header == null || !header.startsWith(PREFIX)) {
            chain.doFilter(request, response);          // anonymous request
            return;
        }
        try {
            Claims claims = jwtService.parse(header.substring(PREFIX.length()));
            List<?> roles = claims.get("roles", List.class);
            List<SimpleGrantedAuthority> authorities = roles.stream()
                    .map(r -> new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + r))
                    .toList();

            var auth = new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
                    claims.getSubject(), null, authorities);   // principal = user id
            auth.setDetails(new WebAuthenticationDetailsSource().buildDetails(request));
            SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth);
        } catch (JwtException | IllegalArgumentException e) {
            SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();       // bad token: stay anonymous
            request.setAttribute("auth.error", e.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}

The three-argument UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken constructor creates an authenticated token (the two-argument one is "not yet authenticated"). The principal here is the user id as a string, so authentication.getName() returns "42". We read the roles from the token and trust the signature; there is no database call per request. If you need fresh account status (disabled users blocked immediately), load the user inside the filter instead, at the cost of one query per request (or a short cache).

Registering the filter and exposing the AuthenticationManager

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity
@EnableConfigurationProperties(JwtProperties.class)
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http, JjwtService jwtService,
                            JsonSecurityHandlers handlers) throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(s ->
                    s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .httpBasic(b -> b.disable())
            .formLogin(f -> f.disable())
            .exceptionHandling(e -> e
                    .authenticationEntryPoint(handlers)      // 401 JSON
                    .accessDeniedHandler(handlers))          // 403 JSON
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                    .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                    .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/jobs/**").permitAll()
                    .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .addFilterBefore(new JwtAuthenticationFilter(jwtService),
                    UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean
    AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration cfg)
            throws Exception {
        return cfg.getAuthenticationManager();
    }

    @Bean
    PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
    }
}

JsonSecurityHandlers is defined in the error-response article. Note that the filter is created with new inside the configuration and is not annotated with @Component: Spring Boot registers every Filter bean in the servlet container too, so a @Component filter would run twice (once outside and once inside the security chain). If you prefer a bean, add a FilterRegistrationBean with setEnabled(false).

The login controller

public record LoginRequest(@NotBlank @Email String email, @NotBlank String password) {}

public record TokenResponse(String accessToken, String tokenType, long expiresIn) {}
@PostMapping("/login")
public TokenResponse login(@Valid @RequestBody LoginRequest req) {
    Authentication auth = authenticationManager.authenticate(
            UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(
                    req.email().toLowerCase(), req.password()));
    AppUserDetails user = (AppUserDetails) auth.getPrincipal();
    String token = tokenService.issueAccessToken(user);
    return new TokenResponse(token, "Bearer", 1800);
}
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/auth/login \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"email":"asha@example.com","password":"S3cret#2026"}'
{"accessToken":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...","tokenType":"Bearer","expiresIn":1800}

$ curl -s localhost:8080/api/jobs/mine -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi..."
[ {"id":7,"title":"Java Developer"} ]

A wrong password makes authenticate throw BadCredentialsException. Because this happens inside a controller (after the filter chain), ExceptionTranslationFilter is not involved; handle AuthenticationException in your @RestControllerAdvice and return 401 with the same generic message for every cause.

@ExceptionHandler(AuthenticationException.class)
ProblemDetail loginFailed(AuthenticationException ex) {
    ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
            HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Invalid email or password");
    pd.setTitle("Authentication failed");
    return pd;
}

Expired and invalid tokens

With this design an expired token makes the filter catch ExpiredJwtException, leave the request anonymous, and the protected URL returns 401. The client reads 401, uses its refresh token (or sends the user to the login screen) and retries. To tell the client why, read the auth.error request attribute in your entry point and put "token_expired" or "token_invalid" in the JSON body.

Common mistakes

  • Annotating the filter with @Component (double registration) or forgetting addFilterBefore, so the filter never runs.
  • Catching the exception and writing a 500 or a stack trace, or swallowing it and still authenticating.
  • Mixing seconds and milliseconds in exp, or using the 0.11 API names with the 0.12 jar.
  • Reading the secret with getBytes() when it is stored as Base64 (or the other way round); both ends must agree.
  • Forgetting permitAll() on the login URL, so nobody can ever log in.

Interview angle

"Walk me through JWT authentication in Spring Boot." Login controller authenticates through the AuthenticationManager and returns a signed token; a OncePerRequestFilter placed before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter reads the Bearer header, validates it, sets the SecurityContext; the stateless session policy means every request repeats this. Mention failure behaviour: invalid token leaves the request anonymous, so the entry point returns 401.

JWT way 2 (recommended): OAuth2 Resource Server with JwtEncoder and JwtDecoder

Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server, define a JwtDecoder and JwtEncoder from your key, and Spring Security's BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter does the parsing, validation and Authentication for you; you only write the token issuing and a role converter.

Why this way

Spring Security ships a complete, well-tested Bearer-token implementation called the OAuth2 Resource Server support. A resource server is simply an API that accepts access tokens. It reads Authorization: Bearer, validates the JWT with a JwtDecoder (built on the Nimbus library, a dependency of the starter), maps claims to authorities, and produces the standard 401 responses. You do not write a filter, you do not catch parser exceptions, and moving later to RS256 keys or to an external identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta) is a configuration change. Use it for new code; it is the approach Spring Security's documentation recommends.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>

Keep spring-boot-starter-security too. Remove the jjwt dependencies and the custom filter, or leave them unused while you compare.

Step 1: the key, encoder and decoder

The decoder verifies tokens; the encoder creates them (the encoder is only needed because this application also issues tokens at login). Both use the same HS256 secret from app.jwt.secret (same properties as before).

import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.source.ImmutableSecret;
import javax.crypto.SecretKey;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jose.jws.MacAlgorithm;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.*;

@Configuration
@EnableConfigurationProperties(JwtProperties.class)
public class JwtConfig {

    @Bean
    SecretKey jwtSecretKey(JwtProperties props) {
        byte[] bytes = Base64.getDecoder().decode(props.secret());
        return new SecretKeySpec(bytes, "HmacSHA256");
    }

    @Bean
    JwtEncoder jwtEncoder(SecretKey key) {
        return new NimbusJwtEncoder(new ImmutableSecret<>(key));
    }

    @Bean
    JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(SecretKey key, JwtProperties props) {
        NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = NimbusJwtDecoder.withSecretKey(key)
                .macAlgorithm(MacAlgorithm.HS256)
                .build();
        // default validators (exp, nbf) + the issuer must match
        decoder.setJwtValidator(JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(props.issuer()));
        return decoder;
    }
}

Step 2: issue the token at login

@Service
public class NimbusTokenService implements TokenService {

    private final JwtEncoder encoder;
    private final JwtProperties props;

    public NimbusTokenService(JwtEncoder encoder, JwtProperties props) {
        this.encoder = encoder;
        this.props = props;
    }

    @Override
    public String issueAccessToken(AppUserDetails user) {
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        JwtClaimsSet claims = JwtClaimsSet.builder()
                .issuer(props.issuer())
                .issuedAt(now)
                .expiresAt(now.plus(Duration.ofMinutes(props.accessTtlMinutes())))
                .subject(String.valueOf(user.getId()))
                .claim("email", user.getUsername())
                .claim("roles", List.of(user.getRole().name()))
                .build();
        JwsHeader header = JwsHeader.with(MacAlgorithm.HS256).build();   // see below
        return encoder.encode(JwtEncoderParameters.from(header, claims)).getTokenValue();
    }
}

Edge case: set the header algorithm yourself

If you call JwtEncoderParameters.from(claims) without a header, the encoder defaults to RS256 and fails with a "Failed to select a JWK signing key" error when your key is an HMAC secret. Pass JwsHeader.with(MacAlgorithm.HS256).build() as shown. Also keep only one TokenService bean: delete @Service from JjwtService (or the class itself) when you switch.

The login controller from the previous article is unchanged: it authenticates with the AuthenticationManager and calls tokenService.issueAccessToken(user).

Step 3: turn on the resource server and map roles

By default the converter looks at the scope or scp claim and prefixes each value with SCOPE_. Our tokens carry a roles claim, so we tell the converter to read that claim and prefix ROLE_, which makes hasRole("RECRUITER") work.

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http, JsonSecurityHandlers handlers)
            throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(s ->
                    s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                    .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                    .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/jobs/**").permitAll()
                    .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                    .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth
                    .jwt(jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(jwtConverter()))
                    .authenticationEntryPoint(handlers)     // 401 JSON
                    .accessDeniedHandler(handlers));        // 403 JSON
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean
    JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtConverter() {
        JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter authorities = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
        authorities.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
        authorities.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");
        JwtAuthenticationConverter converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
        converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(authorities);
        return converter;
    }

    @Bean
    AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration cfg)
            throws Exception {
        return cfg.getAuthenticationManager();
    }

    @Bean
    PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
    }
}

What you get for free: BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter in the chain; for each request the token goes to the JwtDecoder, then the converter builds a JwtAuthenticationToken whose principal is a Jwt object (claims accessible by jwt.getClaim("email")) and whose getName() is the sub claim, the user id. In a controller:

@GetMapping("/api/me")
public Map<String, Object> me(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    return Map.of(
            "id", jwt.getSubject(),
            "email", jwt.getClaimAsString("email"),
            "roles", jwt.getClaimAsStringList("roles"));
}

Expired and invalid tokens

If the token is missing the entry point answers 401. If it is present but bad, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter catches the failure and calls the entry point with an InvalidBearerTokenException. The default entry point returns an empty body with:

HTTP/1.1 401
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Jwt expired at 2026-11-10T10:15:00Z"

That follows the OAuth2 standard (RFC 6750). Our JsonSecurityHandlers replaces it with a JSON body but can keep the header. Note the difference from the custom filter: here a bad token on a public URL is rejected with 401 too, not ignored.

Asymmetric keys and external providers

With RS256 the application that issues tokens keeps the private key; other services only need the public key. With the resource server you can configure that with properties alone:

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://login.example.com/realms/jobs    # discovers the JWKS
          # or: jwk-set-uri: https://login.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
          # or: public-key-location: classpath:app.pub

When Boot sees one of these properties it builds the JwtDecoder for you, and you do not define the decoder bean. This is how a microservice trusts tokens from Keycloak without any security code of its own (module 7).

Comparison: custom filter vs resource server

Custom filter + jjwtOAuth2 Resource Server
Code you writeFilter, parsing, error casesDecoder/encoder beans, role converter
ValidationWhatever you remember to checkSignature, expiry, not-before, issuer, standard
401 for bad tokensYou build it (request attribute + entry point)Built in, RFC 6750 header
RS256 / JWKS / KeycloakMore codeA few properties
TestingGenerate real tokensjwt() post-processor (module 5)
Learning valueShows every stepHides the steps behind framework classes
RecommendedFor learning; legacy codebasesNew code

Real codebases you join will contain both, so you should be able to read either.

Common mistakes

  • Roles never work: the default converter uses scope and SCOPE_, so hasRole fails with 403 until you add the converter above.
  • A secret shorter than 32 bytes: the HS256 key is rejected or insecure.
  • Forgetting the HS256 header when encoding (see the edge case).
  • Defining both your own JwtDecoder bean and the issuer-uri property and expecting both to work: your bean wins.

Interview angle

"How would you secure a Spring Boot API with JWT today?"
