Resource Server with a JwtDecoder and a converter for roles; mention Nimbus, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter, and that issuing tokens uses JwtEncoder (or an external identity provider). Contrast with the hand-written filter and say why the framework version is safer.

JSON error responses for 401 and 403: AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler

Security filters run before Spring MVC, so @RestControllerAdvice cannot handle their errors; implement AuthenticationEntryPoint for 401 and AccessDeniedHandler for 403 and write the JSON yourself.

Why a separate mechanism

Your @RestControllerAdvice from module 2 only sees exceptions thrown inside DispatcherServlet. Security filters run before it. When AuthorizationFilter denies a request, or the token is bad, the exception is caught by ExceptionTranslationFilter which delegates to two strategies:

InterfaceCalled whenStatusDefault behaviour
AuthenticationEntryPointAnonymous user hits a protected URL, or authentication failed401Empty body (and a WWW-Authenticate header)
AccessDeniedHandlerAuthenticated user lacks permission403Empty 403

A client that gets an empty body cannot show a good message. We write one handler class that implements both interfaces and returns a ProblemDetail-style JSON (the same shape as the rest of the API, module 2).

The handlers

@Component
public class JsonSecurityHandlers implements AuthenticationEntryPoint, AccessDeniedHandler {

    @Override   // 401
    public void commence(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                         AuthenticationException ex) throws IOException {
        String detail = "Authentication is required or the token is invalid.";
        if (ex instanceof InvalidBearerTokenException) {
            detail = "The access token is invalid or has expired.";
        }
        response.setHeader(HttpHeaders.WWW_AUTHENTICATE, "Bearer");
        write(response, 401, "Unauthorized", detail, request.getRequestURI());
    }

    @Override   // 403
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                       AccessDeniedException ex) throws IOException {
        write(response, 403, "Forbidden",
                "You do not have permission to do this.", request.getRequestURI());
    }

    private void write(HttpServletResponse response, int status, String title,
                       String detail, String path) throws IOException {
        response.setStatus(status);
        response.setContentType("application/problem+json");
        response.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8");
        response.getWriter().write("""
                {"type":"about:blank","title":"%s","status":%d,\
                "detail":"%s","instance":"%s"}"""
                .formatted(title, status, detail, path.replace("\"", "")));
    }
}
HTTP/1.1 401
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type":"about:blank","title":"Unauthorized","status":401,
 "detail":"Authentication is required or the token is invalid.",
 "instance":"/api/jobs/mine"}

The detail texts are fixed strings, so no user input reaches the JSON except the path, whose quotes we remove. If you build bigger bodies, use your JSON mapper (JsonMapper/ObjectMapper) instead of string formatting; its package differs between Jackson 2 in Boot 3 and Jackson 3 in Boot 4, which is why this example avoids it.

Register the handlers as shown in the earlier configurations: exceptionHandling(e -> e.authenticationEntryPoint(h).accessDeniedHandler(h)) for the custom filter, or the same two calls inside oauth2ResourceServer(...) for the resource server.

Method-security exceptions inside controllers

An AccessDeniedException thrown by @PreAuthorize or by your service code is raised inside MVC. If you have a catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) returning 500, it swallows it and the user gets a wrong status. Handle it explicitly in the advice (or rethrow it):

@ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class)
ProblemDetail denied(AccessDeniedException ex) {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN,
            "You do not have permission to do this.");
}

Common mistakes

  • Expecting @RestControllerAdvice to format the 401/403 for URL rules.
  • A catch-all handler that turns AccessDeniedException into 500.
  • Putting stack traces or "user not found" details into the 401 body.
  • Forgetting the WWW-Authenticate header (it is part of the 401 contract, and clients and tools use it).

Interview angle

"Where do you customise the 401 and 403 responses?" AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler, set in exceptionHandling (or in the resource-server DSL). Explain why controller advice does not apply: the filters run before the DispatcherServlet.

Authorization: roles, hasRole, @PreAuthorize and owner-only checks

Use URL rules for coarse role checks, @PreAuthorize for method-level rules, and an ownership check in the service layer for "only the owner can edit"; roles need the ROLE_ prefix and the current user comes from the Authentication.

Roles vs authorities and the ROLE_ prefix

Spring Security has one concept: a GrantedAuthority, a string. A role is just an authority whose name starts with ROLE_. A finer-grained authority (also called permission) has any other name, e.g. job:write.

ExpressionChecks for
hasRole("ADMIN")Authority ROLE_ADMIN (prefix added for you)
hasAnyRole("ADMIN", "RECRUITER")Either role
hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")The exact string, same result as hasRole("ADMIN")
hasAuthority("job:write")A permission name, exactly as stored
authenticated(), permitAll(), denyAll()Any user / everyone / nobody

The classic bug: the database stores RECRUITER, the authority list contains RECRUITER, and hasRole("RECRUITER") returns 403 because it looks for ROLE_RECRUITER. Add the prefix when you build authorities (we did in both implementations).

Roles suit a small fixed set (CANDIDATE, RECRUITER, ADMIN). If you need "can edit jobs but not delete" across many roles, use permissions and map roles to permission sets.

URL rules vs method security

URL rules (authorizeHttpRequests)Method security (@PreAuthorize)
WhereCentral, in SecurityConfigOn controller or service methods
SeesPath, HTTP method, rolesMethod arguments, return value, the Authentication
Good forCoarse rules: public vs login vs admin areaFine rules: "owner only", argument-based checks
RiskPath patterns that miss a URL variantSelf-invocation skips the proxy (as with @Transactional)

Use both: URL rules as the outer wall, method security next to the business code.

@EnableMethodSecurity and @PreAuthorize

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/jobs")
public class JobController {

    @PostMapping
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('RECRUITER')")
    public JobResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateJobRequest req,
                              Authentication auth) { ... }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

    @GetMapping("/admin/stats")
    @PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('ADMIN', 'RECRUITER')")
    public Stats stats() { ... }
}

The annotation holds a SpEL expression (Spring Expression Language). The useful pieces: authentication (the Authentication), principal, method arguments with #name (needs the -parameters compiler flag, which Spring Boot's Maven parent sets), and bean calls with @beanName. Related annotations: @PostAuthorize (checks the returned object), @PreFilter / @PostFilter (filter collections; avoid on big lists, filter in the query instead).

// Principal is a UserDetails with getId() (session / custom-filter style)
@PreAuthorize("#id == authentication.principal.id or hasRole('ADMIN')")
public UserResponse getProfile(Long id) { ... }

// Resource server style: authentication.name is the "sub" claim
@PreAuthorize("#id.toString() == authentication.name or hasRole('ADMIN')")
public UserResponse getProfile(Long id) { ... }

// Call a bean for anything that needs the database
@PreAuthorize("@jobSecurity.isOwner(#jobId, authentication)")
public JobResponse update(Long jobId, UpdateJobRequest req) { ... }
@Component("jobSecurity")
public class JobSecurity {

    private final JobRepository jobRepository;

    public JobSecurity(JobRepository jobRepository) {
        this.jobRepository = jobRepository;
    }

    public boolean isOwner(Long jobId, Authentication auth) {
        Long userId = Long.valueOf(auth.getName());
        return jobRepository.existsByIdAndPostedById(jobId, userId);
    }
}

If a rule fails, AuthorizationDeniedException (a subclass of AccessDeniedException) is thrown and becomes 403 through the handler above.

Ownership: "recruiters edit only their own jobs"

Roles answer "may a recruiter edit jobs?". Ownership answers "may this recruiter edit this job?". No role expression can know that, so a check against the data is needed. Do it in the service layer, where the entity is already loaded, so it works for every caller (controllers, scheduled jobs, other services) and cannot be forgotten by a new controller.

@Service
public class JobService {

    @Transactional
    public JobResponse update(Long jobId, UpdateJobRequest req, CurrentUser me) {
        Job job = jobRepository.findById(jobId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Job " + jobId));

        boolean owner = job.getPostedBy().getId().equals(me.id());
        if (!owner && !me.isAdmin()) {
            throw new AccessDeniedException("You can only edit your own jobs");
        }
        job.update(req.title(), req.description(), req.salaryMin(), req.salaryMax());
        return JobResponse.from(job);                    // dirty checking saves it
    }
}

Notes: the first lookup returns 404 for an unknown job, then 403 for someone else's. Some APIs return 404 in both cases so outsiders cannot discover ids; pick one. In list queries, filter by owner in the query itself: findByPostedById(userId, pageable) for "my jobs"; never load all and filter in Java. For candidates, "only owners can edit their data" means applications: application.getApplicant().getId() must equal the current user, and a recruiter may see applications only for jobs they posted.

Getting the current user

// 1. Parameter of the controller method (simplest and testable)
@GetMapping("/me")
UserResponse me(Authentication authentication) { ... }

// 2. The principal itself
@GetMapping("/me")
Object me(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) { ... }                 // resource server
Object me(@AuthenticationPrincipal AppUserDetails user) { ... }     // UserDetails style

// 3. Static access (anywhere, but hidden dependency)
Authentication a = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

// 4. A small value object used by services
public record CurrentUser(Long id, Set<String> roles) {
    public static CurrentUser from(Authentication a) {
        Set<String> roles = a.getAuthorities().stream()
                .map(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority)
                .collect(Collectors.toSet());
        return new CurrentUser(Long.valueOf(a.getName()), roles);
    }
    public boolean isAdmin() { return roles.contains("ROLE_ADMIN"); }
}

Resolving CurrentUser once in the controller and passing it to the service keeps services free of SecurityContextHolder and easy to unit test (module 5). Do not accept the user id from the request body or URL for "my data" endpoints: POST /api/applications with {"userId": 5} lets anyone apply as someone else.

Project 2 access matrix

ActionAnonymousCANDIDATERECRUITERADMIN
Browse jobs (GET)YesYesYesYes
Post a jobNoNoYesYes
Edit or close a jobNoNoOwn jobs onlyAny
Apply to a jobNoYesNoNo
See applications of a jobNoNoOwn jobs onlyAny
See / withdraw my applicationNoOwn onlyNoAny
Manage usersNoNoNoYes

Rule: authorize on the server, with data, every time

Hiding a button in React is not security. Every endpoint must check role and ownership on the server. Missing ownership checks are called IDOR (insecure direct object reference, also "broken object-level authorization") and top the OWASP API list.

Common mistakes

  • hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN") double prefix, or authorities stored without prefix and hasRole used.
  • Forgetting @EnableMethodSecurity: the annotations silently do nothing.
  • Calling a @PreAuthorize method from another method of the same class (no proxy, no check).
  • Checking the role but not the owner: any recruiter edits any job.
  • Using the old @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true); it is replaced by @EnableMethodSecurity.

Interview angle

"Role vs authority?" Role is an authority with the ROLE_ prefix. "hasRole vs hasAuthority?" Prefix handling. "How do you stop one user editing another's data?" Ownership check against the loaded entity in the service (or @PreAuthorize calling a bean), plus query filtering; mention IDOR. "Where do you put authorization: controller or service?" URL/role rules at the edge, ownership in the service.

CORS: same-origin policy, preflight and Spring Security configuration

Browsers block JavaScript from reading responses of another origin unless that server allows it with CORS headers; configure one CorsConfigurationSource bean with your exact frontend origins, connect it with cors(withDefaults()), and never combine * with credentials.

The same-origin policy and what an origin is

A browser lets a page talk freely to its own server, but a page from one site must not read data from another site (otherwise any web page could call your bank in the background). This rule is the same-origin policy. An origin is the triple scheme + host + port.

Page at http://localhost:5173 callsSame origin?Why
http://localhost:5173/api/jobsYesSame scheme, host, port
http://localhost:8080/api/jobsNoDifferent port: React dev server vs Spring Boot
https://localhost:5173/xNoDifferent scheme
http://api.jobportal.in/xNoDifferent host

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the standard way for a server to say "this other origin may read my responses". It is a browser rule: Postman and curl ignore it, and the server still receives the request. The classic symptom is a React console error: "Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8080/api/jobs' from origin 'http://localhost:5173' has been blocked by CORS policy". The fix is on the server (or a dev proxy), not in React.

Simple requests and the preflight

For simple requests (GET, or POST with a form content type, no custom headers) the browser sends the request and then checks the response header Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For anything else, for example PUT, DELETE, Content-Type: application/json or an Authorization header, the browser first sends a preflight: an OPTIONS request asking permission, without credentials.

OPTIONS /api/jobs HTTP/1.1
Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type

HTTP/1.1 200
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE,OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization,content-type
Access-Control-Max-Age: 3600

Max-Age lets the browser cache the preflight answer, so it does not repeat before every call.

Configuring CORS with Spring Security

Define a CorsConfigurationSource bean and enable it with http.cors(withDefaults()). This puts CorsFilter early in the security chain, so a preflight (which carries no token) is answered before authentication rejects it with 401.

@Configuration
public class CorsConfig {

    @Bean
    CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource(
            @Value("${app.cors.allowed-origins}") List<String> origins) {
        CorsConfiguration cfg = new CorsConfiguration();
        cfg.setAllowedOrigins(origins);                    // exact origins, no wildcard
        cfg.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
        cfg.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type"));
        cfg.setExposedHeaders(List.of("Location"));        // headers JS may read
        cfg.setAllowCredentials(false);                    // true only for cookie auth
        cfg.setMaxAge(3600L);

        UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
        source.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", cfg);
        return source;
    }
}
app:
  cors:
    allowed-origins: http://localhost:5173,https://jobportal.example.com

Then .cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) in the SecurityFilterChain picks up the bean named corsConfigurationSource. Origins come from properties so development and production differ without code changes.

@CrossOrigin and WebMvcConfigurer

@CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:5173")      // one controller or method
@RestController
class JobController { ... }

@Configuration
class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {         // MVC-level global config
    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**").allowedOrigins("http://localhost:5173");
    }
}

These work for plain Spring MVC, but with Spring Security present the CorsConfigurationSource bean above is the better single place: one list of allowed origins for the whole app and it also covers requests that security rejects (401/403 responses still carry CORS headers, so the browser can show the real error instead of a confusing CORS failure). Scattered @CrossOrigin annotations are easy to forget on new controllers.

Credentials and wildcards

When the frontend sends cookies (fetch(..., { credentials: "include" })), the server must answer with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and a specific origin. The wildcard * is forbidden together with credentials; Spring throws IllegalArgumentException: When allowCredentials is true, allowedOrigins cannot contain the special value "*". If you need patterns (all subdomains), use setAllowedOriginPatterns(List.of("https://*.jobportal.in")). For a Bearer-token API, allowCredentials can stay false, because the token travels in a header the JavaScript sets itself.

Avoiding CORS in development

Vite's dev server can proxy /api to localhost:8080, so the browser sees one origin and no preflight is needed. Production behind one domain with a reverse proxy (Nginx) has the same effect. Keep the CORS config anyway for separate frontend domains. See Frontend · Module 6.

Common mistakes

  • Allowing * for every origin on an API that uses cookies. Any website can then call it as the logged-in user.
  • Fixing the error by disabling CORS in the browser or by adding @CrossOrigin("*") everywhere "to make it work".
  • Forgetting cors(withDefaults()): the MVC mapping exists, but security answers the preflight with 401 first.
  • Allowing the origin but not the Authorization header in allowedHeaders.
  • Trailing slash or wrong port in the origin: http://localhost:5173/ does not match http://localhost:5173.
  • Believing CORS protects the API. It only restricts browsers; authentication does the protecting.

Interview angle

"What is CORS and why does the preflight exist?" Same-origin policy, origin = scheme+host+port, browser enforced; preflight asks permission before non-simple requests so a foreign page cannot trigger a state-changing call that the server never agreed to. "Why can't I use * with credentials?" Spec forbids it, because it would let any site act as the user. "Does CORS stop curl?" No.

CSRF: the attack, and when protection can be off

CSRF tricks a logged-in browser into sending a request the user never intended, which works only when the browser attaches credentials automatically (cookies); stateless APIs that need an Authorization header set by your own code can turn CSRF protection off, but tokens kept in cookies bring it back.

The attack, as a story

Ravi is logged in to jobportal.com; his browser holds the session cookie. In another tab he opens a harmless-looking page, cute-cats.example. That page contains a hidden form:

<form action="https://jobportal.com/api/account/email" method="POST" id="f">
  <input name="email" value="attacker@evil.example">
</form>
<script>document.getElementById("f").submit();</script>

The browser sends the POST to jobportal.com and, because that is the cookie's site, attaches Ravi's session cookie automatically. The server sees a valid session and changes the account email to the attacker's. The attacker then resets the password. Ravi clicked nothing. This is Cross-Site Request Forgery. The attacker cannot read the response (the same-origin policy and CORS prevent that), but a state-changing request is enough.

The requirement: the credential is attached automatically by the browser. Cookies and HTTP Basic credentials both behave this way.

How Spring Security defends: the CSRF token

The defence is a secret value that the attacker's page cannot know. The server gives the legitimate page a random CSRF token; for every unsafe request (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) the page must send it back in a header (X-CSRF-TOKEN) or a hidden form field (_csrf). CsrfFilter compares it to the expected value and answers 403 when it is missing or wrong. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are exempt because they must not change data. Spring Security has this on by default, which is why your first POST after adding the starter returned 403.

  • Thymeleaf forms add the hidden field automatically.
  • For a JavaScript SPA with cookie sessions, store the token in a cookie that JavaScript can read and echo it back in the header: .csrf(c -> c.csrfTokenRepository(CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse())) (the token cookie must be readable by JS, so it is not HttpOnly).
  • Defence in depth: SameSite=Lax or Strict on the session cookie. Modern browsers default to Lax, which already blocks the cross-site POST above; it still does not replace the token for all cases.

Why a stateless Bearer-token API can disable it

In our JWT design, the JavaScript code reads the token from memory and writes Authorization: Bearer ... on each request. A page on cute-cats.example cannot do that: it cannot read your token (different origin), and a browser never adds an Authorization header to a cross-site form post on its own. There is nothing automatic for the attacker to ride on. So the CSRF filter protects against an attack that cannot happen, and Spring's documentation says it is fine to disable it for such APIs:

http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
    .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
    .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
// 1. no session cookie  2. credentials only in the Authorization header
// 3. no HTTP Basic or form login left enabled

When tokens in cookies bring CSRF back

Some teams keep the JWT (or refresh token) in an HttpOnly cookie, so JavaScript cannot steal it with XSS. That is a good idea for XSS, but now the browser attaches the credential automatically, and the whole CSRF argument above applies again. If you store the access token in a cookie, you must keep CSRF protection (or rely strictly on SameSite=Strict plus a custom-header check), and CORS with credentials becomes relevant. A refresh-token cookie scoped to /api/auth/refresh is a smaller risk, because the worst the attacker can do is force a token refresh whose result they cannot read, but protect that endpoint too.

SetupCredential sentCSRF protection
Server-rendered site, session cookieCookie, automaticallyOn (default)
SPA + session cookieCookie, automaticallyOn, token in cookie + header
SPA + Bearer token in memory or localStorageHeader, by your codeCan be off
SPA + JWT stored in a cookieCookie, automaticallyOn (or SameSite=Strict + checks)
Service-to-service with API keys in headersHeaderCan be off

Rule: CSRF is about automatic credentials, not about "REST"

Do not disable CSRF just because "it is an API". Disable it because nothing in your design is attached to the request automatically. If a session cookie or Basic auth is anywhere in play, leave it on.

Common mistakes

  • Calling csrf.disable() on an app that still uses JSESSIONID sessions or httpBasic().
  • Making state-changing endpoints with GET (GET /api/jobs/5/delete); GET is not CSRF-protected.
  • Confusing CSRF with XSS. CSRF abuses the browser's automatic credentials; XSS runs the attacker's JavaScript inside your page and can read tokens in localStorage.
  • Confusing CSRF with CORS. CORS controls who may read responses; it does not stop the sending of a form post.

Interview angle

"What is CSRF and how is it prevented?" Give the forged-form story, the automatic cookie, then the synchronizer token and SameSite cookies. "Why do you disable CSRF in your JWT API?" Bearer header is not sent automatically by the browser; stateless; no session cookie. "When would you re-enable it?" When the token lives in a cookie.

Refresh tokens: short-lived access tokens, rotation and logout

Keep the access JWT short (minutes), give the client a long-lived random refresh token stored hashed in your database, rotate it on every use, and revoke it on logout or when reuse is detected.

The problem

An access JWT cannot be revoked, so the longer it lives, the longer a stolen one works. But a 15-minute token means the user would log in every 15 minutes. The answer is two tokens:

  • Access token: a JWT valid for 5–30 minutes, sent with every API call.
  • Refresh token: a long-lived (days to weeks) opaque random string, sent only to one endpoint (/api/auth/refresh) to get a new access token.

The refresh token is not a JWT: it is stored on the server, so it can be checked, rotated and deleted. That gives you the revocation that pure JWTs lack.

Rotation and reuse detection

Rotation means every refresh call returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. A stolen token then works at most once before the real user's next refresh fails. Reuse detection goes further: if an already-used refresh token is presented again, somebody has a copy (either the thief or the user, after the thief rotated it). The server cannot tell which, so it revokes the whole family (all tokens that descend from that login), forcing a fresh login on every device of that session chain.

Storing refresh tokens

create table refresh_token (
    id          bigserial primary key,
    user_id     bigint not null references app_user(id) on delete cascade,
    family_id   uuid not null,
    token_hash  varchar(64) not null unique,   -- SHA-256 hex of the token
    expires_at  timestamp not null,
    used        boolean not null default false,
    revoked     boolean not null default false,
    created_at  timestamp not null default now()
);

Store a hash of the token, never the token. If the table leaks, the attacker still cannot use the values. A fast hash (SHA-256) is fine here, unlike passwords, because the token is 256 bits of randomness, not a guessable password.

@Service
public class RefreshTokenService {

    private static final SecureRandom RANDOM = new SecureRandom();
    private final RefreshTokenRepository repo;

    public RefreshTokenService(RefreshTokenRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    /** Create a token for a fresh login: new family. */
    @Transactional
    public String create(Long userId) {
        return store(userId, UUID.randomUUID());
    }

    /** Validate, rotate and return the new raw token plus the user id. */
    @Transactional(noRollbackFor = InvalidRefreshTokenException.class)
    public Rotation rotate(String rawToken) {
        RefreshToken stored = repo.findByTokenHash(sha256(rawToken))
                .orElseThrow(() -> new InvalidRefreshTokenException("Unknown token"));

        if (stored.isUsed() || stored.isRevoked()) {
            repo.revokeFamily(stored.getFamilyId());         // reuse detected
            throw new InvalidRefreshTokenException("Token reuse detected");
        }
        if (stored.getExpiresAt().isBefore(Instant.now())) {
            throw new InvalidRefreshTokenException("Expired");
        }
        stored.markUsed();
        String next = store(stored.getUserId(), stored.getFamilyId());
        return new Rotation(stored.getUserId(), next);
    }

    private String store(Long userId, UUID family) {
        byte[] bytes = new byte[32];
        RANDOM.nextBytes(bytes);
        String raw = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(bytes);
        repo.save(new RefreshToken(userId, family, sha256(raw),
                Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofDays(7))));
        return raw;
    }

    private static String sha256(String s) {
        try {
            byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
                    .digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return HexFormat.of().formatHex(d);
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    public record Rotation(Long userId, String newRefreshToken) {}
}

Notes: noRollbackFor matters. The reuse branch revokes the family and then throws; with the default rule the exception would roll the revocation back (@Transactional rollback rules) if the exception were unchecked. The refresh controller calls rotate, loads the user (check that the account is still enabled!) and issues a new access token with the TokenService. Delete expired rows with a scheduled job (module 6).

Where does the client keep tokens?

PlaceStolen by XSS?CSRF?Survives refresh / new tab?
JavaScript memory (a variable)Harder, short windowNoNo: lost on page reload
localStorage / sessionStorageYes, any script can read itNoYes (session storage: per tab)
HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookieCannot be read by JS (but requests can still be made)Yes, needs protectionYes

A widely used compromise: keep the access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie restricted to the refresh path. On page load, React calls /api/auth/refresh to get a new access token silently. Setting such a cookie in Spring:

ResponseCookie cookie = ResponseCookie.from("refresh_token", rawToken)
        .httpOnly(true)
        .secure(true)                  // HTTPS only
        .sameSite("Strict")
        .path("/api/auth")             // sent only to auth endpoints
        .maxAge(Duration.ofDays(7))
        .build();
response.addHeader(HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE, cookie.toString());

How the React side wires this up (an Axios interceptor that refreshes on 401 and retries) is in Frontend · Module 6.

Logout and revocation

  • Logout: revoke the user's current refresh token (or family) in the database, clear the cookie, and have the client forget the access token. The access token stays valid until it expires (minutes).
  • Logout everywhere / password change / account disabled: revoke all refresh tokens of the user.
  • Immediate access-token revocation (rarely needed): keep a deny list of jti values in Redis with a TTL equal to the token lifetime, and check it in the filter; or add a per-user "token version" claim and compare it with the database. This gives back some statefulness; use only if the short expiry is not enough.

Common mistakes

  • Making the refresh token another long-lived JWT that is never stored: nothing can be revoked.
  • Storing raw refresh tokens in the database.
  • No rotation: a stolen refresh token works for weeks.
  • Sending the refresh token with every API call, which defeats the purpose.
  • Not re-checking that the user is still enabled when refreshing.

Interview angle

"How do you log out with JWT?" Short access token plus revocable refresh tokens in the database; optionally a jti deny list. "What is refresh-token rotation?" New refresh token on each use, old one invalid; reuse of an old one revokes the family. "Where do you store tokens in the browser?" Memory for access, HttpOnly cookie for refresh; explain the XSS vs CSRF trade-off against localStorage.

OAuth2, OpenID Connect and "Login with Google/GitHub"

OAuth2 lets an app act with a user's permission without seeing their password, and OpenID Connect adds identity on top; with spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client a few properties give you social login, after which you may still issue your own JWT.

OAuth2 vocabulary

OAuth 2.0 is a standard for delegated authorization: "let this app access my data at that service, without giving the app my password". OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin layer on top that adds authentication: it returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Login with Google" is OIDC.

Resource owner
The user who owns the data.
Client
The application that wants access (your Spring Boot app or your React app).
Authorization server
Authenticates the user and issues tokens (Google, GitHub, Keycloak, Okta).
Resource server
The API that accepts access tokens (Google's APIs; your own API from the earlier articles).
Scope
What the client asks for, e.g. openid profile email.

Authorization code flow with PKCE

The recommended flow for web apps and SPAs is the authorization code flow. The user is sent to the provider to log in (the client never sees the password), the provider returns a short-lived code through the browser, and the client exchanges that code for tokens on a direct, back-channel call. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, "pixy") adds a random secret created at the start (code_verifier, sent as a hash called code_challenge) and proved at the end, so a stolen code is useless. It is required for public clients (SPAs, mobile) and recommended for all.

The state parameter is a random value the client checks on return; it prevents CSRF on the login redirect.

Login with Google in Spring Boot

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client</artifactId>
</dependency>

Create credentials in the Google Cloud console (OAuth client of type "Web application") and register the redirect URI http://localhost:8080/login/oauth2/code/google. The pattern is {baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}.

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          google:
            client-id: ${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID}
            client-secret: ${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}
            scope: openid,profile,email
          github:
            client-id: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
            client-secret: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
            scope: read:user,user:email

Google, GitHub, Facebook and Okta are known providers (Spring has their endpoints built in), so only client-id and client-secret are needed. Other providers (Keycloak) also need a provider section with an issuer-uri.

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/", "/public/**").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults());
    return http.build();
}

@GetMapping("/profile")
Map<String, Object> profile(@AuthenticationPrincipal OidcUser user) {
    return Map.of("name", user.getFullName(), "email", user.getEmail());
}

Opening a protected URL now redirects to a generated page with "Google" and "GitHub" links; after login the principal is an OidcUser (Google) or OAuth2User (GitHub, which does not support OIDC). On your database you map the provider's email to a local User row (create it on first login) so that roles and ownership still work.

Social login vs your own JWT login

Own email + password + JWTLogin with Google / GitHub
PasswordsYou store and protect hashesNone; the provider handles them and MFA
Sign-up frictionForm, email verificationOne click
ControlFullDepends on the provider; users without an account there
ResultYour JWTA Spring session by default (see below)

oauth2Login creates a normal session after the redirect. For an SPA with a stateless API there are two common patterns: (1) after a successful social login, an AuthenticationSuccessHandler issues your own JWT and redirects to the frontend with it (best done with a short-lived code or a cookie rather than putting the token in the URL), or (2) put a dedicated authorization server (Keycloak, Spring Authorization Server) in front of everything, and let all apps be resource servers (module 7). For Project 2, own login is enough; social login is a good extension.

Common mistakes

  • Redirect URI mismatch: the value in the provider console differs from {baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/google in scheme, host, port or path. The provider shows a redirect_uri_mismatch error.
  • Committing the client secret. Use environment variables.
  • Treating an OAuth2 access token as proof of identity. Use the OIDC ID token for "who is this".
  • Trusting the provider's email without checking that it is verified, then linking to an existing local account (account takeover).
  • Using the old implicit flow or putting tokens in the URL fragment of an SPA; use code + PKCE.

Interview angle

"OAuth2 vs OpenID Connect?" OAuth2 = authorization (access tokens); OIDC = authentication on top (ID token). Name the four roles, draw the authorization code flow, say why PKCE exists, and explain that the client never sees the user's password. "How would you add Google login to Spring Boot?" Starter, two properties, redirect URI, oauth2Login().

Security best practices checklist and the OWASP Top 10

Most real breaches come from missing basics: plain HTTP, leaked secrets, no rate limit, missing ownership checks, verbose errors and outdated libraries; walk this checklist before every release.

Checklist for a Spring Boot API

  1. HTTPS only. Terminate TLS at the load balancer or reverse proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Without it, passwords and tokens travel in clear text. Add HSTS (Spring Security adds the header on HTTPS requests).
  2. Secrets in environment variables or a secret manager (JWT key, database password, OAuth2 client secret). Never in Git, never in the Docker image. Rotate them when someone leaves (DevOps · Module 5).
  3. Hash passwords with BCrypt/Argon2; enforce minimum length; never log them.
  4. Short access tokens, rotating refresh tokens, an explicit issuer check.
  5. Rate-limit login, register and password reset (per IP and per account), using a gateway, Bucket4j, or a small Redis counter. Lock an account (or add delays) after repeated failures, and notify the user.
  6. Authorize on the server for every endpoint: role plus ownership. Deny by default with anyRequest().authenticated().
  7. Validate all input (@Valid, size limits); use parameterised queries (Spring Data does) so there is no SQL injection; never build SQL by string concatenation.
  8. Do not leak details. One message for "wrong email or password"; no stack traces, SQL or class names in error JSON; server.error.include-stacktrace=never; return DTOs, never entities.
  9. Security headers. Spring Security sets X-Content-Type-Options and cache headers; add Content-Security-Policy and Referrer-Policy if you serve HTML.
  10. CORS with exact origins; CSRF on whenever cookies carry credentials.
  11. Protect operational endpoints. Expose only health (and what you need) from Actuator, and secure the rest (module 6). Disable the H2 console outside development.
  12. Keep dependencies updated. Run OWASP Dependency-Check or Dependabot/Renovate; a vulnerable library (the Log4Shell case) is a vulnerability in your app.
  13. Log security events (logins, failures, denials, role changes) without secrets, and monitor them.
  14. Least privilege. The application's database user should not be a superuser; containers run as non-root.
  15. Test security: 401/403 and ownership cases belong in your suite (module 5).

OWASP Top 10 in one table

The OWASP Top 10 is a widely used list of the most serious web application risks (the 2021 edition is the most common reference; a newer edition has been in preparation, so check owasp.org for the current list).

RiskMeaningIn Spring Boot, do this
A01 Broken Access ControlUsers act outside their rights (IDOR)Ownership checks, @PreAuthorize, deny by default
A02 Cryptographic FailuresWeak or missing encryption, plain HTTPHTTPS, BCrypt, strong keys, no secrets in code
A03 InjectionSQL, JPQL, OS command injection; XSSParameterised queries, @Param, validation, output encoding
A04 Insecure DesignMissing security thinking in the designThreat model, rate limits, least privilege
A05 Security MisconfigurationDefaults, open consoles, verbose errorsLock down Actuator and H2, hide stack traces, profiles
A06 Vulnerable ComponentsOld libraries with known CVEsDependency scanning, update Spring Boot regularly
A07 Identification and Authentication FailuresWeak passwords, credential stuffing, session flawsBCrypt, rate-limit, lockout, MFA, short tokens
A08 Software and Data Integrity FailuresUntrusted updates, insecure deserialization, CI/CD tamperingVerify artifacts, avoid Java native serialization, protect pipelines
A09 Logging and Monitoring FailuresAttacks go unnoticedLog auth events, alerts
A10 Server-Side Request ForgeryServer fetches attacker-chosen URLsAllow-list outgoing hosts, validate URLs

Security headers and input handling in practice

http.headers(h -> h
    .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives("default-src 'self'"))
    .httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts
            .includeSubDomains(true).maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)));

For a pure JSON API these headers matter less than for HTML pages; for the React app served by Nginx or a CDN, set them there.

Real projects

Teams usually add: a dependency scanner in CI, a secrets scanner (to catch committed keys), rate limiting at the API gateway, and a yearly penetration test. As a developer, your daily share is the first, sixth and seventh items: authorization on every endpoint, validated input, no leaked details.

Interview angle

"How do you secure a REST API?" Walk through: HTTPS, authentication (JWT/OAuth2), role and ownership authorization, input validation, hashed passwords, rate limiting, safe errors, CORS/CSRF decisions, secrets management, dependency updates. Naming broken access control (IDOR) as the top risk and giving the ownership-check example impresses interviewers.

Interview questions — Security

What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication proves who you are (password, token); authorization decides what you may do once identified (roles, ownership). Authentication comes first. Failures map to HTTP 401 and 403. In Spring Security: AuthenticationManager for the first, AuthorizationFilter and @PreAuthorize for the second.

What happens when you add spring-boot-starter-security to a project?

Every endpoint becomes authenticated. A default user named user with a random password printed in the log is created, form login and HTTP Basic are enabled, CSRF protection is on (POST without a token gets 403), a session is used, and default security headers are added. You take control by defining a SecurityFilterChain, a UserDetailsService and a PasswordEncoder.

Explain the Spring Security filter chain.

Security is a list of servlet filters before DispatcherServlet. DelegatingFilterProxy hands the request to FilterChainProxy, which selects the first matching SecurityFilterChain. Important filters: CORS, CSRF, an authentication filter (Bearer token, form login), ExceptionTranslationFilter (turns exceptions into 401/403), and AuthorizationFilter (URL rules). Authentication results are stored in the thread-local SecurityContextHolder.

How does Spring check a username and password?

AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager) delegates to DaoAuthenticationProvider. It calls UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername, checks account flags (enabled, locked, expired) and then PasswordEncoder.matches(raw, hash). A mismatch gives BadCredentialsException, which becomes 401.

Why hash passwords with BCrypt instead of encrypting or using SHA-256?

Encryption is reversible (the key can leak). SHA-256 is fast, so attackers test billions of guesses per second and use rainbow tables. BCrypt is one-way, adds a random salt automatically (equal passwords give different hashes) and has a tunable cost factor that makes each guess slow. Verify with matches, never equals.

What is a JWT, and is its payload secret?

A JSON Web Token has three base64url parts: header, payload (claims such as sub, iat, exp, roles) and signature. The signature proves integrity; the payload is only encoded, so anyone can read it. Never put secrets in it. The server verifies the signature and expiry on every request and needs no session storage.

HS256 vs RS256?

HS256 uses one shared secret for both signing and verifying: simple and fast, but every verifier can also forge tokens. RS256 uses a private key to sign and a public key to verify, so many services can verify without being able to issue tokens; it fits microservices and external identity providers (JWKS).

How do you implement JWT login in Spring Boot?

A login endpoint authenticates through the AuthenticationManager and returns a signed token. On later requests either a custom OncePerRequestFilter (placed before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter) parses the Bearer header and sets the SecurityContext, or, preferably, the OAuth2 Resource Server support with a JwtDecoder does it. The session policy is STATELESS and CSRF is disabled for header-based tokens.

What is the difference between 401 and 403?

401 means unauthenticated: no or invalid credentials, so the client should log in or refresh. 403 means authenticated but not permitted; logging in again does not help. In Spring, AuthenticationEntryPoint produces 401 and AccessDeniedHandler produces 403; customise both to return JSON.

What is the difference between hasRole and hasAuthority?

Both check GrantedAuthority strings. hasRole("ADMIN") adds the ROLE_ prefix and checks ROLE_ADMIN; hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN") checks the exact text. A frequent bug is storing roles without the prefix and getting 403 from hasRole.

How do you make sure a recruiter can edit only their own jobs?

The role check says recruiters may edit jobs; ownership needs data. Load the job in the service, compare job.getPostedBy().getId() with the current user's id (from the Authentication), and throw AccessDeniedException (403) otherwise; admins may bypass. Alternatively use @PreAuthorize("@jobSecurity.isOwner(#id, authentication)"). Filter list queries by owner. Never trust a user id from the request body.

What is CORS and why is there a preflight request?

Browsers apply the same-origin policy (origin = scheme + host + port); CORS is the server's way to allow other origins to read its responses. For non-simple requests (JSON content type, Authorization header, PUT/DELETE) the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight asking whether the real request is allowed. In Spring Security register a CorsConfigurationSource bean and call cors(withDefaults()); do not use * together with credentials.

What is CSRF? Can you disable it for a JWT API?

CSRF makes a victim's browser send a state-changing request to a site where they are logged in, using credentials the browser attaches automatically (cookies). Defence: CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies. For a stateless API where the token goes in the Authorization header set by your JavaScript, there is nothing automatic to abuse, so you can disable it. If the token lives in a cookie, keep CSRF protection.

How do refresh tokens work, and how do you log out a JWT user?

The access JWT lives minutes; a random refresh token (stored hashed in the database) lives days and only buys new access tokens. Rotate it on each use and revoke the whole family if an old one is reused. Logout revokes the refresh tokens (and clears the cookie); the access token stays valid until it expires, unless you keep a jti deny list.

Explain the OAuth2 authorization code flow and PKCE.

The client redirects the user to the authorization server, the user logs in there and consents, the server redirects back with a short-lived code (plus state), and the client exchanges the code on the back channel for tokens. PKCE adds a one-time secret (verifier and its hash, the challenge) so a stolen code cannot be redeemed; it is mandatory for SPAs and mobile apps. OIDC adds an ID token for identity.

Cheat sheet — Security

  • AuthN vs AuthZ who are you (401 on failure) vs what may you do (403 on failure).
  • Starter default everything secured, user user + generated password, form login, Basic, CSRF on.
  • Filter chain DelegatingFilterProxy to FilterChainProxy to SecurityFilterChain; ExceptionTranslationFilter then AuthorizationFilter at the end.
  • SecurityContextHolder thread-local; holds the Authentication (principal, credentials, authorities).
  • Password check AuthenticationManager to DaoAuthenticationProvider to UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder.
  • Config a SecurityFilterChain bean with the lambda DSL; WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is removed.
  • Rule order first match wins; end with anyRequest().authenticated().
  • API chain csrf.disable(), cors(withDefaults()), STATELESS, Basic and form login off.
  • Passwords BCrypt (salted, cost 10 default), matches not equals, never log, max 72 bytes.
  • DelegatingPasswordEncoder stores {bcrypt}...; supports migration between algorithms.
  • JWT header.payload.signature, base64url; payload readable; claims sub iat exp iss aud.
  • HS256 / RS256 shared secret (at least 32 bytes) / key pair.
  • Custom filter OncePerRequestFilter + jjwt, addFilterBefore(..., UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class), do not make it a @Component.
  • Resource server spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server, JwtDecoder (NimbusJwtDecoder.withSecretKey), JwtEncoder, set the HS256 header.
  • Roles from JWT JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter: claim name roles, prefix ROLE_.
  • 401 / 403 JSON AuthenticationEntryPoint / AccessDeniedHandler (advice cannot see filter errors).
  • hasRole adds ROLE_; hasAuthority is exact text.
  • Method security @EnableMethodSecurity + @PreAuthorize; proxy-based, so no self-invocation.
  • Ownership check in the service against the loaded entity; filter queries by owner; admin bypass explicit.
  • Current user Authentication parameter, @AuthenticationPrincipal, never the id from the body.
  • CORS exact origins in a CorsConfigurationSource bean; preflight is OPTIONS; no * with credentials.
  • CSRF needed when credentials are sent automatically (cookies); off for Bearer-header APIs.
  • Refresh token random, hashed in DB, rotated, family revoked on reuse; access token in memory.
  • OAuth2 roles: owner, client, authorization server, resource server; code flow + PKCE; OIDC adds ID token.
  • Checklist HTTPS, secrets in env, rate-limit login, validate input, generic errors, update dependencies.

Practice — Security

  1. Meet the defaults. Add spring-boot-starter-security to Project 2. Find the generated password in the log, call GET /api/jobs with curl (expect 401), then with -u user:password (200). Then POST without a CSRF token and note the 403. Done when you can explain each of the three results.
  2. Register with BCrypt. Add role, passwordHash, enabled to the User entity and migration; build POST /api/auth/register (CANDIDATE or RECRUITER only; duplicate email gives 409). Done when the database column holds a 60-character hash starting with $2a$ and two users with the same password have different hashes.
  3. Load users from the database. Implement AppUserDetails and DbUserDetailsService; expose the AuthenticationManager. Done when a wrong password returns 401 with a generic message and a disabled user cannot log in.
  4. JWT login, way 1. Implement JjwtService, the filter and POST /api/auth/login. Done when a token from login opens GET /api/me, a tampered token or a token with a past exp returns 401 JSON, and no endpoint besides login/register and public GETs works without a token.
  5. JWT login, way 2. Switch to the OAuth2 Resource Server with JwtEncoder/JwtDecoder and the role converter, removing the custom filter. Done when the same requests behave identically and you can write down three differences between the two versions.
  6. Roles for Project 2. Enforce the access matrix: only RECRUITER posts jobs, only CANDIDATE applies, ADMIN manages users. Use URL rules for the broad cases and @PreAuthorize for at least two methods. Done when each cell of the matrix is verified by a curl call.
  7. Owner-only edits. Make recruiters edit and close only their own jobs and see applications only for their jobs, candidates see only their own applications. Done when recruiter B gets 403 on recruiter A's job, "my jobs" returns only own rows, and a client-supplied user id is ignored.
  8. CORS and CSRF decisions. Run the React app from localhost:5173, watch the CORS error, add the CorsConfigurationSource bean, and verify the preflight with curl -X OPTIONS and the three Access-Control-Request-* headers. Write two sentences on why CSRF is disabled in your design.
  9. Refresh tokens (stretch). Add the refresh_token table, /refresh and /logout, rotation and reuse detection. Done when reusing an old refresh token returns 401 and the newest one stops working as well.
  10. Social login (stretch). Add Google or GitHub login to a small sandbox project with oauth2Login and print the logged-in email at /profile. Then write the security tests for all of the above in module 5.
5

Module 5·Week 9, then alwaysMust

Testing

10 topics · about 1 h of reading

Code that is not tested is code you are afraid to change. In a real job you do not get to say "it works on my machine": a pull request is merged only when the tests pass, and reviewers expect tests next to every new service and endpoint. Testing is also one of the most common interview topics for Spring Boot developers, and one of the first things that separates a job-ready developer from a tutorial follower.

This module teaches testing the way Spring Boot projects do it: fast unit tests with JUnit 5, Mockito and AssertJ; slice tests that load only one layer (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest); full @SpringBootTest integration tests; and Testcontainers, which runs a real PostgreSQL in Docker so tests behave like production. It also covers coverage with JaCoCo and what makes a test good. The examples test Project 2 (REST, JPA, Security) and finish with the goal "Project 2 passes all its tests with mvn test".

After this module you will be able to:

  • Choose the right kind of test (unit, slice, integration) for each layer and name and structure tests clearly.
  • Write unit tests with JUnit 5, Mockito (@Mock, @InjectMocks, when, verify, ArgumentCaptor) and AssertJ.
  • Test controllers with @WebMvcTest and MockMvc, including validation errors and secured endpoints.
  • Test repositories with @DataJpaTest and integration flows with @SpringBootTest.
  • Run tests against a real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection.
  • Measure coverage, run tests in Maven and CI, and avoid flaky tests.

Why test: the testing pyramid, structure and naming

Tests give you the confidence to change code; write many fast unit tests, fewer slice tests, a few integration tests and very few end-to-end tests, and keep every test in Arrange-Act-Assert shape with a name that says what is expected.

Why write tests

  • Catch bugs early. A failing test on your laptop costs minutes; the same bug in production costs a night.
  • Refactor safely. With tests you can restructure a service and know within seconds whether behaviour changed.
  • Documentation that runs. A test named apply_whenJobClosed_throwsConflict states a business rule and never goes out of date.
  • Design pressure. Code that is hard to test (static calls, new everywhere, huge methods) is usually badly designed. Constructor injection from module 1 makes testing easy.
  • CI gate. The pipeline runs the tests on every push (DevOps · Module 4).

The testing pyramid

LevelWhat is loadedSpeedTest in a Spring Boot app
UnitOne class, collaborators mocked, no SpringMillisecondsServices (business rules), mappers, validators, utilities
SlicePart of the context: web layer or JPA layer onlyUnder a second to a few secondsControllers (status, JSON, validation, security) and repositories (queries)
IntegrationWhole context, real database (Testcontainers)SecondsKey flows: register, login, post job, apply; Flyway migrations; transactions
End-to-endDeployed app, real browser or API clientSlowestA handful of critical user journeys (Playwright, Cypress); not in this module

The shape matters because tests higher up are slower, need more setup, and fail for more reasons. A pyramid turned upside down (hundreds of end-to-end tests, few unit tests) gives a suite that takes an hour and fails randomly. Put each check at the lowest level that can prove it: a price calculation is a unit test; "an unauthenticated call returns 401" is a slice test; "this query works on PostgreSQL" needs a real database.

Arrange-Act-Assert (Given-When-Then)

Every test has three parts: Arrange (prepare data and mocks), Act (call the one thing under test), Assert (check the result). BDD people call it Given-When-Then; it is the same idea. Separate the parts with a blank line or a comment.

@Test
void applyFee_forPremiumJob_addsTwoPercent() {
    // Arrange (given)
    var calculator = new FeeCalculator();
    var job = JobTestData.premiumJob(100_000);

    // Act (when)
    long fee = calculator.feeFor(job);

    // Assert (then)
    assertThat(fee).isEqualTo(2_000);
}

Rules: one behaviour per test; at most one "Act" call; no if or loops in the test body (a test with logic needs its own test).

Naming

The test name should tell what failed without opening the file. Two common styles:

  • methodName_condition_expectedResult: update_whenNotOwner_throwsAccessDenied
  • shouldDoXWhenY: shouldRejectApplicationWhenJobIsClosed

Pick one per project. Add @DisplayName("...") if the team prefers sentences in reports. Name classes JobServiceTest (unit), JobControllerTest (web slice), JobRepositoryTest (JPA slice) and JobFlowIT (integration, see the Failsafe note in the Maven article).

Folder structure

The test tree mirrors the main tree, so a class and its test are in the same package (this also lets tests use package-private members):

src/main/java/com/example/jobs/job/JobService.java
src/main/java/com/example/jobs/job/JobController.java
src/test/java/com/example/jobs/job/JobServiceTest.java        (unit)
src/test/java/com/example/jobs/job/JobControllerTest.java     (@WebMvcTest)
src/test/java/com/example/jobs/job/JobRepositoryTest.java     (@DataJpaTest)
src/test/java/com/example/jobs/AbstractIntegrationTest.java   (Testcontainers base)
src/test/java/com/example/jobs/JobFlowIT.java                 (@SpringBootTest)
src/test/resources/application-test.yml

What spring-boot-starter-test gives you

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
LibraryPurpose
JUnit Jupiter (JUnit 5)The test framework: @Test, lifecycle, parameterized tests
MockitoMocks and verification
AssertJFluent assertions: assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y)
HamcrestOlder matcher library, still used by some MockMvc examples
JSONassert, JsonPathCompare and query JSON
Spring Test and Spring Boot TestMockMvc, @SpringBootTest, test slices, @MockitoBean
Awaitility, XMLUnitWaiting for async results; XML comparison

Add separately: spring-security-test for secured endpoints, Testcontainers for real databases, and JaCoCo for coverage.

Versions

Each Spring Boot release manages the versions of JUnit, Mockito and AssertJ, so you normally never write their version numbers. Newer Boot lines ship newer JUnit Jupiter releases, but the annotations in this module stay the same. Boot 4 also reorganised the test support into smaller modules and moved some test annotations to new packages (for example @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest); the annotation names are unchanged, so let the IDE fix imports and check the release notes of your version.

Common mistakes

  • Making every test a @SpringBootTest. The suite becomes slow, and nobody runs it.
  • Testing getters and setters, or the framework itself, for coverage numbers.
  • Tests that depend on the order of other tests or on leftover data.
  • A test named test1, or one test that checks ten things.

Interview angle

"Explain the testing pyramid." Draw it, give a Spring example per level, and explain why the base is wide (speed, precision). "What do you test in a Spring Boot app, and how?" Services with unit tests, controllers with @WebMvcTest, repositories with @DataJpaTest on a real database, a few @SpringBootTest flows.

JUnit 5 essentials for Spring developers

JUnit 5 gives you @Test, lifecycle hooks, @DisplayName, @Nested groups, parameterized tests and assertThrows; Spring Boot projects need just these plus AssertJ.

JUnit 5 (also called JUnit Jupiter) is the test framework behind spring-boot-starter-test. A test method is any method annotated @Test. Test classes and methods need no public modifier; package-private is the convention. For core Java background on JUnit see Core Java · Module 8.

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class SalaryRangeTest {

    @Test
    void midpoint_ofRange_isAverage() {
        var range = new SalaryRange(600_000, 1_000_000);
        assertThat(range.midpoint()).isEqualTo(800_000);
    }
}
[INFO] Running com.example.jobs.job.SalaryRangeTest
[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

What is inside "JUnit 5"

JUnit 5 is not one library but three parts. Knowing them explains many dependency questions.

JUnit Platform
The launcher that finds and runs tests. Maven Surefire, Gradle and IDEs talk to the Platform, not to your tests directly.
JUnit Jupiter
The new programming model (@Test, @BeforeEach, assertions, extensions in the package org.junit.jupiter.api) and its test engine.
JUnit Vintage
An engine that runs old JUnit 3 and 4 tests on the Platform. Boot's starter no longer includes it by default, so an old org.junit.Test is simply not found.

spring-boot-starter-test bundles Jupiter, AssertJ, Mockito, Hamcrest, JsonPath and the Spring test support, so you add one dependency with test scope and nothing else (testing overview).

Lifecycle annotations

AnnotationRunsTypical use
@BeforeEachBefore every test methodCreate the object under test, reset data
@AfterEachAfter every test methodClean up files or static state
@BeforeAllOnce before all tests; method must be staticStart an expensive shared resource
@AfterAllOnce after all tests; staticStop it

JUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so instance fields are never shared between tests: that is what keeps tests independent. (@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) changes this and lets @BeforeAll be non-static; avoid it unless needed.) The order for one test is: @BeforeAll once, then for each test @BeforeEach, the test, @AfterEach, and finally @AfterAll once.

class LifecycleDemoTest {
    @BeforeAll static void beforeAll() { System.out.println("beforeAll"); }
    @BeforeEach void beforeEach()      { System.out.println("  beforeEach"); }
    @Test void a()                     { System.out.println("    test a"); }
    @Test void b()                     { System.out.println("    test b"); }
    @AfterEach void afterEach()        { System.out.println("  afterEach"); }
    @AfterAll static void afterAll()   { System.out.println("afterAll"); }
}
beforeAll
  beforeEach
    test a
  afterEach
  beforeEach
    test b
  afterEach
afterAll

JUnit runs test methods in a deterministic but intentionally not obvious order. Never depend on it. If you really need an order (rare, mostly for slow end-to-end flows), add @TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class) and @Order(1) on the methods.

@DisplayName, @Nested, @Disabled, @Tag

@DisplayName("ApplicationService")
class ApplicationServiceTest {

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("apply()")
    class Apply {

        @Test
        @DisplayName("saves an application for an open job")
        void openJob_savesApplication() { ... }

        @Test
        @DisplayName("rejects a second application to the same job")
        void duplicate_throwsConflict() { ... }
    }

    @Nested
    class Withdraw {
        @Test void byOwner_marksWithdrawn() { ... }

        @Disabled("fails until JIRA-123 is fixed")
        @Test void byOtherUser_isForbidden() { ... }
    }
}
  • @Nested inner classes group tests per method or per scenario; the reports show the tree. An outer @BeforeEach runs before each nested test.
  • @Disabled("reason") skips a test; always give a reason and a ticket. A disabled test is a debt.
  • @Tag("slow") labels tests; run only some with Maven: mvn test -Dgroups=fast or exclude with -DexcludedGroups=slow.
  • @Timeout(2) fails a test that takes longer than 2 seconds.
  • @DisplayNameGeneration(DisplayNameGenerator.ReplaceUnderscores.class) on the class turns saves_application into "saves application" in reports, so you can skip @DisplayName on every method.

Parameterized tests

One test body, many inputs. Needs the junit-jupiter-params module, already included in the starter.

@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(strings = {"", " ", "ab", "not-an-email"})
void isValidEmail_forBadInput_returnsFalse(String input) {
    assertThat(EmailValidator.isValid(input)).isFalse();
}

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} years -> {1}")
@CsvSource({
        "0, JUNIOR",
        "2, JUNIOR",
        "3, MID",
        "8, SENIOR"
})
void levelFor_experience(int years, Level expected) {
    assertThat(Level.forYears(years)).isEqualTo(expected);
}

@ParameterizedTest
@MethodSource("invalidSalaryRanges")
void create_withInvalidRange_isRejected(int min, int max) {
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> new SalaryRange(min, max))
            .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
}

static Stream<Arguments> invalidSalaryRanges() {
    return Stream.of(
            Arguments.of(100, 50),
            Arguments.of(-1, 10),
            Arguments.of(0, 0));
}

@ParameterizedTest
@EnumSource(value = Role.class, names = {"CANDIDATE", "RECRUITER"})
void selfRegistration_isAllowedFor(Role role) { ... }

The test name template {0}, {1} shows the arguments in the report. The factory method for @MethodSource is static (unless PER_CLASS). Also available: @NullSource, @EmptySource, @CsvFileSource. For a factory in another class, give the full name: @MethodSource("com.example.Data#cases"). Each row runs as its own test, so one bad row does not hide the others.

levelFor_experience
  0 years -> JUNIOR   ✓
  2 years -> JUNIOR   ✓
  3 years -> MID      ✓
  8 years -> SENIOR   ✓

Testing exceptions and grouping assertions

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

@Test
void divide_byZero_throws() {
    ArithmeticException ex = assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class,
            () -> calculator.divide(1, 0));
    assertEquals("/ by zero", ex.getMessage());      // expected FIRST, then actual
}

@Test
void response_hasAllFields() {
    var r = service.getJob(7L);
    assertAll("job response",                        // all failures are reported
            () -> assertEquals(7L, r.id()),
            () -> assertEquals("Java Developer", r.title()),
            () -> assertTrue(r.open()));
}

JUnit's assertEquals(expected, actual) takes the expected value first; swapping them gives confusing failure messages. AssertJ (next articles) reads better and is the usual choice in Spring projects. assertThrows passes only if the thrown exception is the given type or a subtype, and it returns the exception so you can check the message.

JUnit assertionUseFailure
assertEquals, assertNotEqualsValues equal or notAssertionFailedError with expected and actual
assertTrue, assertFalseA boolean conditionAssertionFailedError
assertNull, assertNotNullNull checksAssertionFailedError
assertThrowsAn exception is thrownFails if nothing, or another type, is thrown
assertAllSeveral checks togetherMultipleFailuresError lists every failing check
assertTimeoutCode finishes in timeFails if too slow

JUnit with Spring: extensions

JUnit 5 replaced the single "runner" of JUnit 4 with extensions; you can use several at once. Two matter in Spring work:

  • @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) creates @Mock and @InjectMocks fields for a plain unit test, with no Spring at all (Mockito). This is the fastest kind of test.
  • SpringExtension loads the Spring context and injects beans into the test. You normally do not write it: @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest already include it (SpringBootTest).
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class JobServiceTest {
    @Mock JobRepository jobRepository;
    @InjectMocks JobService jobService;
    @Test void find_missing_throws() { ... }
}

@SpringBootTest
class JobRepositoryIT {
    @Autowired JobRepository jobRepository;     // injected by SpringExtension
    @Test void contextLoads() { assertThat(jobRepository).isNotNull(); }
}

JUnit 5 also lets a test constructor or method take parameters. Spring supplies beans for them, and JUnit supplies built-in ones such as @TempDir Path dir (a temporary folder deleted after the test), TestInfo and RepetitionInfo. A parameter nobody can resolve fails with ParameterResolutionException.

Comparison: JUnit 4 and JUnit 5

JUnit 4JUnit 5
org.junit.Testorg.junit.jupiter.api.Test
@Before, @After@BeforeEach, @AfterEach
@BeforeClass, @AfterClass@BeforeAll, @AfterAll
@Ignore@Disabled
@RunWith(...), @Rule@ExtendWith(...)
@Test(expected = ...)assertThrows
Test classes and methods publicPackage-private is fine

Rules

  • Test methods must not be private or static, and must return void.
  • @BeforeAll / @AfterAll must be static in the default lifecycle.
  • Do not mix JUnit 4 (org.junit.Test, @RunWith) and JUnit 5 (org.junit.jupiter.api.Test) imports; a test with the wrong @Test is silently not run. Use @ExtendWith instead of @RunWith.
  • Name test classes so the build finds them: Surefire runs *Test, Test* and *Tests; integration tests named *IT go to Failsafe (Maven setup).

Conventions

  • Name the test class after the class under test (OrderServiceTest) and methods as method_condition_result or with @DisplayName (naming).
  • One logical behaviour per test, and the arrange-act-assert shape with blank lines between the parts.
  • Prefer parameterized tests over copy-pasted tests that differ only in the data.
  • Put the test in the same package as the class, so package-private code is reachable.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on test order or on state left by another test. Each test must set up its own data.
  • Catching an exception with try/catch and forgetting fail(), so the test passes when nothing is thrown. Use assertThrows.
  • @Disabled without a reason, left for months.

Wrong: passes even if nothing is thrown

@Test
void withdraw_tooMuch() {
    try {
        account.withdraw(10_000);
    } catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {
        assertEquals("Not enough balance", e.getMessage());
    }
}

Right: fails unless it is thrown

@Test
void withdraw_tooMuch() {
    var ex = assertThrows(InsufficientFundsException.class,
            () -> account.withdraw(10_000));
    assertEquals("Not enough balance", ex.getMessage());
}

Exceptions and edge cases

  • PreconditionViolationException: @BeforeAll method must be static unless the test class is annotated with @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS): you forgot static. The same rule applies to a @MethodSource factory.
  • ParameterResolutionException: No ParameterResolver registered for parameter: a test method takes a parameter that JUnit and your extensions cannot supply. Often a missing @ParameterizedTest or @Autowired.
  • AssertionFailedError: expected: <5> but was: <4>: a normal failed assertion. MultipleFailuresError comes from assertAll and lists every failure; assertThrows reports "Unexpected exception type thrown" when the type differs.
  • If a test run reports "No tests found" or runs zero tests, the usual reasons are a JUnit 4 @Test import, a name that Surefire does not match, or a missing junit-platform provider on an old Surefire version.
  • An exception in @BeforeEach marks every test of the class as failed, and an exception in @AfterEach fails the test that already passed. Keep hooks simple.
  • A static field shared between tests is shared state again: the new-instance rule does not protect static data or Spring singletons.

Tip: run one test quickly

From the command line: ./mvnw test -Dtest=JobServiceTest runs one class, and -Dtest=JobServiceTest#find_missing_throws runs one method. In IntelliJ, click the green arrow beside the method.

Interview angle

"What is new in JUnit 5?" Jupiter API, extensions via @ExtendWith (instead of runners), @Nested, @ParameterizedTest, assertThrows/assertAll, Java 8+ lambdas. "Does JUnit share the test instance?" No: new instance per method, which is why tests do not leak state through fields. Also ready: the three parts (Platform, Jupiter, Vintage), the difference between @BeforeEach and @BeforeAll, how to test an exception, and why @BeforeAll is static. A good extra point is that unit tests with MockitoExtension are far faster than tests that start Spring.

Mockito in depth: mocks, stubbing, verification and a full service test

Mockito replaces a class's collaborators with fakes you control: @Mock creates them, @InjectMocks wires them into the class under test, when(...).thenReturn(...) scripts answers, and verify(...) and ArgumentCaptor check what the class did.

Why mocks

A unit test of JobService should test the service's logic, not the database and not the e-mail sender. A mock is a fake object that has the same type as the real collaborator (JobRepository), returns whatever you script, and records how it was called. The test stays fast and is only about the class under test (the SUT, system under test).

Setup

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.*;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)         // JUnit 5 integration; no Spring context
class JobServiceTest {

    @Mock JobRepository jobRepository;
    @Mock UserRepository userRepository;

    @InjectMocks JobService jobService;     // gets the mocks through its constructor
    ...
}
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
Creates the mocks before each test, injects them, and checks strictness after each test.
@Mock
A mock of the field's type. Every method returns a default: null, 0, false, an empty List/Optional.
@InjectMocks
Creates the real object under test and injects the mocks. It tries the biggest constructor first, then setters, then fields. If a constructor argument has no matching mock it passes null, so a missing @Mock shows up as a NullPointerException in your service.
@Spy
A real object whose methods run for real unless you stub them; used rarely (partial mocking).

Without the extension you can create mocks by hand: JobRepository repo = mock(JobRepository.class);. The annotations are shorter.

Stubbing: when ... then

when(jobRepository.findById(7L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(job));
when(jobRepository.findById(99L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());
when(userRepository.findById(any())).thenThrow(new IllegalStateException("db down"));

// consecutive calls: first returns a, then b
when(jobRepository.count()).thenReturn(1L, 2L);

// compute the answer from the arguments
when(jobRepository.save(any(Job.class))).thenAnswer(inv -> {
    Job j = inv.getArgument(0);
    ReflectionTestUtils.setField(j, "id", 7L);       // simulate the generated id
    return j;
});

For methods that return void, and for spies, when(...) does not work (the call would run for real or does not compile). Use the other form, action first:

doThrow(new MailException("smtp down")).when(mailSender).send(any());
doNothing().when(auditLog).record(anyString());
doReturn(42).when(spyCalculator).slowCompute();       // on a @Spy, avoids calling the real method

Argument matchers: the all-or-none rule

Matchers (any(), anyLong(), anyString(), eq(x), argThat(...), isNull()) say "any value of this kind". If one argument uses a matcher, all arguments of that call must use matchers; wrap plain values in eq().

Wrong: mixing a matcher and a raw value

when(repo.findByTitleAndCity(anyString(), "Pune")).thenReturn(list);
// InvalidUseOfMatchersException: 2 matchers expected, 1 recorded

Right: matchers for all arguments

when(repo.findByTitleAndCity(anyString(), eq("Pune"))).thenReturn(list);

With Mockito 5 (used by current Boot), any(Job.class) matches only a non-null instance of that type; any() matches anything including null.

Verification

Stubbing controls what the mock returns; verify checks what the SUT did to it.

verify(jobRepository).save(any(Job.class));                // exactly once (default)
verify(jobRepository, times(2)).findById(anyLong());
verify(jobRepository, never()).deleteById(anyLong());
verify(jobRepository, atLeastOnce()).findById(7L);
verifyNoInteractions(mailSender);                          // never touched
verifyNoMoreInteractions(jobRepository);                   // nothing else was called

Use verify for side effects that matter (an e-mail was sent, a row was saved, nothing was deleted). Do not verify every call of every mock: verifyNoMoreInteractions in every test makes tests break whenever you refactor, which is the "testing implementation details" trap (good tests). If the method returns a value, assert the value instead of verifying the call that produced it.

ArgumentCaptor

Sometimes the SUT builds an object internally and passes it to a collaborator. A captor lets you grab it and assert on it.

ArgumentCaptor<Job> captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Job.class);
verify(jobRepository).save(captor.capture());
Job saved = captor.getValue();
assertThat(saved.getTitle()).isEqualTo("Java Developer");
assertThat(saved.getPostedBy().getId()).isEqualTo(5L);

You can also declare @Captor ArgumentCaptor<Job> captor; as a field with the extension.

BDDMockito: given / then

The same API with names that match Given-When-Then, in org.mockito.BDDMockito:

import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.*;

given(jobRepository.findById(7L)).willReturn(Optional.of(job));        // given
JobResponse r = jobService.getJob(7L);                                 // when
then(jobRepository).should().findById(7L);                             // then
then(mailSender).shouldHaveNoInteractions();

Strict stubs and UnnecessaryStubbingException

With MockitoExtension the default is strict stubs: if you stub something the test never uses, the test fails with org.mockito.exceptions.misusing.UnnecessaryStubbingException. This is useful: it finds dead set-up code and wrong assumptions about what the SUT calls. Also, strict stubs report a PotentialStubbingProblem if the SUT calls a stubbed method with different arguments than you stubbed. Fix by removing the stub or correcting the arguments. Use lenient().when(...) only for set-up shared by many tests in @BeforeEach.

Mocking static methods (brief)

Since Mockito 5 (Mockito 3.4+ with the inline mock maker) you can mock a static method. It is limited to a block and thread, via try-with-resources:

Instant fixed = Instant.parse("2026-11-10T10:00:00Z");
try (MockedStatic<Instant> mocked = mockStatic(Instant.class, CALLS_REAL_METHODS)) {
    mocked.when(Instant::now).thenReturn(fixed);
    assertThat(service.isExpired(job)).isFalse();
}   // the static mock is closed here

A static mock is a design smell more often than a solution. Inject a java.time.Clock into the service (clock.instant()) and pass Clock.fixed(...) in the test; that is simpler and thread-safe.

What not to mock

  • The class under test. A test that mocks the SUT tests the mock.
