  • Value objects and records (JobResponse, Money, LocalDate, String): just create them.
  • Collections and simple data holders: use List.of(...).
  • Types you do not own (the JDBC driver, RestTemplate, EntityManager) in deep chains: wrap them in your own class and mock that, or test with a real thing (Testcontainers, MockWebServer).
  • Everything. If a test has six mocks and eleven stubs, it is probably re-implementing the code. Test that logic at a higher level instead.

A complete service test: JobServiceTest

The service under test (simplified from the earlier modules):

@Service
public class JobService {

    private final JobRepository jobRepository;
    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public JobService(JobRepository jobRepository, UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.jobRepository = jobRepository;
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    @Transactional
    public JobResponse create(CreateJobRequest req, CurrentUser me) {
        User recruiter = userRepository.findById(me.id())
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("User " + me.id()));
        Job saved = jobRepository.save(new Job(req.title(), req.description(), recruiter));
        return JobResponse.from(saved);
    }

    @Transactional
    public JobResponse update(Long jobId, UpdateJobRequest req, CurrentUser me) {
        Job job = jobRepository.findById(jobId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Job " + jobId));
        if (!job.getPostedBy().getId().equals(me.id()) && !me.isAdmin()) {
            throw new AccessDeniedException("You can only edit your own jobs");
        }
        job.update(req.title(), req.description());
        return JobResponse.from(job);
    }
}
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class JobServiceTest {

    @Mock JobRepository jobRepository;
    @Mock UserRepository userRepository;
    @InjectMocks JobService jobService;

    private User recruiter;
    private final CurrentUser asRecruiter = new CurrentUser(5L, Set.of("ROLE_RECRUITER"));

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        recruiter = TestData.user(5L, "asha@example.com", Role.RECRUITER);
    }

    @Nested
    class Create {

        @Test
        void create_savesJobPostedByCurrentUser() {
            when(userRepository.findById(5L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(recruiter));
            when(jobRepository.save(any(Job.class))).thenAnswer(inv -> {
                Job j = inv.getArgument(0);
                ReflectionTestUtils.setField(j, "id", 7L);
                return j;
            });

            JobResponse response = jobService.create(
                    new CreateJobRequest("Java Developer", "Spring Boot, SQL"), asRecruiter);

            assertThat(response.id()).isEqualTo(7L);
            ArgumentCaptor<Job> captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Job.class);
            verify(jobRepository).save(captor.capture());
            assertThat(captor.getValue().getPostedBy()).isSameAs(recruiter);
        }

        @Test
        void create_whenUserMissing_throwsNotFound() {
            when(userRepository.findById(5L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());

            assertThatThrownBy(() -> jobService.create(
                    new CreateJobRequest("x", "y"), asRecruiter))
                    .isInstanceOf(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
                    .hasMessageContaining("User 5");

            verify(jobRepository, never()).save(any());
        }
    }

    @Nested
    class Update {

        @Test
        void update_byOwner_changesFields() {
            Job job = TestData.job(7L, "Old title", recruiter);
            when(jobRepository.findById(7L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(job));

            JobResponse r = jobService.update(7L,
                    new UpdateJobRequest("New title", "New text"), asRecruiter);

            assertThat(r.title()).isEqualTo("New title");
        }

        @Test
        void update_byAnotherRecruiter_isForbidden() {
            Job job = TestData.job(7L, "Old title", recruiter);
            when(jobRepository.findById(7L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(job));
            var other = new CurrentUser(6L, Set.of("ROLE_RECRUITER"));

            assertThatThrownBy(() -> jobService.update(7L,
                    new UpdateJobRequest("Hacked", "x"), other))
                    .isInstanceOf(AccessDeniedException.class);

            assertThat(job.getTitle()).isEqualTo("Old title");     // unchanged
        }

        @Test
        void update_byAdmin_isAllowed() {
            Job job = TestData.job(7L, "Old title", recruiter);
            when(jobRepository.findById(7L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(job));
            var admin = new CurrentUser(1L, Set.of("ROLE_ADMIN"));

            jobService.update(7L, new UpdateJobRequest("By admin", "x"), admin);

            assertThat(job.getTitle()).isEqualTo("By admin");
        }

        @Test
        void update_whenJobMissing_throwsNotFound() {
            when(jobRepository.findById(99L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());

            assertThatThrownBy(() -> jobService.update(99L,
                    new UpdateJobRequest("t", "d"), asRecruiter))
                    .isInstanceOf(ResourceNotFoundException.class);
        }
    }
}

TestData is a small helper class in src/test that builds entities (see test data builders); it uses reflection to set generated ids. Notice what the tests check: returned values and state for the main behaviour, verify only for the important side effect ("nothing saved" when the user is missing), and no real database. No save call is verified in update because the service relies on dirty checking (module 3); in a unit test we assert the entity changed.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NullPointerException inside the SUT: a dependency has no @Mock (it was injected as null), or an unstubbed mock returned null from a method returning a non-collection object.
  • InvalidUseOfMatchersException: mixed matchers and raw values, or a matcher used outside a stubbing/verification call.
  • UnnecessaryStubbingException: a stub was never used (strict stubs).
  • WantedButNotInvoked / TooManyActualInvocations: verify failed; the message lists the actual calls.
  • MockitoException: Cannot mock/spy class ... final: very old Mockito versions could not mock final classes; Mockito 5 can.
  • Stubbing when(mock.voidMethod()) does not compile; use doThrow/doNothing.

Common mistakes

  • Testing the mock: stub repo.findById to return X and then assert the service returned X, with no logic in between.
  • Mocking User, Job or other entities; create real objects.
  • Using @Mock with @SpringBootTest: that is @MockitoBean (see the MockMvc article); @Mock is for pure unit tests.
  • Over-verifying every call, so every refactor breaks tests.

Interview angle

"@Mock vs @InjectMocks?" Mock creates a fake; InjectMocks builds the real SUT and injects the fakes. "Mock vs spy?" Mock is a full fake, spy wraps a real object. "When do you use doReturn?" Void methods and spies. "What is ArgumentCaptor for?" Inspecting arguments passed to a collaborator. "What does UnnecessaryStubbingException mean?" Strict stubs found a stub that was not used. Also expect: "What would you not mock?"

AssertJ: fluent assertions for objects, collections and exceptions

AssertJ's assertThat(actual) starts a chain of readable checks with helpful failure messages; it is the default assertion library in Spring Boot tests and clearly better than JUnit's assertEquals for collections and exceptions.

AssertJ comes with spring-boot-starter-test. Import one static method and let the IDE's auto-complete show what you can check, because the available methods depend on the type of the value:

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;

Objects, numbers, strings, booleans

assertThat(job.getTitle()).isEqualTo("Java Developer");
assertThat(job.getSalaryMax()).isGreaterThan(job.getSalaryMin());
assertThat(rate).isBetween(0.0, 1.0);
assertThat(0.1 + 0.2).isCloseTo(0.3, within(0.0001));          // floating point
assertThat(job.isOpen()).isTrue();
assertThat(job.getDescription()).isNotBlank();

assertThat(email)
        .startsWith("asha")
        .contains("@")
        .endsWith(".com")
        .doesNotContain(" ");
assertThat("JAVA").isEqualToIgnoringCase("java");

assertThat(user).isNotNull();
assertThat(a).isSameAs(b);                      // same reference (==)
assertThat(response.status()).isEqualTo(ApplicationStatus.SUBMITTED);
assertThat(maybeJob).isPresent().hasValueSatisfying(j -> assertThat(j.getId()).isEqualTo(7L));
assertThat(Optional.empty()).isEmpty();

Chaining makes one statement check several things. Add a description with .as("job title") before the check to get a clearer failure message.

Collections

List<JobResponse> jobs = service.findOpenJobs();

assertThat(jobs).hasSize(3);
assertThat(jobs).isNotEmpty();
assertThat(jobs).extracting(JobResponse::title)
        .containsExactly("Java Developer", "QA Engineer", "DevOps Engineer");   // order matters
assertThat(jobs).extracting(JobResponse::title)
        .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("QA Engineer", "Java Developer", "DevOps Engineer");
assertThat(jobs).extracting(JobResponse::title).contains("QA Engineer");        // at least
assertThat(jobs).extracting(JobResponse::title).doesNotContain("Cook");

assertThat(jobs).filteredOn(j -> j.salaryMax() > 1_000_000)
        .extracting(JobResponse::title)
        .containsExactly("DevOps Engineer");
assertThat(jobs).allMatch(JobResponse::open);
assertThat(jobs).anySatisfy(j -> assertThat(j.title()).startsWith("Java"));

assertThat(map).containsEntry("city", "Pune").containsKey("country");
assertThat(page.getContent()).isSortedAccordingTo(Comparator.comparing(JobResponse::id));
contains
Contains these elements (and maybe others), any order.
containsOnly
Only these elements, duplicates and order ignored.
containsExactly
Exactly these elements in exactly this order.
containsExactlyInAnyOrder
Exactly these elements, any order. The usual choice when SQL order is not specified.
extracting
Maps each element to a field first; check the field values instead of whole objects.

To compare two objects by their fields (when equals is not implemented or is by id only), use assertThat(actual).usingRecursiveComparison().isEqualTo(expected), optionally with .ignoringFields("id", "createdAt").

Exceptions

assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.update(99L, request, me))
        .isInstanceOf(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
        .hasMessage("Job 99")
        .hasMessageContaining("99");

assertThatExceptionOfType(AccessDeniedException.class)
        .isThrownBy(() -> service.update(7L, request, stranger))
        .withMessageContaining("own jobs");

assertThatNoException().isThrownBy(() -> service.update(7L, request, owner));

// the cause chain
assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.importJobs(file))
        .hasRootCauseInstanceOf(IOException.class);

Put only the one call that should throw inside the lambda. If you put the whole arrange block in it, an exception from the set-up code makes the test pass for the wrong reason.

Soft assertions

Normal assertions stop at the first failure. Soft assertions collect all failures and report them together, which is nice when checking many fields of one response:

SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(softly -> {
    softly.assertThat(response.id()).isEqualTo(7L);
    softly.assertThat(response.title()).isEqualTo("Java Developer");
    softly.assertThat(response.open()).isTrue();
});

AssertJ vs JUnit assertions

JUnit (Assertions.*)AssertJ
StyleassertEquals(expected, actual)assertThat(actual).isEqualTo(expected)
Argument orderEasy to swap, wrong failure textActual first, no confusion
CollectionsBasic (assertIterableEquals)Rich: extracting, filteredOn, containsExactly
ExceptionsassertThrows (returns the exception)assertThatThrownBy with chained checks
Failure messagesShortDetailed, shows both values and the difference
DiscoverabilityFew methodsIDE shows only methods valid for the type

Using AssertJ everywhere is a good habit; just do not mix both styles inside one test. Hamcrest matchers (assertThat(x, is(5))) still appear in old MockMvc examples; use AssertJ or jsonPath there.

Common mistakes

  • Writing assertThat(x) and forgetting the check: assertThat(list.size() == 3); compiles but verifies nothing. Always end with a method such as isTrue() or use hasSize(3).
  • Using isEqualTo on arrays of entities without a useful equals.
  • Asserting the order of a result that SQL does not order (use containsExactlyInAnyOrder or add ORDER BY).
  • Comparing floating-point numbers with isEqualTo instead of isCloseTo.

Interview angle

"Why AssertJ over JUnit assertions?" Fluent, type-aware, better messages, strong collection and exception support. Be ready to write a collection assertion with extracting(...).containsExactly(...) and an exception assertion from memory.

@WebMvcTest and MockMvc: testing controllers, validation and security

@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, advice, filters, JSON, security) so you can test status codes, JSON, validation and 401/403 with MockMvc while the service is replaced by @MockitoBean.

What it loads, and what it does not

A test slice starts a small part of the Spring context. @WebMvcTest starts only the MVC infrastructure:

LoadedNot loaded
@Controller / @RestController (the ones you name), @ControllerAdvice, @JsonComponent, converters, Filter beans, WebMvcConfigurer, Jackson, validation, MockMvc, Spring Security auto-configuration@Service, @Repository, @Component beans, DataSource, JPA, Flyway, your @Configuration classes (import what you need)

Because services are not loaded, a controller that needs JobService fails to start the context with "No qualifying bean of type JobService". You supply a mock with @MockitoBean. This keeps the test fast (typically about a second) and focused on HTTP behaviour: URL mapping, request parsing, validation, status codes, JSON shape, error handling and security rules.

A first controller test

import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.*;

@WebMvcTest(JobController.class)
@Import({SecurityConfig.class, JsonSecurityHandlers.class})
class JobControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @MockitoBean JobService jobService;
    @MockitoBean JwtDecoder jwtDecoder;      // required by the resource server config

    @Test
    void getJob_returnsJson() throws Exception {
        when(jobService.getJob(7L)).thenReturn(new JobResponse(7L, "Java Developer", true));

        mvc.perform(get("/api/jobs/{id}", 7L))                    // public endpoint
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(content().contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(7))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Java Developer"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.open").value(true));
    }

    @Test
    void getJob_whenMissing_returns404Problem() throws Exception {
        when(jobService.getJob(99L)).thenThrow(new ResourceNotFoundException("Job 99"));

        mvc.perform(get("/api/jobs/{id}", 99L))
                .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.status").value(404))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("Job 99"));
    }
}
MockMvc
Sends fake HTTP requests straight into DispatcherServlet without opening a network port. Fast and in the same thread.
perform(request)
Executes the request built with get, post, put, delete, patch.
andExpect(matcher)
Checks the response: status(), content(), jsonPath(), header(), cookie().
andDo(print())
Prints the request and response; the fastest way to debug a failing test (MockMvcResultHandlers.print).
@Import(...)
Adds beans the slice does not scan. Your SecurityConfig is a @Configuration, so import it explicitly (with its handlers), otherwise default security rules apply.

The @ControllerAdvice from module 2 is picked up automatically, so error responses (ProblemDetail) are tested here too.

@MockitoBean and @MockBean

@MockitoBean (package org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito) puts a Mockito mock into the Spring test context in place of the real bean of that type, and resets it after each test. It exists since Spring Framework 6.2 (Spring Boot 3.4) and replaces @MockBean, which Boot deprecated in 3.4 and removed in Boot 4. On Boot 3.0 to 3.3 you still use @MockBean (package org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito). Inside test slices and @SpringBootTest use @MockitoBean; @Mock is only for plain unit tests with MockitoExtension. Similarly @MockitoSpyBean replaces @SpyBean.

Posting JSON and testing validation

private static final String VALID_JSON = """
        {"title": "Java Developer", "description": "Spring Boot, SQL"}""";

@Test
void createJob_asRecruiter_returns201() throws Exception {
    when(jobService.create(any(), any())).thenReturn(new JobResponse(7L, "Java Developer", true));

    mvc.perform(post("/api/jobs")
                    .with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_RECRUITER"))
                            .jwt(j -> j.subject("5")))
                    .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                    .content(VALID_JSON))
            .andExpect(status().isCreated())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(7));
}

@Test
void createJob_withBlankTitle_returns400() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/api/jobs")
                    .with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_RECRUITER")))
                    .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                    .content("""
                            {"title": "", "description": "x"}"""))
            .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.status").value(400));

    verifyNoInteractions(jobService);                 // service was never called
}

@Test
void createJob_withoutToken_returns401() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/api/jobs")
                    .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                    .content(VALID_JSON))
            .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
}

@Test
void createJob_asCandidate_returns403() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/api/jobs")
                    .with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_CANDIDATE")))
                    .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                    .content(VALID_JSON))
            .andExpect(status().isForbidden());

    verifyNoInteractions(jobService);
}

Text blocks (""") keep JSON readable. For bigger bodies serialize a record with the ObjectMapper (autowire JsonMapper/ObjectMapper, which differs by Boot line), but hand-written JSON also checks the real field names that clients use. The 400/401/403 tests are cheap and protect your security rules from accidental change.

Testing secured endpoints

Add spring-security-test (scope test). With it, MockMvc can pretend a user is logged in without a real token:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
ToolUse when
@WithMockUser(roles = "RECRUITER")Session/Basic style or when the principal type does not matter. Annotation on the test; creates a user with ROLE_RECRUITER. Does not apply to JWT resource-server authentication tokens, but method security and URL rules see its authorities.
.with(jwt())Resource server. Replaces the JwtDecoder: no real token is needed. Customise with .authorities(...), .jwt(j -> j.subject("5").claim("email", "...")).
.with(user("asha").roles("ADMIN"))Per-request user for form/Basic setups.
.with(csrf())When CSRF protection is enabled (cookie/session apps): adds a valid token to POST/PUT/DELETE. Without it you get 403. Not needed in our stateless API.
httpBasic("user", "pw")Basic authentication in the request.
 
@Test
@WithMockUser(username = "5", roles = "ADMIN")
void adminEndpoint_asAdmin_returns200() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/api/admin/users")).andExpect(status().isOk());
}

@Test
@WithMockUser(roles = "CANDIDATE")
void adminEndpoint_asCandidate_returns403() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/api/admin/users")).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
}

Note that roles = "ADMIN" already adds the ROLE_ prefix, while authorities in jwt().authorities(...) are used as written. If your controller reads jwt.getSubject() (for example through @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt), use jwt() with a subject; @WithMockUser does not provide a Jwt principal.

Useful matchers

.andExpect(status().isCreated())                              // 201
.andExpect(header().string("Location", "/api/jobs/7"))
.andExpect(jsonPath("$.items", hasSize(3)))                    // Hamcrest matcher from jsonPath
.andExpect(jsonPath("$.items[0].title").value("Java Developer"))
.andExpect(jsonPath("$.items[*].open", everyItem(is(true))))
.andExpect(jsonPath("$.password").doesNotExist())              // never leak a hash
.andExpect(content().json("{\"id\":7}"))                       // lenient JSON compare
.andExpect(content().string(containsString("Java")))

Read a value from the response for a later step with MvcResult result = mvc.perform(...).andReturn(); and result.getResponse().getContentAsString(). To test pagination parameters use .param("page", "0").param("size", "10").

MockMvcTester (brief)

Spring Framework 6.2 added MockMvcTester, an AssertJ-style wrapper around MockMvc, auto-configured for MVC tests in recent Boot versions. It avoids the throws Exception and the matcher imports:

@Autowired MockMvcTester mvc;

@Test
void getJob_returnsJson() {
    when(jobService.getJob(7L)).thenReturn(new JobResponse(7L, "Java Developer", true));

    assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/jobs/{id}", 7L))
            .hasStatusOk()
            .bodyJson()
            .extractingPath("$.title").isEqualTo("Java Developer");
}

It is optional; many codebases still use classic MockMvc, which you must be able to read. Check the API of your Spring version before using it.

Rules

  • A @WebMvcTest never touches a database. If the test needs one, it is the wrong kind of test.
  • Name the controller in @WebMvcTest(JobController.class) so only it is loaded; a bare @WebMvcTest loads all controllers and needs mocks for all their services.
  • Mock the layer below (the service), assert the HTTP contract. Business rules belong to the service unit test.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type JobService: add @MockitoBean for every dependency of the controller (and of imported filters/config).
  • 401/403 in a test where you expected 200: security is active; add jwt()/@WithMockUser, or csrf() when CSRF is on. If the real security config is missing, you get the default (everything secured, CSRF on).
  • Missing JwtDecoder: UnsatisfiedDependencyException when the imported config uses oauth2ResourceServer; mock it.
  • HttpMessageNotReadableException (400): malformed JSON in the test body or a missing Content-Type.
  • Empty body with jsonPath: the status was an error; use andDo(print()).

Common mistakes

  • Using @SpringBootTest + @AutoConfigureMockMvc for every controller test: slower, and loads the database you wanted to avoid.
  • Forgetting contentType(APPLICATION_JSON) on POST (you get 415 Unsupported Media Type).
  • Disabling security in tests (addFilters = false) so the 401/403 behaviour is never tested.
  • Putting business logic assertions here instead of in the service test.

Interview angle

"What does @WebMvcTest load?" Only web-layer beans; services are mocked with @MockitoBean. "How do you test a secured endpoint?" spring-security-test: @WithMockUser or jwt() post-processor; csrf() when needed; test 401 (no auth) and 403 (wrong role). "@MockBean vs @MockitoBean?" Same purpose; the latter is the replacement from Spring 6.2, while @MockBean was removed in Boot 4.

@DataJpaTest: testing repositories and queries

@DataJpaTest loads only JPA entities and repositories with a transaction that rolls back after each test; use it for derived and custom queries, and run it against the real database type (Testcontainers) instead of the default embedded H2.

What it loads

@DataJpaTest starts the persistence slice: entity scanning, Spring Data repositories, the DataSource, Hibernate, EntityManager, Flyway/Liquibase migrations when present, and a TestEntityManager. It does not load services, controllers or web configuration. By default it also replaces your configured database with an embedded one (H2 or HSQLDB, if on the classpath) and runs each test in a transaction that is rolled back at the end, so tests do not leave data behind (@Transactional in tests).

@DataJpaTest
class JobRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired JobRepository jobRepository;
    @Autowired UserRepository userRepository;
    @Autowired TestEntityManager em;

    @Test
    void findByPostedById_returnsOnlyThatRecruitersJobs() {
        User asha = em.persist(TestData.newUser("asha@example.com", Role.RECRUITER));
        User ravi = em.persist(TestData.newUser("ravi@example.com", Role.RECRUITER));
        em.persist(TestData.newJob("Java Developer", asha));
        em.persist(TestData.newJob("QA Engineer", asha));
        em.persist(TestData.newJob("DevOps Engineer", ravi));
        em.flush();           // send INSERTs to the database
        em.clear();           // forget loaded entities, so the query really hits the DB

        List<Job> jobs = jobRepository.findByPostedById(asha.getId());

        assertThat(jobs).extracting(Job::getTitle)
                .containsExactlyInAnyOrder("Java Developer", "QA Engineer");
    }

    @Test
    void existsByEmailIgnoreCase_isCaseInsensitive() {
        em.persist(TestData.newUser("Asha@Example.com", Role.CANDIDATE));
        em.flush();

        assertThat(userRepository.existsByEmailIgnoreCase("asha@example.com")).isTrue();
    }
}
TestEntityManager
A test helper around EntityManager with persist, persistAndFlush, find, flush, clear. Use it to arrange data without going through the repository you test.
flush()
Writes pending SQL to the database. Hibernate delays INSERTs until flush or commit, and the test transaction never commits, so without it your query may not see the data (or constraint violations never appear).
clear()
Empties the persistence context. Without it, findById returns the cached Java object and the test does not prove the SQL works.

What to test with it

  • Derived query methods with tricky names (findTop5ByCityAndOpenTrueOrderBySalaryMaxDesc).
  • Custom @Query JPQL and native SQL (joins, join fetch, projections, paging).
  • Constraints and mappings: unique email gives DataIntegrityViolationException on flush; @Enumerated(STRING) columns; cascade and orphanRemoval.
  • Pagination and sorting with PageRequest.of(0, 10, Sort.by("id")).
@Test
void saveTwoUsersWithSameEmail_violatesUniqueConstraint() {
    em.persist(TestData.newUser("asha@example.com", Role.CANDIDATE));
    em.flush();

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> {
        em.persist(TestData.newUser("asha@example.com", Role.RECRUITER));
        em.flush();                                   // the exception happens here
    }).isInstanceOf(PersistenceException.class);
}

Do not test Spring Data's built-in methods (save, findById); they are already tested. Test your own queries and mappings.

The H2 trap, and the fix

An embedded H2 database is fast and needs no setup, but it is not PostgreSQL. It can hide bugs and cause false failures:

  • PostgreSQL-only SQL in native queries (ILIKE, jsonb, array types, DISTINCT ON, RETURNING, window-function details) fails on H2.
  • Different rules for case sensitivity, null ordering, GROUP BY strictness and function-based indexes (lower(email)), so a test passes on H2 and fails in production, or the reverse.
  • Your Flyway migrations (written for PostgreSQL) may not run on H2 at all.
  • Different locking and transaction isolation behaviour.

The fix: test against the same database type you run in production. Tell @DataJpaTest not to replace the database, and supply a real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers (next articles):

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class JobRepositoryPgTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired JobRepository jobRepository;
    // tests as before
}

With Replace.NONE Spring Boot keeps the DataSource that @ServiceConnection created from the container. Put the container in a shared base class so it starts once, as shown in the Testcontainers article.

Versions

In Boot 4 the packages of @DataJpaTest and @AutoConfigureTestDatabase changed with the new modular test support; the names and behaviour are the same. Let the IDE import them. With Flyway on the classpath its migrations run in the slice, which is a good thing: the tests then also check your schema scripts.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • A test passes but production fails: the SQL ran on H2, or the entity came from the first-level cache. Use flush() + clear() and a real database.
  • DataIntegrityViolationException/PersistenceException only appears at flush(), not at save().
  • LazyInitializationException does not appear in a @DataJpaTest because the test transaction keeps the session open; you can miss this bug. Test the service with a real transaction boundary in an integration test, or map to DTOs.
  • Auditing fields (@CreatedDate) need @Import(JpaAuditingConfig.class) because your configuration classes are not scanned.
  • Hibernate sequence/identity ids: do not hard-code expected ids; read them from the saved entity.

Common mistakes

  • Asserting on an entity returned by findById without clear(): you are testing the cache.
  • Test data written with SQL files in H2 syntax and never run on PostgreSQL.
  • Marking the test @Transactional(propagation = NOT_SUPPORTED) or @Commit to "see data", then leaking rows into other tests.

Interview angle

"What does @DataJpaTest do?" Slice with entities and repositories, embedded DB by default, rollback per test, TestEntityManager. "Why not just use H2?" Dialect and feature differences hide real bugs; use Testcontainers PostgreSQL with Replace.NONE. "Why flush and clear?" Force SQL and bypass the first-level cache.

@SpringBootTest: full integration tests, profiles, test data and context caching

@SpringBootTest starts the whole application context so you can test real flows end to end through the layers; keep these tests few, share one context between them, and give each test its own clean data.

What it does

@SpringBootTest searches upwards for your @SpringBootApplication class and starts the full application context: all beans, security, JPA, Flyway, everything. Use it to prove the parts work together: controller to service to repository to database, with real security and real transactions. It is slower (seconds to start), so you write fewer of these.

webEnvironmentWhat happensCall the app with
MOCK (default)Full context, but a mock servlet environment; no port is openedMockMvc with @AutoConfigureMockMvc
RANDOM_PORTReal embedded server on a random free port@LocalServerPort + an HTTP client (RestClient, TestRestTemplate, WebTestClient)
DEFINED_PORTReal server on the configured port (can clash)Rarely used
NONEContext without any web environmentTest services or batch jobs directly

Prefer MOCK + MockMvc for most API flows: it is faster, runs in the same thread, and works with @Transactional rollback. Choose RANDOM_PORT when you need the real servlet container, real HTTP (filters at container level, cookies, serialisation over the wire) or to simulate a client.

An integration test through MockMvc

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@ActiveProfiles("test")
@Import(TestcontainersConfig.class)             // real PostgreSQL, see next article
class JobFlowIT {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @Test
    void recruiterPostsJob_candidateApplies() throws Exception {
        register("asha@example.com", "S3cret#2026", "RECRUITER");
        register("ravi@example.com", "S3cret#2026", "CANDIDATE");
        String recruiterToken = login("asha@example.com", "S3cret#2026");
        String candidateToken = login("ravi@example.com", "S3cret#2026");

        String jobBody = mvc.perform(post("/api/jobs")
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + recruiterToken)
                        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                        .content("""
                                {"title":"Java Developer","description":"Spring Boot"}"""))
                .andExpect(status().isCreated())
                .andReturn().getResponse().getContentAsString();
        int jobId = JsonPath.read(jobBody, "$.id");

        mvc.perform(post("/api/jobs/{id}/applications", jobId)
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + candidateToken))
                .andExpect(status().isCreated());

        // the candidate may not edit the job
        mvc.perform(put("/api/jobs/{id}", jobId)
                        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + candidateToken)
                        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                        .content("""
                                {"title":"Hacked","description":"x"}"""))
                .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }

    private void register(String email, String password, String role) throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/api/auth/register")
                        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                        .content("""
                                {"name":"Test","email":"%s","password":"%s","role":"%s"}"""
                                .formatted(email, password, role)))
                .andExpect(status().isCreated());
    }

    private String login(String email, String password) throws Exception {
        String body = mvc.perform(post("/api/auth/login")
                        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                        .content("""
                                {"email":"%s","password":"%s"}""".formatted(email, password)))
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andReturn().getResponse().getContentAsString();
        return JsonPath.read(body, "$.accessToken");
    }
}

This one test exercises registration, BCrypt, JWT, role rules, ownership and the database, using the real security chain instead of mocks. That is its value: the wiring that unit tests cannot see.

Calling a real server

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Import(TestcontainersConfig.class)
class HealthIT {

    @LocalServerPort int port;

    @Test
    void healthEndpoint_isUp() {
        RestClient client = RestClient.create("http://localhost:" + port);

        String body = client.get().uri("/actuator/health")
                .retrieve().body(String.class);

        assertThat(body).contains("UP");
    }
}

RestClient (Spring 6.1+) works the same in Boot 3 and 4. TestRestTemplate and WebTestClient also work with a random port, but how they are provided (extra dependencies or annotations) differs between Boot lines, so check your version's documentation; the idea is identical. Remember that a test method annotated @Transactional does not roll back the server's work with RANDOM_PORT: the server handles the request in another thread and its own transaction.

Profiles and test configuration

  • @ActiveProfiles("test") activates the test profile, so src/test/resources/application-test.yml overrides the main settings: a short JWT secret for tests, lower BCrypt cost, a fixed clock, disabled mail sending. Files in src/test/resources shadow those of the same name in src/main/resources.
  • @TestPropertySource(properties = "app.jwt.access-ttl-minutes=1") or @SpringBootTest(properties = "...") set single properties for one class.
  • @TestConfiguration adds or replaces beans for tests only, for example a fixed Clock. A static nested @TestConfiguration class is picked up automatically; a top-level one must be imported with @Import. (A normal @Configuration in src/test would be found by component scanning of every test, which is usually not what you want.)
@SpringBootTest
@Import(FixedClockConfig.class)
class DeadlineIT { ... }

@TestConfiguration
class FixedClockConfig {
    @Bean
    @Primary
    Clock clock() {
        return Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-11-10T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    }
}

Test data: @Sql, and cleaning up

@Test
@Sql("/sql/jobs.sql")                                   // run before the test method
@Sql(scripts = "/sql/cleanup.sql",
     executionPhase = Sql.ExecutionPhase.AFTER_TEST_METHOD)
void listJobs_returnsSeededJobs() throws Exception { ... }
insert into app_user (id, name, email, password_hash, role, enabled, locked)
values (1, 'Asha', 'asha@example.com', '{bcrypt}$2a$10$...', 'RECRUITER', true, false);
insert into job (id, title, description, posted_by_id)
values (10, 'Java Developer', 'Spring Boot', 1);

Three ways to keep tests independent in integration tests: (1) @Transactional on the test class with MockMvc (same thread, rolled back after each test), (2) @Sql cleanup scripts or repository.deleteAll() in @AfterEach, (3) unique data per test (random emails), so no cleanup is needed and tests can even run in parallel.

Context caching

Starting a Spring context takes seconds. The test framework therefore caches contexts and reuses one for all test classes with the same configuration. The cache key includes the configuration classes, active profiles, properties, @MockitoBean definitions, @TestConfiguration imports, and webEnvironment. Any difference creates and caches another context, and every cached context keeps its beans and connection pool alive.

Started JobFlowIT in 4.1 seconds
Started ApplicationFlowIT in 3.8 seconds     (different mocks: new context)
Started AuthIT in 3.9 seconds                (another property: new context)
  • Use one shared base class for integration tests with the same annotations, so most of them share a context.
  • Avoid scattering @MockitoBean and @TestPropertySource across many classes; each variant costs one more startup.
  • @DirtiesContext marks the context as dirty and discards it after the test or class. It is a last resort: it throws away the cache and makes the suite slow. Reset state explicitly instead.

Rules

  • Use @SpringBootTest for flows across layers; use slices and unit tests for everything else.
  • Integration tests need a real database of the production type (Testcontainers), not H2.
  • Each test creates the data it needs and must not rely on another test.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • Unable to find a @SpringBootConfiguration: the test class is in a package that is not under your application class. Move it or give classes = ....
  • ApplicationContext failure threshold exceeded / Failed to load ApplicationContext: the real cause is in the first "Caused by" lines, often a missing property or bean in the test profile.
  • @Transactional + RANDOM_PORT: no rollback of the server side (see above).
  • Port conflicts with DEFINED_PORT; prefer RANDOM_PORT.

Common mistakes

  • Using @SpringBootTest for a test that only needs one service and two mocks. Use a plain unit test.
  • Sharing mutable data between tests, then seeing tests pass alone and fail together.
  • A different set of @MockitoBean in every class, giving ten contexts and a ten-minute build.
  • Reaching for @DirtiesContext to clean the database.

Interview angle

"@SpringBootTest vs slice tests?" Full context vs one layer; mention speed and when you need each. "MOCK vs RANDOM_PORT?" No server, MockMvc vs real server and HTTP client. "Why are my tests slow?" Too many contexts: different mocks/properties break the cache; @DirtiesContext; Testcontainers started per class. Good answer: base class, shared container, fewer integration tests.

Testcontainers: tests against a real PostgreSQL in Docker

Testcontainers starts a throwaway Docker container (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka) for your tests; with @ServiceConnection Spring Boot wires it in automatically, and a shared configuration or base class starts it once for the whole suite.

Why

H2 is not PostgreSQL, and a database installed on your laptop differs from your colleague's and from CI. Testcontainers is a Java library that starts a real database in a Docker container, from an exact image tag (postgres:16-alpine), for the duration of the tests, and removes it afterwards. Every developer and every CI run gets the same database, with your real Flyway migrations, real SQL features and real locking. You trade a few seconds of startup for tests that mean something.

Requirement: Docker must be running. On Windows start Docker Desktop (with the WSL 2 backend) before running the tests; on Linux the Docker daemon. Without it you get IllegalStateException: Could not find a valid Docker environment. CI runners such as GitHub-hosted Ubuntu already have Docker.

Dependencies

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-testcontainers</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Spring Boot's dependency management supplies the versions. Your normal PostgreSQL JDBC driver must be on the classpath too.

Versions

Testcontainers 2.x (used by newer Boot lines) renamed its modules with a testcontainers- prefix (for example testcontainers-postgresql, testcontainers-junit-jupiter) and moved PostgreSQLContainer to the package org.testcontainers.postgresql without the generic type parameter. The ideas and the Spring annotations stay the same. Use the artifact names and imports that match the Testcontainers version your Boot version manages; the code below uses the 1.x style.

Way 1: @Testcontainers, @Container and @ServiceConnection

import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class JobRepositoryIT {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired JobRepository jobRepository;

    @Test
    void connectsToRealPostgres() {
        assertThat(postgres.isRunning()).isTrue();
        assertThat(jobRepository.count()).isZero();     // Flyway ran on a clean database
    }
}
  • @Testcontainers adds the JUnit extension that manages containers.
  • @Container on a static field: started once before the first test of the class and stopped after the last. On a non-static field: a new container per test method (slow).
  • @ServiceConnection (Spring Boot 3.1+) tells Boot to create the connection details from the container (JDBC URL, user, password) and use them instead of spring.datasource.*. No manual property mapping.

Way 2: @DynamicPropertySource (before 3.1, or when @ServiceConnection does not fit)

@DynamicPropertySource
static void dbProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
    registry.add("spring.datasource.url", postgres::getJdbcUrl);
    registry.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername);
    registry.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword);
}

The values are suppliers because the container's mapped port is known only after it starts. This also works for containers that @ServiceConnection does not support.

A reusable setup for the whole suite

Starting one PostgreSQL per test class wastes time (about 2 to 5 seconds each) and gives each class its own Spring context. Share one container. The cleanest way in modern Boot is a test configuration that defines the container as a bean:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class TestcontainersConfig {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres() {
        return new PostgreSQLContainer<>(DockerImageName.parse("postgres:16-alpine"));
    }
}
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@ActiveProfiles("test")
@Import(TestcontainersConfig.class)
public abstract class AbstractIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired protected MockMvc mvc;
}

class JobFlowIT extends AbstractIntegrationTest { ... }
class ApplicationFlowIT extends AbstractIntegrationTest { ... }

All subclasses have identical annotations, so Spring caches one context, which holds one container for the entire test run. Flyway runs its migrations once on startup. Isolate tests by unique data or cleanup.

The older, widely seen alternative is the singleton container pattern, which does not need the Spring bean approach:

public abstract class AbstractPgTest {

    static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> POSTGRES =
            new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    static { POSTGRES.start(); }                 // started once per JVM, no @Container

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
        r.add("spring.datasource.url", POSTGRES::getJdbcUrl);
        r.add("spring.datasource.username", POSTGRES::getUsername);
        r.add("spring.datasource.password", POSTGRES::getPassword);
    }
}

Testcontainers starts a helper container (called Ryuk) that removes your containers when the JVM exits, even if the test run crashes, so you do not stop the singleton yourself.

Container reuse, other containers, dev time

  • Reuse between runs (local development only): call .withReuse(true) on the container and set testcontainers.reuse.enable=true in ~/.testcontainers.properties. The container then stays running after the tests and the next mvn test starts in a second. Data persists, so such tests must clean up after themselves. Do not enable it in CI.
  • Other services: the same pattern works for Redis (new GenericContainer<>("redis:7").withExposedPorts(6379) with @ServiceConnection(name = "redis")), Kafka (KafkaContainer), RabbitMQ, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, and a mock HTTP server. See module 7 for messaging.
  • Dev-time Testcontainers (Boot 3.1+): a class in src/test with SpringApplication.from(Application::main).with(TestcontainersConfig.class).run(args) starts your real application with a containerised database, no local PostgreSQL install needed. Combined with @RestartScope it survives DevTools restarts. It reuses the same configuration class as your tests.

Speed tips

  • One container per suite (above); pin a small image (postgres:16-alpine) so CI caches it.
  • Use a tmpfs for the data directory only if tests are I/O heavy: .withTmpFs(Map.of("/var/lib/postgresql/data", "rw")).
  • Keep the number of distinct Spring contexts low (context caching).
  • Use @DataJpaTest with Replace.NONE for query tests: it starts less than the full application but shares the same container class.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • IllegalStateException: Could not find a valid Docker environment: Docker is not running or not reachable. Start Docker Desktop; check docker ps.
  • ContainerLaunchException: Container startup failed: image could not be pulled (no network, proxy), or the database crashed on start. Read the container logs printed above the exception.
  • Connection refused to localhost:5432: the test connects to a fixed port instead of the container's mapped port. Always read the port from the container (getJdbcUrl()).
  • Tests pass locally and fail in CI: CI has no Docker (for example Docker-in-Docker not enabled) or lacks permissions.
  • Flyway fails with "Found non-empty schema" or checksum errors when a reused container holds old data.

Common mistakes

  • A non-static @Container field: a fresh database for every test method.
  • Using the latest image tag: a surprise upgrade breaks CI. Pin the major version to match production.
  • Hard-coding jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/... in application-test.yml, which overrides the container wiring.
  • Forgetting that @DataJpaTest replaces the database unless Replace.NONE is set.

Interview angle

"How do you test repositories against a real database?" Testcontainers with @ServiceConnection; Docker required; one shared container per suite; Flyway migrations run for real. "Why not H2?" Behaviour and SQL dialect differ. "What is @ServiceConnection?" Boot 3.1+ feature that derives connection details from the container, replacing @DynamicPropertySource boilerplate.

Coverage with JaCoCo, Surefire vs Failsafe, and tests in CI

JaCoCo measures which lines and branches your tests execute; read the HTML report to find untested code, aim for sensible targets, never treat the percentage as proof of quality, and run unit tests with mvn test and integration tests (*IT) with mvn verify.

What coverage tells you

Code coverage is the share of your code that ran while the tests ran. JaCoCo is the standard Java tool: it attaches an agent to the test JVM and records executed instructions.

Line coverage
Percentage of source lines executed at least once.
Branch coverage
Percentage of decision outcomes taken: for if (a && b) both the true and false path of each condition. More honest than line coverage, because one line can hide several paths.
Other counters
Instruction, method, class and cyclomatic complexity.
return job.isOpen() ? apply(job) : reject(job);   // a test with an open job gives 100% line,
                                                  // but only 50% branch coverage

Setting up the JaCoCo Maven plugin

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
    <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>0.8.12</version>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>prepare-agent</id>
            <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>
        </execution>
        <execution>
            <id>report</id>
            <phase>verify</phase>
            <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

prepare-agent adds the JaCoCo agent to the JVM arguments of the test runs (Surefire and Failsafe). report turns the recorded data into HTML after the tests. Use the latest 0.8.x release that supports your JDK; an old JaCoCo fails on classes compiled by a newer Java ("Unsupported class file major version").

$ mvn clean verify
...
[INFO] Loading execution data file target/jacoco.exec
[INFO] Analyzed bundle 'jobs' with 48 classes
$ start target/site/jacoco/index.html          # Windows (macOS: open, Linux: xdg-open)

Reading the report

The first page lists packages with bars for instruction and branch coverage, plus missed/total counts. Click a package, then a class, then a method: the source view colours each line green (fully covered), yellow (some branches missed, with a diamond marker) and red (never executed). Start with red lines in service classes that hold business rules; ignore generated code, DTOs and the main method. The right questions are "which rules are untested?" and "which branches did I forget (404, 403, validation, empty list)?", not "how do I reach 100%?".

Exclude classes that add noise (configuration, generated mappers, entities with only getters) in the plugin <configuration><excludes>. To fail the build under a threshold add a check goal:

<execution>
    <id>check</id>
    <phase>verify</phase>
    <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
    <configuration>
        <rules>
            <rule>
                <element>BUNDLE</element>
                <limits>
                    <limit>
                        <counter>LINE</counter>
                        <value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
                        <minimum>0.70</minimum>
                    </limit>
                </limits>
            </rule>
        </rules>
    </configuration>
</execution>

Sensible targets, and why coverage is not quality

  • Many teams ask for roughly 70 to 80 percent line coverage on new code and watch the trend; 100 percent is rarely worth the cost. Services and domain logic deserve more than configuration or DTOs.
  • A test with no assertions gives coverage and no protection. service.update(...) called without checking anything is "covered".
  • Coverage tells you what is definitely untested; it cannot tell you what is well tested. Review assertions in pull requests, not just the percentage.
  • Mutation testing (PIT) goes further by changing your code and checking that tests fail; use it to learn, not necessarily in every build.

Surefire vs Failsafe

Maven SurefireMaven Failsafe
PurposeUnit and slice testsIntegration tests
Default name patterns*Test, Test*, *Tests, *TestCase*IT, IT*, *ITCase
Phasetest (mvn test)integration-test and verify (mvn verify)
On test failureBuild stops immediatelyRuns the post-integration-test phase first (cleanup), then fails in verify
SetupIncluded by defaultAdd the plugin (Spring Boot's parent configures its version)
 
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>integration-test</goal>
                <goal>verify</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
$ mvn test                              # unit + slice tests (Surefire), fast
$ mvn verify                            # all tests, including *IT, plus JaCoCo report
$ mvn test -Dtest=JobServiceTest        # one class
$ mvn test -Dtest=JobServiceTest#update_byOwner_changesFields   # one method
$ mvn verify -DskipITs                  # skip Failsafe tests
$ mvn test -Dgroups=fast                # JUnit @Tag("fast") only

A common layout: name pure unit and slice tests *Test and Docker-based ones *IT. Developers run mvn test constantly (no Docker needed, seconds); CI runs mvn verify (everything). If your whole project uses only Surefire and you name Testcontainers tests *Test, that also works; the split is about speed and feedback. To meet the goal "Project 2 passes all its tests with mvn test", either keep all tests under Surefire naming, or decide that the full check is mvn verify and say so in the README.

Running tests in CI

name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest          # Docker is preinstalled, Testcontainers works
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 21
          cache: maven
      - run: mvn -B verify          # unit, slice, integration tests + coverage
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: reports
          path: |
            target/site/jacoco
            target/surefire-reports

Make the pipeline required on pull requests so that red tests block the merge. Details of GitHub Actions are in DevOps · Module 4.

Common mistakes

  • Chasing a percentage with tests that have no assertions.
  • Naming an integration test MyFlowTest and wondering why it runs on every mvn test (or naming it MyFlowIT and wondering why mvn test skips it).
  • Checking JaCoCo only on unit tests and concluding that controllers are "untested" when integration tests cover them: aggregate both runs (verify).
  • A JaCoCo version too old for your Java version.

Interview angle

"What coverage is enough?" There is no number; useful targets are around 70 to 80 percent on business code, with branch coverage and good assertions. "Line vs branch coverage?" One line can have several branches. "Surefire vs Failsafe?" Unit vs integration, test vs verify phases, *Test vs *IT names.

Good tests: FIRST, test data builders and avoiding flaky tests

A good test is fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating and written at the right time; it checks behaviour not implementation, builds its data with readable helpers, and never depends on time, order or luck.

The FIRST principles

Fast
Unit tests run in milliseconds, the whole unit suite in seconds. Slow tests are not run, so they do not protect you.
Independent
No test depends on another or on their order. Each creates its own data and cleans up. You can run one test alone or all in parallel.
Repeatable
Same result in every environment and on every run: no dependence on the clock, random numbers, network, the machine's time zone or leftover files.
Self-validating
The test says pass or fail by itself, through assertions. No reading console output to decide.
Timely
Written together with the code (or before it, TDD), when you still remember the rules. Not "after the release".

Test behaviour, not implementation

A test should fail when behaviour breaks and keep passing when you refactor. Tests that mirror the code line by line (verify that private helper A called B twice) break on every refactoring and teach nothing. Ask: "what would a caller notice?" Test the public result, the stored state, the response, and the side effects that matter.

Wrong: tests how, not what

verify(jobRepository).findById(7L);
verify(jobRepository).save(job);
verify(mapper).toResponse(job);
verifyNoMoreInteractions(jobRepository, mapper);

Right: tests the outcome

JobResponse r = service.close(7L, owner);
assertThat(r.open()).isFalse();
assertThat(job.getClosedAt()).isNotNull();

Test data builders

Creating a Job needs a user, a title and more fields; repeating a ten-line set-up in every test hides what matters. A test data builder creates a valid object with defaults and lets the test override only what it cares about.

public final class TestData {

    private TestData() {}

    public static User user(Long id, String email, Role role) {
        User u = new User("Test " + email, email, "{bcrypt}hash", role);
        ReflectionTestUtils.setField(u, "id", id);
        return u;
    }

    public static User newUser(String email, Role role) {      // no id: for persist
        return new User("Test " + email, email, "{bcrypt}hash", role);
    }

    public static Job job(Long id, String title, User owner) {
        Job j = new Job(title, "Description of " + title, owner);
        ReflectionTestUtils.setField(j, "id", id);
        return j;
    }

    public static Job newJob(String title, User owner) {
        return new Job(title, "Description of " + title, owner);
    }
}

// A builder with fluent overrides, when objects have many fields:
public class JobBuilder {
    private String title = "Java Developer";
    private boolean open = true;
    private User owner = TestData.newUser("owner@example.com", Role.RECRUITER);

    public static JobBuilder aJob() { return new JobBuilder(); }
    public JobBuilder withTitle(String t) { this.title = t; return this; }
    public JobBuilder closed() { this.open = false; return this; }
    public Job build() {
        Job j = new Job(title, "Some description", owner);
        if (!open) j.close();
        return j;
    }
}
// usage: Job closed = aJob().withTitle("QA").closed().build();

Test data should be minimal and meaningful: names like asha@example.com help readers; magic numbers do not. Avoid giant shared fixtures loaded for all tests (changing one row breaks twenty tests).

Flaky tests

A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change. It destroys trust: people re-run the pipeline "until green" and real failures get ignored. Typical causes and fixes:

CauseExampleFix
Time and datesLocalDate.now(); a test fails at midnight or on month endInject Clock; use a fixed instant
RandomnessRandom emails that sometimes collideSeeded random or UUIDs; assert on properties, not values
Test order and shared stateOne test leaves a row that another countsOwn data per test, cleanup, rollback
Unordered resultsAsserting list order from a query with no ORDER BYAdd ordering or containsExactlyInAnyOrder
Async and threadsThread.sleep(500) then assertAwaitility: await().atMost(5, SECONDS).untilAsserted(...)
External systemsCalling a real payment or mail APIMock, WireMock/MockWebServer, or a container
EnvironmentFixed ports, time zone, locale, file paths, Windows vs Linux newlineRandom ports, explicit time zone and locale, Path APIs
ResourcesDocker not ready, CI under load, timeouts too tightWait strategies, generous timeouts, retry only the infrastructure step

Never "fix" a flaky test by adding a retry or @Disabled without finding the cause. Reproduce it by running the test in a loop, read the failure, fix the cause.

Habits of strong teams

  • Test the unhappy paths: not found, validation failure, duplicate, forbidden, empty list, boundary values (0, 1, max).
  • When you fix a bug, first write a test that fails because of it (regression test).
  • Keep tests readable: a new teammate should understand a test without opening the production code. Prefer clear duplication over clever shared helpers that hide the scenario.
  • Treat test code like production code: review it, refactor it, delete obsolete tests.
  • Do not assert on log output or private methods. Do not test third-party libraries.

Real projects

A typical Spring Boot pull request contains: unit tests for new service logic, a @WebMvcTest for a new endpoint (success plus 400/401/403/404), a repository test for any new query, and the existing integration flows still green. Reviewers reject changes that lower coverage on business code or that add Thread.sleep.

Interview angle

"What makes a good unit test?" FIRST, one behaviour, Arrange-Act-Assert, descriptive name, no logic, no real I/O. "What is a flaky test and how do you handle it?" Name causes (time, order, async, shared state) and fixes (Clock, isolation, Awaitility), and say you never ignore it. "TDD in one minute?" Red (failing test), green (smallest code), refactor.

Interview questions — Testing

Explain the testing pyramid and what you test at each level in a Spring Boot app.

Many fast unit tests at the base (services with Mockito), fewer slice tests (@WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories), a few @SpringBootTest integration flows with a real database, and very few end-to-end tests. Each check goes to the lowest level that can prove it, because upper levels are slower and fail for more reasons.

What is the difference between @Mock, @InjectMocks, @MockBean/@MockitoBean and @Spy?

@Mock creates a Mockito fake (plain unit tests with MockitoExtension). @InjectMocks creates the real object under test and injects those fakes. @MockitoBean (earlier @MockBean) puts a Mockito mock into the Spring context, replacing the bean, for slice and integration tests. @Spy wraps a real object so that only the stubbed methods are faked.

What is UnnecessaryStubbingException?

With MockitoExtension stubs are strict: a when(...) that the test never triggers fails the test. It points to dead set-up or a wrong assumption about what the code calls. Remove the stub, or use lenient() for shared set-up in @BeforeEach.

Why can't you write when(mock.voidMethod()) and what do you use instead?

A void method has no value to pass to when, so it does not compile. Use the action-first forms doThrow(...).when(mock).voidMethod() or doNothing(). The same style, doReturn(x).when(spy).method(), is needed with spies so the real method is not called while stubbing.

What is the rule for argument matchers?

If any argument of a call uses a matcher (any(), anyString()), all arguments must use matchers; wrap literals in eq(). Mixing them throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException.

When do you use verify, and when does it hurt?

Use verify for side effects that are the point of the behaviour: an e-mail was sent, a save happened, nothing was deleted. Over-verifying every interaction (or verifyNoMoreInteractions everywhere) couples tests to the implementation, so refactoring breaks them. When a result is returned, assert the result instead.

What does @WebMvcTest load, and how do you test a secured endpoint?

Only the web layer: controllers, advice, filters, converters and security auto-configuration; services need @MockitoBean. Import your SecurityConfig. With spring-security-test use @WithMockUser(roles = ...) or .with(jwt().authorities(...)), add csrf() when CSRF is enabled, and test both 401 (no auth) and 403 (wrong role).

How do you test validation errors and error responses for a POST endpoint?

Post invalid JSON with MockMvc (content type JSON), expect status().isBadRequest(), assert the ProblemDetail fields with jsonPath, and verifyNoInteractions(service) to show the service was never reached. Likewise, make the mocked service throw ResourceNotFoundException and expect 404.

What does @DataJpaTest do and why not use H2 for it?

It starts only JPA: entities, repositories, TestEntityManager, a transaction rolled back after each test. By default it swaps your database for an embedded one. H2 differs from PostgreSQL in SQL dialect, functions, case rules, locking and migrations, so tests can pass while production fails. Use Testcontainers with @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE). Call flush() and clear() so SQL really runs.

@SpringBootTest MOCK vs RANDOM_PORT?

MOCK (default) loads the full context with a mock servlet environment and no port; you call it with MockMvc, in the same thread, so @Transactional rollback works. RANDOM_PORT starts a real embedded server on a free port, injected with @LocalServerPort, and you use an HTTP client; the server handles requests on its own threads and transactions.

Why is my Spring test suite slow, and what is context caching?

Spring caches each distinct application context and reuses it across test classes. Different @MockitoBean sets, properties, profiles or @DirtiesContext create new contexts (seconds each), and starting a Testcontainers database per class adds more. Fix with one shared base class, a shared container, fewer integration tests and no @DirtiesContext.

How does Testcontainers work with Spring Boot, and what does @ServiceConnection do?

Testcontainers starts a real PostgreSQL in Docker for the tests. A static @Container field (or a container bean in a @TestConfiguration) annotated with @ServiceConnection (Boot 3.1+) makes Boot derive the datasource URL, user and password from the container; before that you used @DynamicPropertySource. Docker must be running, and a shared container keeps the suite fast.

Line coverage vs branch coverage, and is 100% coverage the goal?

Line coverage counts executed lines; branch coverage counts the outcomes of decisions (both sides of an if), so it is stricter. 100 percent is not the goal: coverage shows what is untested, not whether tests assert anything. Use it to find missing scenarios, set a modest threshold on business code, and review assertion quality.

What is a flaky test and how do you fix one?

One that passes and fails without code changes. Causes: time (now()), randomness, test order or shared data, unordered results, Thread.sleep with async code, external services, environment differences. Fix the cause: inject a Clock, isolate data, containsExactlyInAnyOrder or ORDER BY, Awaitility, mocks or containers. Do not just retry or disable it.

Cheat sheet — Testing

  • Pyramid unit (many, ms) then slice then integration then end-to-end (few).
  • AAA Arrange, Act, Assert (= Given, When, Then); one behaviour per test.
  • Naming method_condition_expected or shouldXWhenY; test tree mirrors main.
  • Starter spring-boot-starter-test: JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Spring Test, JsonPath; add spring-security-test.
  • JUnit @Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, static @BeforeAll, @Nested, @DisplayName, @Disabled, @Tag.
  • Parameterized @ParameterizedTest with @ValueSource, @CsvSource, @MethodSource, @EnumSource.
  • Mockito setup @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), @Mock, @InjectMocks, @Spy, @Captor.
  • Stubbing when(x).thenReturn/thenThrow/thenAnswer; void or spy: doThrow/doNothing/doReturn(...).when(m).
  • Matchers any(), eq(); all-or-none rule.
  • Verify verify(m), times(n), never(), verifyNoInteractions; use sparingly.
  • Strict stubs unused stub gives UnnecessaryStubbingException; lenient() as exception.
  • Do not mock the SUT, value objects, collections; prefer a Clock to static mocks.
  • AssertJ assertThat, extracting, containsExactly, hasSize, assertThatThrownBy, SoftAssertions.
  • @WebMvcTest controller + advice + security only; MockMvc, @MockitoBean for services, @Import your config.
  • MockMvc perform(post(...).contentType(JSON).content(...)), status(), jsonPath(), andDo(print()).
  • Security tests @WithMockUser, jwt(), csrf(); always test 401 and 403.
  • @MockitoBean replaces @MockBean (Boot 3.4+, only one in Boot 4).
  • @DataJpaTest JPA slice, rollback per test, TestEntityManager, flush() + clear(), Replace.NONE for real DB.
  • @SpringBootTest full context; MOCK + MockMvc or RANDOM_PORT + client; few of them.
  • Test config @ActiveProfiles("test"), application-test.yml, @TestConfiguration, @Sql, avoid @DirtiesContext.
  • Context cache same config gives same context; vary mocks or properties and you pay a new startup.
  • Testcontainers Docker running; static @Container + @ServiceConnection; shared container via config/base class.
  • Surefire / Failsafe *Test with mvn test; *IT with mvn verify.
  • JaCoCo prepare-agent + report; HTML in target/site/jacoco; branch coverage is stricter; coverage is not quality.
  • FIRST Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely; fix flaky tests at the cause.

Practice — Testing

  1. Warm-up unit tests. Write SalaryRangeTest or a similar pure-Java test with JUnit 5 and AssertJ: a normal case, a boundary, and a @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource for invalid input. Done when mvn test -Dtest=SalaryRangeTest is green and each test name states the expected result.
  2. Unit-test the services of Project 2. Write JobServiceTest and ApplicationServiceTest with Mockito: create, update by owner, update by another recruiter (forbidden), admin override, not found, duplicate application, apply to a closed job. Use ArgumentCaptor once and verify(..., never()) once. Done when every branch of the services' public methods is covered and no test starts Spring.
  3. Break it on purpose. Add an unused stub and a mixed-matcher call, read the two Mockito exceptions, and fix them. Done when you can explain both messages.
  4. MockMvc tests for controllers. For JobController and AuthController write @WebMvcTest tests: 200 and 201 responses, 400 for invalid JSON, 404 via a mocked ResourceNotFoundException, 401 without token, 403 for a CANDIDATE posting a job. Done when each endpoint has a success test and at least two failure tests, and $.password never appears in any response.
  5. Repository tests. Write a @DataJpaTest for every custom query (for example jobs by recruiter, search by title ignoring case, applications by job). Use flush() and clear(). Done when a deliberately broken query (wrong field) makes a test fail.
  6. One Testcontainers integration test. Add TestcontainersConfig and AbstractIntegrationTest with PostgreSQL and your Flyway migrations. Write JobFlowIT: register a recruiter and a candidate, log in, post a job, apply, and check that the candidate cannot edit the job and the other recruiter gets 403. Done when it passes with Docker Desktop running and your Flyway migrations are applied on startup.
  7. Switch repository tests to PostgreSQL. Run the @DataJpaTest tests with Replace.NONE and the shared container. Add a native query using a PostgreSQL feature (such as ilike) and show it would fail on H2. Done when all repository tests run against the container.
  8. Measure coverage. Add JaCoCo and run mvn clean verify. Open target/site/jacoco/index.html, find the three least-covered service methods, and add tests for the missed branches. Done when business packages are above 70 percent line coverage, with a short note on one thing the percentage cannot tell you.
  9. Make the suite green and fast. Check the log for how many Spring contexts start; reduce them with a common base class. Split names into *Test and *IT, enable Failsafe, and run both mvn test and mvn verify. Done when Project 2 passes all its tests with mvn test (and mvn verify if you keep ITs separate) with no @Disabled and no sleeps.
  10. CI. Add the GitHub Actions workflow from this module and push a deliberately failing test to a branch. Done when the pull request shows a red check and turns green after the fix (DevOps · Module 4).
6

Module 6·Weeks 10–11Good to know

Production features

12 topics · about 1.5 h of reading

A project that "works on my laptop" is not yet a project that runs well in production. This module is about everything around your business code that makes an application operable: you can see what it is doing (logs, health, metrics), it is fast enough (caching), it does work in the background (scheduling, async), it handles files and email, it calls other APIs safely, and it protects itself from abuse (rate limiting).

Most of these features are a starter dependency plus a few properties, and most are built on the proxy mechanism from module 1, so the same traps repeat (self-invocation, wrong thread, wrong transaction). We use the Project 2 job portal (User, Company, Job, Application) for examples: a resume upload, an email to the recruiter when someone applies, a cached job list and a health endpoint for Docker.

The next module, Microservices and messaging, builds on these: Actuator and Micrometer feed tracing, and RestClient meets Resilience4j.

  • Configure logging with levels, files, JSON output and a correlation id, and know what never to log.
  • Expose health, info and metrics with Actuator, secure it, and write a custom health check and custom metrics.
  • Cache with @Cacheable using Caffeine or Redis, and invalidate correctly.
  • Run scheduled and asynchronous jobs safely, with virtual threads where they help.
  • Upload and download files and send email (HTML, attachments) without security holes.
  • Call other services with RestClient and declarative HTTP clients, with timeouts.
  • Add rate limiting and walk through a production-readiness checklist.

Logging with SLF4J and Logback: levels, files, JSON and MDC

Log through the SLF4J API, let Spring Boot's default Logback do the work, control it with logging.level.* and a few properties, switch to JSON in production, tag every line with a request id using MDC, and never log secrets.

What and why

System.out.println is not logging. A log is a stream of timestamped, levelled events that you can filter, search, ship to a central system and turn up or down without redeploying. When a user says "my application did not go through at 3 pm", the log is often your only evidence.

Java has many logging libraries, so Spring Boot uses a facade. SLF4J is the API you write against (Logger, LoggerFactory); Logback is the implementation that actually writes lines. spring-boot-starter-logging is included by every starter, so logging works with zero setup. Basic Java logging ideas are in Core Java · Module 8.

Writing log statements

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

@Service
public class ApplicationService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ApplicationService.class);

    public ApplicationResponse apply(Long jobId, Long userId) {
        log.info("User {} applying to job {}", userId, jobId);   // placeholders, no concatenation
        try {
            // ... save the application
            log.debug("Application saved, id={}", saved.getId());
            return mapper.toResponse(saved);
        } catch (DuplicateResourceException ex) {
            log.warn("Duplicate application: user={}, job={}", userId, jobId);
            throw ex;
        } catch (RuntimeException ex) {
            log.error("Could not save application for user {} job {}", userId, jobId, ex);
            throw ex;                    // the last argument, an exception, prints the stack trace
        }
    }
}

With Lombok you can write @Slf4j on the class and use log directly. Rules for the statements themselves:

  • Use {} placeholders. The message is built only if the level is enabled, so log.debug("x " + big) (which builds the string always) is a small performance bug.
  • Pass the exception as the last argument, without a placeholder, to get the stack trace. log.error("failed: " + ex.getMessage()) throws the stack trace away.
  • Do not log and rethrow the same exception at every layer; you get the same stack trace five times. Log it once, where you handle it (usually the @RestControllerAdvice from module 2).

Log levels

LevelUse it forExample
ERRORThe operation failed and someone should lookDatabase down, unexpected exception
WARNSomething odd, but the app handled itRetry succeeded, deprecated API used, rate limit hit
INFOImportant business events, few per request"Application submitted", startup, job finished
DEBUGDetails for developers, off in productionMethod arguments, decisions taken
TRACEVery fine detailEvery loop iteration, raw payloads

Levels are ordered: setting a logger to INFO prints INFO, WARN and ERROR. Spring Boot's default is INFO for everything. A bad request from a client (validation failure, 404) is not an ERROR in your system; log it at INFO or DEBUG, or not at all. Reserve ERROR for things you would wake up for.

Configuring Logback through properties

Boot's defaults need no XML. Everything below goes in application.yml (or .properties):

logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example.jobs: DEBUG              # your packages
    org.springframework.web: WARN
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG             # print SQL (see the JPA module)
  file:
    name: logs/jobs-api.log              # also write to a file (path relative to working dir)
  logback:
    rollingpolicy:
      max-file-size: 10MB                # roll over when the file reaches this size
      max-history: 14                    # keep 14 days of archives
      total-size-cap: 1GB
  pattern:
    console: "%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} %-5level [%X{requestId:-}] %logger{36} - %msg%n"
  group:
    persistence: org.hibernate.SQL, org.springframework.orm.jpa   # one name for many loggers
  • logging.level.<logger> sets the level for a package or class. Loggers form a tree: com.example.jobs also controls com.example.jobs.job.JobService unless that has its own level.
  • logging.file.name (or logging.file.path, which writes spring.log inside that folder) adds a file. Boot rolls files by size and date once you set the logging.logback.rollingpolicy.* properties.
  • logging.pattern.console and logging.pattern.file change the line format. %X{requestId:-} prints a value from the MDC (below), or nothing.
  • logging.group.<name> lets you write logging.level.persistence: DEBUG for several loggers at once.
  • Quick debugging: start with --debug (or debug=true) to see Boot's auto-configuration report. This is not the same as DEBUG for your own code.

You can also change a level of a running application without a restart through the Actuator loggers endpoint (see Actuator).

logback-spring.xml: profiles and rolling files

When properties are not enough, add src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml. Use the name logback-spring.xml, not logback.xml: the "-spring" version is loaded by Spring Boot, so you can use <springProfile> and <springProperty>.

<configuration>
  <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/defaults.xml"/>
  <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/console-appender.xml"/>

  <springProperty scope="context" name="APP" source="spring.application.name"
