                  defaultValue="jobs-api"/>

  <appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
    <file>logs/${APP}.log</file>
    <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy">
      <fileNamePattern>logs/${APP}-%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.%i.log.gz</fileNamePattern>
      <maxFileSize>10MB</maxFileSize>
      <maxHistory>14</maxHistory>
      <totalSizeCap>1GB</totalSizeCap>
    </rollingPolicy>
    <encoder>
      <pattern>%d %-5level [%thread] [%X{requestId:-}] %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
    </encoder>
  </appender>

  <springProfile name="dev">
    <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/></root>
    <logger name="com.example.jobs" level="DEBUG"/>
  </springProfile>

  <springProfile name="prod">
    <root level="INFO">
      <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
      <appender-ref ref="FILE"/>
    </root>
  </springProfile>
</configuration>

Think about whether you need files at all. In Docker and Kubernetes the standard is: write to the console (stdout) and let the platform collect it. Files and rotation are for plain VM deployments (DevOps · Module 6).

Structured (JSON) logging

Plain text lines are easy for humans but hard for log tools: to search "all errors for user 42" you must parse text. Structured logging writes each event as one JSON object with fields (@timestamp, level, message, traceId, your MDC values), so tools like Loki, Elasticsearch or CloudWatch can filter by field.

logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs          # also: logstash, gelf
      # file: ecs           # same for the log file
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-10T09:15:03.412Z",
  "log.level": "INFO",
  "message": "User 42 applying to job 7",
  "service.name": "jobs-api",
  "log.logger": "com.example.jobs.application.ApplicationService"
}

Version note

Built-in structured logging (logging.structured.format.console) arrived in Spring Boot 3.4 and works the same in 4.x. On older versions you would add a JSON encoder library such as logstash-logback-encoder in logback-spring.xml. The exact field names depend on the format you pick (ECS, Logstash, GELF).

MDC: a request id on every line

The MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is a per-thread map that Logback can print on every line. Put a correlation id (request id) in it at the start of each request, and every log line from that request, from any class, carries the same id. When a user reports a problem, you search for one id and see the whole story.

import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.core.Ordered;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

@Component
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private static final String HEADER = "X-Request-Id";

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        String id = request.getHeader(HEADER);
        if (id == null || id.isBlank() || id.length() > 64) {
            id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        }
        MDC.put("requestId", id);
        response.setHeader(HEADER, id);          // the client can quote it in a bug report
        try {
            chain.doFilter(request, response);
        } finally {
            MDC.remove("requestId");             // threads are reused: always clean up
        }
    }
}
09:15:03.412 INFO  [a1b2c3d4-...] c.e.jobs.application.ApplicationService - User 42 applying to job 7
09:15:03.430 WARN  [a1b2c3d4-...] c.e.jobs.application.ApplicationService - Duplicate application

Two details matter. First, the MDC is bound to the thread; a new thread (@Async, an executor, a Kafka listener) starts with an empty MDC. Copy it with a TaskDecorator (see Async). Second, if you add Micrometer Tracing later (tracing), it puts traceId and spanId in the MDC for you, and the request id becomes less necessary.

What to log, and what never to log

  • Log: business events with ids (application submitted, job closed), calls to other systems with duration and status, scheduled job start/end with counts, security events (login failed, access denied), and the exception at the place you handle it.
  • Never log: passwords, JWTs, API keys, OTPs, card numbers, Aadhaar/PAN, full email bodies, full request bodies of sensitive endpoints. This is both a security and a legal problem (privacy laws, PCI rules). Log ids, not personal data: userId=42, not the user's phone number.
  • Watch out for: toString() of entities (lazy loading and sensitive fields), Lombok @Data printing a password field, and logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG in production, which can print request details.

Logging in tests

Keep a src/test/resources/application-test.yml with quieter levels so test output is readable. To assert on log output, use the OutputCaptureExtension from Spring Boot (@ExtendWith(OutputCaptureExtension.class), then take a CapturedOutput parameter and check output.getOut()). Prefer asserting on behaviour, and only check logs for things like "secret is not printed". See module 5 for test setup.

Common mistakes

  • String concatenation in log calls, or ex.printStackTrace() (goes to stderr, outside the log).
  • Logging a whole request DTO that contains a password.
  • DEBUG left on in production: slow, huge disk use, and leaks data.
  • Forgetting MDC.remove in finally, so the next request on that thread shows the old id.
  • Logging inside a tight loop (a million lines for one batch). Log a summary.

Edge cases

  • Both logging.file.name and logging.file.path set: name wins.
  • If a second logging library is on the classpath (log4j-slf4j and Logback together), SLF4J prints "multiple bindings" and may pick the wrong one. Exclude one in the build.
  • A logback.xml (without "-spring") is read before Boot starts, so <springProfile> will not work there.
  • Logging cannot fail the request: Logback swallows its own I/O errors (a full disk loses logs, but requests continue).

Interview angle

"SLF4J vs Logback?" Facade vs implementation. "Why placeholders?" No string building when disabled. "How do you trace one request across many log lines?" MDC correlation id in a filter, or tracing ids. "How do you change the log level without restart?" Actuator loggers. "What do you never log?" Secrets and personal data. Mention JSON logs for log platforms.

Spring Boot Actuator: health, info, endpoints and securing them

Add spring-boot-starter-actuator to get ready-made endpoints (health, info, metrics, loggers and more); expose only what you need, secure the rest, and use the liveness and readiness probes for Docker and Kubernetes.

What and why

Actuator adds production endpoints to your application with no code: "is it up?", "what is its version?", "how many requests failed?", "what is the log level?". Load balancers, Docker, Kubernetes and monitoring tools call these endpoints. Without a health endpoint, your platform can only guess whether the application works.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

With the starter alone, only /actuator/health is exposed over HTTP (and it shows just {"status":"UP"}). The other endpoints exist but are hidden for safety, because some of them (env, heapdump) reveal sensitive data.

The main endpoints

EndpointWhat it shows or doesRisk
healthUP/DOWN of the app and its parts (database, disk, Redis...)Low (details can leak)
infoApp name, version, git commit, build timeLow
metricsMicrometer metric names and values (JVM, HTTP, pool)Medium
prometheusAll metrics in Prometheus text format (needs the Prometheus registry)Medium
loggersList and change log levels at runtimeMedium (writeable)
envProperties and environment (values of secrets are masked by default, not always)High
mappingsAll URL mappingsMedium
beansAll Spring beansMedium
conditionsWhy each auto-configuration did or did not applyLow
threaddumpStack of every thread (find deadlocks and stuck requests)High
heapdumpDownloads a JVM heap dump, which contains everything in memoryVery high

Exposure settings

Every endpoint has two switches: enabled and exposed (over HTTP or JMX). You choose what is exposed:

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, info, metrics, prometheus, loggers   # list what you need
        # exclude: heapdump, env
        # include: "*"                                         # everything: dev only
      base-path: /actuator                                     # default
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized      # never | when-authorized | always
      probes:
        enabled: true                    # adds /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness
  server:
    port: 9090                           # optional: serve actuator on a separate port

A separate management port (management.server.port) is a strong, simple protection: do not publish port 9090 to the internet, only to your monitoring network. Your gateway or Nginx only forwards the API port.

Securing Actuator

If Spring Security is on the classpath, actuator endpoints are protected by your filter chain like any URL. The rule is: health (and the probes) open or limited to the platform, everything else for an admin role.

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain actuatorChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())          // only actuator URLs
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to("health", "info")).permitAll()
            .anyRequest().hasRole("ADMIN"))
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());
    return http.build();
}

Put this chain before your main API chain with @Order(1), or merge the rules into your existing chain. Prometheus scrapers usually use a separate port or a basic-auth user. Rule of thumb: health may be public; env, heapdump, threaddump, loggers must never be.

Health in depth

The health endpoint combines many health indicators. Boot adds them automatically when the related library is present: db (runs a validation query on your DataSource), diskSpace, redis, mail, rabbit, and so on. The overall status is the worst one: if the database is DOWN, the app is DOWN (HTTP 503).

{
  "status": "UP",
  "components": {
    "db":        { "status": "UP", "details": { "database": "PostgreSQL" } },
    "diskSpace": { "status": "UP", "details": { "free": 91234816000, "threshold": 10485760 } },
    "ping":      { "status": "UP" }
  }
}

Liveness and readiness probes

Orchestrators ask two different questions, and Boot answers both when management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true (it is on automatically when Boot detects Kubernetes):

  • Liveness (/actuator/health/liveness): "Is the process broken beyond repair?" If it fails, the platform restarts the container. Keep it simple: it should not check the database, or a database outage would restart every pod and make things worse.
  • Readiness (/actuator/health/readiness): "Can it accept traffic now?" If it fails, the platform stops sending requests but does not restart. It goes OUT_OF_SERVICE during startup and during graceful shutdown.

You can define your own health groups that pick specific indicators, for example a group the Docker healthcheck uses:

management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db, redis       # DB and Redis needed to serve traffic
        liveness:
          include: livenessState

A custom HealthIndicator

Add your own check by implementing HealthIndicator; the bean name (minus "HealthIndicator") becomes the component name. Example: is the resume storage folder writeable?

import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.health.Health;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.health.HealthIndicator;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component("storage")                         // shows as components.storage
public class StorageHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final Path root;

    public StorageHealthIndicator(@Value("${app.upload-dir}") Path root) {
        this.root = root;
    }

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        if (Files.isWritable(root)) {
            return Health.up().withDetail("path", root.toString()).build();
        }
        return Health.down().withDetail("path", root.toString())
                .withDetail("reason", "not writable").build();
    }
}

Keep indicators fast (they run on each call, and the platform may call every few seconds). Do not call a slow external API from one; if you must, cache the result.

The info endpoint: build and git information

The info endpoint answers "which version is running?" You can feed it from properties, the build, and git:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals><goal>build-info</goal></goals>   <!-- creates META-INF/build-info.properties -->
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
management:
  info:
    env:
      enabled: true          # show properties that start with "info."
    git:
      mode: simple           # needs git.properties (git-commit-id plugin)
info:
  app:
    name: Jobs API
    owner: platform-team

With the git-commit-id Maven plugin generating git.properties, info shows the commit id and branch, which is gold when you ask "is the fix deployed?".

Changing log levels at runtime

The loggers endpoint lets you raise one logger to DEBUG on a live system, find the problem, then put it back, with no restart:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.example.jobs.application
{"configuredLevel":null,"effectiveLevel":"INFO"}

$ curl -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.example.jobs.application \
       -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'

$ curl -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.example.jobs.application \
       -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":null}'     # reset

The change is in memory only; it is lost on restart. This is why loggers must be admin-only.

Rules

  • Expose only the endpoints you use. Never expose env, heapdump or threaddump publicly.
  • Liveness must not depend on external systems; readiness may.
  • Do not put secrets into info or health details.

Common mistakes

  • include: "*" copied from a tutorial into production.
  • Using /actuator/health (with the DB check) as the liveness probe, so a short database outage restarts all pods.
  • A Docker healthcheck that calls an endpoint behind authentication, so the container is "unhealthy" forever.
  • Forgetting that show-details: always leaks database names and paths on a public URL.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • A DOWN health returns HTTP 503, not 200 with a body saying DOWN. Docker or Kubernetes probes use the status code.
  • With a separate management port, Spring Security rules for the main port do not apply to it; protect it by the network.
  • Boot 3 and 4 both read management.endpoints.web.exposure.*; JMX exposure has different defaults (JMX is off unless enabled).

Interview angle

"What is Actuator?" Production-ready endpoints. "Liveness vs readiness?" Restart vs stop sending traffic. "How do you secure it?" Expose few endpoints, separate port, role-based access. "How do you add a custom check?" Implement HealthIndicator. "How do you find which version is deployed?" The info endpoint with build and git info.

Metrics with Micrometer and the Prometheus endpoint

Micrometer is the metrics facade inside Spring Boot: it records JVM, HTTP and pool metrics automatically, you add your own counters, timers and gauges through MeterRegistry, and Prometheus scrapes them from /actuator/prometheus.

What and why

Logs tell you what happened in one request. Metrics are numbers over time: requests per second, error rate, 95th percentile latency, heap used, database connections in use. They answer "is the system healthy right now, and is it getting worse?" and they drive alerts and dashboards.

Micrometer is to metrics what SLF4J is to logging: a facade. You write code against Micrometer, and a registry for your monitoring system (Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch...) turns it into that system's format. With Actuator you already get many metrics:

  • jvm.memory.used, jvm.gc.pause, jvm.threads.live
  • http.server.requests (count, total time and max, tagged by method, URI, status, outcome)
  • hikaricp.connections.active, hikaricp.connections.pending
  • system.cpu.usage, process.uptime, logback.events, cache metrics for caches that expose stats
$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/metrics | head -c 120
{"names":["application.ready.time","hikaricp.connections.active", ...

$ curl -s "localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=status:500"
{"name":"http.server.requests","baseUnit":"seconds","measurements":[
 {"statistic":"COUNT","value":3.0},{"statistic":"TOTAL_TIME","value":0.41}, ...

Meter types

TypeMeaningExample
CounterA value that only goes upApplications submitted, emails sent, errors
GaugeA value that goes up and down; read when scrapedQueue size, open jobs, cache size
TimerCount and duration of short events, with percentilesTime to send an email, time of a job run
DistributionSummaryDistribution of non-time valuesUploaded file size

Custom metrics with MeterRegistry

Inject MeterRegistry (Boot provides it) and create meters. Names use dots (jobs.applications.submitted); each registry converts them to its own style (Prometheus: jobs_applications_submitted_total).

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Counter;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Gauge;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Timer;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class ApplicationMetrics {

    private final Counter submitted;
    private final Timer emailTimer;

    public ApplicationMetrics(MeterRegistry registry, JobRepository jobRepository) {
        this.submitted = Counter.builder("jobs.applications.submitted")
                .description("Applications submitted by candidates")
                .tag("source", "web")
                .register(registry);

        this.emailTimer = Timer.builder("jobs.email.send")
                .description("Time to send one email")
                .publishPercentileHistogram()          // allows percentiles in Prometheus
                .register(registry);

        Gauge.builder("jobs.open", jobRepository, repo -> repo.countByStatus(JobStatus.OPEN))
                .description("Jobs currently open")
                .register(registry);                   // read on every scrape: keep it cheap
    }

    public void applicationSubmitted() { submitted.increment(); }

    public <T> T timeEmail(java.util.function.Supplier<T> work) {
        return emailTimer.record(work);                // records duration, returns the result
    }
}

Use it from a service: metrics.applicationSubmitted();. A gauge keeps only a weak reference to the object it observes, so keep a reference (a bean, as here) or the gauge may report NaN after garbage collection.

Rule: keep tag values low-cardinality

Every unique combination of tag values creates a new time series in memory and in Prometheus. Tags like status, method, outcome are fine. A tag with a user id, an email or a full URL with ids creates millions of series and can bring the monitoring system down. For ids, use logs or traces, not metric tags.

@Timed and @Observed (brief)

To time a method without writing the Timer code, use @Timed("jobs.search"). For controllers Boot already times every request, but for ordinary beans you must register the aspect once (it needs spring-boot-starter-aop or the AOP libraries on the classpath):

@Configuration
public class MetricsConfig {
    @Bean
    TimedAspect timedAspect(MeterRegistry registry) {
        return new TimedAspect(registry);
    }
}

@Service
public class JobSearchService {
    @Timed(value = "jobs.search", description = "Job search time", histogram = true)
    public Page<JobResponse> search(JobFilter filter, Pageable pageable) { ... }
}

Like all proxy-based annotations, it does not work on self-invocation (module 1). Micrometer's Observation API (@Observed) goes one step further: one annotation produces both a timer and a trace span, which we use in distributed tracing.

The Prometheus endpoint

Prometheus is a monitoring system that pulls: every few seconds it calls /actuator/prometheus on each application, stores the numbers, and Grafana draws graphs from it. To enable it, add the registry and expose the endpoint:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, info, prometheus
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: ${spring.application.name}      # added to every metric: filter by app
    distribution:
      percentiles-histogram:
        http.server.requests: true                 # latency histogram for p95/p99 in Grafana
# HELP jobs_applications_submitted_total Applications submitted by candidates
# TYPE jobs_applications_submitted_total counter
jobs_applications_submitted_total{application="jobs-api",source="web"} 17.0
http_server_requests_seconds_count{method="GET",status="200",uri="/api/jobs"} 412.0
jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap",id="G1 Eden Space"} 5.2428800E7

The Prometheus side is one scrape config (job name, metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus, target host:port). Setting up Prometheus, Grafana and alert rules belongs to DevOps · Module 6.

The four golden signals

A useful first dashboard has four graphs, all available from the metrics above: latency (p95 of http.server.requests), traffic (requests per second), errors (share of status 5xx), and saturation (CPU, heap, Hikari connections pending, thread pool queue). Alert on symptoms users feel (errors, latency), not on every internal number.

Common mistakes

  • High-cardinality tags (user id, raw URL) that explode the number of series.
  • Creating a new Counter on every call without caching it; building meters is cheap but not free. Create once, increment many times (or use registry.counter(name) which looks it up).
  • Exposing /actuator/prometheus publicly. It reveals internals; put it on the management port or behind auth.
  • Heavy database queries inside a gauge supplier; it runs on every scrape.

Tip

Start simple: Actuator + Prometheus + Grafana with a ready-made "Spring Boot / JVM (Micrometer)" dashboard gives 80% of the value in an hour. Add 3 or 4 business counters (applications submitted, emails failed) after that.

Interview angle

"What is Micrometer?" Vendor-neutral metrics facade, like SLF4J. "Counter vs gauge vs timer?" Up-only, up-and-down snapshot, duration with count. "Push vs pull monitoring?" Prometheus pulls from /actuator/prometheus. "Why is cardinality dangerous?" Each tag combination is a time series. "Logs vs metrics vs traces?" Events, aggregates, request paths (see tracing).

Caching with @Cacheable, @CachePut and @CacheEvict

Spring's cache abstraction puts a proxy in front of a method so that repeated calls with the same arguments return a stored result; you choose the cache provider separately (a simple map, Caffeine or Redis) and must plan how entries are invalidated.

What and why

A cache keeps the result of expensive work (a slow query, a call to another service) so the next request gets it from memory. The job list page of Project 2 is read thousands of times and changes a few times a day: running the same SQL on every request wastes the database. Caching trades freshness for speed; the hard part is not storing, it is knowing when the stored value is wrong (invalidation). The general theory (cache-aside, write-through, eviction policies) is in System Design · Module 5.

How it works

Like @Transactional, caching is an AOP proxy feature (module 1). Spring wraps your bean; when you call a cached method from another bean, the proxy computes a key from the arguments, looks in the named cache, and calls your method only on a miss.

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableCaching                       // without this, the annotations do nothing
public class JobsApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(JobsApplication.class, args); }
}

With no provider on the classpath, Boot uses a simple ConcurrentHashMap cache: good for learning and tests, but it never expires and has no size limit.

The annotations

AnnotationWhat it doesTypical use
@CacheableReturn the cached value if present; otherwise call the method and store the resultReads: findById, search
@CachePutAlways call the method and store the result (no skip)Update: refresh the entry after a change
@CacheEvictRemove one entry (or all with allEntries = true)Delete, or any change that makes entries stale
@CachingCombine several of the above on one methodUpdate that evicts a list and puts an item
@CacheConfigClass-level defaults (cacheNames)Avoid repeating the cache name
 
@Service
@CacheConfig(cacheNames = "jobs")
public class JobService {

    private final JobRepository jobRepository;
    private final JobMapper mapper;

    public JobService(JobRepository jobRepository, JobMapper mapper) {
        this.jobRepository = jobRepository;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }

    @Cacheable(key = "#id")                              // key = the argument
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public JobResponse getJob(Long id) {
        return mapper.toResponse(jobRepository.findById(id).orElseThrow(
                () -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Job " + id)));
    }

    @CachePut(key = "#id")                               // runs always, refreshes the entry
    @Transactional
    public JobResponse updateJob(Long id, JobRequest request) {
        Job job = jobRepository.findById(id).orElseThrow();
        mapper.update(job, request);
        return mapper.toResponse(job);
    }

    @CacheEvict(key = "#id")
    @Transactional
    public void deleteJob(Long id) {
        jobRepository.deleteById(id);
    }

    @CacheEvict(allEntries = true)                       // clear the whole "jobs" cache
    public void clearAll() { }
}

Keys and SpEL

The default key is built from all method arguments (a single argument is the key itself; several become a SimpleKey; no arguments use a constant). You almost always want to write the key explicitly with SpEL (Spring Expression Language):

@Cacheable(key = "#id")                                   // a parameter by name
@Cacheable(key = "#filter.city + ':' + #filter.page")     // property of a parameter
@Cacheable(key = "T(java.util.Objects).hash(#city, #type)")
@Cacheable(key = "#root.methodName + ':' + #id")          // method name in the key
@Cacheable(key = "#user.id")                              // per-user cache

Parameter names work only if the code is compiled with -parameters (Spring Boot's Maven and Gradle plugins do this) or you use #p0, #a0 for positions. Two arguments that mean the same thing must produce the same key, and different things must never collide: a per-user result with a key that ignores the user would leak one user's data to another.

condition and unless

  • condition is checked before the call and decides whether caching applies at all: @Cacheable(condition = "#id > 0"). If false, the method runs and nothing is read or stored.
  • unless is checked after the call and can veto storing the result; it can use #result: @Cacheable(unless = "#result == null || #result.isEmpty()").

Use unless to avoid caching empty results or errors you do not want to remember. @Cacheable on a method that returns Optional caches the unwrapped value.

@CacheEvict options and @Caching

@Caching(
    put   = { @CachePut(cacheNames = "jobs", key = "#result.id()") },
    evict = { @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "jobList", allEntries = true) }
)
@Transactional
public JobResponse createJob(JobRequest request) { ... }

@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "jobs", key = "#id", beforeInvocation = true)
public void forceReload(Long id) { ... }      // evict even if the method throws

By default eviction happens after a successful call, so a method that throws leaves the cache intact. beforeInvocation = true evicts first. allEntries = true clears the cache; with Redis it can be slow on large caches because it scans keys.

The two cache names pattern: items and lists

A single-item cache (jobs::7) is easy to keep correct. A list or search cache (jobList::Pune:page0) is hard: any new job makes every list stale. Options: keep list caches short-lived (TTL of a minute), evict the whole list cache on any write (allEntries = true), or do not cache lists and cache only single items and expensive aggregates.

Concurrency: sync = true

When a popular entry expires, many requests may miss at once and all hit the database (a cache stampede). @Cacheable(sync = true) makes one thread compute the value while the others wait. It works only with one cache name and is not supported with unless. For Redis it locks per JVM, not across servers.

The self-invocation pitfall

Exactly the same as @Transactional: the call must go through the proxy.

Wrong: same-class call skips the cache

@Service
public class JobService {
    public JobResponse view(Long id) {
        return getJob(id);               // this.getJob(): proxy bypassed, NOT cached
    }
    @Cacheable("jobs")
    public JobResponse getJob(Long id) { ... }
}

Right: call from another bean

@RestController
public class JobController {
    private final JobService jobService;
    @GetMapping("/api/jobs/{id}")
    JobResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return jobService.getJob(id);    // goes through the proxy: cached
    }
}

Also: only public methods, and the bean must be created by Spring (not new).

Providers: simple, Caffeine, Redis

Simple (default)CaffeineRedis
WhereJVM memoryJVM memorySeparate server
Shared between instancesNoNoYes
Size limit and TTLNoneYes (size, expire after write/access)TTL; memory limit on the server
SpeedFastestFastest (no network)Network call (about a millisecond)
Survives restartNoNoYes (depends on persistence)
Use forTests, demosSingle instance, or data where slight differences between instances are fineSeveral instances, large data, shared state

Caffeine is a high-performance local cache library. Add com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine next to the cache starter and Boot configures it:

spring:
  cache:
    type: caffeine
    cache-names: jobs, companies                       # fixed set of caches
    caffeine:
      spec: maximumSize=1000,expireAfterWrite=10m      # size limit + TTL

With several application instances, a local cache means each instance has its own copy: after an update on instance A, instance B still serves the old value until its TTL ends. That is acceptable for slowly changing data with a short TTL; for anything stricter use Redis (next article).

What to cache, what not to cache

  • Good candidates: read-heavy data that changes rarely (job categories, company profiles, config), results of expensive calculations, responses of slow third-party APIs.
  • Bad candidates: data that must be exactly current (account balance, stock count), per-user data without the user in the key, huge results, anything cheap to compute, and entities with lazy associations (cache DTOs instead; module 3).
  • Cache DTOs/records, not JPA entities. A cached entity is detached, may have uninitialised lazy fields, and cannot be serialised cleanly.
  • Always set a TTL. It is your safety net if an eviction is missed.

Invalidation strategy

  1. Time-based: every entry expires after a TTL (60 seconds to a few hours). Simple and always works; data may be a little stale.
  2. Event-based: evict or update on every write (@CacheEvict, @CachePut). Fresher, but you must cover every write path (also bulk updates, SQL scripts, other services).
  3. Combine both: evict on writes and keep a TTL as a backstop.

Transactions and caches

Eviction runs when the method returns, which is before the transaction commits if the cache annotation and @Transactional sit on the same method. Another thread can then reload the old row and put the stale value back. For strictness, evict after commit (a @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)) or accept the short TTL.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting @EnableCaching and wondering why nothing is cached.
  • Caching without a TTL, so wrong data lives for ever.
  • A key that ignores a parameter (the second page returns the first page).
  • Caching a method that returns a mutable object, then modifying the object (with a local cache you modify the cached instance itself).
  • Caching exceptions or null by accident; use unless.

Edge cases

  • NoSuchCacheException or "Cannot find cache named 'x'": the name is not in spring.cache.cache-names when the list is fixed.
  • @Cacheable on a method with void return caches nothing useful.
  • A key of null (null argument) throws IllegalArgumentException: Null key returned for cache operation.
  • Caches that store null: Caffeine does not by default; Redis can (cache-null-values, default true).

Interview angle

"How does @Cacheable work?" Proxy, key, cache lookup, call on miss. "Why does it not work when I call the method from the same class?" Proxy bypass. "@CachePut vs @Cacheable?" Always run and store vs skip on hit. "How do you avoid stale data?" TTL plus eviction on writes. "Local vs distributed cache?" Caffeine vs Redis trade-offs in the table above.

Redis as a cache: setup, TTL, JSON serialization and RedisTemplate

Add the Redis and cache starters, set spring.cache.type=redis with a TTL, configure JSON serialization so cached values are readable and safe to change, and use StringRedisTemplate directly for counters, locks and other non-cache uses.

What Redis gives you

Redis is an in-memory key-value server. All your application instances talk to the same Redis, so a value cached by one is visible to all, and an eviction on one removes it for all. It is fast (sub-millisecond on a local network), supports TTL on every key, and also offers counters, sets, sorted sets, pub/sub and atomic operations. Keep it for data you can lose: a cache is a copy, the database stays the source of truth. More on Redis internals in SQL · Module 6.

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost                  # the service name in Docker Compose, e.g. redis
      port: 6379
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:}     # empty for local development
      timeout: 2s
  cache:
    type: redis
    redis:
      time-to-live: 10m                # default TTL for every cache
      key-prefix: "jobs-api::"
      use-key-prefix: true
      cache-null-values: false
$ docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7
$ docker exec -it redis redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> KEYS *
1) "jobs-api::jobs::7"
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL "jobs-api::jobs::7"
(integer) 583

Use the property spring.data.redis.* on Boot 3.x and 4.x (older Boot 2 used spring.redis.*). The default client is Lettuce, which is thread-safe and works with the connection pooling Boot sets up.

Serialization: the important detail

Redis stores bytes. By default the Spring cache uses JDK serialization, which has three problems: your cached classes must implement Serializable; the stored bytes are unreadable in redis-cli; and a change to the class (a new field) can make old entries fail to deserialize after a deployment. Most projects switch to JSON.

import java.time.Duration;
import org.springframework.cache.annotation.EnableCaching;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.data.redis.cache.RedisCacheConfiguration;
import org.springframework.data.redis.cache.RedisCacheManager;
import org.springframework.data.redis.connection.RedisConnectionFactory;
import org.springframework.data.redis.serializer.GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer;
import org.springframework.data.redis.serializer.RedisSerializationContext.SerializationPair;
import org.springframework.data.redis.serializer.StringRedisSerializer;

@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig {

    @Bean
    RedisCacheConfiguration defaultCacheConfig() {
        return RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
                .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
                .disableCachingNullValues()
                .serializeKeysWith(SerializationPair.fromSerializer(new StringRedisSerializer()))
                .serializeValuesWith(SerializationPair.fromSerializer(
                        new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer()));
    }

    @Bean
    RedisCacheManager cacheManager(RedisConnectionFactory factory,
                                   RedisCacheConfiguration defaults) {
        return RedisCacheManager.builder(factory)
                .cacheDefaults(defaults)
                .withCacheConfiguration("jobs", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofHours(1)))
                .withCacheConfiguration("jobList", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
                .build();
    }
}

The per-cache TTL is the main reason to define the manager yourself: categories can live for hours, search results for a minute. GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer writes the class name into the JSON (@class) so it can rebuild the right type. Records and immutable DTOs work with Jackson, but they must be deserializable (a record is fine). The stored JSON is readable:

{"@class":"com.example.jobs.job.JobResponse","id":7,"title":"Java Developer",
 "company":"Acme","city":"Pune"}

Version note

Spring Boot 4 moves to Jackson 3, and Spring Data Redis 4 adds serializers for it next to the Jackson 2 ones. The idea above is the same on every version (key serializer = string, value serializer = JSON), but the exact serializer class name differs; check the Spring Data Redis reference for your version before you copy the code. Properties under spring.cache.redis.* do not change.

Rule: cached data is a contract between deployments

During a rolling deploy, old and new application versions share one Redis. If the new version changes a cached class, old entries may not deserialize and every request throws SerializationException. Include a version in the key prefix (jobs-v2::) when you change a cached class, or flush the cache on deployment. Also treat a Redis failure as a cache miss, not an error (below).

If Redis is down

By default a cache error becomes an exception and the request fails, although the database is healthy. For a cache that is only an optimisation, you can register a CacheErrorHandler that logs and continues:

@Configuration
public class CacheErrorConfig implements CachingConfigurer {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(CacheErrorConfig.class);

    @Override
    public CacheErrorHandler errorHandler() {
        return new SimpleCacheErrorHandler() {
            @Override
            public void handleCacheGetError(RuntimeException ex, Cache cache, Object key) {
                log.warn("Cache get failed: {} {}", cache.getName(), key, ex);   // act as a miss
            }
            @Override
            public void handleCachePutError(RuntimeException ex, Cache cache, Object key,
                                            Object value) {
                log.warn("Cache put failed: {} {}", cache.getName(), key, ex);
            }
        };
    }
}

Combine it with a short connection timeout (spring.data.redis.timeout) so a dead Redis does not hang every request for 60 seconds. Circuit breakers for this kind of problem appear in Resilience4j.

RedisTemplate and StringRedisTemplate

The cache abstraction hides Redis. When you want Redis features directly, inject a template. StringRedisTemplate (keys and values are plain strings) is the simplest and the one you will use most; RedisTemplate<K, V> is generic and needs serializers configured.

@Service
public class OtpService {

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public OtpService(StringRedisTemplate redis) { this.redis = redis; }

    public void store(String email, String otp) {
        redis.opsForValue().set("otp:" + email, otp, Duration.ofMinutes(5));   // SET with TTL
    }

    public boolean verify(String email, String otp) {
        String key = "otp:" + email;
        String saved = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
        if (saved != null && saved.equals(otp)) {
            redis.delete(key);                  // one-time use
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    public long viewCount(Long jobId) {
        Long n = redis.opsForValue().increment("views:job:" + jobId);   // atomic INCR
        return n == null ? 0 : n;
    }
}
Operations objectRedis typeTypical use
opsForValue()StringCache entries, counters, OTP, tokens
opsForHash()HashSmall objects, sessions
opsForList()ListSimple queues, recent items
opsForSet()SetUnique members, "already seen" checks
opsForZSet()Sorted setLeaderboards, sliding-window rate limits

Typical real uses beyond caching: login/OTP tokens with expiry, rate-limit counters (rate limiting), distributed locks, a blacklist of revoked JWTs (module 4), and Spring Session to share HTTP sessions between instances.

Testing with Redis

In tests, run a real Redis with Testcontainers (@ServiceConnection with GenericContainer for Redis, see module 5) instead of mocking it; serialization bugs only show against the real thing. For unit tests that do not care, set spring.cache.type=none.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving JDK serialization on: unreadable values and NotSerializableException for DTOs.
  • No TTL at all: Redis memory grows until it evicts keys or runs out.
  • Running KEYS * on a production Redis (it blocks the single-threaded server); use SCAN.
  • Keeping the only copy of important data in Redis without persistence.
  • Hard-coded host localhost in a container; use the service name from Compose (Compose).

Edge cases

  • RedisConnectionFailureException: Unable to connect to Redis when the server is down or the host is wrong.
  • SerializationException when the stored JSON no longer matches the class.
  • A key with a prefix: allEntries = true deletes only keys that match the cache name prefix, so one cache does not clear another.
  • Redis eviction policy (maxmemory-policy) can drop keys even before their TTL when memory is full.

Interview angle

"How do you set up Redis caching in Spring Boot?" Two starters, spring.cache.type=redis, @EnableCaching, TTL, JSON serializer. "Why not default serialization?" Needs Serializable, unreadable, brittle. "Redis down: what happens?" Add a CacheErrorHandler and timeouts. "Local vs distributed cache?" Consistency across instances. "What else is Redis used for?" OTP, counters, locks, sessions, rate limits.

Scheduled jobs with @Scheduled

Enable scheduling, annotate a no-argument method with fixedRate, fixedDelay or a six-field cron expression, remember that the default scheduler uses one thread, and use a lock such as ShedLock when several instances must run the job only once.

What and why

Some work is not triggered by a user: close expired jobs every night, send a daily digest at 9 am, clear old uploads, retry failed emails. A scheduled job is a method that Spring calls repeatedly on a timetable, inside your application, with no extra tool.

@Configuration
@EnableScheduling                       // switches the feature on
class SchedulingConfig { }

@Component
public class JobExpiryTask {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(JobExpiryTask.class);
    private final JobService jobService;

    public JobExpiryTask(JobService jobService) { this.jobService = jobService; }

    @Scheduled(cron = "0 30 0 * * *", zone = "Asia/Kolkata")     // 00:30 IST every day
    public void closeExpiredJobs() {
        int closed = jobService.closeJobsPastDeadline();
        log.info("Closed {} expired jobs", closed);
    }
}

The annotated method must return void (a returned value is ignored) and take no parameters. The bean can be any Spring component.

Timing options

AttributeMeaningExample
fixedRateStart every N ms, measured from the start of the previous runfixedRate = 60000
fixedDelayWait N ms after the previous run finishedfixedDelay = 30000
initialDelayWait before the first run (with fixedRate/fixedDelay)initialDelay = 10000
cronA calendar expressioncron = "0 0 9 * * MON-FRI"
zoneTime zone for cronzone = "Asia/Kolkata"

Use fixedDelay when runs must never overlap and you want a rest between them (polling a table). Use fixedRate for a steady rhythm, but note that if a run takes longer than the period, the next run starts as soon as the previous ends, because by default runs of the same task never overlap on one scheduler thread. Both accept string forms that read properties or use Duration text: @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${app.poll-delay:PT30S}").

@Scheduled(fixedRate = 60_000, initialDelay = 10_000)    // every minute, first after 10 s
void heartbeat() { ... }

@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${app.mail.retry-delay:PT5M}")   // 5 minutes after finishing
void retryFailedEmails() { ... }

@Scheduled(cron = "${app.digest.cron}", zone = "Asia/Kolkata")  // cron from configuration
void dailyDigest() { ... }

Spring cron vs Unix cron

Spring's cron has six fields, with seconds first; classic Unix cron has five.

┌──────── second (0-59)
│ ┌────── minute (0-59)
│ │ ┌──── hour (0-23)
│ │ │ ┌── day of month (1-31)
│ │ │ │ ┌ month (1-12 or JAN-DEC)
│ │ │ │ │ ┌ day of week (MON-SUN, or 0-7)
0 0 9 * * MON-FRI        weekdays at 09:00
0 */15 * * * *           every 15 minutes
0 0 2 1 * *              1st of every month at 02:00
0 0 0 * * *              midnight; also written with the macro  @daily  /  "@midnight"

Common surprises: a Unix expression like 0 9 * * 1-5 has five fields and Spring rejects it (IllegalStateException: Encountered invalid @Scheduled method ... cron expression must consist of 6 fields). Without zone, the time zone is the server's, which in a Docker container is usually UTC, so "9 am" silently means 2:30 pm in India. Always set zone. Spring also supports L (last day), # (nth weekday) and macros such as @hourly, @daily.

The single-thread default and a thread pool

By default all @Scheduled methods in the application share one thread (Boot's auto-configured ThreadPoolTaskScheduler has pool size 1). If one job takes ten minutes, every other job waits. Give the scheduler more threads:

spring:
  task:
    scheduling:
      thread-name-prefix: sched-
      pool:
        size: 5                          # default is 1

Even with a pool, one task still does not run concurrently with itself. For truly parallel work, hand the job to an executor (@Async, next article) and keep the scheduled method short. Exceptions: if a scheduled method throws, Spring logs it and the schedule continues (for fixedRate/cron the next run still happens). Catch exceptions yourself to log with context and to avoid half-finished batches.

Running the job only once in a cluster

If you run three instances of the application, every instance runs the scheduled job, so every candidate gets three digest emails. Options:

  • A lock in the database or Redis: ShedLock. A small library; before the job runs, an instance tries to write a lock row. Only the winner runs the job.
  • One dedicated instance (a "worker" profile) runs scheduling; others disable it with a property or profile.
  • An external scheduler (Kubernetes CronJob, Quartz cluster, a cloud scheduler) that triggers an HTTP endpoint or runs a container.
// Table: shedlock(name varchar(64) primary key, lock_until timestamp,
//                 locked_at timestamp, locked_by varchar(255))

@Configuration
@EnableScheduling
@EnableSchedulerLock(defaultLockAtMostFor = "PT10M")
class SchedulingConfig {
    @Bean
    LockProvider lockProvider(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new JdbcTemplateLockProvider(dataSource);
    }
}

@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 9 * * *", zone = "Asia/Kolkata")
@SchedulerLock(name = "dailyDigest", lockAtMostFor = "PT5M", lockAtLeastFor = "PT1M")
public void dailyDigest() { ... }

lockAtMostFor releases the lock even if the instance crashes; set it longer than the longest normal run. lockAtLeastFor stops a fast job from running again on another instance with a slightly different clock. ShedLock needs a lock provider (JDBC, Redis, Mongo and others) from its own dependencies; check its README for the current artifact names.

Designing good scheduled jobs

  • Idempotent: running twice must not do harm (the job may run twice after a crash or on two instances). Mark processed rows, or select rows with status = 'PENDING'.
  • Batch size: process 100 rows at a time, not a million in one transaction.
  • Log start, end and count, and add a counter or timer metric (Micrometer) so you notice when it stops.
  • Transactions: the scheduled method has no transaction; call a @Transactional service method (from another bean, not this).
  • Make it testable: put the logic in a service and test the service; test the schedule by calling the method directly.
  • Virtual threads: with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true Boot runs scheduled tasks on virtual threads too (Async).

Programmatic scheduling is possible with TaskScheduler.schedule(runnable, trigger), useful when the schedule comes from the database.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting @EnableScheduling (nothing runs, no error).
  • A five-field cron, or no time zone.
  • Long job blocking a pool of one, so other jobs are late.
  • Three instances sending three emails.
  • Annotating a method that takes parameters.
  • Calling a @Transactional method of the same class (self-invocation).

Interview angle

"fixedRate vs fixedDelay?" Start-to-start vs end-to-start. "What if the app runs on three servers?" Every instance runs it; use ShedLock, a single worker, or an external scheduler. "Why did my 9 am job run at the wrong time?" Missing zone, server in UTC. "Default number of scheduler threads?" One.

@Async, thread pools and virtual threads

@Async runs a method on another thread through a proxy so the caller does not wait; configure your own ThreadPoolTaskExecutor, handle exceptions explicitly, remember that transactions, security context and MDC do not follow the new thread, and consider virtual threads for blocking work.

What and why

When a candidate applies for a job, the API must save the application and then email the recruiter. Sending email takes 300 ms to 3 seconds and can fail. The candidate should not wait for it. Asynchronous execution means: start the work on another thread and return immediately. Spring does this with @Async. (Threads, executors and CompletableFuture themselves are explained in Core Java · Module 6.)

Setup and basic use

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
class AsyncConfig { }

@Service
public class NotificationService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(NotificationService.class);

    @Async                                          // fire and forget
    public void sendNewApplicationMail(Long applicationId) {
        log.info("Sending mail on thread {}", Thread.currentThread().getName());
        // ... load data, build and send the mail
    }

    @Async
    public CompletableFuture<Integer> countInactiveUsers() {     // caller can wait for the result
        int n = userRepository.countInactive();
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(n);
    }
}
  • A method may return void or Future/CompletableFuture<T> (wrap the value with completedFuture). Any other return type gives null to the caller.
  • With CompletableFuture the caller can combine results: CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join().
  • The call returns at once; the work runs on a pool thread (task-1 in the log).

How it works: the same proxy trap

@Async is another proxy feature (module 1): the proxy does not run your method but submits it as a task to an Executor and returns. Therefore:

  • Self-invocation does not work. this.sendMail() from the same class runs synchronously on the caller's thread. Call it from another bean.
  • The method must be public and not final/private.
  • The caller must be another bean holding the proxy.

Configuring the executor

Boot auto-configures an applicationTaskExecutor (a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor) that @Async uses. Tune it with properties:

spring:
  task:
    execution:
      thread-name-prefix: app-async-
      pool:
        core-size: 4
        max-size: 16
        queue-capacity: 200
        keep-alive: 60s
      shutdown:
        await-termination: true
        await-termination-period: 30s       # finish queued work on shutdown

How the pool behaves is a classic interview point: threads up to core-size are created first; further tasks go into the queue; only when the queue is full does the pool grow up to max-size; when both are full, the executor rejects the task (TaskRejectedException). A queue of "unbounded" capacity (the old default) means max-size is never used and memory can grow without limit.

For different kinds of work, define named executors, so slow email sending cannot starve report generation (the bulkhead idea):

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig {

    @Bean("mailExecutor")
    public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor mailExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        ex.setCorePoolSize(2);
        ex.setMaxPoolSize(5);
        ex.setQueueCapacity(100);
        ex.setThreadNamePrefix("mail-");
        ex.setTaskDecorator(new MdcTaskDecorator());          // copy request id (below)
        ex.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        ex.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true);
        ex.setAwaitTerminationSeconds(30);
        return ex;                       // Spring initialises it as a bean
    }
}

@Async("mailExecutor")                    // choose the executor by bean name
public void sendNewApplicationMail(Long applicationId) { ... }

CallerRunsPolicy makes the caller run the task when the pool is full, which slows the producer down (back-pressure) instead of losing work or throwing.

Exception handling

  • For methods returning CompletableFuture, the exception is stored in the future: handle it with .exceptionally(...) or .handle(...), or you get it at get()/join().
  • For void methods the caller is already gone, so nobody can catch the exception. Spring passes it to an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler; the default only logs it.
@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncErrorConfig implements AsyncConfigurer {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(AsyncErrorConfig.class);

    @Override
    public AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler getAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler() {
        return (ex, method, params) ->
                log.error("Async method {} failed with params {}", method.getName(),
                        java.util.Arrays.toString(params), ex);
    }
}

A failed email is lost unless you record it. For important work, catch inside the method, save a "FAILED" status, and let a scheduled job retry (scheduling), or use a message queue (messaging) which gives you retries and durability.

Transactions, security and MDC do not follow the thread

Transactions, the Spring Security context and the MDC are all stored in thread-locals (per-thread storage), so a new thread starts with none of them:

  • Transaction: the async method does not run in the caller's transaction. If the caller has not committed yet, the async method may not see the new row (it can fail with "not found"). Pass ids, not entities, and load again in the async method with its own @Transactional. Better, trigger it after commit:
public record ApplicationSubmitted(Long applicationId) { }

@Service
public class ApplicationService {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
    // ...
    @Transactional
    public ApplicationResponse apply(Long jobId, Long userId) {
        Application saved = applicationRepository.save(new Application(jobId, userId));
        events.publishEvent(new ApplicationSubmitted(saved.getId()));   // nothing sent yet
        return mapper.toResponse(saved);
    }
}

@Component
public class ApplicationMailListener {
    private final NotificationService notifications;
    // ...
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    public void onSubmitted(ApplicationSubmitted event) {
        notifications.sendNewApplicationMail(event.applicationId());    // @Async method
    }
}

If the transaction rolls back, the event is dropped and no email is sent. That is exactly what you want, and it is the in-process cousin of the outbox pattern (delivery semantics).

  • Security context: SecurityContextHolder is empty in the async thread. Wrap the executor with DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor, or pass the user id explicitly. Passing explicit values is simplest (module 4).
  • MDC: use a TaskDecorator to copy the map:
import java.util.Map;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.core.task.TaskDecorator;

public class MdcTaskDecorator implements TaskDecorator {
    @Override
    public Runnable decorate(Runnable task) {
        Map<String, String> context = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();   // captured on the caller
        return () -> {
            try {
                if (context != null) MDC.setContextMap(context);
                task.run();
            } finally {
                MDC.clear();
            }
        };
    }
}

Virtual threads in Spring Boot

A normal (platform) thread maps to an operating-system thread and costs about a megabyte of stack, so pools hold tens or hundreds of them. A virtual thread (Java 21+) is a cheap thread managed by the JVM: you can have hundreds of thousands, and a virtual thread that blocks (waiting for a database or HTTP response) frees the underlying carrier thread. Blocking code scales without becoming reactive. Details: Core Java · Module 6.

spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true

One property (Spring Boot 3.2+, Java 21+) makes Boot use virtual threads for: Tomcat/Jetty request handling (one virtual thread per request), the @Async executor, @Scheduled tasks, and several other places (Kafka and RabbitMQ listeners among them). In effect, core-size/max-size pool settings no longer limit these.

Platform thread poolVirtual threads
Best forCPU-heavy workBlocking I/O: database, HTTP, files
CountSmall, bounded poolOne per task, no pool needed
Limiting concurrencyPool size does itYou must limit yourself (a Semaphore, a connection pool)
Thread-localsReused threads need clean-upWork, but are not shared: each task has its own

Things to know about virtual threads

  • They do not make CPU-bound code faster, and they do not remove the bottleneck of your database: 10,000 concurrent requests still share a Hikari pool of 10 connections. The pool becomes the limit (and requests wait for a connection), so size it consciously.
  • Pinning: on Java 21 a virtual thread blocked inside a synchronized block holds its carrier thread. Java 24 and later fixed most of this. Prefer ReentrantLock in your own code, and keep your libraries current.
  • Do not pool virtual threads, and do not put unbounded ThreadLocal caches on them.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting @EnableAsync, or calling the async method from the same class: it runs synchronously and nobody notices.
  • An unbounded queue or pool: memory grows or threads explode.
  • Passing a JPA entity into the async method; its session is closed (LazyInitializationException). Pass an id.
  • Sending the async message inside the transaction, then rolling back: the email says "application received" for an application that does not exist.
  • Blocking on future.get() immediately, which removes all the benefit.

Interview angle

"How does @Async work and when does it fail?" Proxy submits to an executor; fails on self-invocation, missing @EnableAsync, private methods. "Which thread runs it?" The applicationTaskExecutor or the named one. "Is the async method in the caller's transaction?" No. "How do you handle exceptions?" Future, or AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler. "What do virtual threads change?" Cheap blocking, one property to enable; not for CPU-bound work.

File upload and download: MultipartFile, storage and safe file names

Receive files as MultipartFile, limit their size, check type and content yourself, never trust the original file name, store the file under a generated name (on disk or S3) with metadata in the database, and send it back with ResponseEntity<Resource> and a Content-Disposition header.

What and why

In Project 2 a candidate uploads a resume (PDF) when applying. Browsers send files using the multipart/form-data encoding: one HTTP request with several parts (text fields and files), each part with its own headers. Spring parses it for you and gives each file as a MultipartFile.

Limits first

spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      enabled: true
      max-file-size: 5MB          # one file (default is 1MB)
      max-request-size: 6MB       # whole request: all files + fields (default is 10MB)
      file-size-threshold: 1MB    # above this size Spring writes to a temp file instead of memory
app:
  upload-dir: ${UPLOAD_DIR:./uploads}

If a client sends more, Spring throws MaxUploadSizeExceededException before your controller runs. Map it to 413 Payload Too Large in your @RestControllerAdvice (module 2). Also set limits at the proxy (Nginx client_max_body_size) so huge bodies are rejected before they reach Java.

The controller

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/applications")
public class ResumeController {

    private final ResumeService resumeService;

    public ResumeController(ResumeService resumeService) { this.resumeService = resumeService; }

    @PostMapping(path = "/{applicationId}/resume", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
    public ResponseEntity<ResumeResponse> upload(@PathVariable Long applicationId,
                                                 @RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file,
                                                 @AuthenticationPrincipal UserPrincipal user) {
        ResumeResponse saved = resumeService.store(applicationId, user.getId(), file);
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(saved);
    }
}
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/applications/12/resume \
       -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
       -F "file=@./asha-resume.pdf;type=application/pdf"
{"id":5,"originalName":"asha-resume.pdf","size":184320,"contentType":"application/pdf"}

Useful MultipartFile methods:

MethodReturnsTrust it?
getOriginalFilename()Name chosen by the clientNo (may contain ../)
getContentType()Type the client claimsNo (client controlled)
getSize()Size in bytesYes (counted by the server)
isEmpty()No file chosen or zero bytesYes
getInputStream()Stream of the contentYes, read from this
transferTo(Path)Moves the content to a destinationYes

Security: validate everything about the file

  • Size: check getSize() again in the service, with a business limit (a resume: 2 MB) even if the global limit is 5 MB.
  • Type by content, not by name: the extension and Content-Type are written by the client; an attacker uploads shell.jsp labelled image/png. Check the first bytes (a PDF starts with %PDF-) or use a detection library such as Apache Tika. Keep an allow-list (pdf, docx), never a block-list.
  • The file name: getOriginalFilename() can be ../../etc/cron.d/job or contain a null byte. This is a path traversal attack: writing outside your upload folder. Defence: do not use the client name for the path at all. Generate your own stored name, and keep the original only as a display name in the database (after cleaning it with StringUtils.cleanPath and taking only the last segment).
  • Where to store: never inside the web root or a folder served as static files, so an uploaded HTML or script file can never be fetched and run. Serve downloads only through your controller.
  • Authorisation: check that the logged-in user may upload to / download this application's resume. Using a guessable id (/files/5) without checking ownership is an IDOR bug (module 4).
  • Malware and image bombs: for public uploads, scan with an antivirus service and limit image dimensions.

Storing: generated name, safe path, metadata in the DB

@Service
public class ResumeService {

    private static final long MAX_SIZE = 2L * 1024 * 1024;           // 2 MB
    private static final byte[] PDF_MAGIC = "%PDF-".getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);

    private final Path root;
    private final ResumeRepository resumeRepository;
    private final ApplicationRepository applicationRepository;

    public ResumeService(@Value("${app.upload-dir}") Path root,
                         ResumeRepository resumeRepository,
                         ApplicationRepository applicationRepository) throws IOException {
        this.root = root.toAbsolutePath().normalize();
        this.resumeRepository = resumeRepository;
        this.applicationRepository = applicationRepository;
        Files.createDirectories(this.root);
    }

    @Transactional
    public ResumeResponse store(Long applicationId, Long userId, MultipartFile file) {
        Application app = applicationRepository.findById(applicationId)
                .filter(a -> a.getApplicant().getId().equals(userId))     // ownership
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Application " + applicationId));

        if (file.isEmpty() || file.getSize() > MAX_SIZE) {
            throw new BadRequestException("File must be between 1 byte and 2 MB");
        }
        try (InputStream in = file.getInputStream()) {
            byte[] head = in.readNBytes(PDF_MAGIC.length);
            if (!Arrays.equals(head, PDF_MAGIC)) {
                throw new BadRequestException("Only PDF files are accepted");
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
        }

        String storedName = UUID.randomUUID() + ".pdf";                   // our name, our extension
        Path target = root.resolve(storedName).normalize();
        if (!target.startsWith(root)) {                                    // belt and braces
            throw new BadRequestException("Invalid path");
        }
        try (InputStream in = file.getInputStream()) {
            Files.copy(in, target, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not store file", e);
        }

        String display = StringUtils.getFilename(StringUtils.cleanPath(
                file.getOriginalFilename() == null ? "resume.pdf" : file.getOriginalFilename()));
        Resume resume = resumeRepository.save(
                new Resume(app, storedName, display, "application/pdf", file.getSize()));
        return new ResumeResponse(resume.getId(), display, resume.getSize(), "application/pdf");
    }
}

The table behind it keeps what the database should know: id, application_id, stored_name, original_name, content_type, size_bytes, uploaded_at. The file system holds only bytes; the database holds meaning and permissions. Add a Flyway migration for the table (module 3). If the database save fails after the file was written, delete the file in a catch block (or run a clean-up job for orphan files), because a file system is not part of the transaction.

Downloading

@GetMapping("/{applicationId}/resume")
public ResponseEntity<Resource> download(@PathVariable Long applicationId,
                                         @AuthenticationPrincipal UserPrincipal user) {
    DownloadableFile f = resumeService.load(applicationId, user);   // checks permission
    Resource resource = new FileSystemResource(f.path());

    ContentDisposition disposition = ContentDisposition.attachment()
            .filename(f.displayName(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)      // safe encoding of the name
            .build();

    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
            .contentLength(f.size())
            .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, disposition.toString())
            .header("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
            .body(resource);
}
  • Content-Disposition: attachment makes the browser download the file; inline shows it in the browser (fine for PDFs and images that you trust).
  • Return Resource (a FileSystemResource, UrlResource or InputStreamResource). Spring streams it to the response in chunks; it does not load the whole file into memory.
  • Set contentType from your stored value, not from a guess, and add nosniff so a browser does not reinterpret it.
  • Return 404 when the row or the file is missing, and 403/404 when the user is not allowed.

Streaming large files

For big downloads (exports, videos) use StreamingResponseBody, which lets you write to the output stream from your own code on a separate thread, without buffering. For huge uploads, avoid byte[] getBytes(); use getInputStream() and copy in chunks. For data exports (CSV of 1 million rows), stream from a database cursor and write rows as you read them.

@GetMapping("/export/jobs.csv")
public ResponseEntity<StreamingResponseBody> export() {
    StreamingResponseBody body = out -> {
        var writer = new BufferedWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(out, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        writer.write("id,title,city\n");
        jobService.streamAll(job -> {                         // iterates, no full list in memory
            try { writer.write(job.id() + "," + job.title() + "," + job.city() + "\n"); }
            catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
        });
        writer.flush();
    };
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, "attachment; filename=\"jobs.csv\"")
            .contentType(MediaType.parseMediaType("text/csv"))
            .body(body);
}

Escape CSV fields properly in real code (commas and quotes inside titles) or use a CSV library, and beware of CSV injection (cells starting with =).

Disk vs object storage

Local diskObject storage (S3 and similar)
SetupNoneBucket, credentials, SDK
Several app instancesEach has its own disk: file not found on another instance (needs a shared volume)All instances see the same bucket
ContainersLost when the container is replaced unless a volume is mountedIndependent of the container
Durability, backupYour jobBuilt in (replication, versioning)
Large downloadsGo through your appCan use a time-limited pre-signed URL: the browser downloads directly from S3

Local disk is fine for development and a single server. In production on several instances or containers, use object storage (see DevOps · Module 5). Hide the choice behind an interface (FileStorage with save, load, delete) with a disk implementation and an S3 implementation, selected by a property; the controller and service never know. For large uploads to S3, many systems let the browser upload directly with a pre-signed URL, and the API only records the metadata.

Common mistakes

  • Saving with the client's file name ("uploads/" + file.getOriginalFilename()): path traversal and overwrites.
  • Trusting Content-Type or the extension.
  • Storing uploads inside src/main/resources/static or any served folder.
  • Reading the whole file into memory with getBytes().
  • No ownership check on download; sequential ids let users read each other's resumes.
  • Not handling MaxUploadSizeExceededException: the client gets a confusing 500 or 413 HTML page.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • MissingServletRequestPartException (400): the part name is not file, or the request is not multipart.
  • MultipartException / "Current request is not a multipart request": missing Content-Type: multipart/form-data, often caused by setting the header manually in a client (the boundary is then missing; let the HTTP client set it).
  • Temporary files: Spring writes large parts to a temp folder and deletes them after the request; on small disks watch the temp space.
  • Names with non-ASCII characters (हिंदी.pdf) need the RFC 5987 encoding that ContentDisposition.filename(name, UTF_8) produces.

Interview angle

"How do you handle file upload securely?" Size limits, content-based type check with an allow-list, generated storage names, path normalisation, storage outside the web root, authorisation, metadata in the DB. "What is path traversal?" ../ in a file name writes outside the folder. "How do you send a file?" ResponseEntity<Resource> with Content-Disposition. "Disk or S3?" S3 for multiple instances and containers.

Sending email with JavaMailSender, HTML, attachments and local testing

Add spring-boot-starter-mail, set the SMTP properties from environment variables, send plain mail with SimpleMailMessage and HTML or attachments with MimeMessageHelper, render bodies with Thymeleaf, send asynchronously after commit, and test locally with Mailpit.

What and why

Email is the oldest notification channel: welcome mails, password reset, "a candidate applied to your job". Mail travels with SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol). Your application is an SMTP client: it connects to a mail server (a provider such as SES, SendGrid, Brevo, or Gmail) with a host, port, username and password, and hands over the message. The server delivers it. Your code never talks to the recipient's server.

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-mail</artifactId>
</dependency>
spring:
  mail:
    host: ${MAIL_HOST:smtp.gmail.com}
    port: ${MAIL_PORT:587}
    username: ${MAIL_USERNAME}
    password: ${MAIL_PASSWORD}           # never commit this; use an environment variable
    properties:
      mail:
        smtp:
          auth: true
          starttls:
            enable: true                 # upgrade the connection to TLS on port 587
          connectiontimeout: 5000        # ms: do not wait for ever
          timeout: 5000
          writetimeout: 5000
app:
  mail:
    from: "Jobs Portal <no-reply@jobs.example.com>"

With these properties set, Boot creates a JavaMailSender bean. Provider notes: Gmail needs 2-step verification on the account and an app password (a 16-character password made for apps; your normal password does not work). It is fine for learning but limited (about 500 mails a day) and unsuitable for production. Real systems use a transactional email provider (SES, SendGrid, Mailgun, Brevo) with their SMTP credentials or HTTP API, and set up SPF/DKIM/DMARC DNS records for your sending domain, otherwise your mail lands in spam. Port 587 with STARTTLS is the usual choice; port 465 uses implicit TLS (spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.ssl.enable=true).

Plain text mail

@Service
public class MailService {

    private final JavaMailSender mailSender;
    private final String from;

    public MailService(JavaMailSender mailSender, @Value("${app.mail.from}") String from) {
        this.mailSender = mailSender;
        this.from = from;
    }

    public void sendPlain(String to, String subject, String text) {
        SimpleMailMessage msg = new SimpleMailMessage();
        msg.setFrom(from);
        msg.setTo(to);
        msg.setSubject(subject);
        msg.setText(text);
        mailSender.send(msg);              // throws MailException (unchecked) on failure
    }
}

HTML mail and attachments

For HTML, an attachment, an inline image or a non-ASCII text, use a MimeMessage (MIME is the format of structured email) with the helper class:

public void sendNewApplication(String to, String subject, String html,
                               String attachmentName, Path attachment) {
    try {
        MimeMessage message = mailSender.createMimeMessage();
        MimeMessageHelper helper = new MimeMessageHelper(message, true, "UTF-8");   // true = multipart
        helper.setFrom(from);
        helper.setTo(to);
        helper.setSubject(subject);
        helper.setText(html, true);                                   // true = this is HTML
        helper.addAttachment(attachmentName, new FileSystemResource(attachment));
        mailSender.send(message);
    } catch (MessagingException e) {
        throw new MailPreparationException("Could not build mail", e);
    }
}

Pass true for multipart whenever you add attachments or inline images. Always send a plain-text alternative for important mail with helper.setText(plain, html). Attach only when needed: many providers cap messages at 10 to 25 MB, and sending a link is often better.

Templates with Thymeleaf (brief)

Do not build HTML with string concatenation. Use a template engine; Thymeleaf is the common choice with Spring (spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf). Put src/main/resources/templates/mail/new-application.html in place:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html xmlns:th="http://www.thymeleaf.org">
  <body>
    <p>Hello <span th:text="${recruiterName}">Recruiter</span>,</p>
    <p><strong th:text="${candidateName}">Candidate</strong> applied for
       <em th:text="${jobTitle}">Job</em>.</p>
    <p><a th:href="${link}">Open the application</a></p>
  </body>
</html>
@Service
public class ApplicationMailService {

    private final TemplateEngine templateEngine;      // org.thymeleaf.TemplateEngine
    private final MailService mailService;
    // constructor omitted

    public void notifyRecruiter(RecruiterMailData d) {
        Context ctx = new Context();                  // org.thymeleaf.context.Context
        ctx.setVariable("recruiterName", d.recruiterName());
        ctx.setVariable("candidateName", d.candidateName());
        ctx.setVariable("jobTitle", d.jobTitle());
        ctx.setVariable("link", d.link());
        String html = templateEngine.process("mail/new-application", ctx);   // th:text escapes HTML
        mailService.sendHtml(d.recruiterEmail(), "New application: " + d.jobTitle(), html);
    }
}

th:text escapes HTML, which protects you from a candidate whose name contains a script tag. Never use th:utext with user input.

Send asynchronously and after commit

SMTP is slow and flaky. If send() runs inside the request, a slow mail server makes the API slow, and a mail failure can roll back (or fail) the business operation. The standard design for Project 2 combines three pieces from earlier in this module:

  1. The service saves the application and publishes an ApplicationSubmitted event.
  2. A @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) receives it only if the transaction committed.
  3. It calls an @Async("mailExecutor") method that loads the data, renders the template and sends, with a try/catch that logs failures and records them (Async).
@Async("mailExecutor")
public void sendNewApplicationMail(Long applicationId) {
