    try {
        RecruiterMailData data = loader.load(applicationId);        // own @Transactional(readOnly)
        applicationMailService.notifyRecruiter(data);
        log.info("Recruiter mail sent for application {}", applicationId);
    } catch (MailException | RuntimeException ex) {
        log.error("Recruiter mail failed for application {}", applicationId, ex);
        // optionally: save a FAILED row so a scheduled job can retry
    }
}

This is "good enough" for a small system. Its weakness: if the app crashes between commit and sending, the mail is lost. A table of pending mails (an outbox) plus a scheduler, or a message queue, solves it; see the outbox idea.

Testing email locally

Never test with real recipients. Run a fake SMTP server that catches all mail and shows it in a web page. Mailpit (successor of MailHog) is a small Docker image:

services:
  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit
    ports:
      - "1025:1025"      # SMTP: the application sends here
      - "8025:8025"      # web UI: open http://localhost:8025 to read the mails
spring:
  mail:
    host: localhost
    port: 1025
    properties:
      mail.smtp.auth: false
      mail.smtp.starttls.enable: false

MailHog (mailhog/mailhog) works the same way with the same ports. In automated tests, either use Testcontainers with Mailpit and call its HTTP API, or mock JavaMailSender and capture the MimeMessage (module 5); GreenMail is a popular in-process test SMTP server.

Common mistakes

  • Committing the SMTP password to Git. Use environment variables or a secret manager.
  • Sending email inside the database transaction: a mail goes out for data that is later rolled back.
  • No timeouts: a stuck SMTP server hangs the thread for minutes.
  • Sending to a user-supplied address without limit: your "forgot password" form becomes a spam cannon (rate-limit it, next topics).
  • Putting user-controlled text in the subject or headers without removing line breaks (header injection). MimeMessageHelper checks this for you; do not build headers by hand.

Exceptions

  • MailAuthenticationException: wrong username/password (Gmail without an app password).
  • MailSendException: delivery to some recipients failed; it contains the failed messages.
  • MailParseException / MailPreparationException: bad address or content.
  • All extend the unchecked MailException, so no throws clause; MessagingException (checked) comes from the Jakarta Mail API when you build a MimeMessage.
  • The health indicator mail (Actuator) connects to the SMTP server; it can mark the app DOWN when the mail server is unreachable. Disable it with management.health.mail.enabled=false if mail is not critical.

Interview angle

"How do you send email in Spring Boot?" Starter, SMTP properties, JavaMailSender, SimpleMailMessage vs MimeMessageHelper. "Why asynchronous?" Slow, unreliable external call; do not block the request or the transaction. "How do you make sure it is sent only if the data was saved?" After-commit listener or outbox. "How do you test it?" Mailpit/MailHog or GreenMail.

Calling other APIs: RestClient, HTTP service clients, WebClient and RestTemplate

Use RestClient (Spring 6.1+, Boot 3.2+) for synchronous HTTP calls with a fluent API, wrap it in an @HttpExchange interface for a declarative client, always set timeouts, and map error statuses deliberately.

What and why

Your backend often calls other services: a payment gateway, a resume parser, an email API, another microservice. This is an outgoing HTTP call, the mirror image of a controller. It is where production systems fail most: the other side is slow, down or returns something unexpected. So the three rules are: set timeouts, handle errors explicitly, and decide what to do when the call fails (retry, fallback, circuit breaker; see Resilience4j).

The four clients: which one?

ClientStyleStatusUse it for
RestClientSynchronous, fluentCurrent (since Spring 6.1 / Boot 3.2)New code in a servlet (blocking) application
HTTP service client (@HttpExchange)Declarative interface on top of RestClient or WebClientCurrentA typed client for one remote API; the least code
WebClientReactive (Mono/Flux), also works blockingCurrent, part of WebFluxReactive apps, streaming, parallel calls
RestTemplateSynchronous, template methodsMaintenance mode; will not get new featuresExisting code; do not start new code with it

You will meet RestTemplate in most older codebases and interviews, so know its methods (getForObject, postForEntity, exchange). RestClient was created to give the same blocking model with the modern fluent style of WebClient, without needing the reactive stack.

RestClient basics

Boot provides a RestClient.Builder bean already configured (message converters, observability). Inject it, set a base URL and defaults once, and keep the built client in a bean:

@Configuration
public class PaymentClientConfig {

    @Bean
    RestClient paymentRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
                                 @Value("${payments.base-url}") String baseUrl,
                                 @Value("${payments.api-key}") String apiKey) {

        SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
        factory.setConnectTimeout(2000);        // ms to open the connection
        factory.setReadTimeout(5000);           // ms to wait for the response

        return builder
                .baseUrl(baseUrl)
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION, "Bearer " + apiKey)
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .requestFactory(factory)
                .build();
    }
}
@Service
public class PaymentGateway {

    private final RestClient client;
    public PaymentGateway(@Qualifier("paymentRestClient") RestClient client) { this.client = client; }

    public PaymentStatus status(String paymentId) {
        return client.get()
                .uri("/payments/{id}", paymentId)               // URI template: encoded safely
                .retrieve()
                .body(PaymentStatus.class);                     // deserialises JSON into a record
    }

    public ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> pay(PaymentRequest request) {
        return client.post()
                .uri("/payments")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(request)                                  // serialised to JSON
                .retrieve()
                .toEntity(PaymentResponse.class);               // status, headers and body
    }

    public List<PaymentStatus> recent(int days) {
        return client.get()
                .uri(b -> b.path("/payments").queryParam("days", days).build())
                .retrieve()
                .body(new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<PaymentStatus>>() { });  // generics
    }
}
  • retrieve() is the simple path: send, check status, give the body. exchange() gives full control of the raw response when you need it.
  • body(Class) returns the object; toEntity(Class) keeps headers and status; toBodilessEntity() ignores the body; .body(new ParameterizedTypeReference<...>(){}) keeps generic types.
  • Use URI templates ("/payments/{id}") instead of string concatenation, so values are encoded and you do not get injection into the URL.

Error handling with onStatus

By default, retrieve() throws HttpClientErrorException (4xx) or HttpServerErrorException (5xx), both subclasses of RestClientResponseException. Turn these into your own domain exceptions, so the rest of your code does not depend on HTTP:

public PaymentStatus status(String paymentId) {
    return client.get()
            .uri("/payments/{id}", paymentId)
            .retrieve()
            .onStatus(status -> status.value() == 404, (request, response) -> {
                throw new PaymentNotFoundException(paymentId);
            })
            .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError, (request, response) -> {
                throw new PaymentProviderException("Provider error " + response.getStatusCode());
            })
            .body(PaymentStatus.class);
}

Other failures: a connection refused or a timeout surfaces as ResourceAccessException (wrapping ConnectException or SocketTimeoutException). Catch it where you decide to retry or fall back. Never log the full request when it holds API keys or personal data.

Timeouts: always

The default of many HTTP clients is "wait for ever". One slow dependency then occupies all your threads and your whole application stops answering: a cascading failure. Always set a connect timeout (1 to 3 s) and a read timeout (based on the remote service's normal speed, for example 3 to 10 s). Three ways, from simplest:

  • Boot properties (Boot 3.4+): spring.http.client.connect-timeout and spring.http.client.read-timeout apply to clients built from the auto-configured builder.
  • A request factory in code, as above (SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory, JdkClientHttpRequestFactory, or the Apache / Jetty factories when those libraries are present).
  • Resilience4j @TimeLimiter as an outer deadline for the whole operation.

Retries are the next layer; they belong with circuit breakers and backoff in module 7. Retry only idempotent calls (GET, PUT, DELETE), not a payment POST unless the API supports idempotency keys.

HTTP service clients: a declarative interface

Instead of writing a class full of client.get().uri(...), describe the remote API as an interface. Spring creates the implementation (a proxy) at runtime; the style is like Feign or Retrofit.

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.service.annotation.GetExchange;
import org.springframework.web.service.annotation.HttpExchange;
import org.springframework.web.service.annotation.PostExchange;

@HttpExchange("/api/companies")
public interface CompanyDirectoryApi {

    @GetExchange("/{id}")
    CompanyDto byId(@PathVariable("id") Long id);

    @GetExchange
    List<CompanyDto> search(@RequestParam("q") String query);

    @PostExchange
    CompanyDto create(@RequestBody CompanyDto company);
}
@Configuration
public class DirectoryClientConfig {

    @Bean
    CompanyDirectoryApi companyDirectoryApi(RestClient.Builder builder,
                                            @Value("${directory.base-url}") String baseUrl) {
        RestClient restClient = builder.baseUrl(baseUrl).build();
        RestClientAdapter adapter = RestClientAdapter.create(restClient);
        HttpServiceProxyFactory factory = HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(adapter).build();
        return factory.createClient(CompanyDirectoryApi.class);
    }
}

Now other beans just inject CompanyDirectoryApi and call api.byId(5L). The same interface with a WebClientAdapter works on WebClient. Methods can return the body type, ResponseEntity<T>, or void. It uses the Spring MVC annotations for parameters (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @RequestHeader) and its own @HttpExchange family for the verb and path (@GetExchange, @PostExchange, @PutExchange, @DeleteExchange, @PatchExchange).

Version note

HttpServiceProxyFactory is available from Spring Framework 6.0, and RestClient support from 6.1. Spring Framework 7 / Boot 4 adds simpler registration of such clients (annotations and properties so you do not write the factory bean yourself); the interface you write stays the same, only the bean wiring becomes shorter. Check the Spring reference for your version if you use 7 or later.

WebClient and RestTemplate in short

WebClient webClient = WebClient.builder().baseUrl("https://api.example.com").build();

Mono<PaymentStatus> mono = webClient.get().uri("/payments/{id}", id)
        .retrieve().bodyToMono(PaymentStatus.class);          // reactive: nothing happens until subscribed

PaymentStatus blocking = mono.block(Duration.ofSeconds(5));   // blocking style, with a timeout
RestTemplate rest = new RestTemplateBuilder()
        .rootUri("https://api.example.com")
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))        // method names differ between Boot versions
        .readTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .build();

PaymentStatus s = rest.getForObject("/payments/{id}", PaymentStatus.class, id);
ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> r = rest.postForEntity("/payments", request, PaymentResponse.class);

Do not add the WebFlux starter to a servlet app just for WebClient; use RestClient. Choose WebClient when your whole stack is reactive or you must call many services in parallel without blocking threads.

Testing outgoing calls

Test your client against a fake server: MockRestServiceServer (bind it to the RestClient.Builder with MockRestServiceServer.bindTo(builder)), or WireMock / MockWebServer for real HTTP. Test the error cases too: 404, 500, a slow response, an invalid JSON. See module 5.

Common mistakes

  • No timeouts, so one slow dependency freezes the application.
  • Creating a new client (RestClient.create()) for each call: lose pooling and configuration. Build once, reuse.
  • Calling a remote API inside a database transaction, holding a connection while waiting.
  • Catching Exception and returning an empty object: the failure becomes invisible.
  • Retrying non-idempotent POSTs and charging a customer twice.
  • Building URLs with string concatenation of user input.

Interview angle

"RestTemplate vs RestClient vs WebClient?" Legacy blocking, modern blocking, reactive. "What is an HTTP service client?" A proxy generated from an @HttpExchange interface. "What happens if the remote service is slow?" Timeouts, then circuit breaker and fallback. "How do you handle 4xx and 5xx?" onStatus, map to domain exceptions.

Rate limiting: algorithms, Bucket4j, 429 responses and distributed limits

Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may make in a time window; implement a token bucket per user or IP (Bucket4j) in a filter, return 429 with Retry-After, store counters in Redis when you run several instances, and prefer doing coarse limiting at the gateway or Nginx.

What and why

Rate limiting restricts how often a client may call your API. Reasons:

  • Abuse and attacks: brute-force logins, OTP guessing, scraping, a denial-of-service attempt.
  • Cost: every request that sends an email or calls a paid API costs money.
  • Fairness and stability: one noisy client must not slow the service for everyone.
  • Protecting downstream systems (database, third-party APIs with their own limits).

Algorithms in brief

AlgorithmHow it worksGoodWeak
Fixed windowCount requests per clock window (per minute); reset at the boundarySimplest; one Redis keyBurst at the boundary: 100 at 10:00:59 and 100 at 10:01:00
Sliding windowCount the last N seconds continuously (log of timestamps, or weighted two windows)Smooth, accurateMore memory and work
Token bucketBucket holds up to N tokens; each request takes one; tokens refill at a steady rateAllows short bursts, enforces the average rate; cheapTwo parameters to tune
Leaky bucketRequests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rateVery smooth outputAdds delay; queue can fill

Token bucket is the most common. Example: capacity 20, refill 10 tokens per minute: a client can burst 20 requests at once, then is held to one every 6 seconds. Design notes for the algorithms are in System Design · Module 5.

In-app implementation with Bucket4j

Bucket4j is a Java library that implements the token bucket correctly and thread-safely. Add the bucket4j-core dependency (check the Bucket4j site for the current group and artifact name for your Java version). We keep one bucket per client key and consult it in a servlet filter:

import com.github.benmanes.caffeine.cache.Cache;
import com.github.benmanes.caffeine.cache.Caffeine;
import io.bucket4j.Bucket;
import io.bucket4j.ConsumptionProbe;
import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.time.Duration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

@Component
public class RateLimitFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    // one bucket per client; entries unused for 10 minutes are dropped (no memory leak)
    private final Cache<String, Bucket> buckets = Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .expireAfterAccess(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .maximumSize(100_000)
            .build();

    private Bucket newBucket() {
        return Bucket.builder()
                .addLimit(limit -> limit.capacity(20).refillGreedy(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
                .build();
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean shouldNotFilter(HttpServletRequest request) {
        return !request.getRequestURI().startsWith("/api/");     // limit the API only
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        String key = clientKey(request);
        Bucket bucket = buckets.get(key, k -> newBucket());
        ConsumptionProbe probe = bucket.tryConsumeAndReturnRemaining(1);

        if (probe.isConsumed()) {
            response.setHeader("X-RateLimit-Remaining", String.valueOf(probe.getRemainingTokens()));
            chain.doFilter(request, response);
        } else {
            long waitSeconds = Math.max(1, probe.getNanosToWaitForRefill() / 1_000_000_000L);
            response.setStatus(HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS.value());          // 429
            response.setHeader("Retry-After", String.valueOf(waitSeconds));
            response.setContentType("application/problem+json");
            response.getWriter().write("{\"title\":\"Too many requests\",\"status\":429,"
                    + "\"detail\":\"Try again in " + waitSeconds + " seconds\"}");
        }
    }

    private String clientKey(HttpServletRequest request) {
        var auth = org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder
                .getContext().getAuthentication();
        if (auth != null && auth.isAuthenticated() && !"anonymousUser".equals(auth.getPrincipal())) {
            return "user:" + auth.getName();                 // logged in: limit per user
        }
        return "ip:" + request.getRemoteAddr();              // anonymous: limit per IP
    }
}
  • The filter needs a Caffeine dependency here; a plain ConcurrentHashMap works too but never forgets old clients.
  • If you want to limit authenticated users, register the filter after the security filter that sets the authentication; for login and OTP endpoints (anonymous) use the IP.
  • You can give different endpoints different limits: strict for /api/auth/login (5 per minute) and loose for reads. Select the bucket configuration by path.

Returning 429 properly

Status 429 Too Many Requests is the standard answer. Add a Retry-After header (seconds to wait) so well-behaved clients back off, and optionally informal headers such as X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining. Use the same error body format as the rest of your API (ProblemDetail, module 2). Log rejections at WARN with the key, and count them with a Micrometer counter so you can see attacks.

Which client key? Be careful with proxies

Behind Nginx, a load balancer or a gateway, request.getRemoteAddr() is the proxy's address, so everyone shares one bucket and gets blocked together. Set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework (or native for Tomcat) so Spring reads the X-Forwarded-For header, and make sure only your trusted proxy can set it; otherwise an attacker sends a fake header with a new value on each request and escapes the limit. Authenticated user id or an API key is a better key than IP, because many people share one IP (a college or an office network behind NAT).

Distributed rate limiting with Redis

With three instances of the app, each with its own in-memory buckets, a client effectively gets three times the limit. Counters must live in a shared store, and Redis is the usual choice because it is fast and has atomic operations. Two ways:

  • Bucket4j with a Redis backend (extension modules for Lettuce, Redisson, Jedis and others): the same bucket API, with the state kept in Redis.
  • A simple fixed-window counter with StringRedisTemplate:
public boolean allow(String clientKey, int limit, Duration window) {
    long slot = System.currentTimeMillis() / window.toMillis();          // current window number
    String key = "rl:" + clientKey + ":" + slot;
    Long count = redis.opsForValue().increment(key);                     // atomic
    if (count != null && count == 1L) {
        redis.expire(key, window);                                       // first hit sets the TTL
    }
    return count != null && count <= limit;
}

This has a tiny race (the app can crash between INCR and EXPIRE, leaving a key with no TTL); production code puts both steps in a Lua script that Redis runs atomically. It also has the fixed-window boundary burst. For a sliding window use a sorted set (opsForZSet()): add the timestamp, remove entries older than the window, count the rest, all in one script. Decide what happens if Redis is down: fail open (allow requests, accept the risk) or fail closed (reject). Most public APIs fail open, with an alert.

Limit at the edge instead

The cheapest request to handle is the one that never reaches Java. Put coarse limits in front of the application:

http {
    limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;     # 10 requests per second per IP

    server {
        location /api/ {
            limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay;                     # allow short bursts
            limit_req_status 429;
            proxy_pass http://backend;
        }
    }
}

Spring Cloud Gateway has a built-in RequestRateLimiter filter backed by Redis (gateway article), and cloud API gateways and CDNs offer limits too. A good layering: Nginx or gateway for coarse per-IP limits and DDoS protection; the application for business limits (5 resume uploads per hour per user, 3 password-reset mails per hour per address) that need to know who the user is.

PlaceStrengthWeakness
Nginx / CDN / WAFBlocks before Java; very cheapKnows IP and URL, not your users
API gatewayOne place for all services; can use user or API keyAnother component to run
Application filterBusiness rules, per-user, per-planUses app resources; needs Redis for several instances
Resilience4j @RateLimiterLimits your calls to another serviceOutgoing, not for protecting your API from clients

Common mistakes

  • An unbounded HashMap of buckets: one attacker with a million fake IPs fills memory.
  • Rate limiting by getRemoteAddr() behind a proxy (everybody is "the proxy").
  • Trusting X-Forwarded-For from anyone.
  • Same limit for login and for reading job lists.
  • Returning 500 or 403 instead of 429, with no Retry-After.
  • In-memory limits on several instances (limit multiplied by the instance count).

Interview angle

"How would you rate-limit an API?" Pick key (user/IP/API key), algorithm (token bucket for bursts), shared store (Redis) for several instances, answer 429 + Retry-After, and do coarse limiting at the edge. "Token bucket vs fixed window?" Bursts allowed with a steady average vs boundary double-burst. "What if Redis fails?" Fail open or closed, a stated decision.

Production-readiness checklist

Before you deploy, check that configuration comes from the environment, health checks and logs work, shutdown is graceful, every external call has a timeout, pools are sized, the schema is migrated by a tool, and the API is documented.

"It works" is not "it is ready". This checklist collects the lessons of the whole module and ties them to Project 2. Go through it before the first real deployment, and again when a service misbehaves.

1. Configuration and secrets

  • 12-factor style: the same JAR runs everywhere; only environment variables change. Spring's relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url.
  • No passwords, API keys or JWT secrets in Git, in application.yml defaults, or in logs. Use environment variables, Docker/Kubernetes secrets or a vault.
  • Profiles (dev, test, prod) for differences; prod must not fall back to development defaults silently.
  • Fail fast: validate required properties at startup with @ConfigurationProperties and @Validated.
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate           # Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only checks it
  flyway:
    enabled: true
server:
  shutdown: graceful
  forward-headers-strategy: framework
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, info, prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs

2. Database

  • Migrations with Flyway or Liquibase, never ddl-auto=update in production (module 3). Migrations run on startup before traffic is served.
  • Connection pool sizing: HikariCP maximum-pool-size defaults to 10. More is not better: a pool larger than the database can serve only moves the queue into the database. Start at about 10 to 20 per instance and make sure (instances x pool size) stays below the database's max_connections. Watch hikaricp.connections.pending.
  • Set spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout (default 30 s) lower, so overloaded requests fail fast.
  • Indexes for your real queries, slow-query log on, open-in-view=false, N+1 checked.

3. Health, shutdown and timeouts

  • Actuator health with liveness and readiness probes; the container or Kubernetes uses them (Actuator).
  • Graceful shutdown: server.shutdown=graceful makes Tomcat stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight ones, then exit; spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s sets how long it waits. Without it, a deployment cuts requests in half (HTTP 502 for users). Match it with the platform's termination grace period.
  • Timeouts everywhere: outgoing HTTP (clients), database (spring.jpa.properties.jakarta.persistence.query.timeout or per-transaction timeout), Redis, SMTP. A missing timeout is a future outage.
  • Executors have bounded queues; scheduled jobs are idempotent and single-run in a cluster.

4. Observability

  • Structured logs to stdout with a request or trace id; correct levels; no secrets (Logging).
  • Metrics scraped by Prometheus; dashboards for latency, traffic, errors and saturation; alerts on error rate and latency (Micrometer).
  • Version in /actuator/info (build and git info), so you know what is running.
  • Later: tracing across services (module 7).

5. Performance and protection

  • Caching for hot read paths with TTL and invalidation (Caching); pagination on every list endpoint; compression (server.compression.enabled=true) if not handled by Nginx.
  • Rate limiting on login, OTP, upload, email-sending endpoints (Rate limiting).
  • Request size limits (max-file-size, Tomcat max-http-form-post-size where relevant).
  • Security: HTTPS at the edge, CORS limited to your frontend origin, security headers, actuator locked, dependencies updated (module 4).

6. API quality

  • API documentation with springdoc-openapi (Swagger UI) from your controllers and DTOs (module 2). Disable or protect Swagger UI in production if the API is not public.
  • Consistent error responses (ProblemDetail), correct status codes, validation, idempotency for payments.
  • Versioning strategy (/api/v1) and a deprecation policy before you have many clients.

7. Build and deploy

  • A multi-stage Dockerfile, non-root user, small base image, JVM that respects container memory limits (DevOps · Module 3). Layered JARs make rebuilds faster.
  • CI runs tests and builds the image on every push (DevOps · Module 4).
  • A rollback plan; migrations that are backward-compatible for one release (add a column first, remove it later).
  • Backups of the database and a tested restore.

In real projects

Teams turn this list into a template: a company "service starter" with logging, Actuator, metrics, Dockerfile and CI already configured, so every new service is production-ready on day one. The same list is also a good outline for the "how do you take a Spring Boot app to production?" interview question.

Common mistakes

  • Treating production as "dev with a bigger server": same ddl-auto=update, same passwords, debug logs.
  • Health check that returns UP while the database is unreachable (or the opposite: liveness depending on the database).
  • A 200-connection pool times ten instances, killing PostgreSQL.
  • No graceful shutdown, so every deploy shows errors to users.

Interview questions — Production features

What is the difference between SLF4J and Logback, and why use placeholders in log calls?

SLF4J is the logging API (a facade) that your code uses; Logback is the implementation that formats and writes the lines, and it is Spring Boot's default. The facade lets you change the implementation without touching code. Placeholders (log.info("user {}", id)) build the message only when the level is enabled, and they keep the exception as a separate last argument so the stack trace is printed.

How do you follow one request through many log lines, including across threads?

Put a correlation id into the MDC in a servlet filter at the start of the request, print %X{requestId} in the log pattern, and clear the MDC in finally. The MDC is thread-local, so for @Async or executors you copy it with a TaskDecorator. With Micrometer Tracing the trace and span ids are put in the MDC for you and propagated between services.

What is Spring Boot Actuator, and how do you secure it?

It adds production endpoints (health, info, metrics, loggers, env, threaddump and others). Only health is exposed over HTTP by default. You choose exposure with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include, restrict sensitive endpoints to an admin role with Spring Security, and/or serve them on a separate management.server.port that is not reachable from the internet. Never expose heapdump or env publicly.

Liveness vs readiness probe?

Liveness answers "is the process broken?"; failure makes the platform restart the container, so it should not depend on external systems. Readiness answers "can it serve traffic now?"; failure removes the instance from the load balancer but does not restart it, and it may include the database. Boot exposes /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness when probes are enabled.

What are counters, gauges and timers in Micrometer, and why is tag cardinality dangerous?

A counter only increases (requests, errors); a gauge reports a current value that can rise and fall (queue size); a timer records count and duration of events. Each unique combination of tag values becomes a separate time series, so a tag such as user id or a raw URL creates millions of series and overloads Prometheus and your application's memory. Use low-cardinality tags only.

How does @Cacheable work, and why might it not work?

A proxy intercepts the call, builds a key from the arguments, looks it up in the named cache and calls the method only on a miss. It fails silently when @EnableCaching is missing, when the method is called from the same class (self-invocation bypasses the proxy), when the method is private or final, or when the bean is not created by Spring. The key can also be wrong, for example when it ignores a parameter.

@Cacheable vs @CachePut vs @CacheEvict?

@Cacheable skips the method if the value is cached. @CachePut always runs the method and updates the cache with the result (use on updates). @CacheEvict removes an entry, or all entries with allEntries = true (use on deletes and on changes that make other cached results stale). @Caching combines several on one method.

Caffeine or Redis for a cache? What serialization would you use with Redis?

Caffeine is in-process memory: fastest, no network, but every instance has its own copy, so entries can differ between instances. Redis is shared and survives restarts of the application, at the cost of a network hop. With Redis, replace the default JDK serialization by JSON (and string keys) so values are readable, need not be Serializable, and are less fragile to class changes; always set a TTL.

What is the difference between fixedRate, fixedDelay and cron? What problems appear in a cluster?

fixedRate measures the period from the start of one run to the start of the next; fixedDelay from the end of one run to the start of the next; cron uses a calendar expression (six fields in Spring, with seconds) and a time zone. In a cluster each instance runs the job, so use ShedLock, a dedicated worker instance, or an external scheduler. The default scheduler also has one thread, so a long job delays the others.

Why can an @Async method run synchronously, and what does not propagate to the async thread?

It runs synchronously when @EnableAsync is missing or when it is called from within the same class, because the proxy is bypassed. Thread-local state does not propagate: the caller's transaction, the Spring Security context and the MDC are not available in the new thread. Pass ids instead of entities, start async work after commit, and copy context with a decorator if needed.

What do virtual threads change in Spring Boot?

With Java 21+ and Boot 3.2+, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true runs request handling, @Async and scheduled tasks on cheap virtual threads. Blocking calls (JDBC, HTTP) no longer hold an OS thread, so a blocking-style application scales to many concurrent requests. They do not speed up CPU-bound work, and your connection pool and downstream services still limit the throughput. Older Java versions could pin carrier threads in synchronized blocks.

How do you implement a secure file upload?

Limit sizes (spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and a business limit), check the content type by looking at the bytes with an allow-list, never use the client's file name for the path (path traversal), generate a UUID name, normalise and verify that the path stays inside the upload folder, store outside the web root, keep metadata and ownership in the database, authorise downloads and send them with Content-Disposition. In production use object storage such as S3.

RestTemplate, RestClient and WebClient: which one do you use, and what must you configure?

For new blocking code use RestClient (Spring 6.1+); RestTemplate is in maintenance mode but common in old code; WebClient is for reactive stacks. Whatever the client, set connect and read timeouts, map 4xx/5xx errors to domain exceptions (onStatus), reuse the client bean, and add retry and circuit breaking for unreliable dependencies. An @HttpExchange interface gives a declarative client.

How would you rate-limit the login endpoint across three instances of a service?

Use a shared counter store, normally Redis, with a token bucket or sliding window keyed by IP (and username for login). Local in-memory buckets would give each instance its own allowance. Respond with 429 and Retry-After, decide fail-open or fail-closed if Redis is down, make sure the real client IP is read correctly behind the proxy, and add coarse limits at Nginx or the gateway as well.

What would you check before putting a Spring Boot service in production?

Config and secrets from the environment, Flyway migrations with ddl-auto=validate, open-in-view=false, sized connection pool, timeouts on every external call, health and readiness probes, graceful shutdown, structured logs without secrets, metrics and alerts, rate limits on sensitive endpoints, locked-down Actuator, API docs, a multi-stage Docker image and a rollback plan.

Cheat sheet — Production features

  • Logger LoggerFactory.getLogger(X.class) or Lombok @Slf4j; use {} placeholders; exception as the last argument
  • Levels ERROR > WARN > INFO > DEBUG > TRACE; Boot default is INFO; set with logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
  • Log files logging.file.name, logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-file-size, max-history; in containers log to stdout
  • JSON logs logging.structured.format.console=ecs (Boot 3.4+); MDC filter puts requestId, clear in finally
  • Never log passwords, tokens, OTPs, card or ID numbers, full bodies
  • Actuator spring-boot-starter-actuator; expose with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include; separate management.server.port
  • Probes /actuator/health/liveness (restart) and /readiness (traffic); custom check = HealthIndicator
  • Runtime log level POST /actuator/loggers/<logger> with {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}
  • Micrometer Counter (up), Gauge (current), Timer (duration); low-cardinality tags; /actuator/prometheus needs micrometer-registry-prometheus
  • Caching @EnableCaching; @Cacheable(key, condition, unless), @CachePut, @CacheEvict(allEntries), @Caching
  • Cache pitfalls self-invocation, no TTL, wrong key, cached entities; cache DTOs
  • Redis cache spring.cache.type=redis, spring.cache.redis.time-to-live, JSON value serializer, string keys; StringRedisTemplate for direct use
  • Caffeine local, spring.cache.caffeine.spec=maximumSize=1000,expireAfterWrite=10m
  • @Scheduled @EnableScheduling; fixedRate (start to start), fixedDelay (end to start), 6-field cron + zone="Asia/Kolkata"
  • Scheduler pool default 1 thread: spring.task.scheduling.pool.size; cluster: ShedLock
  • @Async @EnableAsync; returns void or CompletableFuture; named executor @Async("mailExecutor"); bounded queue
  • Async limits no caller transaction, no security context, no MDC; start after commit with @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)
  • Virtual threads spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true (Boot 3.2+, Java 21+); for blocking I/O, not CPU work
  • Upload MultipartFile; spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size/max-request-size; check bytes, UUID name, normalised path, outside web root
  • Download ResponseEntity<Resource> + ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(n, UTF_8); big data: StreamingResponseBody
  • Email spring-boot-starter-mail, spring.mail.*; SimpleMailMessage vs MimeMessageHelper (HTML, attachments); test with Mailpit (SMTP 1025, UI 8025)
  • RestClient builder.baseUrl().build(); .get().uri(..).retrieve().body(T.class); onStatus; always timeouts
  • HTTP service client @HttpExchange interface + HttpServiceProxyFactory
  • Rate limiting token bucket (Bucket4j) per user/IP; 429 + Retry-After; Redis for several instances; coarse limits in Nginx/gateway
  • Production env-var config, Flyway + ddl-auto=validate, open-in-view=false, server.shutdown=graceful, timeouts, pool sizing, probes

Practice — Production features

  1. Logging (easy). In your Project 2 API, add an SLF4J logger to the application service, log "application submitted" at INFO with ids, and set logging.level.com.example to DEBUG in a dev profile. Done when the console shows the line with the right level and no secret appears.
  2. Correlation id (easy). Write the RequestIdFilter, print %X{requestId} in the pattern, and return the id in an X-Request-Id response header. Done when two requests show different ids across several log lines each, and the id does not leak into the next request.
  3. Actuator health and info (easy). Add Actuator, expose health,info,metrics,prometheus, enable probes, add build info, and write a custom HealthIndicator for the upload folder. Done when /actuator/health shows your component, turns DOWN (503) if the folder is removed, and the other endpoints need the ADMIN role.
  4. Custom metric (medium). Add a counter for submitted applications and a timer for the mail sending, then scrape /actuator/prometheus. Done when the counter increases after each application and the timer appears in the output.
  5. Caching (medium). Cache getJob(id) and the company list with Caffeine (TTL 10 minutes), evict on update and delete, and prove it with a test that counts repository calls. Then switch to Redis with JSON values and a per-cache TTL, and inspect keys with redis-cli. Done when the second call does not hit the database and an update makes the next read fresh.
  6. Project 2: resume upload (medium). Add POST /api/applications/{id}/resume (PDF only, 2 MB, UUID name, metadata table through a Flyway migration) and an owner-only download endpoint. Done when a renamed .exe is rejected, a file called ../../x.pdf cannot escape the folder, and another user gets 404/403.
  7. Project 2: email to the recruiter (medium). When someone applies, send an HTML mail to the job's recruiter (Thymeleaf template, resume attached) asynchronously after commit using a dedicated executor, tested against Mailpit in Docker. Done when the API answers quickly, the mail appears in Mailpit, and no mail is sent if the transaction rolls back.
  8. Scheduled job (medium). Close jobs whose deadline passed every night at 00:30 IST, idempotently and in batches, with a log line and a counter. Done when running it twice changes nothing the second time; bonus: protect it with ShedLock and start two instances.
  9. Rate limiting (hard). Limit /api/auth/login to 5 requests per minute per IP using Bucket4j, returning 429 with Retry-After. Then move the counter into Redis and verify with two instances. Done when the sixth call in a minute fails on both instances.
  10. Project 2 finishing steps (hard). Complete the production side of the job portal: Swagger/OpenAPI docs for all endpoints, Flyway migrations for the whole schema with ddl-auto=validate, an Actuator health endpoint with probes, proper logging (levels, request id, JSON in the prod profile), graceful shutdown, and a README that lists the endpoints and contains the ER diagram of User, Company, Job and Application. Done when a new developer can clone the repository, start it with one command and find every endpoint and the data model in the README, and the checklist in this module is ticked.

Module 7·Month 9Later

Microservices and messaging

11 topics · about 1.5 h of reading

Everything in modules 1 to 6 built one application. Large companies run hundreds of small services that call each other and talk through message brokers. This module explains why they do that, what it costs, and how Spring supports it: gateways, service discovery, central configuration, resilience patterns, Kafka and RabbitMQ, tracing, and running many containers together with Docker Compose.

This is a "later" topic: most first jobs are in a monolith or a handful of services, and a wrong early move to microservices is a classic mistake. But interviews ask about it a lot, and the ideas (timeouts, retries, idempotency, events) improve ordinary applications too. Design theory lives in System Design · Module 6; here we focus on the Spring and Docker side.

  • Compare monolith, modular monolith and microservices and say when each is right.
  • Draw service boundaries and choose between synchronous calls and events.
  • Configure Spring Cloud Gateway routes, and explain discovery and central configuration.
  • Protect calls with Resilience4j: timeout, retry with backoff, circuit breaker, bulkhead.
  • Produce and consume messages with Kafka and RabbitMQ, with retries and dead-letter handling.
  • Explain delivery semantics, idempotent consumers and the outbox pattern.
  • Follow a request across services with Micrometer Tracing.
  • Run two Spring Boot services, a database, Kafka and Redis with one compose.yaml.

Monolith, modular monolith and microservices

Start with a well-structured modular monolith and split into microservices only when team size, scaling needs or release independence justify the cost of a distributed system.

The three architectures

A monolith is one deployable application: one JAR, one process, usually one database. Everything you built in Project 2 is a monolith. A microservice architecture splits the system into many small, independently deployable services, each owning its data and talking to the others over the network. A modular monolith is a middle path: one deployable, but inside it the code is divided into strongly separated modules with clear interfaces, so it could be split later.

MonolithModular monolithMicroservices
DeploymentOne unitOne unitMany units, each its own pipeline
ScalingWhole app togetherWhole app togetherEach service by itself
DataOne shared schemaOne database, schema or tables per moduleDatabase per service
Calls between partsMethod callsMethod calls through module APIsNetwork calls and events
TransactionsACID across everythingACID (use sparingly across modules)No distributed ACID; sagas and eventual consistency
ComplexityLow at first, grows into a "big ball of mud"MediumHigh: networking, observability, DevOps
Team size that fits1 to 15 people5 to 40 peopleMany teams that must ship independently

What microservices really buy you

  • Independent deployment: a team ships its service without coordinating a release of everything.
  • Independent scaling: the search service needs 20 instances, the admin service needs 1.
  • Fault isolation and technology freedom: a crash in the recommendation service need not take down checkout; a service may use another language or database.
  • Organisation: small teams own services end to end (Conway's law: system structure mirrors the communication structure of the organisation).

What they cost

  • Network instead of method calls. A call that took nanoseconds now takes milliseconds and can fail, time out or arrive twice. You need timeouts, retries and circuit breakers (Resilience4j).
  • Distributed data. No joins across services and no single transaction. Consistency becomes eventual, and you need patterns like events, sagas and the outbox (delivery semantics).
  • Observability. One user request touches six services; you need central logs, metrics and distributed tracing (tracing).
  • DevOps load. Many pipelines, containers, configs, secrets, versions and environments (Docker, Kubernetes).
  • Testing gets harder: contracts between services, end-to-end environments.
  • Latency and duplication: more hops per request, and the same code (auth, DTOs) repeated.

The distributed monolith anti-pattern

The worst result is a distributed monolith: services that must be deployed together, share one database, call each other in long synchronous chains, or break whenever another service changes. You pay all the costs of microservices and get none of the benefits. Warning signs: a change always touches three services; services cannot start without each other; two services read each other's tables; a release needs a "deployment order".

Why a modular monolith is often the better start

  1. You do not yet know the right boundaries. Wrong boundaries in a monolith cost a refactor; wrong boundaries across services cost API versions, data migration and meetings.
  2. You keep simple transactions, simple debugging, one deployment and fast local development.
  3. If you structure it well (packages by business capability, no cross-module repository access, events between modules), extracting a module into a service later is a mechanical job.

Many well-known companies run a monolith or a few large services successfully. Move to microservices when you have a concrete reason: several teams blocked on each other's releases, a part of the system with very different scaling or availability needs, or regulatory isolation.

Spring Modulith (brief)

Spring Modulith is a Spring project that helps you build and keep a modular monolith. Each top-level package under your application class is an application module; other modules may use only its public API (the types in the module's base package), and a test verifies this:

// com.example.jobs.job          -> module "job"   (public API: JobApi, events)
// com.example.jobs.job.internal -> hidden implementation
// com.example.jobs.application  -> module "application"
// com.example.jobs.notification -> module "notification"

class ModularityTests {
    @Test
    void verifyModularity() {
        ApplicationModules.of(JobsApplication.class).verify();   // fails on illegal dependencies
    }
}

Modules communicate with application events (and Modulith can persist events so they are not lost), which is the same style you would use between microservices. It also generates documentation diagrams of the modules. Add the Spring Modulith starter and test dependencies from the Spring Modulith documentation.

In real projects

A common path: monolith, then modular monolith, then extract one or two services that really need it (notifications, search, payments, report generation), often because they scale differently or are owned by a separate team. Companies "go back" from microservices to a monolith more often than people admit. Project 4 in this roadmap lets you practise the split on a small scale.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing microservices because it looks good on a CV, with a team of three and no users.
  • Splitting by technical layer (a "database service", a "validation service") instead of business capability.
  • Sharing one database between services.
  • Making every call synchronous, building a chain: A calls B calls C calls D.

Interview angle

"Monolith vs microservices?" Give a balanced table (deployment, scaling, data, transactions, complexity), not "microservices are modern". "When would you not use microservices?" Small team, unclear domain, no DevOps maturity. "What is a distributed monolith?" Coupled services that deploy together. "How would you migrate?" Modular monolith first, then the strangler pattern: extract one capability at a time behind a gateway.

Microservice basics: boundaries, data ownership and communication

Draw service boundaries around business capabilities, give each service its own database, talk synchronously only where the caller needs the answer now, and use events for everything else.

Service boundaries: business capabilities

A good boundary groups things that change together and have one owner. Look at the business, not the code layers. For a food-delivery product the capabilities are: restaurants and menus, orders, payments, delivery tracking, notifications, users and authentication. Each becomes a candidate service with its own team, API and data. For the job portal of Project 2: identity (users), jobs (companies and jobs), applications, notifications (email) and search.

  • A service should be small enough for one team to understand, large enough to do something useful alone. "Micro" does not mean one class.
  • Domain-driven design helps: a bounded context is an area where the words have one meaning ("customer" in billing differs from "customer" in support). Boundaries often follow bounded contexts.
  • If two services must always change together or call each other on every request, they are probably one service.

Database per service

Each service owns its data and is the only one allowed to access it. Others use its API or listen to its events. This keeps services independently changeable: the jobs service can rename a column without breaking applications. The consequences:

  • No SQL joins across services. If the applications service needs a job title, it calls the jobs service, or stores a copy of the fields it needs (updated by events).
  • No single ACID transaction across services. "Place order, charge payment, reserve stock" becomes a saga: a series of local transactions with compensating actions (refund) if a later step fails.
  • Data is eventually consistent: a copy may lag behind for milliseconds or seconds.

"Database per service" may be separate servers or just separate schemas with separate credentials; what matters is that nobody reads another service's tables.

Synchronous vs asynchronous communication

Synchronous (REST, gRPC)Asynchronous (events, messages)
StyleRequest and wait for the responseSend a message and continue; consumers react later
CouplingCaller needs the callee up nowLoose: the producer does not know the consumers
Latency of the callerAdds the callee's time (and failures)Only the time to publish
Good forQueries that need an answer now: "get job details", "validate the token"Notifications, workflows, data replication, spikes
Failure handlingTimeouts, retries, circuit breaker, fallbackBroker buffers; retries, dead-letter queue, idempotent consumers
DebuggingSimpler, a call stack across servicesHarder: need tracing and correlation ids

REST with JSON is the default for synchronous calls (you know it from module 2; call it with RestClient or HTTP service clients, module 6). gRPC uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2: smaller, faster, strongly typed contracts, popular for internal calls between services, less friendly for browsers. Rule of thumb: commands that need an immediate answer go synchronous; facts that happened ("ApplicationSubmitted") are published as events. Details of communication styles: System Design · Module 6.

API composition

When a screen needs data from several services (an application page: job from the jobs service, candidate from identity, status from applications), someone must assemble it, since there is no join. Options:

  • API composition: a gateway, a backend-for-frontend or one service calls the others (in parallel) and merges the answers. Simple, but latency is the slowest call and one failure affects the page; use timeouts and partial results.
  • Data replication / CQRS-style read model: a service keeps its own read-optimised copy built from events, so the page needs one query. More work, much faster reads.

Service-to-service contracts

  • Treat each API as a public contract: add fields, do not remove or rename them; version when you must (/v2). The consumers deploy on their own schedule.
  • Be liberal in what you accept: ignore unknown JSON fields (spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=false is Boot's default).
  • Consider consumer-driven contract tests (Spring Cloud Contract, Pact) so a provider cannot break a consumer unnoticed.
  • Security: services trust the gateway or validate JWTs themselves (module 4); never expose internal services directly to the internet.

Rules

  • One service, one owner, one database. Never share tables.
  • Never design a long synchronous call chain; keep depth to one or two hops.
  • Every network call has a timeout; every message handler is idempotent.
  • Automate: one command to build, test and deploy each service.

Common mistakes

  • Splitting too early into "nano-services" that cannot do anything alone.
  • Replicating whole tables by hand with a cron job instead of events.
  • Distributed transaction attempts (two-phase commit) instead of sagas and idempotency.
  • Putting business logic in the gateway.

Interview angle

"How do you decide service boundaries?" Business capabilities and bounded contexts, data ownership, team ownership. "How do you handle a transaction across services?" Saga with compensation, idempotent steps, eventual consistency. "REST vs messaging between services?" Need-the-answer-now vs facts and decoupling. "How do you get data owned by another service?" API call, composition, or a local copy fed by events.

API gateway with Spring Cloud Gateway

An API gateway is the single entry point that routes client requests to the right service and handles cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, rate limiting, CORS and path rewriting; Spring Cloud Gateway configures this with routes made of predicates and filters.

What and why

Without a gateway, the React frontend would need to know the address of every service, handle each one's CORS and authentication, and the services would be exposed to the internet. An API gateway is one server in front of all of them. Clients call https://api.jobs.example.com/...; the gateway decides where each request goes.

Typical responsibilities:

  • Routing by path, host, method or header, plus path rewriting.
  • Authentication: validate the JWT once at the edge and pass user information on (services may still validate again for defence in depth).
  • Rate limiting and request size limits (rate limiting).
  • CORS and security headers in one place; TLS termination.
  • Load balancing to several instances (with discovery), retries, circuit breaking.
  • Aggregation of several calls into one response, logging, correlation ids.

Keep it thin: routing and cross-cutting rules only, no business logic. A fat gateway becomes a new monolith and a bottleneck owned by nobody.

Spring Cloud Gateway: the model

Spring Cloud Gateway is a gateway built on Spring WebFlux (reactive, non-blocking, on Netty), so it handles many concurrent connections cheaply. It is a separate Spring Boot application, not a library inside your services. Its three core ideas:

Route
The basic building block: an id, a destination URI, a list of predicates and a list of filters.
Predicate
A condition that decides whether a route matches the incoming request (Path, Method, Host, Header, Query, After...).
Filter
A step that changes the request before it is sent on, or the response on its way back (StripPrefix, AddRequestHeader, RequestRateLimiter...).

A route configuration

server:
  port: 8080

spring:
  application:
    name: api-gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: job-service
          uri: http://job-service:8081            # or lb://job-service with service discovery
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/jobs/**, /api/companies/**
          filters:
            - AddRequestHeader=X-Gateway, api-gateway
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args:
                name: jobsCb
                fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/jobs

        - id: application-service
          uri: http://application-service:8082
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/applications/**
            - Method=GET,POST,PUT,DELETE
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10     # tokens per second
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20
                key-resolver: "#{@ipKeyResolver}"        # a KeyResolver bean

        - id: identity-service
          uri: http://identity-service:8083
          predicates:
            - Path=/auth/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=0
            - RewritePath=/auth/(?<segment>.*), /api/auth/${segment}

      globalcors:
        cors-configurations:
          '[/**]':
            allowedOrigins: "https://app.jobs.example.com"
            allowedMethods: [GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS]
            allowedHeaders: "*"
      default-filters:
        - DedupeResponseHeader=Access-Control-Allow-Origin Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
  • Path=/api/jobs/** matches every URL under that path. Multiple predicates in one route are combined with AND.
  • StripPrefix=1 removes the first path segment before forwarding: /job-api/jobs becomes /jobs. RewritePath uses a regex for arbitrary changes.
  • RequestRateLimiter uses Redis (the reactive Redis starter) with a token bucket and a KeyResolver bean that picks the key (IP, user, API key).
  • A CircuitBreaker filter needs the Resilience4j reactive circuit-breaker starter on the gateway's classpath (Resilience4j), and a fallback endpoint.
  • You can also define routes in Java with RouteLocatorBuilder when you need logic:
@Bean
RouteLocator routes(RouteLocatorBuilder builder) {
    return builder.routes()
            .route("job-service", r -> r.path("/api/jobs/**")
                    .filters(f -> f.addRequestHeader("X-Gateway", "api-gateway"))
                    .uri("http://job-service:8081"))
            .build();
}

@Bean
KeyResolver ipKeyResolver() {
    return exchange -> Mono.just(exchange.getRequest().getRemoteAddress()
            .getAddress().getHostAddress());
}

A global filter (a GlobalFilter bean) applies to every route; it is the place for a correlation id, request logging, or JWT validation (with Spring Security's resource server support for WebFlux, module 4).

Version note

Dependency and property names of Spring Cloud Gateway changed in the Spring Cloud 2025.0 release train: the classic starter spring-cloud-starter-gateway is renamed spring-cloud-starter-gateway-server-webflux, and the configuration prefix becomes spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.* (there is also a separate servlet-based gateway-server-webmvc variant). The concepts (routes, predicates, filters) and the route syntax are the same. Always use the Spring Cloud release train that matches your Spring Boot version (the spring-cloud-dependencies BOM) and check its documentation for the property prefix.

Backend for Frontend (BFF)

A Backend for Frontend is a gateway-like service built for one kind of client: a mobile app needs small payloads and fewer calls, a web admin needs big tables. Each BFF aggregates and shapes data for its client. It is useful when clients differ a lot; do not create one until you feel the pain.

Gateway alternatives

Nginx, Kong, Traefik, Envoy, cloud gateways (AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management) and Kubernetes Ingress controllers all do routing and rate limiting. Spring Cloud Gateway is attractive when your team knows Spring and wants route logic in Java; a plain Nginx or ingress is often enough for pure routing (DevOps · Module 2).

Common mistakes

  • Putting blocking code (JDBC, RestTemplate) in a reactive gateway filter: it blocks the Netty event loop and stalls all traffic.
  • CORS configured both in the gateway and in the services, giving duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers (hence DedupeResponseHeader).
  • Trusting a user-id header from clients: the gateway must remove incoming X-User-Id headers and set its own.
  • Leaving the services publicly reachable, so attackers bypass the gateway.

Interview angle

"What does an API gateway do?" Routing, auth, rate limiting, CORS, aggregation, one entry point. "Route, predicate, filter?" Define each. "Why is Spring Cloud Gateway not a normal Spring MVC app?" It is reactive (WebFlux/Netty). "Gateway vs load balancer?" A load balancer spreads traffic across identical instances; a gateway routes to different services and applies policies.

Service discovery and centralized configuration

Services find each other by name instead of fixed addresses (client-side discovery with Eureka, or DNS in Kubernetes), and shared configuration comes from a config server, environment variables, ConfigMaps or Vault instead of files inside each JAR.

The problem: addresses change

In the monolith you called a method. Between services you need a URL. But service instances start and stop all the time (autoscaling, deployments, crashes), and their IP addresses change. Hard-coding http://10.0.4.17:8081 breaks within a day. Service discovery solves it: services register under a logical name (job-service), and callers look the name up to get the current healthy instances.

Client-side discovery: Eureka

Eureka (from Netflix, wrapped by Spring Cloud) is a registry server. Each service instance registers itself at startup, sends heartbeats, and unregisters on shutdown. A caller asks Eureka for the instances of job-service, picks one (client-side load balancing), and calls it directly.

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableEurekaServer
public class DiscoveryServerApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(DiscoveryServerApplication.class, args); }
}
server:
  port: 8761
eureka:
  client:
    register-with-eureka: false        # the registry itself does not register
    fetch-registry: false
spring:
  application:
    name: job-service                  # the logical name in the registry
eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://discovery:8761/eureka
  instance:
    prefer-ip-address: true

With Spring Cloud LoadBalancer on the classpath, a client built from a @LoadBalanced builder understands logical names:

@Configuration
class ClientConfig {
    @Bean
    @LoadBalanced                                   // resolve "job-service" via discovery
    RestClient.Builder loadBalancedBuilder() {
        return RestClient.builder();
    }
}

@Service
class JobLookup {
    private final RestClient client;
    JobLookup(@LoadBalanced RestClient.Builder builder) {
        this.client = builder.baseUrl("http://job-service").build();   // not a real DNS name
    }
    JobDto get(Long id) {
        return client.get().uri("/api/jobs/{id}", id).retrieve().body(JobDto.class);
    }
}

Gateway routes use the same idea: uri: lb://job-service. Eureka tolerates failures by design (it favours availability): the registry may briefly list a dead instance until its lease expires, so callers still need timeouts and retries. Remember to run more than one registry in production.

Server-side discovery: Kubernetes and Docker DNS

On Kubernetes (or Docker Compose) the platform does discovery for you. A Kubernetes Service gets a stable DNS name (job-service, or job-service.default.svc.cluster.local) and a virtual IP; the platform spreads traffic across the healthy pods behind it. Your code simply calls http://job-service:8081. There is no registry to run and no client library, which is why many teams skip Eureka on Kubernetes (DevOps · Module 5). Docker Compose gives the same by service name on a shared network (Compose).

Client-side (Eureka)Server-side / platform DNS
Who picks an instanceThe calling serviceThe platform (kube-proxy, load balancer)
Extra infrastructureA registry clusterNone beyond the platform
Code impactStarter, @LoadBalanced, lb://Plain URLs
FitsVMs and Docker without an orchestratorKubernetes, ECS, Compose

Centralized configuration

With 20 services and 3 environments, copying application.yml files around is a mess; changing a database password means rebuilding images. Principles: keep the build the same everywhere and inject configuration from outside (12-factor). Choices:

  • Environment variables: the simplest. Boot's relaxed binding reads SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL. Works with Docker, Compose and Kubernetes. Hard to manage for hundreds of values.
  • Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets: mounted as environment variables or files. ConfigMaps for plain settings, Secrets for passwords (base64-encoded, so also protect them with RBAC and consider encryption at rest or an external secrets operator).
  • Spring Cloud Config Server: a Spring Boot app that serves configuration files stored in a Git repository over HTTP; clients fetch at startup. Gives history and review (Git), per-service and per-profile files, and optional refresh.
  • HashiCorp Vault / cloud secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) for secrets: access control, auditing, rotation.
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableConfigServer
public class ConfigServerApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(ConfigServerApplication.class, args); }
}
server:
  port: 8888
spring:
  cloud:
    config:
      server:
        git:
          uri: https://github.com/example-org/jobs-config    # files: job-service.yml, job-service-prod.yml
          default-label: main
spring:
  application:
    name: job-service                                  # selects job-service*.yml in the repo
  config:
    import: "optional:configserver:http://config-server:8888"
  profiles:
    active: prod

The client merges the fetched properties with its own, with the usual precedence rules (environment variables and command-line arguments still win). Changing a value at runtime without restart is possible with @RefreshScope and the Actuator refresh endpoint (or Spring Cloud Bus), but many teams prefer to redeploy, which is simpler to reason about. Never store plain-text secrets in the config repository; use encryption support or a vault.

Practical advice

For Project 4 and for most real teams on Kubernetes: environment variables + ConfigMaps + Secrets, no Eureka, no Config Server. Learn Eureka and Config Server so you can explain them and maintain older Spring Cloud systems, but do not add them just because the tutorial does.

OpenFeign vs HTTP service clients

OpenFeign (spring-cloud-starter-openfeign) is a declarative HTTP client from Spring Cloud: you write an interface with @FeignClient(name = "job-service") and Spring Cloud-style mapping annotations, and it creates the client, integrated with discovery and load balancing. It is common in existing microservice code. The newer Spring-native alternative is the @HttpExchange interface from module 6, which needs no extra Spring Cloud library and works with a @LoadBalanced builder as well.

@FeignClient(name = "job-service")                  // logical name, resolved by discovery
public interface JobClient {
    @GetMapping("/api/jobs/{id}")
    JobDto byId(@PathVariable("id") Long id);
}
// @EnableFeignClients on a configuration class turns this on

Common mistakes

  • Hard-coded localhost URLs that work on a laptop and fail in Docker (each container has its own localhost).
  • A config server as a single point of failure with no optional: import or retry.
  • Secrets in the config Git repository, or in an image layer.
  • Starting services in an order that requires the registry to be up, instead of retrying.

Interview angle

"What is service discovery and why?" Dynamic addresses; registry plus load balancing. "Client-side vs server-side discovery?" Eureka vs Kubernetes Service. "How do you manage configuration and secrets across environments?" Same artifact, external config, ConfigMaps/Secrets/Vault or a Config Server backed by Git. "Feign vs RestClient?" Declarative Spring Cloud client vs Spring's own client and HTTP interfaces.

Resilience4j: timeouts, retries, circuit breaker, bulkhead and rate limiter

In a distributed system, calls fail; protect each remote call with a timeout first, then a retry (for idempotent calls only, with exponential backoff and jitter), a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing service, and a bulkhead that limits concurrency, all with a sensible fallback.

Why: failures spread

Suppose the application service calls the payment service for every request, and payments become slow (10 seconds per call). Each request now holds a thread for 10 seconds; soon all of the application service's threads are stuck waiting; it stops answering; services that call it start to hang. One slow dependency has taken down the whole system. This is a cascading failure. Resilience patterns stop it by failing fast, limiting damage and giving the failing service room to recover.

Resilience4j is the standard lightweight Java library for these patterns (it replaced Netflix Hystrix, which is retired). It integrates with Spring Boot through annotations and YAML configuration.

The patterns

PatternWhat it doesAnnotation
Time limiter / timeoutStops waiting after a set time@TimeLimiter
RetryTries again after a failure, with waiting between attempts@Retry
Circuit breakerAfter too many failures, rejects calls immediately for a while@CircuitBreaker
BulkheadLimits concurrent calls to one dependency (like watertight ship compartments)@Bulkhead
Rate limiterLimits calls per time period to a dependency@RateLimiter
FallbackA substitute result when the call failsfallbackMethod

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.resilience4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>resilience4j-spring-boot3</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-aop</artifactId>      <!-- annotations are AOP proxies -->
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

Add the version of Resilience4j that matches your Boot version (use the project's BOM or the version in its release notes). The annotations are AOP proxies like @Transactional, so the same rules apply: public methods, called from another bean, no self-invocation (module 1).

Version note

The artifact resilience4j-spring-boot3 targets Boot 3.x. For Boot 4, check the Resilience4j release notes for the artifact and version that support it. Spring Framework 7 also ships basic resilience features in core (@Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods), which cover simple retry and concurrency limiting without an extra library; circuit breakers, bulkheads and time limiters still come from Resilience4j.

Why timeouts come first

Every other pattern needs the call to end. A retry cannot happen and a circuit breaker cannot count a failure while the call waits for ever. So always set the client's connect and read timeouts (module 6), and keep them shorter than the caller's own timeout: if your API promises an answer in 3 seconds, the sum of timeouts and retries inside it must fit in 3 seconds. @TimeLimiter adds a time limit for an asynchronous call, but it works on CompletableFuture return types, which is why a client-level timeout is usually the first line of defence.

Circuit breaker

It works like the electrical one in your house. In normal state calls go through. If too many calls fail, the breaker "trips" and further calls fail instantly without touching the broken service. After a pause it lets a few test calls through; if they succeed, it closes again.

  • CLOSED: calls pass; the breaker records successes and failures in a sliding window (last N calls, or last N seconds).
  • OPEN: calls are rejected at once with CallNotPermittedException (and your fallback runs). The failing service gets time to recover, and your threads are free.
  • HALF_OPEN: after waitDurationInOpenState, a limited number of probe calls are allowed. Enough successes close the breaker; failures reopen it.

A call counts as failed when it throws an exception (configurable which ones) or when it is slow (above slowCallDurationThreshold). Business exceptions such as "payment declined" or a 404 should usually not count; list them in ignoreExceptions.

Configuration in YAML

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 20                    # judge the last 20 calls
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 10                 # do not decide before 10 calls
        failureRateThreshold: 50                 # open at 50% failures
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s
        slowCallRateThreshold: 80
        waitDurationInOpenState: 15s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 3
        automaticTransitionFromOpenToHalfOpenEnabled: true
        registerHealthIndicator: true
        ignoreExceptions:
          - com.example.jobs.payment.PaymentDeclinedException
  retry:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        maxAttempts: 3                           # first call + 2 retries
        waitDuration: 500ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2          # 500 ms, 1 s, 2 s ...
        enableRandomizedWait: true               # jitter
        randomizedWaitFactor: 0.5
        retryExceptions:
          - java.io.IOException
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException
        ignoreExceptions:
          - com.example.jobs.payment.PaymentDeclinedException
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        maxConcurrentCalls: 10                   # at most 10 calls in parallel
        maxWaitDuration: 0                       # reject at once when full
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        limitForPeriod: 50
        limitRefreshPeriod: 1s
        timeoutDuration: 0
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        timeoutDuration: 3s
        cancelRunningFuture: true

management:
  health:
    circuitbreakers:
      enabled: true
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, circuitbreakers, circuitbreakerevents, retries

Using the annotations with a fallback

@Service
public class PaymentGateway {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentGateway.class);
    private final RestClient client;

    public PaymentGateway(@Qualifier("paymentRestClient") RestClient client) { this.client = client; }

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "paymentService", fallbackMethod = "chargeFallback")
    @Retry(name = "paymentService")
    @Bulkhead(name = "paymentService")
    public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) {
        return client.post().uri("/payments")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", request.idempotencyKey())     // makes retry safe
                .body(request).retrieve().body(PaymentResult.class);
    }

    // same parameters + a Throwable (or a specific exception type) as the last one
    private PaymentResult chargeFallback(PaymentRequest request, Throwable cause) {
        log.warn("Payment service unavailable for order {}: {}", request.orderId(),
                cause.toString());
        return PaymentResult.pending(request.orderId());     // accept the order, charge later
    }
}
  • The fallback method must be in the same class, with the same parameters plus an exception parameter, and the same return type. You can have several fallbacks, one per exception type; the most specific wins.
  • Order of the aspects (outermost first): Retry, CircuitBreaker, RateLimiter, TimeLimiter, Bulkhead. So a retry wraps the circuit breaker: each retry attempt is recorded by the breaker, and when the breaker is open, the retry sees CallNotPermittedException, which you should list in ignoreExceptions of the retry to avoid hammering.

Retries: only when safe

  • Retry only idempotent operations (GET, PUT, DELETE, or a POST with an idempotency key). Retrying "charge 500 rupees" without protection can charge twice, because the first request may have succeeded and only the response got lost.
  • Retry only transient errors: timeouts, connection refused, 502/503/504. Never retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or a validation error; they will fail again.
  • Exponential backoff (wait 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s...) gives the service room to recover. Jitter (random variation) stops all clients retrying at the same instant, which would create a retry storm.
  • Keep maxAttempts small (2 or 3). Retries multiply load: 3 attempts across 3 layers of services is 27 calls.
  • Use a total time budget; a retry loop that takes longer than the user waits is useless.

Fallbacks that make sense

  • Cached or default data: show the last known company logo, or an empty recommendation list.
  • Degraded mode: accept the order as "payment pending", queue it, charge later.
  • A clear error (503 with a message and Retry-After) is also a valid fallback. For money, security and consistency-critical operations, a wrong guess is worse than failing: do not invent "payment succeeded".
  • Do not hide failures: log and count fallbacks.

Bulkhead and rate limiter

A bulkhead reserves a limited capacity for each dependency: with maxConcurrentCalls: 10 for payments, at most ten threads can be busy with payments, so a slow payment service cannot use all your Tomcat threads, and image resizing still works. It throws BulkheadFullException when full. The semaphore type (the default) limits concurrent calls on the caller's thread; a thread-pool type isolates calls on a separate pool (for CompletableFuture methods). A rate limiter here protects a dependency with a quota (for example an SMS provider that allows 50 requests per second); it is the outgoing cousin of the incoming rate limits from module 6.

Observing it
