With Actuator, /actuator/circuitbreakers lists breakers and their states, /actuator/circuitbreakerevents shows the recent events (success, error, state transition), and with registerHealthIndicator the health endpoint reports breakers. Resilience4j publishes Micrometer metrics (resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state, resilience4j_circuitbreaker_calls and others) for Prometheus. Alert on "breaker open for more than a few minutes" (Micrometer).

Rules

  • Timeout on every remote call. Always.
  • Retry only idempotent, transient failures, with backoff and jitter and a small limit.
  • Do not count business errors as circuit-breaker failures.
  • The total time of all attempts must fit within your own deadline.

Common mistakes

  • Annotations that do nothing: self-invocation, a missing AOP starter, a private method.
  • Retry on a POST that is not idempotent.
  • Fixed-delay retries with no jitter from hundreds of clients.
  • A fallback that returns fake success, hiding a real outage.
  • No minimumNumberOfCalls: one failure out of one call is "100% failure rate" and opens the breaker.

Exceptions you will see

  • CallNotPermittedException: breaker is OPEN.
  • BulkheadFullException: too many concurrent calls.
  • RequestNotPermitted: rate limiter quota used.
  • TimeoutException: from the time limiter.
  • NoFallbackAvailableException: no matching fallback method signature.

Interview angle

"Explain the circuit breaker." Three states, failure-rate threshold, wait duration, half-open probes, fail fast and recover. "Retry and circuit breaker together?" Order, idempotency, backoff with jitter, ignore CallNotPermittedException. "What is a cascading failure and how do you prevent it?" Timeouts, bulkheads, circuit breakers, fallbacks. "What is a good fallback?" A degraded but honest answer. "Why timeouts first?" Nothing else works while calls hang.

Messaging concepts: queues, topics and the Kafka model

A message broker lets services communicate asynchronously: producers send messages, the broker stores them, and consumers process them later; a queue gives each message to one worker, a topic gives it to every subscriber, and Kafka stores topics as partitioned, replicated logs that consumer groups read at their own pace.

Why messaging

Take "a candidate applies for a job". After saving the application you want to email the recruiter, update search, add to analytics and notify the candidate. If the application service calls all four synchronously, the user waits for the slowest, and any failure breaks the request. With a message broker in the middle, the service publishes one message, "ApplicationSubmitted", and returns. Other services consume it in their own time.

  • Decoupling: the producer does not know who consumes, or how many.
  • Buffering: a spike (10,000 applications in a minute) is stored in the broker and processed at the consumers' speed.
  • Resilience: if the notification service is down for an hour, messages wait and are processed on recovery.
  • Scalability: add consumer instances to share the work.

The costs: more infrastructure, eventual consistency, harder debugging, and the need to deal with duplicates and ordering (delivery semantics).

Queue vs topic

Queue (point-to-point)
Each message is delivered to one consumer among those listening. Several consumers on one queue are competing consumers: they share the load. Example: a queue of "send this email" tasks.
Topic (publish/subscribe)
Each message is delivered to every subscriber group. Example: "ApplicationSubmitted" is read independently by notifications, analytics and search.

RabbitMQ models both through exchanges and queues; Kafka models everything as topics, and gets queue behaviour with consumer groups.

Kafka: the model

Apache Kafka is a distributed, durable commit log. Unlike a classic queue, a consumed message is not deleted: Kafka keeps messages for a retention period (days or weeks, or by size), and consumers remember how far they have read. That makes replay possible and lets many independent consumers read the same data.

Broker
A Kafka server. A cluster has several brokers.
Topic
A named stream of records, such as application-events.
Partition
A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log. Partitions let a topic scale over many brokers and many consumers.
Offset
The position number of a record inside a partition (0, 1, 2...). A consumer commits the offset it has processed.
Key
An optional value on each record. Records with the same key always go to the same partition (hash of the key), which gives ordering per key.
Producer / Consumer
Clients that write to and read from topics.
Consumer group
Consumers with the same group.id share a topic: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group. Different groups each get all records.
Replication
Each partition has copies on several brokers (replication factor, commonly 3): one leader serves reads and writes, followers replicate. If the leader dies, a follower takes over.
  • Ordering is guaranteed only inside a partition. Use the entity id as key (job id, order id) so all events of one entity stay in order.
  • Parallelism of a group is limited by the number of partitions: 3 partitions can keep at most 3 consumers busy; a fourth consumer sits idle. Choose the partition count with future growth in mind (it can be increased later but then key-to-partition mapping changes).
  • When consumers join or leave a group, Kafka rebalances: partitions are reassigned, with a short pause.
  • Modern Kafka runs without ZooKeeper, in KRaft mode: brokers (some acting as controllers) manage the metadata themselves. Single-node KRaft is easy for development (see Compose).

When to use messaging, and when not

  • Good: notifications, workflows across services, replicating data to other services or search indexes, activity/analytics streams, smoothing spikes, background jobs that must survive restarts.
  • Not good: a user waiting for a result right now (use a synchronous call); tiny apps where @Async plus an after-commit event (module 6) is enough.

Event types you will hear: event notification (a small message "job 7 was updated", consumers call back for details), event-carried state transfer (the message contains the data, so consumers keep their own copy), and commands ("send this email", directed at one service). Name events in the past tense (ApplicationSubmitted); commands in the imperative (SendEmail).

Broker theory (log-structured storage, consensus) appears in System Design · Module 5.

Interview angle

"Why a message broker?" Decoupling, buffering, resilience. "Queue vs topic?" One consumer vs every subscriber. "Explain partitions, offsets and consumer groups." Define each; partition = ordering and parallelism unit; group = load sharing; offset = progress. "How do you keep events of one order in order?" Use the order id as the record key. "What if there are more consumers than partitions?" Extra consumers idle.

Kafka with Spring: KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener, JSON and dead-letter topics

Add spring-kafka, configure serializers and a consumer group in YAML, publish with KafkaTemplate using a business key, consume with @KafkaListener, and handle failures with retries and a dead-letter topic through DefaultErrorHandler.

Setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.kafka</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-kafka</artifactId>
</dependency>
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP:localhost:9092}
    producer:
      acks: all                                  # wait for all in-sync replicas
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true                 # no duplicates from producer retries
        spring.json.add.type.headers: false      # do not tie consumers to our class names
    consumer:
      group-id: notification-service             # consumer group
      auto-offset-reset: earliest                # new group starts from the beginning
      enable-auto-commit: false
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: >-
          org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
        spring.json.trusted.packages: com.example.events
        spring.json.value.default.type: com.example.events.ApplicationSubmitted
    listener:
      ack-mode: record                           # commit the offset after each record
      concurrency: 3                             # 3 consumer threads in this instance
    template:
      observation-enabled: true                  # tracing for sends (see tracing article)
  • acks: all with enable.idempotence: true is the safe producer setting: a message is acknowledged only when all in-sync replicas have it, and a retry cannot create a duplicate in the partition.
  • auto-offset-reset matters only when the group has no committed offset: earliest reads history, latest reads only new records.
  • ErrorHandlingDeserializer wraps the real deserializer so a malformed message does not crash the consumer in an endless loop (a "poison pill"); the error is delivered to the error handler.
  • spring.json.trusted.packages is a security setting: JSON deserialization may only create classes from these packages. Do not use * in production.

Version note

The class names JsonSerializer and JsonDeserializer come from Spring for Apache Kafka and use Jackson 2. Spring Boot 4 moves to Jackson 3, and Spring for Apache Kafka 4 provides matching Jackson 3 serializers; names and packages differ, so use the ones in the reference for your version. The Kafka concepts and the property structure (spring.kafka.*) are unchanged.

The event class

A shared contract. Keep events small, immutable and versionable. Records are perfect:

package com.example.events;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.UUID;

public record ApplicationSubmitted(
        UUID eventId,              // unique id: lets consumers detect duplicates
        Long applicationId,
        Long jobId,
        Long candidateId,
        String recruiterEmail,
        Instant occurredAt) { }

Creating the topic

@Configuration
public class KafkaTopicConfig {

    public static final String APPLICATION_EVENTS = "application-events";

    @Bean
    NewTopic applicationEventsTopic() {
        return TopicBuilder.name(APPLICATION_EVENTS)
                .partitions(3)
                .replicas(1)                   // 3 in a real cluster
                .build();                      // created at startup if it does not exist
    }
}

Producer: KafkaTemplate

@Component
public class ApplicationEventsProducer {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ApplicationEventsProducer.class);
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, ApplicationSubmitted> kafkaTemplate;

    public ApplicationEventsProducer(KafkaTemplate<String, ApplicationSubmitted> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void publish(ApplicationSubmitted event) {
        String key = String.valueOf(event.jobId());              // same job -> same partition
        kafkaTemplate.send(KafkaTopicConfig.APPLICATION_EVENTS, key, event)
                .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {                  // send() is asynchronous
                    if (ex != null) {
                        log.error("Publish failed for application {}", event.applicationId(), ex);
                    } else {
                        var md = result.getRecordMetadata();
                        log.info("Published to {}-{} offset {}", md.topic(), md.partition(), md.offset());
                    }
                });
    }
}
  • send() returns a CompletableFuture<SendResult> in current Spring Kafka versions (older versions returned a ListenableFuture). It is non-blocking; a failure appears only in the callback, so always handle it.
  • Choose the key deliberately. No key means records are spread without ordering. A skewed key (one huge customer) overloads one partition.
  • Do not publish inside the database transaction and hope: if the transaction rolls back, the event is already out; if the app crashes after commit and before publishing, the event is lost. See the outbox pattern in the next articles.

Consumer: @KafkaListener

@Component
public class ApplicationEventsListener {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ApplicationEventsListener.class);
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    private final ProcessedEventRepository processedEvents;

    // constructor omitted

    @KafkaListener(topics = "application-events", groupId = "notification-service")
    @Transactional
    public void onApplicationSubmitted(ApplicationSubmitted event,
                                       @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_PARTITION) int partition,
                                       @Header(KafkaHeaders.OFFSET) long offset) {
        log.info("Received {} from partition {} offset {}", event.eventId(), partition, offset);

        if (!processedEvents.markProcessed(event.eventId())) {     // idempotency: seen already?
            log.info("Duplicate event {} ignored", event.eventId());
            return;
        }
        notificationService.notifyRecruiter(event);                 // do the real work
    }
}
  • The method parameter type is the payload; add @Header parameters for metadata, or take a whole ConsumerRecord<String, ApplicationSubmitted>.
  • Instances with the same groupId share the partitions. A second group (analytics) with its own listener gets every event too.
  • concurrency starts several consumer threads in one instance; the total across all instances cannot usefully exceed the partition count.
  • Listener threads are not request threads: no SecurityContext, no web request. Wrap work in its own transaction.
  • Process quickly. If one poll's processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes by default), Kafka thinks the consumer died and rebalances.

Commit behaviour: with ack-mode: record the offset is committed after the listener method returns normally; if it throws, the error handler decides (retry, skip, dead-letter). With MANUAL ack mode you inject an Acknowledgment and call acknowledge() yourself, useful when work finishes asynchronously.

Error handling: retries and a dead-letter topic

A listener will meet bad data or temporary failures (database down). Without a plan, a failing record is retried again and again and blocks its partition. Spring Kafka's DefaultErrorHandler retries with a back-off, then hands the record to a recoverer. The standard recoverer publishes it to a dead-letter topic (DLT), a parking place for messages that could not be processed, where humans or tools inspect them.

@Configuration
public class KafkaErrorConfig {

    @Bean
    DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
        // after retries are used up, publish to "<topic>.DLT" (same partition number)
        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);

        var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);   // up to 4 retries
        backOff.setInitialInterval(1_000);
        backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
        backOff.setMaxInterval(10_000);

        var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(IllegalArgumentException.class);   // bad data: no retry
        return handler;
    }
}

Boot picks up a single CommonErrorHandler bean for its listener container factory. A dead-letter record carries headers with the original topic, partition, offset and the exception message, so you can diagnose and, after a fix, re-publish it. Alternatively, @RetryableTopic creates retry topics (-retry-0, -retry-1) and a DLT for you, so retries do not block the main partition, at the cost of more topics and weaker ordering.

Monitor the DLT (alert when it is not empty) and the consumer lag, the difference between the latest offset and the group's committed offset, which shows whether consumers keep up.

Testing

Use Testcontainers with a Kafka container (@ServiceConnection sets the bootstrap address, module 5) and Awaitility to wait for the asynchronous result: publish, then await().atMost(10, SECONDS).untilAsserted(...). @EmbeddedKafka from spring-kafka-test is faster to start but less like the real broker.

Common mistakes

  • Ignoring the future returned by send(): failures vanish.
  • No key, then wondering why events of one job are processed out of order.
  • Unlimited retries on a poison message: the partition is blocked for ever.
  • Sharing a Java class between services through a "common" library so every change forces all services to redeploy; prefer a stable, versioned schema (JSON schema, Avro with a schema registry).
  • Using the same group.id for two different services: they steal each other's messages.
  • Doing slow, blocking work in the listener until the poll timeout expires and a rebalance storm begins.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • SerializationException or DeserializationException: bad payload or a missing trusted package; wrapped by the ErrorHandlingDeserializer.
  • TimeoutException: Topic ... not present in metadata: wrong bootstrap server, topic missing, or auto-creation disabled.
  • org.apache.kafka.common.errors.RecordTooLargeException: message above the broker limit (about 1 MB by default); send a reference to the data instead of the data.
  • CommitFailedException / rebalance: processing took too long between polls.

Interview angle

"How do you produce and consume in Spring?" KafkaTemplate.send(topic, key, value) and @KafkaListener(topics, groupId). "How do you handle a failing message?" Retry with back-off, then dead-letter topic; no-retry for bad data; alert on DLT. "How do you avoid duplicates?" Idempotent producer plus idempotent consumer with an event id. "Why a key?" Ordering per entity. "What is consumer lag?" Distance between the log end and the group's committed offset.

RabbitMQ with Spring AMQP, and Kafka vs RabbitMQ

RabbitMQ routes messages from producers through exchanges to queues using bindings and routing keys; Spring AMQP gives you RabbitTemplate to publish and @RabbitListener to consume, with acknowledgements, retries and dead-letter exchanges for failures.

The RabbitMQ model

RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker that implements the AMQP protocol. Its main difference from Kafka: the producer never writes to a queue directly. It publishes to an exchange, and the exchange routes the message to zero or more queues according to bindings and a routing key. Consumers read from queues, and a message is removed from the queue once it is acknowledged.

Exchange typeRouting ruleTypical use
directRouting key must equal the binding key exactlyTask queues, one destination per key
topicBinding patterns with * (one word) and # (zero or more words), e.g. application.*Event routing by category
fanoutCopies the message to every bound queue, ignoring the keyBroadcast: cache invalidation, notifications to many
headersMatches on message headersRare
  • Acknowledgements: the consumer acks after processing; if it dies or rejects (nack), the broker re-queues or dead-letters the message. This gives at-least-once delivery.
  • Durability: mark queues durable and messages persistent so they survive a broker restart.
  • Competing consumers: several consumers on one queue share its messages round-robin (prefetch controls how many unacknowledged messages each holds).
  • Dead-letter exchange (DLX): rejected or expired messages are re-routed to another exchange for inspection.

Spring AMQP setup

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-amqp</artifactId>
</dependency>
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    host: ${RABBIT_HOST:localhost}
    port: 5672
    username: ${RABBIT_USER:guest}
    password: ${RABBIT_PASSWORD:guest}      # guest works only from localhost
    listener:
      simple:
        acknowledge-mode: auto              # ack when the method returns, nack on exception
        prefetch: 10
        retry:
          enabled: true                     # local retries before giving up
          max-attempts: 3
          initial-interval: 1s
          multiplier: 2.0
        default-requeue-rejected: false     # after retries: reject, do not loop (goes to DLX)

Declaring exchange, queue and bindings

Spring declares these on the broker at startup when you create them as beans:

@Configuration
public class RabbitConfig {

    public static final String EXCHANGE = "jobs.events";
    public static final String QUEUE = "notification.application-submitted";
    public static final String DLX = "jobs.events.dlx";
    public static final String DLQ = "notification.application-submitted.dlq";

    @Bean TopicExchange eventsExchange() { return new TopicExchange(EXCHANGE, true, false); }
    @Bean DirectExchange deadLetterExchange() { return new DirectExchange(DLX); }

    @Bean
    Queue notificationQueue() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable(QUEUE)
                .deadLetterExchange(DLX)                    // rejected messages go here
                .deadLetterRoutingKey(DLQ)
                .build();
    }

    @Bean Queue deadLetterQueue() { return QueueBuilder.durable(DLQ).build(); }

    @Bean
    Binding notificationBinding() {
        return BindingBuilder.bind(notificationQueue()).to(eventsExchange())
                .with("application.submitted");             // routing key pattern
    }

    @Bean
    Binding deadLetterBinding() {
        return BindingBuilder.bind(deadLetterQueue()).to(deadLetterExchange()).with(DLQ);
    }

    @Bean
    MessageConverter jsonMessageConverter() {
        return new Jackson2JsonMessageConverter();         // JSON instead of Java serialization
    }
}

Version note

Jackson2JsonMessageConverter uses Jackson 2. Boot 4 moves to Jackson 3, and Spring AMQP offers a Jackson 3 converter with a different class name; check the Spring AMQP reference for your version. Define one MessageConverter bean and Boot wires it into RabbitTemplate and the listener containers.

Producer and consumer

@Component
public class ApplicationEventsPublisher {

    private final RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate;
    public ApplicationEventsPublisher(RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate) { this.rabbitTemplate = rabbitTemplate; }

    public void publish(ApplicationSubmitted event) {
        rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(RabbitConfig.EXCHANGE, "application.submitted", event);
    }
}

@Component
public class NotificationListener {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(NotificationListener.class);

    @RabbitListener(queues = RabbitConfig.QUEUE)
    public void onSubmitted(ApplicationSubmitted event) {
        log.info("Notifying recruiter for application {}", event.applicationId());
        // throw an exception -> retry -> after max attempts the message goes to the DLQ
    }
}

If the listener method returns normally, the message is acknowledged. If it throws, Spring retries locally (the retry settings above), and when retries are exhausted the message is rejected without requeue and RabbitMQ routes it to the dead-letter exchange. Throw AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException to reject at once for unrecoverable data. Publisher-side reliability uses publisher confirms (spring.rabbitmq.publisher-confirm-type=correlated) and returns for unroutable messages.

Kafka vs RabbitMQ

KafkaRabbitMQ
ModelDistributed commit log; consumers pull and track offsetsSmart broker: exchanges, queues, routing; broker pushes to consumers
After consumptionMessages stay until retention expires; replay is possibleMessage is removed after ack
RoutingBy topic and key onlyFlexible: direct, topic, fanout, headers
OrderingPer partitionPer queue (lost with competing consumers and redelivery)
ThroughputVery high (millions of records per second per cluster)High (tens of thousands per second per node)
Best forEvent streaming, event sourcing, analytics, data pipelines, many independent readersTask queues, request routing, per-message TTL, priorities, delayed retries
OperationsHeavier cluster; partitions to planSimpler to start

Rule of thumb: work to be done once (send this email, resize this image) fits RabbitMQ; facts that many parties read and may replay (a stream of order events) fit Kafka. For a small project either works; choose what your team can run. Cloud alternatives exist too: AWS SQS/SNS, Google Pub/Sub, Azure Service Bus.

Common mistakes

  • Non-durable queues, so messages vanish on a broker restart.
  • Requeueing a poison message for ever (default-requeue-rejected: true with a permanent error).
  • A huge prefetch with slow consumers: one consumer holds many messages while others idle.
  • Using the default guest account in production.
  • Expecting Kafka-style replay from RabbitMQ.

Interview angle

"Explain exchange, queue, binding and routing key." Producer to exchange, bindings route to queues. "Exchange types?" Direct, topic, fanout, headers. "How does RabbitMQ avoid message loss?" Durable queues, persistent messages, publisher confirms, consumer acks. "Kafka or RabbitMQ?" Streaming and replay and scale versus routing flexibility and task queues.

Delivery semantics, idempotent consumers and the outbox pattern

Networks make exactly-once delivery impossible in general, so build for at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, and use the outbox pattern to publish events atomically with your database change.

Delivery guarantees

GuaranteeMeaningHow it happensRisk
At-most-once0 or 1 timesSend and forget; commit the offset before processingLost messages
At-least-once1 or more timesRetry until acknowledged; commit the offset after processingDuplicates
Exactly-onceExactly 1 effectIdempotent processing, or transactions inside one system (Kafka transactions)Complex; works only within defined boundaries

Why duplicates? A consumer processes a message, then crashes before acknowledging. The broker redelivers. Or a producer sends, the broker stores it, but the acknowledgement is lost, so the producer retries. You cannot tell "lost request" from "lost response". The practical industry answer: at-least-once delivery + idempotent handling = effectively-once. Kafka's "exactly-once semantics" (idempotent producer plus transactions) is real, but it covers reading from Kafka and writing to Kafka; once you touch an email server or your database, you need your own idempotency.

Idempotent consumers

An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. "Set status to SHORTLISTED" is idempotent; "add 100 to the balance" and "send an email" are not. Make a handler idempotent by recording the ids of events already processed, in the same transaction as the effect:

CREATE TABLE processed_event (
    event_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    consumer     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    processed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
@Transactional
public void handle(ApplicationSubmitted event) {
    try {
        processedEventRepository.saveAndFlush(
                new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId(), "notification-service"));   // unique key
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException duplicate) {
        log.info("Event {} already processed, skipping", event.eventId());
        return;
    }
    notificationRepository.save(Notification.forRecruiter(event));   // same transaction
}

If the handler fails, the transaction rolls back including the "processed" row, and a retry works. Natural idempotence is even better: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, an upsert, "set" instead of "increment", or a unique constraint on (application_id, type). For external side effects (an email), store a "mail sent" flag, or pass an idempotency key to the provider. Producers should include a unique eventId in every event.

The dual-write problem

The application service must (1) save the application in its database and (2) publish an event. These are two systems, and there is no transaction across both:

  • Save, then publish: if the app crashes between, the data exists but no event was sent; the recruiter is never told.
  • Publish, then save: if the save fails, an event describes something that never happened.
  • Publish inside the transaction: the commit may still fail after the event left.

The outbox pattern

Write the event to an outbox table in the same local database transaction as the business data. Because both rows are in one ACID transaction, either both exist or neither. A separate process then reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, marking rows as sent.

@Transactional
public ApplicationResponse apply(Long jobId, Long userId) {
    Application saved = applicationRepository.save(new Application(jobId, userId));

    outboxRepository.save(new OutboxEvent(
            UUID.randomUUID(),
            "application-events",                       // topic
            String.valueOf(jobId),                      // key
            objectMapper.writeValueAsString(ApplicationSubmitted.from(saved)),   // JSON payload
            Instant.now()));
    return mapper.toResponse(saved);                    // one commit covers both rows
}
@Component
public class OutboxRelay {

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000)
    @SchedulerLock(name = "outboxRelay", lockAtMostFor = "PT30S")      // one relay at a time
    public void publishPending() {
        List<OutboxEvent> batch = outboxRepository.findTop100BySentAtIsNullOrderByCreatedAtAsc();
        for (OutboxEvent e : batch) {
            try {
                kafkaTemplate.send(e.getTopic(), e.getKey(), e.getPayload()).get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
                e.markSent(Instant.now());
                outboxRepository.save(e);
            } catch (Exception ex) {
                log.warn("Outbox publish failed for {}, will retry", e.getId(), ex);
                break;                                   // keep order; try again next tick
            }
        }
    }
}

The relay itself is at-least-once (it may publish and crash before marking), which is why consumers must be idempotent. Variants: a polling relay as above (simple, adds a second or so of delay), or change data capture (CDC) with a tool such as Debezium that reads the database's transaction log and publishes outbox rows to Kafka (low latency, no polling, more infrastructure). Delete or archive sent rows regularly. The Spring Modulith project has built-in support for an event publication log with similar goals. Pattern background: System Design · Module 6.

Ordering, retries and sagas in one paragraph

Ordering holds only per partition (Kafka) or per queue (RabbitMQ without competing consumers), so key by the entity id and design handlers that tolerate late or reordered events (include a version or timestamp and ignore older ones). A saga coordinates a multi-service workflow as a chain of local transactions plus compensations, either choreographed (each service reacts to events) or orchestrated (a coordinator tells each service what to do).

A worked event flow: OrderPlaced to payment to notification

Food-delivery example, with three services and one broker:

  1. The order service stores the order as PENDING and an OrderPlaced row in its outbox, in one transaction.
  2. The relay publishes OrderPlaced keyed by order id.
  3. The payment service charges the customer; a duplicate delivery finds the payment for this order id already exists and does nothing. It publishes PaymentCompleted or PaymentFailed.
  4. The order service consumes the result and moves the order to CONFIRMED (or CANCELLED, the compensation).
  5. The notification service sends the SMS and email; it deduplicates by event id.

Notice what the user sees: the order API returns "accepted" immediately; confirmation arrives a moment later. The system is eventually consistent, and the UI must reflect that ("processing payment...").

Rules

  • Assume every message can arrive twice, late or out of order.
  • Give every event a unique id, and every consumer a way to ignore a repeat.
  • Never do "save to DB and publish to broker" as two independent steps; use an outbox or an after-commit mechanism with a recovery path.
  • Check duplicates in the same transaction as the side effect.

Common mistakes

  • Believing a broker setting makes the whole flow "exactly-once".
  • Idempotency check outside the transaction, leaving a window where a crash marks an event processed without its effect (or the reverse).
  • Deleting outbox rows before the broker confirmed.
  • Retrying a non-idempotent step (charging) without a key.

Interview angle

"What delivery guarantees exist?" At-most, at-least, exactly-once; explain why at-least-once plus idempotence is the practical choice. "What is the dual-write problem and how do you solve it?" Outbox with a relay or CDC. "How do you make a consumer idempotent?" Event id table or natural idempotence, in the same transaction. "Orchestration vs choreography?" Central coordinator versus event reactions.

Distributed tracing with Micrometer Tracing

A trace follows one request across all services using a trace id that travels in the traceparent header; Micrometer Tracing creates spans automatically, propagates the context over HTTP and messaging, exports them to Zipkin, Jaeger or Tempo, and puts the trace id in your logs.

The problem and the vocabulary

A user clicks "Apply". The request passes the gateway, the application service, the job service, the payment service and a Kafka consumer. It is slow. Which hop is slow? Logs from five services do not tell the story unless something links them. Distributed tracing records the path and timing of a request across services.

Trace
The whole journey of one request; identified by a trace id (128-bit, 32 hex characters).
Span
One unit of work inside a trace (an incoming HTTP request, a database query, an outgoing call, a Kafka send); has a span id, a parent span id, a start time and a duration, and tags.
Context propagation
Passing the trace id and current span id to the next service, so it continues the same trace. Over HTTP it travels in headers; over messaging in message headers.

The W3C traceparent header

The standard format for HTTP propagation is the W3C Trace Context header:

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01

The fields are: version (00), the 32-hex trace id, the 16-hex parent span id, and flags (01 means "sampled"). The receiving service creates a new child span under that parent. Older Zipkin systems used the B3 headers; Micrometer Tracing can be configured for either.

Micrometer Tracing

Micrometer Tracing is the tracing facade in Spring Boot 3 and later (the successor of Spring Cloud Sleuth, which is not used any more). It is built on the Micrometer Observation API: one instrumented operation produces both a metric and a span. You choose a bridge to a tracer implementation, and an exporter to a backend:

PieceChoices
Bridge (tracer)OpenTelemetry (micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel) or Brave (micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave)
ExporterOTLP (opentelemetry-exporter-otlp) to any OpenTelemetry-compatible backend; or Zipkin reporter for Brave
Backend (UI)Zipkin, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, commercial APM tools
 
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
    <artifactId>opentelemetry-exporter-otlp</artifactId>
</dependency>
spring:
  application:
    name: application-service              # shown as the service name in every span
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0                      # trace 100% in dev; the default is 0.1 (10%)
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://tempo:4318/v1/traces   # OTLP over HTTP

For Zipkin with Brave, use micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave plus io.zipkin.reporter2:zipkin-reporter-brave, and set management.zipkin.tracing.endpoint=http://zipkin:9411/api/v2/spans. Run Zipkin with docker run -p 9411:9411 openzipkin/zipkin and open http://localhost:9411.

Version note

The dependencies and management.tracing.* settings above are for Boot 3.x. Spring Boot 4 adds a dedicated OpenTelemetry starter and its own configuration for OTLP; the concepts (traces, spans, sampling, propagation) are identical. Check the Boot 4 reference for the exact starter name before copying the dependencies.

What is traced automatically

  • Incoming HTTP requests (Spring MVC and WebFlux).
  • Outgoing calls made with the Boot-provided RestClient.Builder, RestTemplateBuilder or WebClient.Builder: they add the traceparent header. You must build clients from the injected builders (RestClient.create() or new RestTemplate() are not instrumented).
  • Messaging: set spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled=true and spring.kafka.listener.observation-enabled=true for Kafka; Spring AMQP has similar observation settings. The trace id then travels in message headers and the consumer continues the trace.
  • JDBC and others, with extra libraries (datasource-micrometer, OpenTelemetry instrumentation).
  • Your own code: annotate with @Observed (needs ObservedAspect bean) or create a span by hand:
@Service
public class ResumeScoringService {

    private final ObservationRegistry observationRegistry;
    public ResumeScoringService(ObservationRegistry observationRegistry) {
        this.observationRegistry = observationRegistry;
    }

    public int score(Long applicationId) {
        return Observation.createNotStarted("resume.score", observationRegistry)
                .lowCardinalityKeyValue("type", "pdf")
                .observe(() -> doScore(applicationId));        // a timer metric AND a span
    }
}

Trace ids in your logs

When tracing is on, Spring Boot 3.2 and later add the trace and span ids to the log lines automatically (the application name, trace id and span id appear in the default pattern), and they are fields in the JSON log formats. Then the loop closes: find a slow trace in Tempo or Zipkin, copy the trace id, and search the central log system for every log line of that request across all services. If you write your own pattern, use %X{traceId:-} and %X{spanId:-}, or the property logging.pattern.correlation. Return the trace id to clients in an error response or header, so a bug report can include it. This replaces the hand-made request id from module 6.

Sampling and cost

Tracing every request in a busy system produces a lot of data. Sampling keeps a percentage: management.tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1 keeps 10%. The decision is made at the start of the trace and respected by all services (the "sampled" flag). Production systems often sample 1 to 10%, or use tail-based sampling in a collector (keep all slow or failed traces). Errors you care about may be missed at low rates, which is the trade-off.

The three pillars of observability

PillarQuestion it answersSpring tool
LogsWhat happened, exactly, in this component?SLF4J + Logback (JSON)
MetricsIs the system healthy, and how is it trending?Micrometer + Prometheus
TracesWhere did this one request spend its time, across services?Micrometer Tracing + OTLP/Zipkin

The usual workflow: an alert on a metric (error rate up) leads to traces of failing requests, which lead to the logs of the failing span, joined by the trace id. Setting up Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Tempo is covered in DevOps · Module 6.

Common mistakes

  • Creating new RestTemplate() or RestClient.create() by hand: no propagation, broken traces.
  • Leaving the default 10% sampling and wondering why the trace for a failing request is missing during a test.
  • Forgetting spring.application.name: every service shows as unknown_service.
  • Tracing everything at 100% in production without a plan for the storage cost.
  • Putting personal data (emails, tokens) into span tags.

Interview angle

"What is distributed tracing?" Trace, span, trace id, parent-child, propagation via traceparent. "How do you add it in Spring Boot?" Actuator, Micrometer Tracing bridge (OTel or Brave), exporter, sampling property. "How do you correlate logs and traces?" Trace id in MDC and in the log pattern. "What are the three pillars?" Logs, metrics, traces, and what each answers.

Running several services together with Docker Compose

Docker Compose describes all your containers (services, databases, broker, cache) in one compose.yaml; use healthchecks with depends_on conditions so services start in a working order, a shared network so they reach each other by service name, and environment variables for configuration.

What and why

A microservice system is many processes. Starting PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis and three Spring Boot applications by hand with long docker run commands is slow and error-prone. Docker Compose lets you write the whole setup once in compose.yaml and start it with docker compose up. It is the standard tool for local development and for simple single-host deployments. (Docker basics, images and Dockerfiles: DevOps · Module 3; Kubernetes replaces Compose for large production systems.)

Compose creates a private network for the project. Containers reach each other by service name as hostname: from application-service, the database is simply jobs-db:5432 and Kafka is kafka:9092. localhost inside a container means that container itself, a very common mistake.

A complete compose.yaml

Two Spring Boot services (jobs and notifications), each with its own PostgreSQL (database per service), plus Kafka and Redis:

name: jobs-platform

services:
  jobs-db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: jobs
      POSTGRES_USER: jobs
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${JOBS_DB_PASSWORD:?set JOBS_DB_PASSWORD in .env}
    volumes:
      - jobs-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U jobs -d jobs"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    networks: [backend]

  notify-db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: notify
      POSTGRES_USER: notify
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${NOTIFY_DB_PASSWORD:?set NOTIFY_DB_PASSWORD in .env}
    volumes:
      - notify-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U notify -d notify"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    networks: [backend]

  redis:
    image: redis:7
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    networks: [backend]

  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.9.0
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 20s
    networks: [backend]

  jobs-service:
    build: ./jobs-service                       # folder with its Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8081:8080"                             # host:container
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://jobs-db:5432/jobs
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: jobs
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${JOBS_DB_PASSWORD}
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: redis
      SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
      MANAGEMENT_TRACING_SAMPLING_PROBABILITY: "1.0"
    depends_on:
      jobs-db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      # needs curl inside the image; or use a tiny Java/wget check
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -fs http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 40s
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [backend]

  notification-service:
    build: ./notification-service
    ports:
      - "8082:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://notify-db:5432/notify
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: notify
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${NOTIFY_DB_PASSWORD}
      SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
      SPRING_MAIL_HOST: mailpit
      SPRING_MAIL_PORT: "1025"
    depends_on:
      notify-db:
        condition: service_healthy
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [backend]

  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit
    ports:
      - "8025:8025"                             # open the mail UI on the host
    networks: [backend]

volumes:
  jobs-db-data:
  notify-db-data:

networks:
  backend:

Reading the file

  • depends_on with condition: service_healthy makes Compose wait until the dependency's healthcheck passes. A plain depends_on: [kafka] only waits until the container has started, which is not the same as "ready to accept connections", the usual reason for startup crashes.
  • Healthchecks are commands that Docker runs repeatedly; the container becomes healthy after one succeeds. start_period gives slow starters (Spring Boot, Kafka) time before failures count. Your services can reuse the Actuator readiness endpoint (Actuator); the image needs a tool such as curl to call it.
  • Environment variables override application.yml via relaxed binding: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL becomes spring.datasource.url, SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS becomes spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers. Hostnames are service names (jobs-db, kafka, redis).
  • ${VAR} and .env: Compose reads a .env file next to compose.yaml for substitutions. ${VAR:?message} stops with an error if the variable is missing. Add .env to .gitignore; commit a .env.example instead.
  • volumes (named volumes) keep database files when containers are recreated. docker compose down -v deletes them.
  • networks: by default all services share one network anyway; naming networks lets you separate, for example, a frontend network (gateway, UI) from a backend network (databases not reachable from outside).
  • ports publish a container port to the host. Do not publish databases and Kafka in anything but local development; services on the network reach them without publishing.
  • Kafka needs an advertised listener that clients can reach: kafka:9092 works for other containers. For an application running on your host (outside Docker), you would add a second listener on a host-visible address such as localhost:9094.

A Dockerfile for a Spring Boot service

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --system --create-home app
USER app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

The multi-stage build keeps the build tools out of the final image, and the non-root user is a basic security measure. Spring Boot can also build an image without a Dockerfile (./mvnw spring-boot:build-image, using buildpacks).

Everyday commands

$ docker compose up -d --build        # build images and start everything in the background
$ docker compose ps                   # status and health of each service
$ docker compose logs -f jobs-service # follow one service's logs
$ docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh \
      --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list
$ docker compose stop notification-service   # simulate an outage: do events queue up?
$ docker compose up -d notification-service  # bring it back: does it catch up?
$ docker compose down                 # stop and remove containers (keeps volumes)
$ docker compose down -v              # also delete volumes (all data!)

The "stop a service and restart it" experiment is the best way to see the value of Kafka buffering and of timeouts and circuit breakers in the other services.

Spring Boot's Docker Compose support for development

While developing, you usually run the application from your IDE and only want the infrastructure (databases, Kafka, Redis) in Docker. Spring Boot 3.1+ can manage this for you. Add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-docker-compose</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

Put a compose.yaml with only the infrastructure services in the project root. When you start the application, Boot runs docker compose up, waits for the containers, and configures the connections automatically (datasource URL, Redis host, Kafka bootstrap server, the mapped random ports), so you write no connection properties for local development. On shutdown it stops the containers. You control it with spring.docker.compose.lifecycle-management (start-and-stop, start-only, none) and spring.docker.compose.file. The same idea with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection is used for tests (module 5). Keep the full multi-service file above for running the whole system.

Common mistakes

  • localhost in SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL inside a container: connection refused. Use the service name.
  • Plain depends_on and a race condition: the app starts before the database accepts connections (or before Kafka is ready) and exits.
  • Committing secrets in compose.yaml or .env.
  • Publishing database and broker ports on a server.
  • Forgetting that docker compose down -v deletes the data volume.
  • One shared database for all services: it works, but it breaks the main microservice rule.

Tip

Add Prometheus, Grafana and Zipkin (or Grafana's all-in-one grafana/otel-lgtm image) as extra Compose services, point your services at them with environment variables, and your laptop becomes a complete observability lab (DevOps · Module 6).

Interview angle

"What is Docker Compose for?" Define and run multi-container applications locally. "How do containers find each other?" Service-name DNS on the Compose network. "How do you make a service wait for the database?" Healthcheck plus depends_on: condition: service_healthy, and application-level retries. "Compose vs Kubernetes?" Single host and development versus orchestration, scaling and self-healing across a cluster.

Interview questions — Microservices and messaging

Monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices: how do you choose?

A monolith deploys as one unit and is simplest; a modular monolith is the same deployment with strict module boundaries; microservices are independently deployable services with their own data. Microservices give independent deployment and scaling for many teams, but cost network failures, distributed data, observability and DevOps effort. Start with a (modular) monolith, and extract services when there is a concrete need such as team independence or different scaling.

What is a distributed monolith?

A system split into services that are still tightly coupled: they share a database, must be deployed together, or call each other in long synchronous chains. It has all the costs of microservices and none of the benefits. Avoid it with clear business boundaries, database per service, and asynchronous events between services.

How do you decide service boundaries, and what does "database per service" mean for queries and transactions?

Use business capabilities and bounded contexts, with one team owning each service. Each service is the only owner of its data, so there are no cross-service joins: you use API composition or a local copy fed by events. Cross-service transactions become sagas with compensating actions and eventual consistency.

What does an API gateway do, and what is a route in Spring Cloud Gateway?

It is the single entry point that routes requests to services and handles authentication, rate limiting, CORS and similar cross-cutting concerns. A route has an id, a destination URI, predicates that decide whether it matches (Path, Method, Header...) and filters that modify the request or response (StripPrefix, RewritePath, RequestRateLimiter, CircuitBreaker). The gateway is reactive (WebFlux/Netty), so avoid blocking calls in it.

How do services find each other, and how is configuration managed across environments?

With client-side discovery (Eureka registry plus load balancing, lb://service-name) or, more commonly today, platform DNS such as Kubernetes Services or Compose service names. Configuration is kept outside the artifact: environment variables, ConfigMaps and Secrets, a Spring Cloud Config Server backed by Git, and a vault for secrets. The same image runs in every environment.

Explain the circuit breaker pattern and its states.

It protects a caller from a failing dependency. In CLOSED state calls pass and failures are counted in a sliding window. When the failure (or slow-call) rate exceeds the threshold, it moves to OPEN and rejects calls immediately, so threads are not blocked and the dependency can recover. After a wait time it becomes HALF_OPEN and allows a few probe calls; success closes it, failure reopens it. Business errors should not count as failures.

How do you configure retries safely?

Retry only idempotent operations and transient errors (timeouts, 503), never 4xx or validation errors. Use few attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, and keep the total time inside your own deadline. For non-idempotent calls like payments, pass an idempotency key. Put timeouts first, since a retry needs the earlier call to end.

Why must every remote call have a timeout, and what is a cascading failure?

Without a timeout, a slow dependency makes threads wait indefinitely; the thread pool fills, the service stops responding, and its callers start hanging too. That chain reaction is a cascading failure. Timeouts, bulkheads (limiting concurrency per dependency), circuit breakers and fallbacks contain the damage.

Kafka: what are topics, partitions, offsets and consumer groups?

A topic is a named stream split into partitions; each partition is an ordered append-only log, and each record has an offset. Records with the same key go to the same partition, so order is guaranteed per key only. A consumer group shares a topic: each partition is read by one consumer in the group, so parallelism is limited by the partition count, while different groups each receive all records. Messages are retained for a set period, so consumers can replay.

Kafka vs RabbitMQ: when would you pick each?

Kafka is a distributed log with high throughput, retention and replay, good for event streaming, many independent consumers and data pipelines. RabbitMQ is a broker with flexible routing (direct, topic, fanout exchanges), per-message acknowledgement and dead-letter exchanges, good for task queues and work distribution. RabbitMQ deletes a message after the ack; Kafka keeps it until retention ends.

What delivery guarantees exist, and how do you achieve effectively-once processing?

At-most-once can lose messages, at-least-once can duplicate them, and true exactly-once is only achievable inside controlled boundaries. In practice you use at-least-once delivery (acks after processing, producer retries with idempotence) together with idempotent consumers that record processed event ids in the same transaction as their side effect, or use naturally idempotent operations.

What is the outbox pattern and what problem does it solve?

It solves the dual-write problem: you cannot atomically update your database and publish to a broker. The service writes the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change. A relay (a polling job or change data capture such as Debezium) publishes outbox rows to the broker and marks them sent. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

How do you handle a message that keeps failing in a Kafka listener?

Configure a DefaultErrorHandler with a back-off (for example exponential, 4 attempts) and a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer that sends the record to a dead-letter topic. Mark non-retryable exceptions (bad data) so they go straight to the DLT, wrap the deserializer in ErrorHandlingDeserializer to survive poison pills, and alert on the DLT and consumer lag. Alternatively use @RetryableTopic for non-blocking retries.

How does distributed tracing work in a Spring Boot system?

Each request gets a trace id; each operation is a span with its own id and a parent. The trace context travels to the next service in the W3C traceparent header (or message headers). Micrometer Tracing with an OpenTelemetry or Brave bridge creates spans for HTTP and messaging automatically, an exporter sends them to Zipkin, Jaeger or Tempo, and sampling controls the volume. The trace id is also added to the logs so you can jump from a trace to all log lines of the request.

How would you run a multi-service system locally, and how do containers wait for each other?

Docker Compose: one compose.yaml with the services, databases, Kafka and Redis on a shared network where service names are hostnames. Each infrastructure container has a healthcheck, and application services use depends_on with condition: service_healthy. Configuration is passed through environment variables. For development, Boot's spring-boot-docker-compose module can start the infrastructure for you and configure connections.

Cheat sheet — Microservices and messaging

  • Modular monolith first one deployable, strict module boundaries; extract services when team or scaling needs prove it
  • Distributed monolith services that share a DB or must deploy together: worst of both worlds
  • Boundaries business capabilities / bounded contexts; one owner, one database per service; no cross-service joins
  • Sync vs async REST/gRPC when you need the answer now; events for facts that happened; keep call chains short
  • Sagas local transactions + compensations instead of distributed ACID; eventual consistency
  • API gateway routing, auth, rate limit, CORS; Spring Cloud Gateway = routes (id, uri, predicates, filters), reactive, no business logic
  • Gateway YAML predicates: - Path=/api/jobs/**, filters: - StripPrefix=1, uri: lb://job-service
  • Discovery Eureka (client-side, @EnableEurekaServer, @LoadBalanced) or Kubernetes / Compose DNS by service name
  • Config env vars, ConfigMaps/Secrets, Spring Cloud Config Server (spring.config.import=configserver:), Vault for secrets
  • Feign vs HTTP interfaces @FeignClient (Spring Cloud) vs @HttpExchange (Spring native)
  • Timeouts first connect + read timeouts on every call; nothing else works without them
  • Retry idempotent + transient only; exponential backoff + jitter; 2 to 3 attempts
  • Circuit breaker CLOSED, OPEN (fail fast), HALF_OPEN (probes); @CircuitBreaker(name, fallbackMethod); ignore business exceptions
  • Bulkhead / rate limiter / time limiter limit concurrency / calls per period / wait time per dependency
  • Resilience4j order Retry, CircuitBreaker, RateLimiter, TimeLimiter, Bulkhead (outermost first); needs AOP starter; see /actuator/circuitbreakers
  • Queue vs topic one consumer gets each message vs every subscriber group gets it
  • Kafka topic, partitions (ordering + parallelism unit), offset, key, consumer group, replication, retention, KRaft
  • Spring Kafka KafkaTemplate.send(topic, key, value) (async), @KafkaListener(topics, groupId), ErrorHandlingDeserializer, spring.json.trusted.packages
  • Kafka errors DefaultErrorHandler + back-off + DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer (topic.DLT); watch consumer lag
  • RabbitMQ producer to exchange (direct/topic/fanout) to queues via bindings + routing key; ack/nack; DLX; RabbitTemplate, @RabbitListener
  • Kafka vs RabbitMQ log with replay and huge throughput vs smart routing and task queues
  • Delivery at-most-once (loss), at-least-once (duplicates), exactly-once (only within boundaries); use at-least-once + idempotent consumer
  • Idempotent consumer unique event id stored in the same transaction as the effect; or upsert / set semantics
  • Outbox event row saved in the same DB transaction, relay or CDC publishes later; fixes the dual-write problem
  • Tracing trace id + span id, W3C traceparent, Micrometer Tracing bridge (OTel/Brave) + exporter; management.tracing.sampling.probability; build clients from injected builders
  • Compose healthcheck + depends_on: condition: service_healthy; service names as hosts; env vars override Spring properties; down -v deletes data

Practice — Microservices and messaging

  1. Draw the boundaries (easy). For the job portal, write down the services you would extract, what data each owns, and which calls are synchronous and which are events. Compare it with a modular-monolith package layout. Done when you can justify each boundary in one sentence and have no shared tables.
  2. Gateway (easy). Create a Spring Cloud Gateway project that routes /api/jobs/** and /api/applications/** to two local services, strips a prefix, adds a header and handles CORS. Done when the frontend calls only the gateway port and both routes work.
  3. HTTP client with timeouts (easy). In the application service, call the job service with an @HttpExchange client with a 2 s connect and 3 s read timeout. Done when stopping the job service makes the call fail fast with a clear exception, not a hang.
  4. Resilience4j (medium). Add a circuit breaker, retry (exponential backoff with jitter) and a fallback to that call; expose the breaker via Actuator. Done when you can watch it go CLOSED, OPEN and HALF_OPEN by stopping and restarting the dependency, and POST calls are not retried without a key.
  5. Kafka producer and consumer (medium). Publish ApplicationSubmitted (JSON, keyed by job id) from the application service and consume it in a notification service. Done when two instances of the consumer in one group split the partitions and a second group receives every event.
  6. Dead-letter topic (medium). Make the listener throw for a specific bad record, configure retries with back-off and a DLT. Done when the bad record lands in the DLT with the exception headers after the retries, and the good records behind it are still processed.
  7. Idempotency and outbox (hard). Replace direct publishing with an outbox table and a scheduled relay; add a processed-event table to the consumer. Done when killing the application between commit and publish does not lose the event, and replaying the same event twice sends only one email.
  8. RabbitMQ variant (medium). Re-implement the notification flow with a topic exchange, durable queue, DLX and @RabbitListener. Done when a rejected message appears in the dead-letter queue, and you can explain in two sentences when you would pick RabbitMQ over Kafka.
  9. Tracing (medium). Add Micrometer Tracing with OTLP or Zipkin export to the gateway and two services, enable Kafka observation, and show the trace id in the logs. Done when one browser request shows up as one trace with spans from the gateway, both services and the Kafka consumer.
  10. Project 4 (hard). Build either a URL shortener with analytics (a redirect service that serves from Redis and publishes a click event, plus an analytics service that consumes events and exposes statistics) or a food-delivery backend split into services (orders, payments, notifications) using Redis, Kafka or RabbitMQ. Run everything with one compose.yaml with healthchecks and depends_on: condition: service_healthy, add a README with an architecture diagram, and add timeouts, a circuit breaker and tracing. Done when docker compose up starts the whole system, a simulated outage of one service does not lose events, and you can walk an interviewer through the event flow.
